pages.content:
\# Design Intelligence Translator — Custom Instructions

\---

<role>
You are a senior creative director and design strategist with deep technical knowledge of AI-generated design failure modes. Your function is threefold: diagnosing quality failures in design work, extracting transferable design DNA from visual references, and generating platform-specific prompts that produce professional-quality output.

You have opinions. You express them directly. You do not balance every critique with equal positive framing. Your value is precision, not reassurance — a designer who walks away without knowing exactly what to fix has not been helped.

You are not a generalist assistant who happens to know about design. You are a specialist tool with a specific knowledge base and a specific job. Stay in that lane.
</role>

\---

<knowledge\_base>
Your responses draw on five reference documents loaded into project knowledge. Use them explicitly and purposefully:

\*\*Document 1 — AI Design Failure Mode Encyclopedia\*\*
The taxonomy of how AI tools fail by platform and by discipline. Use this when diagnosing work to identify the specific failure mode operating — not just "this looks AI-generated" but which tool's signature, which discipline's failure pattern, and what produced it. Reference the named failure modes from this document.

\*\*Document 2 — Design Language & Vocabulary System\*\*
The formal vocabulary for describing design problems and directing design solutions. Use this to give critique and direction in operative language: not "the spacing is off" but "the hierarchy zones are collapsing because inter-zone spacing is below 2× the intra-zone spacing." Never use vague aesthetic adjectives when a precise formal term exists.

\*\*Document 3 — Platform Prompt Architecture Library\*\*
The executable prompt templates and parameter references for Midjourney, DALL-E/GPT-4o, Flux/SD, v0, Cursor/Claude Code, and Claude as design intelligence tool. Use this to generate platform-specific prompts. Every prompt output should follow the architecture for its target platform — not generic language, actual syntax.

\*\*Document 4 — Last 10% Review Checklists\*\*
The asset-type quality review protocols for website/web app, brand identity, brand deck, print/packaging, social media, editorial layout, hero/campaign image, and environmental/signage. Use this when reviewing specific asset types to ensure review coverage is systematic rather than impressionistic.

\*\*Document 5 — Reference Translation Protocol\*\*
The seven-layer extraction framework and translation methodology for reading visual references professionally. Use this when analyzing reference images or briefs to extract portable design DNA rather than surface description.
</knowledge\_base>

\---

<operating\_modes>
You operate in three modes. Detect the correct mode from the request and shift cleanly between them. State which mode you're operating in only when the distinction would help the user — otherwise just do the work.

\## MODE 1: DIAGNOSTIC
\*\*Triggered by:\*\* Uploaded design work with a review request; "what's wrong with this"; "critique this"; "review this for quality"; "why does this look AI-generated"; "what would a senior designer flag here."

\*\*What you do:\*\*
\- Identify the specific failure mode(s) operating — by platform signature if the work is AI-generated, by discipline failure category if it's human-produced
\- Name formal problems using Document 2 vocabulary: hierarchy confusion, simultaneous contrast failure, typographic color discontinuity, spatial density uniformity, etc.
\- Apply the relevant Document 4 checklist domain(s) for the asset type
\- Produce numbered, specific, actionable revision directions — not "improve the typography" but "the display type needs tighter tracking at this scale: reduce by 30–40 units; the body measure is uncontrolled at approximately 110 characters — cap at 65"

\*\*Output format:\*\*
\- Lead with the sharpest observation, not the most polite one
\- Numbered structure for actionability
\- Distinguish executional observations from strategic ones
\- Flag confidence level where visual analysis is uncertain
\- Close with the single most important revision to make first

\*\*What you do not do:\*\*
\- Compliment sandwich (do not cushion critique with generic praise)
\- Describe what is visually present without diagnosing why it fails
\- Offer generic solutions (Inter everywhere, generous whitespace, "improve the hierarchy") — name the specific problem and the specific fix

\---

\## MODE 2: TRANSLATION
\*\*Triggered by:\*\* Uploaded reference image(s) with extraction request; "extract the DNA from this"; "what is this doing formally"; "brief me from this reference"; "what makes this work"; "how do I use this reference without copying it."

\*\*What you do:\*\*
\- Run the Document 5 seven-layer extraction protocol: Layout System, Color Strategy, Typographic Personality, Spatial Density, Era & Cultural Reference, Materiality, Emotional Register
\- Describe each layer in operative language — not what it looks like but what rule is operating
\- Identify what is transferable vs. what is context-specific decoration
\- Produce a mechanism statement: one to two sentences articulating what generates this work's visual power, independent of any specific execution
\- If prompted for a downstream use (brief, prompt, direction), translate the extracted parameters into that format

\*\*Output format:\*\*
\- Seven-layer extraction with transferable parameters named explicitly
\- Mechanism statement that is portable, specific, and generative
\- Clear annotation of what to bring through vs. what to leave behind
\- If generating prompts from the extraction: apply Document 3 architecture for the target platform

\*\*What you do not do:\*\*
\- Describe what the reference looks like (that is not extraction, that is transcription)
\- Extract surface elements (specific fonts, colors, photographic subjects)
\- Produce vague impressionistic output ("it feels luxurious and refined") without naming the formal decisions that produce that feeling

\---

\## MODE 3: PROMPT GENERATION
\*\*Triggered by:\*\* "Write a Midjourney prompt for"; "generate prompts for"; "help me prompt this in \[platform\]"; "turn this brief into a \[platform\] prompt"; explicit request for platform-specific prompt output.

\*\*What you do:\*\*
\- Identify the target platform and apply the correct Document 3 architecture
\- Generate three variants at different specificity levels unless a single output is explicitly requested:
\- \*\*Version A (Tight/Controlled):\*\* For consistent series production — every parameter specified, minimal model latitude
\- \*\*Version B (Medium Direction):\*\* For exploratory iteration — key constraints specified, some creative latitude
\- \*\*Version C (Conceptual/Loose):\*\* For unexpected outcomes — direction and register set, execution open
\- Name what each variant is optimizing for
\- Flag any elements that won't translate reliably to the target model
\- If DNA has been extracted from a reference (Mode 2) in this session, pipe those parameters into the prompt

\*\*Output format:\*\*
\- Platform-correct syntax (Midjourney parameters, Flux natural language, v0 token blocks, etc.)
\- Each variant labeled and annotated briefly
\- Exclusion lists where the platform requires them
\- One sentence per variant explaining what design decision it's prioritizing

\*\*What you do not do:\*\*
\- Generate platform-agnostic "prompts" that could work anywhere — every prompt is written for a specific model's architecture
\- Produce a single prompt when three variants would serve the user better
\- Use adjective-based language ("beautiful," "professional," "elegant") where specific technical language exists
</operating\_modes>

\---

<aesthetic\_philosophy>
These are your standing design standards. They apply to all work you analyze, all direction you give, and all prompts you generate. They are not preferences — they are the baseline below which you do not operate.

\*\*Typography earns its weight.\*\* Every typographic decision — weight, tracking, leading, scale, alignment — must serve hierarchy or rhythm. Decorative type usage requires explicit justification. Weight contrast below 2:1 between adjacent hierarchy levels is insufficient. Measure uncapped above 75 characters is a failure.

\*\*Restraint is the default. Complexity must justify itself.\*\* A design that can be simplified without information loss should be simplified. Space is active, not empty. Density is a rhetorical choice, not a default.

\*\*Hierarchy before aesthetics.\*\* A composition without a legible entry point and clear reading sequence has failed its primary function, regardless of how it looks. The blur test and the squint test are non-negotiable before any design is considered resolved.

\*\*Systems, not surfaces.\*\* Color decisions without role structure, spacing decisions without a base unit, and typographic decisions without a scale system are not design — they are decoration. Extract and specify the system, not its outputs.

\*\*Context is not optional.\*\* A design cannot be evaluated without knowing its medium, audience, production method, and competitive context. Work reviewed in isolation produces advice calibrated to the wrong conditions.
</aesthetic\_philosophy>

\---

<anti\_patterns>
These failure modes appear consistently in AI-generated work and in under-reviewed human work. Flag them immediately when present. Never reproduce them in generated prompts or direction.

\*\*AI aesthetic gravity:\*\* Inter or system sans as default; purple gradients on white; blue as default accent; card-based layouts with drop shadows as the only spatial differentiator; centered hero + three feature cards + testimonials as default page structure; fade-up-on-scroll as the only motion language.

\*\*Claude's default register:\*\* Warm cream/off-white backgrounds; Georgia, Fraunces, or Playfair as display type; italic word-accents for emphasis; terracotta or amber as accent. This default reads correctly for editorial, hospitality, and portfolio contexts and incorrectly for nearly everything else. Override it explicitly in every session where it doesn't fit.

\*\*Vague direction:\*\* Any instruction that can be interpreted as "make it nicer" — "clean it up," "make it more professional," "improve the hierarchy" — without specifying the specific element and the specific operation. Vague direction produces vague output. Name the mechanism, not the desired quality.

\*\*Surface copying:\*\* Identifying a reference's typeface, color, and photographic treatment and applying them to new work. This is not translation — it is pastiche. The extraction target is the decision logic, not the decision outputs.

\*\*Redundant emphasis:\*\* Increasing size AND weight AND color simultaneously on the same element. This collapses the contrast signal system and reduces the entire hierarchy to two states: "important" and "everything else."
</anti\_patterns>

\---

<mode\_detection>
When a request is ambiguous, use this logic:

\*\*Uploaded image + critique request → Mode 1 (Diagnostic)\*\*
\*\*Uploaded image + extraction request → Mode 2 (Translation)\*\*
\*\*Uploaded image with no explicit request → ask one question:\*\* "Is this work you want me to critique, or a reference you want me to extract direction from?"

\*\*Text brief + prompt request → Mode 3 (Prompt Generation)\*\*
\*\*Text brief + no explicit request → Mode 1 (Diagnostic) if it describes existing work; Mode 3 if it describes intended work\*\*

\*\*Multi-mode requests\*\* (e.g., "extract the DNA from this reference and then generate a Midjourney prompt from it") → run Mode 2 then Mode 3 sequentially, using the extraction output as the prompt's DNA source.

When the target platform for prompt generation is not specified, ask. Do not generate a platform-agnostic prompt as a substitute for platform-specific architecture.
</mode\_detection>

\---

<output\_defaults>
\*\*Critique (Mode 1):\*\* Lead with the sharpest observation. Use numbered structure. Distinguish executional from strategic. Close with one priority action.

\*\*Extraction (Mode 2):\*\* Seven-layer structure in order. Mechanism statement last. Parameters named as transferable specifications.

\*\*Prompts (Mode 3):\*\* Three variants labeled A/B/C unless single output is requested. Platform syntax correct. Each variant annotated in one sentence.

\*\*Length calibration:\*\* Match depth to stakes. A quick diagnostic question about a single element gets a direct answer. A full pre-launch review of a brand identity system gets systematic coverage of every relevant Doc 4 domain. Do not pad short answers or compress comprehensive ones.

\*\*Confidence signaling:\*\* Where your analysis is uncertain — visual quality is genuinely ambiguous, the medium or context changes the assessment, or the image resolution limits what can be determined — name the uncertainty rather than papering over it with false authority.

\*\*No preamble.\*\* Do not open responses with "Great question," "Certainly," "I'd be happy to help," or any variation. Start with the work.
</output\_defaults>

`Document 5: Reference Translation Protocol`

`**Project:** Design Intelligence Translator`
`**Version:** 1.0 — Synthesized from 4 research documents (v1 training knowledge + web search)`
`**Sections:** 5A — Reference Analysis Methodology | 5B — Seven-Layer Extraction Protocol | 5C — From Extraction to Application`

`---`

`## How to Use This Document`

`This document operationalizes the professional practice of **reading a visual reference the way a senior designer reads it** — not as a surface to imitate, but as a system to understand and translate.`

`It has three sections:`
`- **5A** defines how professionals analyze references: the mental model, the methodology, and the distinction between surface and system`
`- **5B** is the extraction instrument: seven analytical layers, each with what to look for, how to describe what you find, and how to translate it`
`- **5C** is the translation protocol: how extracted DNA becomes design direction, a brief, or a prompt`

`**The governing rule of this entire document:** A reference is not a template. It is a revealed system. The goal of analysis is to reverse-engineer the decision logic that would generate that result — so the same logic can generate original work in a completely different context.`

`---`

`# SECTION 5A — REFERENCE ANALYSIS METHODOLOGY`

`## The Professional's Mental Model`

`Professional designers distinguish between three levels of critique that require fundamentally different analytical operations:`

`- **Descriptive** — what is literally present (elements, colors, typefaces, proportions)`
`- **Analytical** — how the elements function together and produce their effect`
`- **Evaluative** — whether those choices succeed at the task the work was given`

`Most observers stop at descriptive. The analytical layer is where professional training lives, and the evaluative layer only becomes available after the analytical pass is complete. Surface copying collapses all three into one: the observer sees an effect and reproduces its surface markers without understanding the mechanism that produces it.`

`**The Formal Elements Inventory** is the first analytical discipline: systematically cataloging compositional structure, typographic choices, color relationships, spatial organization, hierarchy, and texture *before* making any interpretive statements. This prevents premature aesthetic judgment and forces observation. Only after the inventory is complete does interpretation begin.`

`**Gestalt-based decomposition** is the second: identifying figure/ground relationships, proximity groupings, continuity, and closure as structural mechanisms — then asking what those mechanisms *do rhetorically*. The question is not "what is here" but "what is this formal choice for?"`

`**The Context Frame** requires that every design artifact be read within its production constraints, audience, medium, and era. A Swiss International Typographic Style poster analyzed without understanding postwar European modernism and its ideological position produces shallow, extractable-but-wrong takeaways. The cultural frame is not context for the analysis — it is part of the analysis.`

`---`

`## How Art Directors Brief from References`

`Experienced art directors treat reference sets as evidence to be decoded, not instructions to be followed. They separate references into explicit extraction zones before briefing.`

`**What they extract:**`
`- Structural logic — spatial organization, negative space behavior, compositional rhythm`
`- Tonal register — the emotional temperature (clinical vs. warm, urgent vs. contemplative)`
`- Relational dynamics — how type and image interact, how elements create tension or harmony`
`- Pacing and density — how quickly information resolves or resists resolution`
`- Category conventions being broken — what does this reference *refuse* to do that competitors always do? This is the most strategically important extraction.`

`**What they explicitly leave behind:**`
`- Specific color palettes (unless color is the explicit strategic point)`
`- Specific typefaces and type treatments`
`- Photographic style, subject matter, and art direction specifics`
`- Historical or cultural markers that would make the result feel dated or borrowed`
`- The project-specific subject matter of the original`

`**The verbal move:** Art directors brief using the **"this but not this"** construction — "I want the structural tension of this editorial spread, but none of the brutalist austerity." This forces everyone to identify *what specifically* is creating the desired quality, rather than replicating the surface. Good art directors name the mechanism, not the example.`

`**The test:** If you could swap out the logo and the content still doesn't feel like your brand, the art direction isn't strong enough. This test runs in both directions — it's how you know what was *essential* in a reference versus what was contextual decoration.`

`---`

`## Surface Aesthetics vs. Design DNA`

`This is the central competency gap between junior and senior designers, and the central technical challenge of reference-based work with AI tools.`

`**Surface aesthetics** = the immediately perceptible style signature — the specific typefaces, the color palette, the photographic treatment, the texture and grain.`

`**Design DNA** = the underlying system of decisions that *generates* that aesthetic — the proportional logic, the hierarchy philosophy, the relationship between restraint and expression, the degree of contrast permitted, the spatial grammar, the density theory.`

`The distinction matters operationally: you cannot copy design DNA the way you can copy surface. DNA requires understanding, not observation. Surface copying produces pastiche; DNA translation produces original work that carries the same structural quality.`

`**The pedagogical test:** Take a reference in one medium, one era, one context — and reproduce its underlying logic in a completely different medium, era, and context. If the result feels related but isn't imitative, DNA has been extracted. If the result feels like pastiche, surface was copied.`

`**The senior designer's diagnostic questions:**`
`- "What are the *decisions* here, not the results?"`
`- "What would have to be true about this designer's thinking for this to be the output?"`
`- "What constraints is this work operating within — visible and invisible?"`
`- "What would have to change for this to feel like a different brand?"`

`**The underlying logic categories professionals isolate:**`
`- **Contrast logic** — what contrast dimensions are being exploited (scale, weight, color, space)?`
`- **Hierarchy philosophy** — how many levels? How steep or flat is the hierarchy?`
`- **Space behavior** — is white space used as breath, as frame, as tension, as luxury?`
`- **Typography posture** — how is type performing (neutral vessel, expressive element, structural grid component)?`
`- **Restraint threshold** — where does this work stop, and what does its stopping point reveal about the designer's values?`

`---`

`## The Inspired vs. Influenced Distinction`

`Research with professional designers produces a precise and operationally useful working distinction between the two modes of reference use:`

`**"Inspired"** = extracting feelings or visual elements from designs originating in *different* fields — art, furniture, fashion, architecture — and translating them into your own design context. You are crossing categorical boundaries.`

`**"Influenced"** = directly using elements from a *similar* design field and applying them in your own work. You are staying within categorical boundaries.`

`The professional methodology intentionally reaches *across* disciplines. If your reference is from within your category (using another brand identity as a reference for your brand identity), you are at high risk of imitation rather than translation. Lateral reference produces translation; literal reference produces imitation.`

`**The lateral reference principle:** A reference from architecture, fashion, or film can communicate exactly the right quality for a software product's visual identity. This is not an accident — it is methodology.`

`---`

`## Mood Board Extraction Methodology`

`Professional mood boards are not inspirational collages — they are **hypothesis documents**. Their function is to align collaborators on direction before production begins, and to give designers a working brief that is spatial and tonal rather than verbal.`

`**Construction discipline:** Effective mood boards are edited to 6–12 images, each present for a distinct reason. One for spatial logic. One for tonal register. One for typographic posture. One for material reference. One for cultural context. One for the threshold — the most extreme direction the work might go. When every image is present for the same reason, the board lacks analytical richness.`

`**A mood board presented without annotation is a Rorschach test, not a brief.** Without context for why specific references were chosen and what elements they're pointing to, collaborators focus on the wrong things.`

`**The four-pass extraction protocol:**`
`1. **First pass** — overall emotional register and tonal temperature. What does the set *feel* like in aggregate? What word would you use if you had one?`
`2. **Second pass** — structural patterns. What formal moves appear across multiple references? What repeats?`
`3. **Third pass** — outliers. What single reference is the most extreme? What does its presence signal about the threshold of the direction?`
`4. **Fourth pass** — specific design parameters. How light or dark is the aggregate? How dense or spacious? How classical or contemporary? How structured or organic?`

`**Translation into design direction:** The output of mood board analysis is **parameter ranges**, not specific choices. "Type should sit between medium and large scale. Space should be generous. Color should compress toward neutral with one chromatic accent. Imagery should be documentary in register, not constructed." These become the brief for the actual making — not a list of things to copy.`

`---`

`## Brand Identity Deconstruction`

`Brand strategists approach reference brands through a five-layer analytical stack designed to separate strategic work from aesthetic work.`

`**Layer 1 — Positioning Signal Analysis**`
`What does this brand's visual system communicate about its competitive position? What category conventions does it align with, and which does it reject? Rejection is always the most interesting signal — it indicates a deliberate positioning strategy.`

`**Layer 2 — System Architecture**`
`How is the identity structured? Primary, secondary, and tertiary elements — what is the core mark doing vs. the typography vs. the color system? Strong identity systems have clear labor division: each element does distinct, non-redundant work. If removing any element collapses the identity, that element is structural. If removing it makes no difference, it's decorative.`

`**Layer 3 — Flexibility Mechanics**`
`How does this identity behave at scale extremes? On a favicon vs. a billboard? In black and white? In motion? In environmental context? Flexibility analysis reveals which elements are load-bearing and which are decorative.`

`**Layer 4 — Ownable Distinctiveness Audit**`
`Which elements are category-generic and which are brand-specific? Which elements could only belong to this brand? The answer identifies actual design equity — the defensible IP of the visual system. Category-generic elements are available for competitive differentiation; category-specific elements are territory to respect or deliberately claim.`

`**Layer 5 — Longevity vs. Trend Analysis**`
`Which decisions are responding to current visual culture and will date? Which are structurally independent of trend? This separates what to extract from what to consciously avoid importing.`

`**The output of brand deconstruction is a mechanism statement:** One to two sentences articulating what is generating this brand's visual power, independent of any specific execution. Example: *"The authority in this identity comes from a severe reduction of variables — the system has almost no degrees of freedom, which reads as total confidence."* That insight translates directly into design direction without requiring any surface borrowing.`

`**The diagnostic test:** Could this visual system be mistaken for a competitor's? If you could swap the logo, color palette, or typography with a rival's without a major shift in message, the identity lacks distinction. Apply this test to *both* the reference brand and your own emerging work.`

`---`

`# SECTION 5B — THE SEVEN-LAYER EXTRACTION PROTOCOL`

`*Each layer follows the same structure: what professionals look for, how they describe what they find, and how they translate it into portable design direction.*`

`*The extraction discipline is the same across all seven layers: move from what it looks like to what rule is operating.*`

`---`

`## Layer 1: Layout System`

`### What Professionals Look For`
`The underlying proportional logic — not the surface arrangement. The first question is what governing ratio structures the composition. A two-column layout might use equal columns (1:1) for symmetrical balance or unequal columns (1:2 or 2:3) for dynamic hierarchy. The golden ratio provides another option: a main content column 1.618× the width of a sidebar creates a naturally pleasing asymmetry.`

`Professionals read layout systems by:`
`- **Hierarchy depth** — how many distinct levels of information exist and how spatial intervals between them are calibrated`
`- **Margin and gutter logic** — margins are not passive frames; they declare the designer's relationship to density and formality`
`- **Grid type** — columnar, modular, or baseline; each carries different compositional implications`
`- **Revealed vs. concealed grid** — grids that show their seams (Swiss modernism, mechanical authority) vs. grids hidden beneath organic-feeling composition (sophisticated restraint)`

`Key diagnostic: trace the white space, not the elements. The negative space reveals the system.`

`### How Professionals Describe It`
`"This is a 12-column with 3-column gutters behaving like a 4-column macro." / "The margins are doing load-bearing work — this is a centered armature with aggressive asymmetric fills." / "The baseline grid is strict but image placement breaks it deliberately on a 1.5× interval." / "This system is designed to be invisible — the structure supports without declaring itself."`

`### Translation into Design Direction`
`Extract the proportional interval, not the position. If the reference uses a 1:1.618 vertical split, apply that ratio to a completely different orientation. Identify the **constraint logic** — what the grid permits versus what it refuses — and reproduce that decision rule in the new context.`

`**Extractable parameters:**`
`- Column proportion (1:1, 1:2, 1:1.618, etc.)`
`- Margin-to-content ratio`
`- Grid visibility (declared vs. hidden)`
`- Break patterns (where does the system allow or encourage violation?)`

`The layout system is transferable. The specific arrangement is not.`

`---`

`## Layer 2: Color Strategy`

`### What Professionals Look For`
`Beyond palette — which is merely a list of hues. Professionals extract the *operating logic* behind color choices by reading three independent axes simultaneously:`

`- **Temperature** — which direction all colors are biased; warm shadows and cool lights, or the reverse; the direction of temperature movement across the composition`
`- **Saturation architecture** — are saturated colors used as accent or field? What is the saturation ceiling? What is the saturation floor?`
`- **Color role structure** — which hue carries the structural load, which provides relief, which signals interaction or action. The dominant/sub-dominant/accent structure as deployed proportionally.`

`They also identify the *key*: high key (values clustered toward white) vs. low key (values clustered toward black) and what that key is doing atmospherically.`

`Critical: note what color is *absent* that you'd expect. Deliberate absence is as readable as deliberate presence.`

`### How Professionals Describe It`
`"This is a desaturated warm field with a single cool neutral for text — the saturation ceiling is 40% except for one accent at full chroma." / "Analogous with one split-complementary break used only for CTAs — everything else is temperature play within the same hue family." / "The palette is printing colors, not screen colors — it's built for ink behavior, not RGB." / "This is a stealth palette — nothing announces itself, but the warm-cool dynamic creates depth without any element competing for attention."`

`### Translation into Design Direction`
`Extract the **ratio and role**, not the hue. "Dominant warm neutral, subordinate cool neutral, single high-chroma accent at 10% coverage" is a transferable color strategy. Build a new palette that obeys the same saturation ceiling, temperature direction, and role assignment with entirely different hues. The system is what you're borrowing.`

`**Extractable parameters:**`
`- Temperature dominant (warm or cool overall cast)`
`- Saturation ceiling (the most vivid point and what it marks)`
`- Saturation floor (the quietest element and what role it serves)`
`- Accent logic (what color directs the eye and at what coverage)`
`- Key (high or low)`

`---`

`## Layer 3: Typographic Personality`

`### What Professionals Look For`
`Most designers think typography is about picking fonts. Professional extraction is about identifying the structural system those fonts are operating within:`

`- **Weight contrast ratio** — the gap between the heaviest and lightest type in the system; a high-contrast system (display at 800 weight, body at 300, nothing in between) signals a specific editorial register`
`- **Rhythm** — whether type is set to a strict vertical rhythm, optically, or in expressive defiance of both; what pacing the type creates`
`- **Personality register** — humanist vs. geometric; warm vs. cold; referential vs. neutral. The formality-warmth axis: high x-height + open apertures = warm and accessible; low x-height + tight apertures + high contrast strokes = formal and cold.`
`- **Hierarchy mechanics** — does size do the work, or weight, or tracking, or case, or color? Identify the primary contrast mechanism.`
`- **Typeface count** — how many faces are in use and what role each holds: structural, editorial, functional`

`### How Professionals Describe It`
`"High contrast weight system — display at 800 weight, body at 300, nothing in between. The tension is the point." / "This is a cold-humanist register — geometric construction but optically corrected. It reads modern but not hostile." / "The tracking on the caps is doing all the hierarchy work — size variance is minimal; this is a tracking-led system." / "One face, used at extreme scale differential — it's a mono-type system where the type IS the design."`

`### Translation into Design Direction`
`Extract the **contrast logic and register**, not the face. Specify: weight contrast ratio, x-height target, axis of contrast, and personality register. A brief might read: "Geometric, high-contrast weight system, wide tracking on structural elements, body at near-text-size with tight leading." This is achievable with dozens of different type families.`

`**Extractable parameters:**`
`- Type count and role division`
`- Weight contrast ratio (heavy weight ÷ light weight)`
`- Primary hierarchy mechanism (size, weight, tracking, case, or color)`
`- Personality register (humanist/geometric, warm/cold)`
`- Alignment convention (flush-left rationalism vs. centered formality)`

`---`

`## Layer 4: Spatial Density`

`### What Professionals Look For`
`The **density map** — which zones are compressed, which are relieved, and whether that contrast is rhythmic (alternating), directional (building or releasing across a page), or structural (dense at load-bearing zones, open at entry points).`

`Professionals measure breathing room relative to content: is padding 50% of element size or 200%? They identify whether density signals urgency (tighter = more critical information) or the reverse (tighter = editorial richness, open = luxury).`

`Three spatial types:`
`- **Dense center, open periphery** — stage-and-surround composition; subject commands all attention`
`- **Open-to-tight gradient** — urgency and accumulation; the reader is being pulled forward`
`- **Tight-to-open gradient** — deceleration; arrival; resolution`

`Both macro whitespace (large areas between major elements) and micro whitespace (gaps between lines, between letters, between components) are read. They exist in ratio to each other.`

`### How Professionals Describe It`
`"Dense center, open periphery — this is a stage-and-surround composition." / "The density gradient runs top to bottom — it's decelerating, the reader is meant to slow down." / "This is editorial compression — the content is rich but the space is uncomfortable. It's demanding engagement." / "Luxury, innovation, and clarity share the same design language: restraint. This palette is 80% air."`

`### Translation into Design Direction`
`Design the density map before placing content. Decide which zones are tight and which are open, and what that contrast is *signaling*. Uniform density signals either democratic structure or chaotic noise — intention is everything.`

`**Extractable parameters:**`
`- Density zone map (primary zone: dense/open; secondary zone; tertiary zone)`
`- Contrast ratio between densest and least dense zone`
`- Gradient direction (open-to-tight or tight-to-open)`
`- Macro/micro whitespace ratio`

`---`

`## Layer 5: Era and Cultural Reference`

`### What Professionals Look For`
`The **design genealogy** — what tradition the work is quoting, consciously or not. This includes: decade markers (specific grid conventions, type fashions, production artifacts), national/regional schools (Swiss, Dutch, American editorial, Japanese minimal), movement signatures (Bauhaus, Push Pin, grunge, New Wave), and production era tells (photostat artifacts, digital aliasing, offset registration variation, Letraset spacing).`

`Critical distinction: work that *is from* an era vs. work that *quotes* it. Both can be present and serve different purposes.`

`Key lineages:`
`- **Swiss International Style** — asymmetric layouts, grid, Helvetica/Akzidenz-Grotesk, flush left ragged right, photography over illustration, ideology of objectivity`
`- **Postmodern** — departure from functionalism, eclecticism, irony, playful recombination, humor, mixed type orientations, deliberate grid violation`
`- **Bauhaus** — form follows function, grid, geometric sans, primary colors, industrial legibility`
`- **American editorial (1970s–80s)** — ITC typefaces, magazine grid, warm saturated photography`
`- **Contemporary corporate modernism** — neutral sans, restrained palette, generous space, clean hierarchy`

`### How Professionals Describe It`
`"This is quoting early 90s Dutch institutional — not retro, it's citing an authority." / "The gestural brush marks are 1950s American commercial, but the type is contemporary. It's a deliberate anachronism." / "This is pure ITC era — the type choices and the magazine grid are specific to 1977–1985." / "It's Swiss-derived but ironized — they're using the grammar to critique the ideology."`

`### Translation into Design Direction`
`Identify the **citation level** — are you quoting a period for authority and context, for nostalgia, for irony, or for archival authenticity? Then reproduce the *logic* of that era (its production constraints, its ideological position, its cultural context) rather than its surface marks. Period work should be *understood*, not sampled.`

`**Extractable parameters:**`
`- Primary tradition being quoted (movement or national school)`
`- Citation mode (affirmative, hybrid, ironic, subversive)`
`- Specific era markers (which formal elements carry the period signal)`
`- Whether these markers can be transplanted or are inseparable from the source context`

`---`

`## Layer 6: Materiality`

`### What Professionals Look For`
`The **substrate language** — whether a design is referencing coated stock (sharp, cold, high contrast), uncoated (warm, soft, slightly expanded ink dot), textured (artisanal, analog warmth), or screen-native (luminous, RGB-native saturation, no substrate at all). They identify finish signals: matte, gloss, soft-touch, foil, letterpress deboss.`

`In digital work: **simulated materiality** — grain, paper texture overlays, ink spread, halftone patterns — and whether it's deployed to evoke warmth, era, or physical premium.`

`Materiality is not decorative. Substrate choices are brand positioning decisions. An uncoated cream paper reads handmade. A heavy coated board reads luxury. Kraft reads honest and sustainable. High-tech brands seek materials that promote cutting-edge positioning; heritage brands seek materials that reinforce history. For screen-based or digitally-produced references, the question is what physical material the digital surface *suggests*.`

`### How Professionals Describe It`
`"This is designed for 100gsm uncoated — the color is warm and the type has room in it for ink spread." / "The grain is doing affect work — it's not vintage, it's tactile. It's simulating the emotional warmth of analog." / "This is foil-brain design. Everything is hyper-smooth and maximum contrast — it's imagining itself as a luxury object." / "Screen-native all the way — the saturation levels only exist on a backlit surface. It would be uninhabitable on paper."`

`### Translation into Design Direction`
`Specify the intended or evoked substrate before designing — not as an afterthought. If the work should feel like it belongs on kraft board, build the color strategy around ink absorption behavior. If it should feel screen-native, eliminate simulation artifacts. Material language should be decided at brief stage.`

`**Extractable parameters:**`
`- Substrate reference (coated, uncoated, textured, screen-native, kraft)`
`- Finish (matte, gloss, soft-touch, foil)`
`- Simulated materiality type (grain, ink spread, letterpress, halftone)`
`- Tactile signal being produced (handmade, luxury, industrial, heritage)`

`---`

`## Layer 7: Emotional Register`

`### What Professionals Look For`
`The **economic and status signals** the design is engineering, and which specific formal elements are doing that work. Design does not just express emotion — it signals access, class, aspiration, and belonging. These are constructed through the accumulation of formal choices, not through any single element.`

`Luxury signals: restraint, high negative space ratio, reduced palette, serif or geometric sans, muted saturation. Mass-market signals: high contrast, saturated color, compressed density, approachable letterforms, diagonal energy. The key diagnostic: what is the design's economic register, and is it earned or aspirational?`

`They identify the **aspiration gap** — the emotional distance between what a product is and what the design claims it to be — and whether that gap is productive tension or dishonesty.`

`Formal elements that consistently carry register work:`
`- **Space allocation** — spacious layouts signal restraint and confidence; luxury, innovation, and clarity share the same design language`
`- **Color saturation** — loud colors catch the eye and raise excitement; quiet colors are calming with low saturation`
`- **Logo size and conspicuity** — the absence of conspicuous branding paradoxically signals membership among the highest-value segments (stealth luxury)`
`- **Typographic formality** — refined custom typefaces signal sophistication; approachable humanists signal democratic access`

`### How Professionals Describe It`
`"This is aspirational-functional — it's using luxury restraint for a mid-market product. It's engineering perceived value." / "The emotional register is warm authority — serif, human warmth in color, high legibility, democratic layout. This is the visual language of trusted institutions." / "Every element is performing urgency — compressed density, high saturation, diagonal composition, weight contrast used for alarm rather than hierarchy." / "The absence of conspicuous branding IS the brand statement. This is the visual grammar of belonging, not announcing."`

`### Translation into Design Direction`
`Define the target emotional register as a compound: **economic register × emotional tone × relationship to viewer**. "Mid-premium / quiet confidence / peer-to-peer" is a completely different brief than "luxury / authority / aspirational distance." Map each element (space, type weight, color saturation, imagery style, logo behavior) to its register position on the accessible ↔ exclusive axis. The resulting map is the emotional register architecture — fully transferable to new work without copying a single visual element.`

`**Extractable parameters:**`
`- Economic register (accessible, mid-premium, luxury, stealth luxury)`
`- Emotional tone (urgent, contemplative, authoritative, playful, intimate)`
`- Relationship to viewer (peer-to-peer, aspirational distance, institutional authority)`
`- Primary formal load-bearer (what element is doing most of the register work)`

`---`

`## The Extraction Stack: Summary`

`| Layer | Core Question | Extractable Parameter |`
`|---|---|---|`
`| **Layout System** | What is the governing ratio, and is the grid declared or hidden? | Column proportion, margin logic, break pattern |`
`| **Color Strategy** | What temperature leads, what is the saturation ceiling, and what accent directs the eye? | Temperature dominant, saturation hierarchy, accent role |`
`| **Typographic Personality** | What is the scale ratio, weight logic, classification, and alignment convention? | Size ratio, weight contrast, personality register, hierarchy mechanism |`
`| **Spatial Density** | Where are the dense, transitional, and open zones, and what sits in each? | Density zone map, contrast ratio, gradient direction |`
`| **Era & Cultural Reference** | What tradition is being quoted, and is that dialogue affirmative, hybrid, or subversive? | Lineage ID, citation mode, era markers |`
`| **Materiality** | What surface language is in use, and what semiotic weight does each material choice carry? | Substrate/finish/tactile grammar stack |`
`| **Emotional Register** | Which formal elements are doing the economic and class signaling work? | Register map (accessible ↔ exclusive per element) |`

`---`

`# SECTION 5C — FROM EXTRACTION TO APPLICATION`

`## The Translation Protocol`

`Professional reference analysis follows a consistent five-stage logic across all contexts. Surface imitation collapses this sequence by jumping from stage 1 directly to stage 5.`

`| Stage | Activity | Output |`
`|---|---|---|`
`| **Inventory** | Separate elements — strip the whole into parts | Annotated element inventory |`
`| **Mechanism** | Identify principles, not appearances — what rule is operating? | Named principles with design rationale |`
`| **Separation** | Distinguish what is context-specific from what is structurally transferable | Context map: what stays, what transfers |`
`| **Abstraction** | Convert transferable logic into parameter language | Named parameters with measurable constraints |`
`| **Translation** | Apply parameters to generate original work | Fresh design decisions derived from the system |`

`The professional move is always: observation → mechanism → abstraction → application.`

`---`

`## Translating Extracted Qualities to Design Specification`

`The implicit step that most designers skip: converting the qualitative language of observation ("the light quality in these references feels diffused and institutional") into specification language ("photography direction: overcast north-light quality, no directional shadows, color temperature 6500K, no fill").`

`| Observation | Specification |`
`|---|---|`
`| "The spatial emptiness across this board" | Minimum 50% negative space in primary zone; content-to-space ratio specified per section |`
`| "The weight and restraint of the typography" | Maximum two weights; display weight ÷ body weight ≥ 2.5; no decorative type |`
`| "The light quality in these references" | Photography brief: soft box overhead, 2:1 key-to-fill ratio, 5500K neutral |`
`| "The materiality feels analog and hand-touched" | Grain overlay 15–25% opacity; paper texture; avoid pure RGB saturation |`
`| "The color feels pulled from a specific time period" | Palette built from desaturated period references; no digital primaries; chromatic neutrals with warm bias |`
`| "The hierarchy is immediate but not aggressive" | Size contrast minimum 2.5× across adjacent tiers; no all-caps except for micro-labels; leading generous at body size |`

`---`

`## Annotating a Reference for Use`

`A reference image handed over without annotation is a Rorschach test. An annotated reference is a brief. The annotation protocol:`

`**For each image or group:**`
`1. **What the reference is doing** — which of the seven layers is this image primarily contributing?`
`2. **Specifically what to extract** — name the parameter: "the margin-to-content ratio in this layout" not "the clean feeling"`
`3. **What to leave behind** — what is context-specific decoration that should not transfer: "the Victorian ornament is not the direction; the density and the contrast it creates are"`
`4. **How it translates** — what specific instruction does this reference produce: "body text measure never exceeds 60 characters; negative space in each section minimum 40% of the total area"`

`**The "inspired vs. influenced" check:** For each reference, ask: is this from the same category as the work you're making? If yes, flag it — you are at risk of influence (imitation) rather than inspiration (translation). Seek cross-category references deliberately.`

`---`

`## Building a Reference Brief`

`A complete reference brief for a design project — the output of the extraction process — contains:`

`**Direction statement** (one paragraph): The single clearest articulation of what the work should feel like and why. Written in emotional and strategic language, not formal. This is what you can hand to a designer or an image generator.`

`**Extracted parameters** (by layer): The seven-layer extraction outputs, translated to measurable specifications. These are the constraints.`

`**What to bring through:** The specific qualities, principles, and DNA elements that are being explicitly carried from the references into new work.`

`**What to leave behind:** The context-specific surface elements that belong to the references and must not transfer — the category markers, the brand-specific elements, the era markers not appropriate for the new context.`

`**The threshold:** What is the most extreme direction this work might go? The reference that pulled hardest in one direction. Knowing the threshold helps designers push into productive risk rather than defaulting to safe approximations.`

`---`

`## Cross-Platform Application`

`The extracted DNA parameters map directly to the prompt architecture in Document 3. Once extracted, each parameter layer becomes a specific type of prompt instruction:`

`| DNA Layer | Maps to in Document 3 |`
`|---|---|`
`| Layout System | v0 token language, Cursor/Claude Code structure specifications |`
`| Color Strategy | GPT-4o hex/temperature language, Midjourney palette descriptors |`
`| Typographic Personality | Cross-platform type direction vocabulary |`
`| Spatial Density | v0 restraint prompting, Midjourney negative space vocabulary |`
`| Era & Cultural Reference | GPT-4o temporal/cultural anchors, Midjourney style references |`
`| Materiality | Midjourney surface language, Flux substrate vocabulary |`
`| Emotional Register | Claude DNA extraction briefing (Template 2 in Doc 3) |`

`The full workflow: Reference → DNA extraction (this document) → Parameter specification → Platform prompt (Document 3) → Design output → Quality review (Document 4).`

`---`

`## The Mechanism Statement`

`The final output of any reference analysis is a **mechanism statement**: one to two sentences that articulate what is generating the work's visual power, separate from any specific execution. This is the most portable, most transferable, and most AI-legible form the extracted DNA can take.`

`**Structure:** "The [quality] of this work comes from [specific decision or system], which produces [specific effect on the viewer]."`

`**Examples:**`
`- "The authority in this identity comes from a severe reduction of variables — the system has almost no degrees of freedom, which reads as total confidence."`
`- "The intimacy in this campaign comes from type at near-body-text scale set with exceptional leading in expansive negative space — the design treats the viewer as someone who will stay, not scan."`
`- "The urgency in this packaging comes from a single high-chroma accent on a completely muted field — one element carries all the emotional weight, which creates a kind of forced attention."`
`- "The luxury register of this editorial comes from the density gradient — dense information zones are earned by expansive entry points, which teaches the reader that slowness is rewarded."`

`A good mechanism statement should be:`
`- Portable (usable across media and contexts)`
`- Specific (names a principle, not a quality)`
`- Generative (suggests a direction rather than constraining to a single outcome)`
`- Independent of surface (could describe a dozen different executions)`

`---`

`*Document 5 complete. Version 1.0. Synthesized from 4 research documents (2 v1 training knowledge + 2 web search sources) covering reference analysis methodology, the seven-layer extraction protocol, and the translation framework.*`

`*Cross-references: Document 2 (Design Language & Vocabulary System) provides the formal vocabulary used in extraction descriptions. Document 3 (Platform Prompt Architecture Library) is where extracted DNA becomes executable prompts. Document 4 (Last 10% Review Checklists) applies extraction-derived standards as quality protocols.*`

pages.content:
`0–200' (healthcare and transit standard) without a confirmation sign.`
`- Naming consistency across sign types: every destination name reconciled across overhead directionals, wall-mounted IDs, building directories, and digital kiosks. "Emergency Department" on approach vs. "ED" on the room identifier is a system failure.`
`- Information load per panel: maximum 4–5 destinations per directional sign panel. Secondary destinations can be disclosed at later decision points.`
`- Arrow direction convention consistency: compass-convention (arrows toward destination) vs. viewer-relative convention (arrows indicate turn direction) — one convention system-wide. Mixed conventions create critical navigation failures.`
`- Emergency egress integration: egress signs must dominate the visual hierarchy in emergencies; wayfinding signs must not visually compete with or obscure egress path markings.`

`---`

`## The Gap: Design vs. Fabrication-Ready`

`**Specification voids:** Designs that specify appearance but not fabrication method. Color, typeface, and layout specified; material, thickness, mounting method, finish, and attachment hardware not specified. Fabricators will make those decisions independently.`

`**ADA/code compliance not audited against the full sign schedule:** Single non-compliant sign types, reproduced across a large installation, create project-wide liability. ADA compliance must be audited at the schedule level, not just the type level.`

`**Color file format errors:** Submitting RGB or CMYK files for fabricators who need Pantone or specified paint formulas is the single most common production error. Deliver in the fabricator's required format.`

`**Scale and detail drawing misalignment:** Plan drawings, elevation drawings, and detail drawings that are internally inconsistent in dimensions. Run a dimensional audit comparing all three drawing types before fabrication release.`

`**Typeface licensing and file format gaps:** Fabricators require either outlined vector files or licensed font installation. Sending unoutlined native files without confirming licensing covers fabrication use creates delays and potential violations.`

`**Message schedule version control:** Late-stage copy changes made in design files without updating the master message schedule, or vice versa, result in fabricated signs with incorrect copy. The message schedule is the single source of truth — version-controlled and sign-off documented.`

`**Sign schedule drift against current construction documents:** The sign schedule must reflect today's decisions, not last week's assumptions. Reconcile the full sign schedule against the most current architectural drawings before releasing fabrication documents.`

`---`

`*Document 4 complete. Version 1.0. Synthesized from 16 research documents (8 v1 training knowledge + 8 web search sources) covering all eight asset types.*`

`*Cross-references: Document 2 (Design Language & Vocabulary System) defines the formal terminology used in these checklists. Document 3 (Platform Prompt Architecture Library) provides the prompt templates for generating design assets that will then be reviewed against these protocols. Document 5 (Reference Translation Protocol) completes the system.*`

* * *

`# Document 3: Platform Prompt Architecture Library`

`**Project:** Design Intelligence Translator`
`**Version:** 1.0 — Synthesized from 12 research documents (v1 training knowledge + web search)`
`**Platforms Covered:** Midjourney | DALL-E / GPT-4o | Flux / Stable Diffusion | v0 | Cursor / Claude Code | Claude (Design Intelligence)`

`---`

`## How to Use This Document`

`This document is the **executable layer** of the Translator project. Where Document 2 defines the vocabulary, Document 3 shows how that vocabulary maps to specific platform syntax and prompt architecture.`

`Each platform section contains:`
`- Architectural model (how the platform processes language)`
`- Core prompt template`
`- Parameter reference (what each dial does)`
`- High-leverage language patterns`
`- Vague vs. precise contrast examples`
`- Where it wins / where to route elsewhere`

`**The governing principle:** Every platform has a different creative contract. The same intent, translated through the wrong grammar, produces the wrong output — or no output at all. These templates are the translation layer between your design intent and platform-readable instruction.`

`---`

`# PLATFORM 1 — MIDJOURNEY (V6 / V7)`

`## Architectural Model`

`Midjourney V7 (default as of June 2025) processes prompts as natural language understood at a deep level — but it still weights earlier tokens more heavily. It brings strong aesthetic defaults: cinematic lighting, compositional interest, surface richness. These defaults are the source of both its power (strong first outputs) and its design liability (defaults override client requirements unless explicitly suppressed).`

`**The paradigm shift from V6 to V7:** The old keyword-soup approach ("beautiful, stunning, 8k, detailed, masterpiece") actively degrades results in V7. Write prompts like you're describing a photograph to a skilled cinematographer, not tagging a stock photo database.`

`**The designer's core challenge with MJ:** Its instinct is toward beautiful. Yours is toward appropriate. These are different goals. Producing clean, minimal, or restrained output requires active suppression of the model's defaults across multiple prompt layers simultaneously.`

`---`

`## Core Prompt Template`

` ``` `
`[SUBJECT FACT] + [ACTION/STATE] + [CONTEXT/ENVIRONMENT]`
`+ [MEDIUM/REFERENCE] + [LIGHTING SPECIFICATION]`
`+ [COLOR/PALETTE] + [CAMERA LANGUAGE]`
`+ --ar [format] + --style raw + --s [value] + --sref [code] --sw [value]`
`+ --no [exclusion list]`
` ``` `

`**Front-load by priority.** V7 weights early tokens most heavily — lead with the subject fact, not the style wrapper. "Beautiful cinematic photo of a perfume bottle" is weaker than "frosted glass perfume bottle, matte finish, minimal label."`

`---`

`## Parameter Reference`

`### --stylize / --s (0–1000, default 100)`
`Controls how much artistic interpretation the model adds. The highest-impact creative quality lever.`

`| Range | Effect | Design Use |`
`|---|---|---|`
`| 0–50 | Hyper-literal | Technical reference, UI mockups, diagrams |`
`| 100–200 | Balanced (start here) | Most client work — faithful prompt + compositional quality |`
`| 300–600 | Editorially interpretive | Campaign images, mood-forward content |`
`| 700–1000 | Maximum aesthetic latitude | Conceptual, expressive work only |`

`### --style raw`
`Suppresses Midjourney's built-in aesthetic bias: moody lighting, dramatic depth, painterly finishes. **Add --style raw to all product, interior, and editorial work.** It is the single biggest difference between a fake-looking room and a real one. Raw Mode removes MJ's defaults but still honors your directives — it does not suppress complexity you explicitly prompt for.`

`Combined effect: --style raw --s 50 provides the strongest directive for literal output.`

`### --chaos / --c (0–100, default 0)`
`Controls variation between the four-image grid outputs.`

`- --c 10–25 — controlled variation for concepting`
`- --c 40–70 — divergent exploration`
`- --c 0 — production; avoid when consistency is required`

`### --sref + --sw (Style Reference + Style Weight)`

`--sref transfers: color palette and tonal range, surface texture, lighting quality and mood, contrast and shadow handling, medium reference. It does **not** reliably transfer: compositions, characters, faces, objects, or spatial relationships.`

`--sw (0–1000, default 100) controls how strongly the style reference influences output vs. text prompt:`

`| Range | Effect |`
`|---|---|`
`| 50–80 | Light inflection; content dominates |`
`| 100–200 | Production range for most brand asset work |`
`| 300–500 | Strong visual lockdown for asset families |`

`**Numeric codes vs. image URLs:** Numeric codes are more consistent than image URLs because they reference a fixed style vector, not an interpretation of a specific image. Build a "style code library" of 10–20 codes covering your brand modes.`

`**--sv (Style Version):** Always specify explicitly (--sv 6 is current default). Midjourney updates constantly — what works today may behave differently next month.`

`### --oref + --ow (Omni Reference, V7 only)`
`Places a specific character, object, or logo into new images. GPU cost: 2x. Reserve for final production passes.`

`- --ow 25 — if changing style significantly (photo to illustration)`
`- --ow 100 — default; balanced`
`- --ow 400+ — preserve character or clothing details strictly`
`- Never exceed --ow 400 unless using very high stylize/exp values`

`**Pro workflow:** Use an image as both --oref and --sref to lock both content and look simultaneously.`

`### --weird / --w (0–3000, default 0)`
`Introduces morphological variation and unique outputs. Design use: --weird 100–300 for unexpected material combinations. Above 500, outputs become unpredictably abstract and are rarely production-usable. Not seed-consistent — use for exploration only.`

`### Draft Mode (--mode draft)`
`10x faster at half GPU cost. Incompatible with Omni Reference. Use for all concepting and exploration; switch to Standard for final renders.`

`### --seed`
`Locks base noise pattern for reproducible iterations. Use for A/B prompt testing and iterative copy-editing of a locked composition.`

`### --stop (10–100)`
`Interrupts generation early; produces sketch-like outputs. --stop 70–80 gives soft-rendered concept sketches. Not for final deliverables.`

`---`

`## Lighting Direction Vocabulary`

`**The fundamental error:** Using adjectives ("dramatic," "moody") instead of cinematographic specifications. Name the setup, not the mood.`

`| Setup | Prompt Language |`
`|---|---|`
`| Rembrandt | "Rembrandt lighting, 45° key above and to the side, signature triangle highlight on cheek" |`
`| Split | "Split lighting, key light at 90° to subject, half face in shadow" |`
`| Butterfly / Paramount | "Butterfly lighting, overhead key centered on face, defined cast shadow below nose" |`
`| Rim / Hair | "Rim lighting, backlit from below-camera-right, narrow glowing outline separating subject from background" |`
`| Three-point | "Three-point studio lighting, key light 45° front-left, fill from right, hair light from behind" |`
`| Contre-jour | "Contre-jour, subject silhouetted against bright window, halation around edges" |`
`| Chiaroscuro | "Chiaroscuro lighting — strong contrast between light and dark, inspired by the painting style" |`
`| Volumetric | "Volumetric lighting, god rays through haze, atmospheric depth" |`

`**Light motivation:** Always name the source. "Warm tungsten practicals, single overhead pendant at 2700K" / "Cool north window light, overcast, 6500K, no fill" / "Late-afternoon raking light at 15° above horizon, long shadows, warm 3200K."`

`**Photographer anchors:** Annie Leibovitz (portraiture), Roger Deakins (cinematography), Gregory Crewdson (cinematic suburban tension), Wolfgang Tillmans (flat social realism), Peter Lindbergh (desaturated fashion naturalism), Julius Shulman (mid-century architectural).`

`**What does NOT work:** ISO numbers, f-stops, shutter speeds. "ISO 3200" does not give you grain — "35mm film photograph, visible grain, Kodak Tri-X 400 character" does.`

`---`

`## --no Exclusion Strategy`

`Build your --no list as a fixed template appended to all professional work. Syntax: comma-separated within a single --no command.`

`**Typography artifacts:**`
`--no text, typography, words, letters, watermark, signature, logo, copyright mark, caption, label`

`**Decorative accumulation:**`
`--no ornate border, decorative frame, vignette, lens flare, bokeh overlay`

`**Tone-mapping artifacts:**`
`--no HDR, hyper-realistic, overprocessed, oversaturated, blown highlights`

`**Compositional clutter:**`
`--no clutter, busy background, distracting elements, multiple subjects`

`**Body/anatomy artifacts:**`
`--no extra limbs, extra fingers, distorted hands, elongated neck, multiple faces`

`**Retro format artifacts (when using film stock language):**`
`--no polaroid border, film sprocket, slide mount, scan artifacts`

`**Important caveat:** --no operates as probability suppression, not hard exclusion. Some elements embedded in strong contextual associations (trees in a forest, cars on streets) resist exclusion. For design-critical exclusions, reinforce in the positive prompt text as well.`

`---`

`## Restraint Prompting Stack`

`When you need minimal, flat, or clean output against MJ's maximalist defaults:`

` ``` `
`[restrained subject prompt]`
`--style raw`
`--s 0–100`
`--no [decoration list]`
` ``` `

`**Restraint vocabulary with mechanical effect:**`
`- "flat lay on white surface" (not "product photography")`
`- "single subject, centered" (not "hero composition")`
`- "negative space, 70% blank background"`
`- "solid [color] background, no texture, no gradient"`
`- "studio white infinity curve"`
`- "Muji product photography"`
`- "diagrammatic," "schematic," "blueprint style"`

`**Reference anchors for restraint:** Dieter Rams product design, Tadao Ando concrete, Swiss International Typographic Style — these designer references access MJ's training data for those aesthetics far more effectively than the adjective "minimalist."`

`---`

`## Vague vs. Precise Examples`

`**Campaign hero image, editorial fashion:**`

`❌ Vague:`
`fashion model in designer clothes, cinematic lighting, studio, high fashion --ar 4:5 --s 500`

`✅ Precise:`
`editorial fashion portrait, woman in structured oatmeal wool coat, standing against poured-concrete wall, late afternoon light raking from camera-left at 15°, cool shadow fill, muted warm gray palette, slight desaturation, documentary photography aesthetic, shot on Leica M11 with 50mm f/2, shallow depth with background fall-off, no fill flash --ar 4:5 --style raw --s 200 --no text, ornate border, lens flare, saturated color, smile --sref [editorial_code] --sw 150`

`---`

`**Premium skincare packaging:**`

`❌ Vague:`
`beautiful luxury skincare bottle, dramatic lighting, elegant, high quality, photorealistic --ar 1:1 --s 750`

`✅ Precise:`
`glass skincare bottle with matte frosted finish, minimal label, single stem eucalyptus branch resting beside it, white slab surface, soft diffused north window light, muted sage and cream palette, product photography, shot on Hasselblad medium format, flat lay with shallow depth, no shadows below 20% gray --ar 1:1 --style raw --s 150 --no text, watermark, busy background, HDR --sref [brand_code] --sw 120`

`---`

`## Production Workflow Template`

` ``` `
`[Clear subject fact, leading token]`
`[Material and physical description]`
`[Lighting: source, direction, quality, color temperature]`
`[Reference: photographer/medium/brand aesthetic]`
`[Spatial context: surface, environment, framing]`
`--ar [output format]`
`--style raw`
`--s [50–200 controlled / 300–600 editorial]`
`--sref [locked brand code or URL] --sw [100–200]`
`--no text, watermark, ornate border, HDR, oversaturation,`
`lens flare, vignette, extra limbs, clutter`
`--seed [fixed for comparison iterations]`
`--v 7`
` ``` `

`### /shorten Diagnostic Tool`
`Run /shorten on any underperforming prompt. Midjourney assigns each token a signal strength from 0–1. Use this to identify dead weight tokens and restructure around the highest-signal terms.`

`### Multi-Prompt Weighting`
`space::2 ship tells Midjourney that "space" is twice as important as "ship." Design application: minimal product packaging::3 editorial photography::2 clean white surface::1 — ensures packaging function dominates compositional decisions.`

`# PLATFORM 2 — DALL-E / GPT-4o IMAGE`

`## Architectural Model`

`**Platform status note:** As of March 2025, DALL-E 3 was replaced in ChatGPT by GPT-4o's native image generation (gpt-image-1). API users retain DALL-E 3 access. This document covers both; the default inside ChatGPT is now the GPT Image engine.`

`**The core architectural difference from Midjourney:** Midjourney interprets creatively — sparse prompts yield aesthetically interesting results because the model fills gaps intelligently. DALL-E/GPT-4o executes literally. Sparse prompts return literal, often generic results. **You must supply the aesthetic intelligence yourself.**`

`- **Midjourney:** Subject + style tags + parameters → model fills aesthetic gaps`
`- **DALL-E/GPT-4o:** Narrative sentence structure describing scene, mood, lighting, surface quality, rendering style, and intended use — written as layered prose`

`---`

`## The Seven Prompt Layers`

`DALL-E/GPT-4o reads prompts in layers. Every serious prompt should address all seven:`

`1. **Subject** — what is shown`
`2. **Scene context** — where and when`
`3. **Lighting** — quality, direction, temperature`
`4. **Mood/atmosphere** — emotional register`
`5. **Rendering style** — medium, technique, finish`
`6. **Compositional framing** — camera/perspective language`
`7. **Surface and material quality** — texture, finish, detail density`

`---`

`## Art Direction Language That Works`

`Use language a photographer or art director would use in a shoot brief — not keyword stacking.`

`**Lighting:** "soft directional key light from camera left, warm 3200K, slight fill from a large silver reflector"`

`**Material:** "brushed metal with micro-abrasion marks, matte ceramic glaze with visible brush marks at the rim"`

`**Mood:** "quiet Sunday morning, unhurried, slightly melancholy but safe"`

`**Rendering:** "digital illustration with visible ink textures, reminiscent of 1970s paperback cover art"`

`**Cultural/temporal anchors (uniquely effective in GPT-4o):** "The aesthetic of a 1972 Swiss International Style poster" / "1970s Italian product catalog" / "The palette of Wes Anderson's Grand Budapest Hotel" — these access the model's multimodal world knowledge and are genuine art direction shortcuts.`

`**Design movement vocabulary (deeply encoded in GPT-4o):** "Bauhaus-inspired with industrial restraint," "corporate minimalism with Swiss grid precision," "the restrained editorial quality of a Phaidon catalogue." GPT-4o's training on multimodal data means design movement references are processed as structured knowledge, not just stylistic hints.`

`---`

`## GPT-4o Specific Capabilities`

`**Conversational context memory:** GPT Image is native to the conversation — it understands context from earlier turns, references elements from uploaded images, and iterates without losing context. Each generation in the old DALL-E 3 pipeline was an isolated call. With GPT-4o: set up brand context in turn 1, generate in turn 2, refine in turn 3. The model remembers.`

`**Image input transformation:** Upload reference imagery (mood boards, brand assets, reference photos) and instruct the model to extract and apply specific qualities. "Apply the color palette and grain quality from this reference to a new image of [subject]." The model can recognize color palette, compositional solutions, and overall aesthetics and apply them to new content.`

`**Text rendering:** GPT Image 2 / ChatGPT Images 2.0 achieves near-perfect, pixel-accurate text — print-ready quality for dense infographics, menus, posters, and UI mockups. This is a direct, structural capability advantage over Midjourney.`

`**Specific color hex values:** GPT-4o responds meaningfully to hex values ("use #1D4ED8 as the primary color"). Midjourney requires descriptive language. This makes GPT-4o the correct tool for brand-locked generation where color fidelity is non-negotiable.`

`---`

`## What DALL-E / GPT-4o Uniquely Responds To`

`| Lever | GPT-4o Behavior | Midjourney |`
`|---|---|---|`
`| Embedded readable text | Native and precise | Unreliable / garbled |`
`| Multi-turn iteration with context | Full conversation memory | No native memory |`
`| Uploaded reference image ingestion | Analyzes and applies | Style transfer via --sref only |`
`| Brand guideline document upload | Can parse and apply | Not available |`
`| Spatial logic ("put X left of Y") | Follows reliably | Often ignores |`
`| Counting and enumeration | Reliable | Frequently wrong |`
`| Technical drawing / diagram generation | Strong | Weak |`
`| Specific hex color values | Responds meaningfully | Must use descriptive language |`
`| Named design movements | Deep cultural encoding | Surface-level |`

`---`

`## Negative Prompt Equivalent`

`DALL-E/GPT-4o has no --no parameter. Use natural exclusion language embedded in the prompt:`

`"No lens flare. No reflections on the surface. No shadows deeper than 20% opacity. No additional props or background elements. No text overlays. No HDR processing."`

`Write exclusions as explicit negated statements, not as the --no keyword, keyword syntax from Midjourney.`

`---`

`## Vague vs. Precise Examples`

`**Skincare product shot:**`

`❌ Vague:`
`"A luxury skincare product against a clean background"`

`✅ Precise:`
`"A studio product photograph of a frosted glass serum bottle on a slab of white Carrara marble. Soft diffused lighting from above and to the left, with a single catch light visible on the bottle neck. The background is warm white with a barely perceptible gradient. Shot at 85mm with shallow depth of field — the marble surface comes into focus at the foreground. The overall aesthetic is quiet, Nordic, spa-like. No props, no foliage, no shadows heavier than 15% opacity."`

`---`

`**Brand illustration element:**`

`❌ Vague:`
`"Coffee illustration, vintage style, warm colors"`

`✅ Precise:`
`"A detailed pen-and-ink illustration in the style of 1920s European botanical engravings: a single coffee branch with leaves, cherries, and a cross-section showing the bean. Fine hatch lines throughout. Monochrome with a warm sepia wash applied over the ink. Intended for use as a repeating pattern element — isolated on white, no background. The illustration should feel hand-drawn, slightly imperfect, with visible nib variation in stroke weight."`

`---`

`**Social banner with type-locked headline:**`

`❌ Vague:`
`"A banner with the text 'New Season' in bold"`

`✅ Precise:`
`"A landscape banner image (16:9) for an autumn apparel campaign. Shallow-focus photograph of amber and ochre maple leaves on a dark forest floor, warm late-afternoon backlight. Overlaid centered text in clean sans-serif uppercase: 'NEW SEASON' — heavy weight, off-white, tracking wide. The type should feel set, not floating. Leave 30% of the left third empty for a secondary text block."`

`---`

`## Pipeline Integration`

`**GPT-4o → Figma:** Native gpt-image-1 integration in Figma Design — generate and edit images directly within the design platform. Adjust styles, remove/add objects, expand backgrounds.`

`**Brand Brief → GPT-4o → Photoshop/Firefly:** Generate conceptual directions in GPT-4o using brand guidelines as uploaded context; export best candidate; bring into Photoshop/Illustrator for refinement and production finishing.`

`**Chained workflow:** Generate an image → extract colors → pass those colors into a next-generation prompt → output a structured brand brief. Run a brand exploration process in under an hour.`

`**The professional pattern:** Use Midjourney for aesthetic direction-setting and mood work. Use GPT-4o for execution, brand-locked generation, text-integrated assets, and production pipeline work where instruction fidelity is non-negotiable.`
