`## PART IV: COLOR PRECISION VOCABULARY`

`*Eight color terms as operative diagnostic and directive tools. The governing principle across all eight: AI treats color as a catalog of individual objects. Professionals orchestrate relationships.*`

`---`

`### TEMPERATURE — WARM VS. COOL AS A DESIGN RELATIONSHIP`

`**Precise Technical Definition**`
`Color temperature is **not a fixed property of a color in isolation — it is a relational condition**. The same orange can read as warm against violet but cool against a redder orange. Warm and cool are perceptual positions, not spectral absolutes. The distinction is based on observed contrast in light between warm daylight or sunset colors and the cooler tones of an overcast day.`

`**As a Design Diagnostic**`
`Warm colors appear to advance toward the viewer; cool colors appear to recede — a perceptual phenomenon rooted in chromatic aberration in the human eye. Designers use warm/cool push-pull to model form, signal foreground/background relationships, and create spatial tension without manipulating value. Temperature also controls emotional register: warm-dominant palettes read as immediate and tactile; cool-dominant palettes recede into authority and distance. The critical question is not "is this warm or cool?" but "what is the temperature *relationship* between this color and its neighbors?"`

`**What AI Gets Wrong**`
`AI treats temperature as a fixed property of individual colors rather than a relational phenomenon. Generated palettes often contain temperatures that don't interact — all warms together, all cools together — producing flat, inert compositions. AI "warm and cool balance" tends toward literal symmetry (three warm, three cool) rather than dynamic tension. AI also fails to resolve ambiguous-temperature hues (green reads warm when yellow-biased, cool when blue-biased; violet shifts similarly) and ignores that a pale, muted warm color might recede more than a bright, saturated cool color.`

`---`

`### SIMULTANEOUS CONTRAST`

`**Precise Technical Definition**`
`Simultaneous contrast (first systematically described by Chevreul, 1839) is the perceptual phenomenon in which adjacent colors mutually alter each other's apparent properties. Each color pushes the perceived properties of its neighbor toward its own complement. A neutral gray placed on orange ground reads as slightly blue; placed on violet, it reads yellow-orange. The effect operates across hue, value, and saturation simultaneously. It intensifies at borders and weakens with spatial separation.`

`**As a Design Diagnostic**`
`Simultaneous contrast is the core reason why color decisions cannot be made in isolation. A color that works in a swatch may fail catastrophically in context. The diagnostic questions: what is this color *doing to* its neighbors, and what are they doing to it? Evaluate: saturation boost (a muted color gains apparent saturation when surrounded by its complement), value shift (mid-tones appear lighter on dark grounds), and hue shift (neutrals pick up the complement of their surrounding color). A text color that passes WCAG contrast ratio checks can still appear low-contrast when placed on a colored background — contrast tools measure luminance, not what the eye actually sees.`

`**What AI Gets Wrong**`
`AI-generated palettes are built as isolated swatches without modeling contextual behavior. A color approved in isolation may catastrophically shift when applied. AI presents colors as static, self-contained objects. The result is palettes that look harmonious in a swatch grid and discordant in deployment — sometimes creating unintended optical vibration (high-contrast complements at similar values) or muddy cancellation (colors too close in hue and value).`

`---`

`### COLOR WEIGHT`

`**Precise Technical Definition**`
`Color weight is the perception of visual heaviness in a color, governed primarily by value (darkness = weight) but significantly modified by saturation and hue. Dark, saturated colors feel heavy; light, desaturated colors feel light. However, hue contributes independently: yellow at equivalent value feels lighter than violet; warm hues generally feel heavier than cool hues at the same value level. Red is considered the heaviest color; yellow the lightest. Color weight is a structural property — it determines whether a composition feels stable, precarious, or intentionally tensioned.`

`**As a Design Diagnostic**`
`Color weight must be **mapped across the entire composition**, not evaluated element-by-element. Heavy colors at the base create stability; heavy colors at the top create tension or prestige. In palette construction, weight determines which colors can carry large areas and which are relegated to accent roles. The diagnostic test: does the visual weight distribution reinforce or contradict the intended hierarchy? Multiple elements with similar visual weights cause them to compete, leaving viewers without direction.`

`**What AI Gets Wrong**`
`AI-generated palettes neglect weight distribution entirely — producing palettes where multiple heavy colors compete or where there is no color capable of anchoring a composition. AI distributes color by area or category (background, primary, accent) without computing weight differentials. Generated color systems feel weightless or equally dense throughout.`

`---`

`### CHROMATIC GRAY`

`**Precise Technical Definition**`
`A chromatic gray is a gray that contains a measurable hue component — it has been mixed with or shifted toward a specific color — while remaining perceptually in the gray family. It is not a neutral gray (equal RGB values) and not a muted color that has been desaturated toward gray. A warm chromatic gray might read as gray with a perceptible yellow-orange lean; a cool chromatic gray as gray with a blue-violet undertone. Hue content may be low in chroma (often 5–15% saturation in HSL) but is present and intentional. Modern colorimetry acknowledges that true neutrality is rarely achievable or even desirable, as slight chromaticity can enhance visual comfort and perceived depth.`

`**As a Design Diagnostic**`
`Chromatic grays are one of the most powerful professional tools for palette cohesion. They allow large neutral areas to participate in the color temperature system without competing with accent colors. By choosing chromatic grays that share temperature relationships with dominant hues, designers create palettes that read as unified even when deploying many distinct colors. The diagnostic use: any palette requiring large neutral areas should specify the hue lean of those neutrals explicitly.`

`**What AI Gets Wrong**`
`AI systems default to neutral grays — achromatic values with no hue component — when populating the neutral zones of a palette. This produces palettes that feel disconnected, with accent colors floating on dead neutral ground. The result is a perceptible "cut" between the chromatic colors and the neutrals — the neutrals read as generic, disconnected placeholders rather than integrated members of the color system.`

`---`

`### DOMINANT / SUB-DOMINANT / ACCENT`

`**Precise Technical Definition**`
`This tripartite role structure describes the proportional and functional hierarchy of colors in a system:`

`- **Dominant** — the color occupying the greatest area; sets the overall character of the palette. Typically 60–70% of visual field. The dominant defines the communicative values of the combination.`
`- **Sub-dominant** — supports and modifies the dominant; occupies 20–30%; creates temperature or value contrast that gives the palette depth. Should either contrast or complement the dominant.`
`- **Accent** — deployed at 5–10%; provides maximum contrast; directs attention and creates punctuation. Can be sympathetic to the dominant/sub-dominant or visually strong and striking.`

`The canonical proportion model: 70% dominant, 20% secondary, 10% accent. This is a structural framework for color deployment, not a decorative convention.`

`**As a Design Diagnostic**`
`The diagnostic question for any palette: have roles been assigned and respected? Common failure modes: treating all palette colors as equivalent (no hierarchy); misassigning roles (highly saturated color as dominant = fatiguing; neutral as accent = invisible). Role inversion — deliberately using accent-register colors at dominant scale — is a valid design decision, but must be intentional and controlled.`

`**What AI Gets Wrong**`
`AI-generated palettes present colors as a flat list of equivalents without role assignment. There is no structural logic governing proportion or function. This forces the designer to impose hierarchy retroactively rather than having it embedded in the palette system. AI tends toward "balanced" palettes with multiple mid-saturation colors — producing systems where no color is positioned to function as a true accent or a true dominant.`

`---`

`### SATURATION STRATEGY`

`**Precise Technical Definition**`
`Saturation strategy is the deliberate management of chroma levels across a palette to produce a specific perceptual and emotional effect. Saturation is not managed color by color but as a system — the relationship between the highest-chroma and lowest-chroma elements determines the palette's overall energy. HSL saturation is a mathematical property, not a perceptual one: yellow at S:80% appears extremely vivid; blue-violet at S:80% at the same lightness appears only moderately vivid. This discrepancy exists because HSL was designed for computational simplicity, not perceptual accuracy.`

`**As a Design Diagnostic**`
`The diagnostic tool is the saturation arc: mapped across the palette, where does chroma peak and trough? The arc should have intentional shape — not flat (no variation), not random (no pattern), not maximized throughout. The arc's peak should coincide with the element requiring the most visual emphasis. Brand register implication: consumers associate lower saturation with higher luxury status — muted, desaturated palettes dominate premium branding. High saturation reads as energetic or affordable. Low saturation reads as refined. One high-saturation accent against desaturated base colors is the most reliable structure.`

`**What AI Gets Wrong**`
`AI-generated palettes default to either uniformly high saturation (everything vivid, nothing emphasized) or arbitrary variation with no strategic logic. The saturation arc is rarely considered as a structural element. AI also tends to avoid the most sophisticated range — mid-to-low saturation where the most complex and durable palettes live — because visually impressive outputs favor higher chroma. AI palettes built in HSL with consistent saturation values look unbalanced: yellow entries look more vivid than blue entries.`

`---`

`### TINTS, SHADES, AND TONES`

`**Precise Technical Definition**`
`Three distinct operations on a base hue, each with different design applications:`

`- **Tint** — hue + white → higher lightness, retained hue, preserved saturation relative to value. Tints retain the hue's character while reducing intensity. Fresh, airy. Application: backgrounds, secondary surfaces, hover states.`
`- **Shade** — hue + black → lower lightness, retained hue, potentially increased chromatic intensity per unit area. Serious, grounded, authoritative. Application: depth, shadows, dark variants. Note: Shades contain no gray — the color can still be intense but darker.`
`- **Tone** — hue + gray (both white and black) → reduced saturation, variable lightness, complex sophistication. Luxury brand websites, editorial layouts, and high-end packaging rarely use pure saturated colors; they use tones.`

`**Technical alert:** Darkening a color by adding black can cause hue shifts toward rose or green (Bezold-Brücke shift). Lightening by adding white can cause noticeable hue shifts (Abney effect). Shade and tint operations are not purely additive — they carry perceptual hue drift that must be corrected in high-fidelity work.`

`**What AI Gets Wrong**`
`AI conflates these operations, producing "lighter versions" of colors that are neither correct tints (too much saturation loss without proper lightness gain) nor tones (no gray component, just desaturation). The failure is particularly acute with tones — AI rarely produces genuine tones because the operation requires adding both white and black simultaneously, which doesn't map neatly to simple HSL adjustments. Generated palettes use tint-only lightness variations, missing the depth and complexity that shade and tone variations provide.`

`---`

`### COLOR GAMUT`

`**Precise Technical Definition**`
`Color gamut is the total range of colors representable within a given color space or reproducible by a given output device. Key gamuts in professional practice:`

`- **sRGB** — the standard for web, consumer displays, and most software. Baseline for web, app, and general digital design. Most images online are created and optimized for sRGB.`
`- **Adobe RGB** — wider working color space for print prepress and photography workflows. Captures more greens and cyans that CMYK printing can reproduce. About 35% larger than sRGB.`
`- **Display P3 / DCI-P3** — Apple's wide-gamut screen standard; approximately 25% larger than sRGB. Increasingly the standard for premium screen design.`
`- **CMYK** — not a fixed gamut but a device-dependent color space for print. Printers layer cyan, magenta, yellow, and black ink; ink on paper absorbs light rather than emitting it, so the printer's gamut is smaller than a monitor's. Neon greens, electric blues, and saturated oranges that look stunning on screen often can't be reproduced in standard CMYK.`

`**As a Design Diagnostic**`
`The decisive professional issue is **output-destination alignment**. Soft proof before you commit — preview how colors will map into a target CMYK profile. This is where you catch "my brand green is going to die" before it dies. A monitor displaying wide gamut will show sRGB content as oversaturated if the display isn't color-managed.`

`**What AI Gets Wrong**`
`AI generates colors in sRGB (or undefined color spaces) without reference to intended output medium or gamut constraints. Colors specified for print are not validated against CMYK reproducibility. AI has no mechanism for gamut warning, soft proofing, or rendering intent selection. For any deliverable crossing from screen to print — brand identity, packaging, publication, environmental graphics — every AI-generated color must be individually verified against the target CMYK profile. The failure is not hypothetical: if you use a color outside the CMYK gamut, the printer picks the closest available match. This often results in muddy or duller tones.`

`---`

`### THE SYSTEM-LEVEL COLOR PRINCIPLE`

`The pattern across all eight terms: **AI generates color properties. Professionals orchestrate color relationships.**`

`Temperature only exists in relation. Simultaneous contrast only exists in adjacency. Color weight only resolves in composition. Chromatic grays only function in context. Role structure only means something deployed at proportion. Saturation strategy only operates across the whole palette. Tint/shade/tone distinctions only matter when applied with intentional register. Gamut only fails at the output boundary.`

`Every definition above is an operative relationship, not a property. These eight terms are eight distinct dimensions of that relationship — each representing a category of decisions that AI color tools currently cannot make.`

`---`

`# SECTION 2B — CREATIVE DIRECTION VOCABULARY`

`*Eleven phrases used between senior creative directors and designers in briefing and review. Each entry defines what it precisely means, what specific operations it calls for, and what resolved looks like.*`

`---`

`### "MAKE IT BREATHE"`

`**What it precisely means:** The composition is spatially congested. Elements are competing for proximity and the eye has no place to rest. The design is treating every available unit of space as waste to be filled — a diagnostic of spatial suffocation at both micro and macro scale.`

`**Specific design operations:**`
`- Increase leading — the single most impactful breath control in type. Increase body text leading by a minimum of 20% above the typeface default`
`- Expand margins and gutters structurally, not cosmetically — cramped margins read as budget-constrained, not designed`
`- Isolate the focal element — surround the hero asset with deliberate emptiness; use the space around content to draw attention to it`
`- Audit all internal spacing — every padding value, every gap between headline and subhead, every inter-column gutter; inconsistent micro-spacing is what CDs feel even when they can't articulate it`
`- Reduce tracking on display type — overly loose tracking fights breathing by spreading letterforms into dead scatter; breath is about generous outer space, not loose internal spacing`

`**What resolved looks like:** The eye can move through the piece in a legible sequence. There are identifiable "pause points" — areas of low visual density that allow primary elements to land with weight. The composition feels confident in what it's leaving out.`

`---`

`### "IT'S FIGHTING ITSELF"`

`**What it precisely means:** Multiple competing design decisions are operating at the same frequency — same visual weight, similar scale, analogous contrast levels — creating tension that isn't productive but cancellative. Nothing dominates; nothing recedes. The eye is trapped in a loop rather than moved through a sequence.`

`**Specific conflicts identified:**`
`- Tonal competition: two elements with equal contrast values fighting for dominance`
`- Color war: multiple hues at full saturation simultaneously demanding priority; no single color acts as a statement`
`- Weight collision: multiple typefaces or weights at similar visual mass — a semi-bold headline competing with a bold subhead at nearly the same point size`
`- Compositional axis conflict: elements aligned to competing grids or axes, creating visual tension without intention`
`- Concept/visual dissonance: the verbal concept says one thing, the visual language says another`

`**What resolved looks like:** One element wins. Clear hierarchy of authority. Contrast is deliberate and directional — not accidental conflict but orchestrated relationship. Every element knows its rank.`

`---`

`### "TOO LITERAL"`

`**What it precisely means:** The design has illustrated the brief rather than interpreted it. It has communicated the surface content without a layer of authorial point-of-view. The design answers the brief at the surface level — it describes instead of communicating. There's no conceptual gap for the audience to close, which means no engagement.`

`**The fix:**`
`- Identify the most expected visual interpretation and deliberately discard it`
`- Ask: what is the emotional or conceptual truth beneath the subject? Design toward that`
`- Use metonymy (represent a concept through an associated part) rather than direct depiction`
`- In advertising: find the unexpected entry point — reductive, oblique, structural`
`- In editorial: let typography and white space *be* the concept rather than illustrating it with imagery`
`- The classic test: if you could remove the logo and still know the brand, you're in conceptual territory. If the design only makes sense with labeling, it's still literal.`

`**What resolved looks like:** There is a conceptual layer that requires a half-second of interpretation. The viewer understands, then slightly enjoys that understanding. The design has a point of view, not just a subject. A resolved concept makes a viewer say "I wish I'd thought of that."`

`---`

`### "MORE TENSION"`

`**What it precisely means:** The composition is too resolved, too harmonious, too comfortable. It needs productive dissonance — the kind that creates visual forward momentum and prevents the eye from settling too easily.`

`**Specific compositional moves:**`
`- Break the grid deliberately — allow one element to violate the margin or column boundary; intentional transgression creates dynamism`
`- Introduce scale extremes — a headline at 200pt next to body copy at 8pt; the dramatic differential creates a gravitational field`
`- Asymmetry over symmetry — move the focal element off-center and counterweight with a smaller opposing element`
`- Proximity pressure — place elements closer than comfortable in one zone; leave other zones emptier; the contrast between compressed and sparse generates energy`
`- Typographic collision — allow display characters to slightly overlap, or crop an image at an unexpected axis; not accident — controlled aggression`
`- In color: introduce a temperature or saturation dissonance — a cool palette punctured by a warm accent at high saturation`

`**What resolved looks like:** The eye is kept moving. There is designed unease that makes the piece feel alive rather than resolved. The tension serves the concept or brand voice.`

`---`

`### "DIAL IT BACK"`

`**What it precisely means:** The design has exceeded the appropriate register. It is over-performing its brief — too loud for the context, too decorative for the function, too expressive for the brand's voice. A volume instruction: reduce intensity, complexity, and the number of active decisions happening simultaneously.`

`**Restraint operations triggered:**`
`- Remove effects applied without structural necessity: drop shadows, gradients, glows, decorative rules`
`- Reduce the typeface weight — a Medium where you've used Bold; a Regular where you've used Medium`
`- Reduce color count — find the version that works in three before using five, then evaluate two`
`- Reduce the number of distinct graphic elements — identify which are structural and which are additive noise`
`- Scale down what's large, give more space to what remains — restraint is often a spatial decision as much as an element decision`
`- In motion: reduce animation parameters, ease more gently, allow beats of stillness`

`**What resolved looks like:** The design is working with less. What remains has more authority precisely because it's not competing with its former neighbors. The restraint reads as confidence, not poverty. John Maeda: "Simplicity is about subtracting the obvious and adding the meaningful."`

`---`

`### "IT FEELS CHEAP"`

`**What it specifically refers to:**`

`*Production signals:*`
`- Low-resolution assets used at scale — texture, photography, or illustration showing compression artifacts or pixel degradation`
`- Poor kerning on headline type — particularly common with all-caps or logotype-adjacent type where optical kerning hasn't been applied`
`- Default drop shadows (multiply, 75% opacity, 5px blur) — they read as unexamined choices`
`- Printing decisions that show in the comp: uncoated simulation not matching, colors unchecked against physical stock`

`*Design signals:*`
`- Gradients that are too steep or use default ramp presets (black-to-transparent applied without refinement)`
`- Typefaces selected for availability rather than fitness — system fonts, unkerned web-safe choices`
`- Color palettes with insufficient separation between values — muddy, built without a color system`
`- Symmetry applied defensively rather than compositionally — centered, equal-weighted layouts that feel undesigned`
`- Stock photography used without image direction — generic compositions, generic lighting, no styling point of view`
`- Typography that's overly compressed or structured will make a brand feel uncertain; people sense that something is off even when they can't articulate it`

`**What resolved looks like:** Every production choice reflects a decision. The typography is optically corrected. Image assets are print-ready or pixel-correctly sized for screen. Color has been built systematically. The piece can survive scrutiny at close range.`

`---`

`### "MORE EDITORIAL"`

`**What it precisely means:** The design is thinking commercially or functionally when it should be thinking like a publication — specifically, like a print magazine that uses typography, proportion, and space as compositional instruments rather than purely as containers for content.`

`**Specific typographic and layout moves:**`
`- Introduce typographic scale drama — editorials use type as image, often running headlines at 80–150pt with considered letterspacing`
`- Deploy pull quotes or callouts as spatial anchors, not just informational accessories — they should interrupt and articulate the grid`
`- Use a more sophisticated column structure — classic editorial uses 3–6 column grids with deliberate column-spanning and text-image counterpoint`
`- Apply considered leading to body text — editorial publishing takes leading seriously as both a readability and tonal decision`
`- Allow text and image to have a compositional relationship rather than a contained one — type overlapping, images bleeding, captions positioned for visual weight not just proximity`
`- Use typeface pairings with historical or tonal sophistication: a sharp serif for display, a neutral grotesque for body, deployed with restraint`

`**What resolved looks like:** The layout has considered every element as a compositional actor. The page (or screen) has been designed, not filled. There is evidence of a typographic system with its own internal logic.`

`---`

`### "IT'S OVERWORKED"`

`**What it identifies:** The design has accumulated decisions — likely across too many revision rounds — until it is visually exhausted. Too many active elements that were each individually reasonable but collectively produce noise. The designer has lost objectivity to earlier choices.`

`**How to fix it:**`
`- Go back to an earlier file state — the overworked version is almost never the right direction to edit from; find the last draft that felt alive and edit *that*`
`- Use subtraction as your primary tool: hide layers, remove elements, evaluate whether their absence is an improvement`
`- Return to an early comp and identify what was working before revision-creep set in`
`- Remove the element you worked hardest on and evaluate the result — overworked pieces often contain one precious element that's dragging the composition`
`- Simplify color to monochrome temporarily — this reveals structural problems that color was masking`
`- Ask: "What is the single thing this design needs to do?" Then audit whether anything is getting in the way of that one thing.`

`**What resolved looks like:** The design has economy. Nothing could be removed without loss, and nothing has been added that doesn't serve. There is still visible evidence of a decision-maker.`

`---`

`### "TRUST THE NEGATIVE SPACE"`

`**What this means as a specific directive:** The designer is compensating for emptiness — filling voids with elements, textures, or copy because the space feels unresolved or risky. The CD is instructing them to treat emptiness as a compositional element with equivalent value to the positive elements. This is both a spatial instruction and a confidence instruction.`

`**Specific implications:**`
`- Stop adding — the empty areas are not gaps to be filled; they are structure`
`- Active negative space has a silhouette; passive negative space doesn't — identify which you have`
`- Emptiness adjacent to a strong element amplifies that element; its removal signals a downshift in quality register`
`- In luxury brand work: negative space is the primary signal of premium positioning — its removal signals a downshift in brand register`
`- In print: resist the temptation to fill "dead" areas with fine print or secondary messaging — if content isn't primary, it belongs in a secondary position`
`- The designer's discomfort with emptiness is almost always incorrect — the audience does not share it`

`**What resolved looks like:** The empty areas are clearly intentional — their scale and proportion feel considered. The positive elements are given room to command their space. Ellen Lupton: "Design is as much an act of spacing as an act of marking."`

`---`

`### "THE HIERARCHY IS CONFUSED"`

`**What it identifies:** The viewer cannot readily determine what to read first, second, or third. The visual entry point is ambiguous — typically caused by competing elements at similar scale and weight, or by a layout that prioritizes aesthetic arrangement over communicative sequence.`

`**Specific diagnostic and remedial operations:**`
`- Squint test: the element your eye goes to at low visual acuity should be the primary message — if it isn't, the hierarchy is wrong`
`- Assign each element a hierarchy rank (1, 2, 3...) and audit whether the design's visual weight distribution matches those ranks`
`- Apply the blur test: Gaussian blur the layout at 20px. What do you see? That should be your tier-1 element, nothing else.`
`- Primary elements should be differentiated from secondary by: size (significant contrast, not incremental — minimum 3:1 ratio between adjacent tiers), weight (bold vs. regular, not bold vs. semibold), color contrast (higher vs. lower), and spatial position`
`- Check that your secondary element doesn't outperform your primary — a beautifully treated subhead can visually outrank a headline that wasn't given enough scale`
`- In digital: confirm that interactive hierarchy matches visual hierarchy — the most important CTA should be visually dominant, not just functionally present`

`**What resolved looks like:** A viewer unfamiliar with the piece can reliably identify and sequence the information in the intended order. The entry point is unambiguous. The design performs its communicative function before its aesthetic one.`

`---`

`### "KILL YOUR DARLINGS"`

`**What this means as an editing principle:** The design contains an element the designer is emotionally attached to that is not serving the work. It is present because the designer made it and likes it, not because the piece needs it. The element is often technically accomplished, which makes its removal feel like a loss. That attachment is precisely why it must go.`

`**How this operates in practice:**`
`- The "darling" is frequently the most elaborate element: a custom illustration, a complex typographic treatment, a refined motion sequence that runs too long`
`- It may be the element that got the most approvals in isolation but doesn't integrate into the whole`
`- Recognize the signal: if you find yourself constructing defenses for an element, you are in darling territory. Resolved design doesn't need to be defended — it needs to be understood.`
`- The test: if you removed it and the piece became cleaner, more direct, and more powerful — it's a darling`
`- The hardest application: killing the element that made the work feel distinctive in the first draft but is actually fighting the final direction`
`- Your favorite idea is usually the one blocking the better one. Delete bravely. Design gets great the moment your ego gets quiet.`

`**What resolved looks like:** The work is tighter, faster, more confident. The viewer receives a unified message with no extraneous moments demanding attention. The design earns its choices rather than accumulating them.`

`---`

`### CROSS-CUTTING PRINCIPLE`

`Nearly all eleven phrases share a single underlying diagnostic: **the ratio of active decisions to available space**. When too many things are happening at once — conceptually, spatially, typographically, tonally — the CD's vocabulary shifts to subtraction.`

`The professional designer's fluency in this vocabulary is not merely terminological. It is the ability to receive an ambiguous instruction and execute a precise spatial, typographic, or conceptual operation in response — translating editorial judgment into production action without requiring a CD to become their own art director.`

`---`

`# SECTION 2C — PLATFORM OPERATIVE VOCABULARY`

`*What each AI design platform actually responds to — the terms and instruction patterns that have measurable leverage on design quality output. For each platform: what has leverage, what is noise, and the vague vs. precise contrast.*`

`---`

`## MIDJOURNEY (V6/V7)`

`**Fundamental architecture:** Midjourney prefers descriptive noun-phrases over conversational sentences. Polite requests, conjunctions, and explanatory prose are noise. Front-load your highest-priority visual intent — the model still pays more attention to words at the beginning.`

`` **Prompt structure:** `[Subject] + [Environment/Setting] + [Lighting] + [Style/Medium] + [Camera/Render specs] + [--parameters]` ``

`**Lighting vocabulary with mechanical effect:**`
``- `volumetric lighting`, `god rays`, `Rembrandt lighting` (45° triangle shadow), `split lighting`, `practical lights` — each produces distinct light source behavior``
`` - `cinematic lighting` is processed as noise unless combined with specific modifiers: `cinematic lighting with hard shadows and motivated source` ``
``- `golden hour` vs. `magic hour` produce different saturation and warmth curves``
``- `studio lighting` alone is generic; `three-point studio lighting with soft fill` is directive``
``- `backlit silhouette` + `rim light` — one of the most reliable architectural/product rendering combos``
`- Camera body references encode entire aesthetic systems: Sony A7R IV = high-resolution clinical sharpness; Fujifilm XT4 = filmic color science; disposable camera = raw flash aesthetic`

`**Lens language with measurable output effect:**`
``- `85mm f/1.4 portrait` vs. `24mm wide angle` changes perspective distortion and depth of field in measurable ways``
``- `tilt-shift` produces authentic miniaturization blur``
``- `macro lens close-up` increases micro-texture rendering``
``- `anamorphic lens flare` adds horizontal streak artifacts authentically``

`**Style and weight parameters:**`
``- `--stylize` (0–1000): Below 250 is literal; 100–400 balances prompt fidelity with aesthetic polish; above 500 overrides content for style``
``- `--style raw` disables MJ's aesthetic opinions — critical for product and editorial work where you don't want beautification. More aggressive in v7.``
``- `--chaos` (0–100): Controls compositional variation across generations; use 20–40 for exploring, 0 for production``
``- `--weird` (0–3000): Introduces morphological variation — useful for surreal editorial, not seed-consistent``

``**`--no` exclusions:**``
``The `--no` parameter is more reliable than negative language in the body prompt. The model reduces probability rather than eliminates — elements may still appear at reduced frequency. Most effective uses: specific objects, text artifacts, specific colors (`--no red`). Reliable: `--no text, watermark, signature`. Inconsistent: `--no people` (works for interiors, not crowds). Mostly ignored: `--no blur`, `--no shadows`.``

``**Personalization (v7 critical workflow note):** V7 enables personalization by default. Two designers with different personalization profiles get meaningfully different outputs from identical prompts. Disable for team consistency: `--no --p`. Use `--sv 4` for compatibility with v6-era sref codes.``

`**Vague vs. Precise:**`
`` - Vague: `beautiful lighting` ``
`` - Precise: `cross-polarized lighting with soft diffusion, no specular highlights, flat product photography` ``

`---`

`## DALL-E / GPT-4o IMAGE`

`**Fundamental architecture:** Art direction language outperforms technical spec language for DALL-E. Training skews toward described scenes, moods, and cultural references rather than photographic parameters. The model executes instructions precisely rather than interpreting atmospherically — write a creative brief, not a mood board.`

`**What gets better results:**`
`` - `shot on Leica M6` is less effective than `understated documentary feel, slightly desaturated, candid framing` ``
`` - `Bauhaus editorial spread, asymmetric grid, bold sans-serif type elements as shapes` lands better than `grid-based layout, 12-column, left-aligned` ``
``- Color references to cultural objects work: `the palette of Wes Anderson's The Grand Budapest Hotel` produces consistent warm coral/dusty rose/mauve results``
``- Temporal/cultural references land well: `1970s Italian product catalog` is a genuine art direction shortcut``
`- Design movement references are deeply encoded: "Bauhaus-inspired with industrial restraint," "corporate minimalism with Swiss grid precision"`

`**GPT-4o specific capabilities:**`
`- Text rendering now near-perfect (print-ready quality) for dense infographics, menus, and UI mockups`
`` - Understands design critique vocabulary: `visual weight`, `hierarchy disruption`, `optical center`, `counter-form` ``
`- Conversational refinement preserves subject identity across turns`
`` - When using image input: `"push the typographic hierarchy"`, `"this reads as busy — identify the three loudest visual elements"` ``

`**For deliberately raw or imperfect output:** Over-specify explicitly. "Brutally rough pencil sketch, deliberately unfinished, messy hatching, not clean, not polished" — otherwise the model corrects toward commercial quality.`

`**Vague vs. Precise:**`
`` - Vague: `make it look professional` ``
`` - Precise: `executive communications aesthetic — restrained palette, generous whitespace, weight carried by single hero image, no decorative elements` ``

`---`

`## V0 (VERCEL)`

`**Fundamental architecture:** V0 responds to component-level and system-level vocabulary because it generates code. Design language must map to implementable decisions. Tailwind utility classes and shadcn/ui tokens are its native vocabulary.`

`**Token language that has leverage:**`
``- `use 8px base unit spacing system` — it will respect this in margin/padding generation``
``- `typographic scale: 12/14/16/20/24/32` specified explicitly produces consistent hierarchy``
``- `neutral-900 for body, accent-500 for interactive` in token syntax gets respected``
``- `card elevation: shadow-sm only` constrains its tendency to over-shadow``

`**What "minimal" and "editorial" mean operationally:**`
`` - `minimal` to v0 = reduced component count, not reduced visual complexity. You must specify: `minimal: single typeface, two weights, no borders, color used only for state` ``
`` - `editorial` is not in its trained vocabulary as a style directive. Use: `magazine-style layout, full-bleed imagery, type as primary visual element, generous leading` ``
`` - `brutalist` is partially understood: it reduces rounded corners and softening, but you must add `no card shadows, high contrast borders, monospace type` ``

`**Reference aesthetics V0 understands:**`
`- "Stripe's documentation design language" → clean, systematic, high information clarity`
`- "Linear's UI aesthetic" → dark, precise, developer-minimal`
`- "Notion's empty state philosophy" → generous space, content-first`

`**Anti-pattern vocabulary that works:**`
``- `no Dribbble aesthetics` — removes gratuitous gradients and glow effects``
``- `no enterprise UI conventions` — removes excessive chrome and utility density``
`` - `no card borders, use whitespace and typographic hierarchy for grouping` ``

`**Vague vs. Precise:**`
`` - Vague: `clean and modern dashboard` ``
`` - Precise: `data-dense layout, 12px body type, zebra-striped table rows, no chart borders, status badges only, no icon decorations` ``

`---`

`## STABLE DIFFUSION / FLUX`

``**Flux vs. SD syntax distinction:** SD/SDXL uses `(keyword:weight)` parenthetical weighting and requires structured negative prompts. Flux responds better to natural language description — parenthetical weighting adds complexity for no gain. Use plain descriptive prose with Flux.``

`**Negative prompt hierarchy (SD) — front-load most critical exclusions:**`
``- `worst quality, low quality, blurry` at the front suppresses low-quality training artifacts more reliably than burying them``
``- `deformed hands, extra fingers, mutation` — functionally necessary for any human subject work``
``- `watermark, signature, text, username` — place early; effective``
``- For product/UI work: `cluttered background, busy, photorealistic` in negative prompt pushes toward illustration styles``

`**LoRA instruction language:**`
``- `<lora:filename:weight>` — weight 0.6–0.8 is the operative range for style influence without distortion; 1.0+ frequently causes artifacts``
`- Multiple LoRAs: keep total combined weight under 1.4`
`- LoRA stacking for style direction is additive but needs CFG adjustment (lower CFG to 5–6 prevents overcooking)`

`**Flux-specific behavior:**`
`- Responds better to natural language than SD's keyword stacking`
`` - Does not require negative prompts in the same way — process absence instructions within the main prompt: `no text overlays, no borders` ``
``- Text rendering is functional; include `legible typography` or specific copy as a prompt element``

`---`

`## CLAUDE (AS DESIGN TOOL)`

`**Image upload framing that improves analysis:**`
`` - Specify your role and output need: `"I'm a senior art director reviewing this for brand consistency — identify hierarchy problems and any elements that contradict the brand's positioning"` ``
`` - Provide comparison context: `"Here are two directions for the same brief. Evaluate which better communicates urgency without aggression"` ``
`` - Ask for operative vocabulary, not impressions: `"Describe this composition in terms a layout director would use in a markup session"` ``

`**Brief structure that gets better output:**`
`` - Lead with constraint before aspiration: `"Budget is low, timeline is 2 weeks, client is risk-averse — now here's what we want to achieve"` ``
`` - Specify deliverable format: `"Output as a design brief with sections: Objective, Audience, Tone, Visual References, Restrictions"` ``

`**Context that unlocks better analysis:**`
`- Industry vertical (fintech vs. consumer lifestyle = completely different treatment recommendations)`
`- Platform context (social vs. OOH vs. packaging changes typographic and compositional guidance)`
`- Audience design literacy level`
`- Brand history and competitive landscape`

`---`

`## CANVA AI`

`**What actually works:**`
``- Brand kit colors must be loaded — `"use brand colors"` only works if the kit is active; otherwise it guesses``
``- `"Match this template style"` with a specific Canva template name produces more consistent output than described aesthetic``
``- Text prompts for image generation respond to `"flat illustration"`, `"photographic"`, `"watercolor"` — these map to trained style clusters``
`- Start with the design type (Instagram story, presentation, business card), be clear on end goal and audience, then specify design style`

`**What's noise:**`
``- Typographic direction beyond `"bold"` or `"minimal"` is largely ignored``
`- Spatial/grid direction has no leverage — Canva AI positions elements according to template logic`
`- Canva AI cannot ingest and enforce a full design system specification`

`**Vague vs. Precise:**`
`` - Vague: `a social post for our sale` ``
`` - Precise: `Instagram story 9:16, Black Friday sale post for handmade candles brand, warm neutral tones, serif headline font, earthy cream and terracotta palette, 'Up to 40% off' as primary message, cozy lifestyle feel, no generic stock photography` ``

`---`

`## FRAMER AI`

`**Layout and interaction direction that has leverage:**`
`` - Specify sections explicitly: `"sticky nav with logo left and two CTAs right, full-width hero with headline, three-column feature section with icon + title + 2-line description, pricing table with three tiers highlighted in center"` ``
``- `"Use auto-layout with 24px gap"` works as a spatial directive``
``- `"Navigation: horizontal with dropdown on hover"` — component-behavior descriptions produce correct component selection``
``- Responsive breakpoints: specify as `"mobile-first, single column below 768px"` — it respects this``
`- Workshop (component-level): describe both the *behavior* and the *exposed controls* explicitly`

`**Critical workflow constraint:** The Wireframer chat is cleared when you close the project and is not aware of any manual changes you make on the canvas. Finish all prompting before making manual edits.`

`**Low leverage:**`
`- Color and typographic direction is mostly overridden by the active theme`
``- `"editorial"` or `"brutalist"` are not functionally parsed; describe the specific layout behavior instead``

`---`

`## NANO BANANA (GEMINI IMAGE)`

`**Model identity:** Two distinct models. Nano Banana (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image) is built for high-speed editing and style transfers. Nano Banana Pro (Gemini 3 Pro) is for tasks requiring complex reasoning and high-fidelity output. Both are autoregressive rather than diffusion-based, generating 1,290 tokens per image.`

`**What it responds to distinctively:**`
`- **Multi-image composition is a native strength** — use multiple reference images to construct a new scene; specify which image controls which aspect (facial features, pose, style)`
``- **Constraint stacking** — `"single color, two type sizes, no icons"` — it performs better with explicit limitations than open-ended style goals; honors an unusual density of constraints``
`` - **Studio lighting language** — `"three-point softbox setup"`, `"Chiaroscuro lighting with harsh, high contrast"`, `"Golden hour backlighting creating long shadows"` ``
``- **Positive framing** — `"empty street"` instead of `"no cars"`; describe what you want rather than what you don't``
`- **Camera-specific terminology** — GoPro for immersive/distorted; Fujifilm for filmic color science; disposable camera for raw nostalgic flash aesthetic`

``**Iterative typography correction pattern:** If title text is distorted, run a second pass focused on typography only: `"Regenerate only the title text; keep all visuals unchanged; enforce clean sans-serif and straight baselines"` — more effective than re-running the full prompt.``

`**Text-first hack for Nano Banana Pro:** First converse with it to generate the text concepts, then ask for an image with that text incorporated.`

`**Vague vs. Precise:**`
`` - Vague: `a product shot of moisturizer` ``
`` - Precise: `High-end, glossy commercial beauty shot of a sleek, minimalist nude-colored face moisturizer jar resting on a warm studio background. Lighting: soft radiant three-point softbox. Camera: Hasselblad medium format. Mood: minimalist luxury. No text, no props, no reflections that obscure the label. Color palette: warm nude, matte cream, soft shadow.` ``

`---`

`## CROSS-PLATFORM OPERATIVE PRINCIPLES`

`| Principle | Operational Rule |`
`|---|---|`
`| **Specificity over adjectives** | "Generous whitespace" is noise; "48px vertical rhythm, 32px section padding" is instruction |`
`| **Cultural/temporal anchors** | One good reference unlocks more than ten descriptors — "1970s Italian product catalog" is a genuine art direction shortcut |`
`| **Constraint-first prompting** | Producing more consistent results than aspiration-first across all platforms |`
`| **Positive framing** | Most platforms handle "include X" better than "exclude Y" — encode intent positively |`
`| **Token/word position** | Both Midjourney and SD weight earlier tokens more heavily; front-load priority intent |`
`| **Aesthetic genre terms** | "Chiaroscuro," "Rembrandt," "Swiss International Style," "editorial grid" are active, not decorative |`
`| **Iteration design** | Changing one variable per iteration reveals causation; multi-variable changes produce unattributable variance |`
``| **Platform-specific syntax** | SD parenthetical weights `(term:1.4)`, Midjourney's `--stylize`/`--no`, v0's Tailwind tokens — syntax is not cross-platform |``
`| **Platform vocabulary maps to training data** | Learn what each model was trained on to predict what language it recognizes as meaningful signal |`

`---`

`*Document 2 complete. Version 1.0. Synthesized from 12 research documents (6 v1 training knowledge + 6 web search sources) read directly from project knowledge.*`

`*Cross-references: Document 1 (Failure Mode Encyclopedia) applies these terms as diagnostic instruments. Document 3 (Platform Prompt Architecture) extends the platform vocabulary in Section 2C into full prompt templates. Document 4 (Last 10% Checklists) applies the formal and typographic vocabulary as review protocols.*`

\# Sŏn— Project Instructions

\## Who You're Working With

\*\*Brandon John Acuña-Cardona\*\* — CEO and founder of Future Nostalgia Hospitality Group. Background: music education, retail management, specialty coffee (national competitive recognition, Director of L&D at Merit Coffee), front-of-house at Launderette and Emmer & Rye, consulting at Alinea, Coqodaq, and Hudson Clearwater, and current hospitality strategy consulting at Pullman Market (Emmer & Rye Hospitality Group / Kevin Fink). Family has deep Texas roots through Cardona Welding, a multi-generational business.

\*\*Co-founders:\*\*
\- \*\*Dominic Thomas\*\* — CFO. Private equity / financial modeling background.

\*\*Open role:\*\*
\- \*\*Executive Chef\*\* — search active. CIA-caliber background required. Live fire Korean fine dining concept. Culinary philosophy is brand-owned; chef executes within it. Mahk standard is an explicit hiring criterion.

\---

\## What We're Building

\*\*Future Nostalgia Hospitality Group\*\* is building the first walled garden in hospitality — an ecosystem of interconnected concepts sharing unified customer profiles, loyalty infrastructure, and operational data that compounds across properties. The flagship and proof-of-concept is \*\*Sŏn\*\* — Korean fine dining in Austin, Texas.

\*Sŏn\* (선) means goodness or virtue. The positioning is "Korean restraint. Texas Warmth. Polished and Playful.

\*\*FNHG ecosystem concepts (company context only — see scope note below):\*\*

| Concept | Format | Daypart | Public-facing |
|---|---|---|---|
| Good Energy | Coffee, matcha, Korean pastry | Early morning | Yes |
| Dosi | Korean QSR / dosirak boxes | Lunch | Yes |
| Sŏn | Korean fine dining | Dinner | Yes |
| Luxx | Late night | Late night | No — internal working name only |
| \[Loyalty layer\] | Membership / network layer | Ongoing | Name TBD |
| Cardona's | Family / neighborhood casual | All-day | Yes |
| Session | Alcohol-free social / listening bar | Evening | Yes |

\*\*Luxx note:\*\* Luxx is a project-internal working name for the late-night daypart at 207 E St. Elmo Rd. It will never appear in public-facing brand expression. There is no public identity to build for this concept. Operational and service posture are scoped internally.

\*\*Loyalty layer note:\*\* The membership and loyalty infrastructure connecting customers across dayparts is a separate, unnamed concept. It requires its own naming session. Do not refer to Luxx as the loyalty layer.

\---

\## ⚠️ Project Scope — Brand Guidelines Work

\*\*This project covers Sŏn only.\*\*

The ecosystem table above is provided for company context — so any chat understands who Future Nostalgia Hospitality Group is and where Sŏn sits within it. It is not a scope definition for this project.

The scope of this brand guidelines build is:

\*\*Sŏn\*\* — Korean fine dining at 207 E St. Elmo Rd, Austin, Texas.

Good Energy, Dosi, and Luxx are internal code names for Sŏn's daypart expressions at this location. They are not separate brands being developed here. They may become standalone concepts at future locations — that is not this project's concern and does not belong in any session prompt, open item, or downstream routing note.

Cardona's, Session, and any other FNHG concept beyond Sŏn are entirely out of scope. Do not reference them in session prompts, open items, extension tests, or future planning within this project. If a session specialist surfaces a future concept by name, that is an error — park it and do not log it.

The token system, visual identity, spatial design, service choreography, and all other deliverables produced in this project are for Sŏn. Extensibility to future concepts is a valid technical consideration (the naming convention should be extensible) but future concepts are never named, referenced, or planned for within this project.

\---

\## Financial Source of Truth — CRITICAL

\*\*All financial figures must come from Airtable. Never generate, estimate, or repeat financial numbers from memory, the pitch deck, or any other document.\*\*

The connected Airtable base is: variable

When any financial question arises — capital requirements, labor costs, pre-opening expenses, reserves, wages — query Airtable first. If the specific table or figure isn't accessible, say so explicitly rather than substituting a number from another source.

\---

\## Strategic Frameworks — How Brandon Thinks

These are load-bearing strategic tools, not decoration. Understand them well enough to deploy selectively.

\*\*Computing efficiency analogy:\*\* Restaurants are throttled computers. Expensive CPUs (talent) bottlenecked by poor information flow. Failure states: CPU (talent wasted on beneath-grade work), Memory (institutional knowledge lost on turnover), I/O (data bottlenecks / verbal handoffs), Bus (inter-department communication failures), Cooling (burnout / no bandwidth).

\*\*Informed late entry / last mover advantage:\*\* From Peter Thiel's \*Zero to One\* and a personal latte art competition story. In competitions, Brandon stalled for competitors to pour first, then poured the same design without their mistakes — won six months straight. Core strategy: enter known categories (coffee, QSR, fine dining) informed by everyone who already failed, on top of architecture nobody else built. Kellogg research: innovative late entrants outperform in 70% of categories. The distinction between noninnovative and innovative late entry is critical.

\*\*Christensen's Innovator's Dilemma applied:\*\* Incumbents can't adapt because their value networks, cost structures, and organizational identities are optimized for the old model. Their excellence at running great rooms is exactly what prevents them from building systems. "Success becomes a cage." Competitors can see what Future Nostalgia is building and still won't copy it — because they're artists, and adoption would require admitting the craft isn't the point.

\*\*Belonging economy over experience economy:\*\* Experiences are commoditized. Belonging creates switching costs and compounding customer value. The mechanism is Nir Eyal's Hooked Model: trigger → action → variable reward → investment. Traditional loyalty optimizes for rewards (discounts that decay). Future Nostalgia optimizes for investment: customers invest preferences, history, status, relationships — leaving means abandoning something they built.

\*\*"Pointed at the plate, not the relationship":\*\* Every operator in the independent segment focuses craft on tonight's experience. Nobody builds the system that makes the customer return Tuesday. No restaurant in the segment can tell you what a specific customer is worth, whether she's coming back, or why she stopped.

\*\*Ecosystem vs. standalone:\*\* Multi-concept independent groups achieve 35% lower profitability and 73% lower revenue per brand vs. focused operators. Architecture fails: hardware without software, portfolio management pretending to be a platform business.

\*\*Systems over heroics:\*\* When the talented GM leaves, quality leaves with them. The answer isn't finding stronger people — it's infrastructure so talent does only what talent can do.

\*\*Bandwidth → Joy → Retention → Results:\*\* The operating formula for employee experience.

\---

\## Phased Launch Strategy — Critical Financial Context

Sŏn does not open all dayparts simultaneously.

\*\*Phase 1 (Opening):\*\* Dinner + Early Morning (Good Energy coffee)
\*\*Phase 2 (Post-revenue):\*\* Dosi QSR lunch — funded by early cash flow, not the raise
\*\*Phase 3 (Property-dependent):\*\* Late night (Fri–Sun only) — funded by operations, all-or-nothing based on property terms

This affects which costs belong in the $2.75M raise vs. which are funded operationally. When reviewing financial content, always confirm which phase is being discussed. "Full multi-daypart" in projections is a scenario, not the opening reality.

\---

\## Voice and Tone

\*\*Investor and client posture:\*\* A brilliant operator explaining why this is inevitable — not a founder pitching for approval. Declarative over aspirational. Statements backed by operational logic, not marketing claims.

\*\*Avoid:\*\*
\- Generic hospitality copy ("curated," "elevated," "thoughtful")
\- Aspirational hedging ("we believe," "we hope to," "our goal is")
\- Invented sub-concepts not in source materials
\- Any financial figure not sourced from Airtable
\- "Guest" — the brand's word is "customer"

\*\*Investor communication:\*\* Confident, concise. Brandon holds leverage in conversations with distressed asset owners and investors who need deal flow. Offering a solution, not seeking approval.

\*\*Framework deployment by investor type:\*\* Operators and street-smart investors (Richie Romero) prefer the latte art story and pattern recognition over academic citations. Financial investors can handle the full stack (Thiel, Christensen, Eyal, Kellogg).

\---

\## Source of Truth Hierarchy

1\. \*\*Airtable\*\* — All financial data. Query before stating any number.
2\. \*\*Project knowledge files\*\* (whitepaper, pitch deck, brand guidelines reference) — Narrative and strategic source of truth.
3\. \*\*ClickUp Technology space\*\* — Tech stack, build docs. Current and authoritative.
4\. \*\*ClickUp Funding Launch space\*\* — Use selectively and on-demand. Contains useful pitch scripts but also outdated material. Do not treat as standing narrative authority.

\---

\## ClickUp Space Reference

\*\*Technology space (current — use freely):\*\*
\- Tech Reference Archive: list ID \`901323733488\`
\- Active Tech Build: list ID \`901325744861\`

\*\*Funding Launch space (selective use only):\*\*
\- Business Strategies Notebook (Whitepaper): doc ID \`2ky45bmy-11873\`
\- Pitch Scripts: doc ID \`2ky45bmy-13213\` (Nexwrk v1/v2/NYC, InKind scripts)
\- Romero Study Guide: doc ID \`2ky45bmy-14073\`

\*\*Brand Guidelines:\*\*
\- Document: \`2ky45bmy-15773\`
\- Session sequence task: \`86ahv9ub2\` (Founding Punch List, Founding Sŏn space)

\---

\## Key Relationships

\- \*\*Derek Gibbons / Nexwrk\*\* — Strategic partner conversation active. Two meetings completed. Not providing full funding; equity proposal being built by Dominic.
\- \*\*Richie Romero\*\* — Hospitality investor/operator. Prefers street smarts over academic citations. Study materials in ClickUp.
\- \*\*Johann Moonesinghe / InKind\*\* — Austin restaurant fintech. Evaluated as capital source.
\- \*\*Kevin Fink / Emmer & Rye / Pullman Market\*\* — Current consulting client. Key advice: "Write the divorce before the marriage."
\- \*\*Simon Kim / Gracious Hospitality\*\* — Cote, Coqodaq.

\---

\## Legal and Regulatory

\- \*\*Holding company structure\*\* required above operating entity — prevents all investors from needing TABC background checks.
\- \*\*TABC:\*\* 90–120 day lead time. 60-day sign posting requirement runs concurrently. Longest lead-time item. Must begin on lease execution day.
\- \*\*Reg D 506(b):\*\* No general solicitation. Investors must have pre-existing relationship.

\---

\## Company Non-Negotiables

\- No Exploitation Ever
\- No Toxicity Ever
\- No Disposable People

Employee-first philosophy influenced by Danny Meyer's Enlightened Hospitality.

\---

\## Current Consulting (Active, Separate from FN)

Brandon is consulting at \*\*Pullman Market\*\* (Emmer & Rye Hospitality Group / Kevin Fink). Active work: reputation management SOPs, guest review response systems, service manager restructuring across multiple properties.

\---

What has been built:
Future Nostalgia Hospitality Group is building Korean fine dining in Austin, Texas under the flagship concept Sŏn. The brand guidelines are being developed section by section through focused specialist sessions. Each session activates one specialist persona from project knowledge, closes a defined set of open decisions, and produces a clean output that comes back here.
