pages.content:
`# Domain 1 Knowledge Base: Exhaust Hood & Ventilation (Live Fire / Solid Fuel)`
`**Project:** Korean Fine Dining — 207 E St. Elmo Rd, Austin, TX`
`**Kitchen:** ~563 SF • **Cook line:** 12–16 LF live fire (wood/charcoal) • **Landlord-furnished:** 10-ton RTU + main trunk; tenant scope is all distribution`
`**Code Basis:** NFPA 96 (2021/2024) Chapter 14 • Austin Mechanical Code (Uniform Mechanical Code 2021/2024, Section 517) • IMC 2021 §§506, 507, 508 (cited where vendors typically reference it)`

`---`

`## TL;DR`
`- **A live-fire wood/charcoal cook line is "Extra-Heavy-Duty / Solid Fuel" cooking under NFPA 96 Chapter 14 and must have its own dedicated hood, dedicated all-welded grease duct, dedicated UL 705 Supplement SC roof exhaust fan, and dedicated fire suppression — it cannot share a hood or duct with gas/electric equipment, period. Any vendor proposing a combined system is non-compliant and must be rejected.**`
`- **A 12–16 LF wall-canopy solid-fuel hood will require roughly 6,000–9,000 CFM of exhaust and a near-equal volume of tempered makeup air. The landlord's 10-ton RTU (≈4,000 CFM total supply) cannot serve as kitchen makeup air for a solid-fuel hood — a separate, interlocked, tempered MUA unit is mandatory in Austin's hot-humid climate, and it is tenant scope.**`
`- **The most common ways vendors get this wrong on solid-fuel jobs are: combining hoods, using mechanical/galvanized duct instead of welded carbon or stainless steel grease duct, using an inline or non-SC-listed fan, undersizing makeup air, omitting spark arresters, and ignoring rooftop grease containment plus the 40-inch discharge requirement. Each is grounds to reject the bid.**`

`---`

`## Key Findings`

`### 1. NFPA 96 Chapter 14 — What Specifically Changes for Solid Fuel`

`NFPA 96 classifies your cook line as *Solid Fuel Cooking Equipment* (NFPA 96 §3.3.40 defines "Solid Cooking Fuel" as briquettes, mesquite, hardwood, or charcoal). The IMC calls this *Extra-Heavy-Duty Cooking* (IMC §507.2.2, definition in IMC Chapter 2). Compared to a standard Type I gas/electric hood, the following rules are added or tightened:`

`| Element | Standard Type I Hood (gas/electric) | Solid Fuel (NFPA 96 Ch. 14 / IMC 507.2.2) |`
`|---|---|---|`
`| Hood / duct sharing | May share with other Type I hoods on a common duct | **Must be wholly separate** (NFPA 96 §14.3.3; IMC §507.2.2) |`
`| Hood listing | UL 710 Type I | UL 710, **rated "Extra-Heavy-Duty / 700°F"** for solid fuel |`
`| Spark arresters | Not required | **Required prior to grease filters** (NFPA 96 §14.1.6 and §14.5.2) |`
`| Filter height above cooking surface | 18" (no flame) / 24" (flame) | **48" minimum above the charcoal/wood cooking surface** (NFPA 96 §14.5.3 — historically referenced as 15.5.3 in older editions) |`
`| Filter material | Steel/SS, UL 1046 listed | Steel/SS, UL 1046 listed, "approved for solid fuel" (NFPA 96 §14.5.1) |`
`| Fire suppression | UL 300 wet-chemical | **Listed system specifically for solid fuel hazard area**, sized to extinguish the entire firebox; gas/electric auxiliary fuels must auto-shut on activation (NFPA 96 §14.7.1, §14.7.3, §14.7.11) |`
`| Portable extinguisher | Class K, 30 ft travel | Firebox ≤5 ft³: Class K wet chemical or 2-A water within **20 ft** (§14.7.8). Firebox >5 ft³: **fixed-pipe water hose, ≥40 psi, ≥5 gpm, mist nozzle** (§14.7.7) |`
`| Cleaning frequency | Quarterly–annual | **Monthly** (NFPA 96 Table 14.8 / §11.4) — non-negotiable for solid fuel |`
`| Combustion chamber | N/A | Scrape to bare metal **weekly** (NFPA 96 §14.8) |`
`| Fuel storage | N/A | Non-combustible enclosure ≥3 ft past appliance, sprinklered if interior (§14.9) |`
`| Auto-fuel shutoff on suppression | Standard | Required on any auxiliary gas/electric ignition fuels too (§14.7.11) |`

`The *reason* for every one of these changes is the same: solid fuel produces (a) airborne sparks and embers that travel into the duct, and (b) **creosote** — a tar-like condensate with a flash point near 165°F — which coats every interior surface and is extraordinarily fire-prone. Solid-fuel hoods routinely see exhaust temperatures of 700°F+, which is also why the hood and duct must be rated to that temperature.`

`Austin note: Austin uses the Uniform Mechanical Code, not the IMC. The Austin Mechanical Code (UMC) places the solid-fuel rules in **Section 517**; UMC §517.3.1 is the separation rule, §517.6 covers makeup air interlocking, §517.7 covers fire suppression, and §517.0 explicitly extracts language from NFPA 96 Chapter 14. Vendors familiar with Texas IMC jurisdictions (most of Texas) will cite IMC §§506–508; Austin reviewers will cite UMC §§508, 510, 511, 517. Both refer to NFPA 96 Chapter 14 as the substantive standard.`

`---`

`### 2. Why a Dedicated Hood and Duct — and What Happens if a Vendor Proposes Combining`

`NFPA 96 §14.3.3 (and identically Austin UMC §517.3.1 / IMC §507.2.2) states that **all solid-fuel cooking equipment served by hood and duct systems shall be separate from all other exhaust systems.** There are only three narrow exceptions, and none apply to a Korean wood/charcoal cook line:`

`1. **§14.3.5 exception:** Cooking equipment that does *not* require automatic fire-extinguishing (i.e., a steamer, low-heat oven) may sit under a *common hood* with the solid-fuel equipment, provided that *the duct serving the solid fuel side is still its own separate duct*. This is rarely useful and does not let you combine with a gas range or charbroiler.`
`2. **§14.3.4 (smoker-box for flavoring only):** A listed gas appliance with an integral solid-fuel smoker box ≤2,000 in³, ≤4.5 lb/hr per 100,000 BTU, with the wood used only for flavor — not your operation.`
`3. **§14.1.2 (self-contained with isolated venting):** Sealed appliances with their own combustion air — not relevant here.`

`**Why the rule exists, in plain language:** Sparks and embers from charcoal/wood are pulled up into ductwork. If that duct also carries grease vapors from a fryer, griddle, or wok, the embers ignite the grease film and you get a duct fire. Beyond fires, mixing also produces draft instability (different appliance temperatures create eddies that defeat capture and containment), and the grease loading rate is so different that any cleaning schedule that works for one will fail for the other.`

`**If a vendor proposes a combined hood/duct over your wood cook line and a gas range:** Reject the bid. It will fail plan review at Austin DSD; if it somehow gets installed, the Travis County / Austin Fire Marshal will red-tag it; your insurance carrier will deny coverage on any subsequent fire; and you carry personal liability under NFPA 96 §4.1.5 (owner is responsible). A vendor who proposes this either (a) doesn't know solid-fuel code, or (b) is trying to save money on duct, fan, and suppression. Either way, walk.`

`What is allowed: **Multiple solid-fuel hoods can manifold into one solid-fuel duct system.** So if your concept has two wood-fire hoods (e.g., one over the charcoal grills, one over a wood-fire oven), they can share a common riser as long as that riser serves *only* solid-fuel hoods.`

`---`

`### 3. Hood Sizing for Solid Fuel — Dimensions and CFM`

`**Mounting Height & Filter Height (NFPA 96 §14.5.3 / §6.2.1):**`
`- **Filter bank minimum 48 inches above the charcoal/wood cooking surface** (vs. 18" for ovens, 24" for open-flame gas). For a typical 36" tall grill, this puts the filters at roughly 7'-0" AFF and the bottom edge of the hood face around 6'-6" AFF.`
`- Hood height (top to bottom of capture area): typically **30 inches minimum** for an extra-heavy-duty wall canopy.`

`**Overhang (IMC §507.3, NFPA 96 §6.2.1, UL 710):**`
`- Wall canopy **front overhang: 12 inches minimum**, 18" preferred when there are doors that open (combi ovens, oven cars). Korean cooking lines with rotating skewers / shelves benefit from 18".`
`- **Side overhang: 6 inches minimum**, 12 inches preferred when a charbroiler is at the end of the line (heavy-duty appliances at hood ends spill more effluent).`
`- **Island (single-island) hoods need overhang on all four sides** and require ~25–40% more CFM than wall canopies because there's no wall to assist capture.`

`**CFM per Linear Foot — the numbers you'll be quoted:**`

`| Hood Type | Standard (Medium-Heavy Duty) | **Solid Fuel / Extra-Heavy-Duty** |`
`|---|---|---|`
`| Wall canopy | 200–300 CFM/ft | **350–550 CFM/ft** (CaptiveAire/ASHRAE: 350–400 typical; **450–500 CFM/ft when charbroiler/solid-fuel appliance >4 ft long**) |`
`| Single-island | 250–400 CFM/ft | **500–700 CFM/ft** |`
`| Double-island (back-to-back) | 150–300 CFM/ft | **400–550 CFM/ft per side** |`

`The IMC §507.5 Table cites a wall-canopy minimum of 550 CFM/ft for unlisted Extra-Heavy-Duty. UL 710-listed hoods can often run lower if their listing supports it (some listings allow 350–400 CFM/ft for solid fuel), so always ask for the manufacturer's listed minimum and the cut sheet — a listed hood saves you exhaust CFM, makeup air CFM, and lifetime energy.`

`**Quick calculation for your 12–16 LF cook line (wall canopy, listed hood):**`

`- 12 LF × 400 CFM/ft = **4,800 CFM** (low end, listed hood, no end-located charbroiler)`
`- 12 LF × 500 CFM/ft = **6,000 CFM** (typical for solid fuel)`
`- 16 LF × 500 CFM/ft = **8,000 CFM** (typical)`
`- 16 LF × 550 CFM/ft = **8,800 CFM** (unlisted / IMC prescriptive)`

`**Plan for 6,000–9,000 CFM of exhaust** depending on final cook-line length and hood listing. This number drives everything downstream — fan size, makeup air unit, gas service, electrical service, roof curb, and the landlord's structural review of the roof. Lock the cook-line LF before sending the hood out for bid; every extra foot adds ~500 CFM and ~$3,000–$5,000 in equipment.`

`---`

`### 4. Spark Arrester Filters`

`**What they are:** A spark arrester is a stainless-steel diamond-mesh screen mounted in front of (upstream of) the conventional baffle grease filter. Required by NFPA 96 §14.1.6 and §14.5.2: *"Solid fuel cooking operations shall have spark arresters to minimize the passage of airborne sparks and embers into plenums and ducts."*`

`**How they differ from a standard baffle filter:**`
`- A **baffle filter** is a centrifugal grease separator — it removes liquid grease droplets but does nothing to stop hot embers.`
`- A **spark arrester** is a diamond-pattern flame-blocking screen that physically intercepts embers and reduces ember passage by orders of magnitude.`
`- A **spark-arrester baffle filter** is a combined unit (e.g., Flame Gard heavy-duty spark arrester / PTFE-coated baffle): the diamond mesh is bonded onto the front face of a UL 1046 baffle. This is what most reputable solid-fuel hood packages include.`

`**What the listing must say:**`
`- **UL 1046 listing** for the underlying grease filter (NFPA 96 §6.1.2). Mesh-only filters are not acceptable as a primary grease filter (NFPA 96 §6.1.3, A.3.3.22.2).`
`- The filter must be **approved/listed for solid-fuel cooking** specifically (NFPA 96 §14.5.1 — "constructed of steel or stainless steel or be approved for solid fuel cooking").`
`- Must be installed at not less than **45° from horizontal** (NFPA 96 §6.2.3.5) and be removable for cleaning.`

`**What to verify on a vendor quote:**`
`- Cut sheet shows "spark arrester" or "spark-arrester baffle" — not "high-velocity baffle" alone.`
`- UL 1046 listing number printed on the filter face.`
`- Quantity is sized for full coverage at the design CFM (filter velocity typically 200–400 fpm).`
`- A spare set is included or specified — they need to be cleaned monthly and rotated.`

`If the vendor quotes "standard galvanized baffle filters" on a solid-fuel hood, that is a code violation and a red flag for the rest of the bid.`

`---`

`### 5. Makeup Air (MUA) — Why Austin Punishes Undersizing`

`**What MUA is:** Outdoor air mechanically introduced into the kitchen to replace the air the hood is exhausting. NFPA 96 §8.2 (and UMC §517.6 / IMC §508) requires that the building not exceed 0.02 in. w.c. of negative pressure during operation.`

`**Sizing relative to exhaust:**`
`- **Industry rule of thumb: MUA = 80–90% of exhaust CFM**, with the remaining 10–20% coming from transfer air across the dining room (the kitchen is intentionally kept slightly negative so smells stay in the kitchen).`
`- For a solid-fuel hood specifically, NFPA 96 §14.6.3 *requires* the MUA system to be **interlocked with the exhaust fan and powered as needed to prevent negative pressure when the solid-fuel appliance is in operation.** This is more aggressive than standard hoods because backdraft of a wood/charcoal firebox is dangerous (CO infiltration, flare-up).`
`- IECC C403.7.5 limits MUA delivered *into the hood cavity* (short-circuit MUA) to **10% of exhaust** — meaning the other 90% must come into the kitchen room itself. Plan reviewers in Austin enforce this.`

`**For a 6,000–9,000 CFM hood, you will need ~5,400–8,100 CFM of dedicated MUA.**`

`**The landlord's 10-ton RTU is NOT your makeup air solution.**`
`- A 10-ton commercial RTU supplies roughly 400 CFM/ton = **~4,000 CFM total** for the *entire tenant space* (dining + kitchen + restrooms + back-of-house).`
`- That 4,000 CFM is sized for cooling load, not for replacing 6,000–9,000 CFM of kitchen exhaust.`
`- The kitchen will pull the dining room into severe negative pressure, doors will be hard to open, the front door will whistle, exhaust fans elsewhere (bathrooms, dryer if any) will reverse, gas pilots will blow out, the wood-fire grill itself will misbehave (back-puffing), and most importantly **the hood will lose 20–30% of its rated capture** because the fan can't move air against the negative pressure.`

`**What's right for an Austin kitchen of this profile:**`
`- A **dedicated tempered MUA unit (DOAS or direct gas-fired MUA)** sized at ~80–90% of exhaust CFM, mounted on the roof, **interlocked with the kitchen exhaust fan**, with a motorized damper that opens automatically.`
`- **Austin climate consideration:** Austin's design summer condition is roughly 99°F dry-bulb and dew points routinely above 72°F — this is a hot-humid climate. Untempered MUA dumps 95–100°F humid outdoor air into your kitchen; cooks won't tolerate it, food safety suffers, and your dining room HVAC fights the hot, wet air bleeding under the kitchen door. In Austin you should specify either:`
`- **DX-cooled tempered MUA (preferred for Austin):** Cools and partially dehumidifies incoming air. Higher capital cost but the right answer in Class 5 dew-point climate.`
`- **Direct gas-fired MUA with evaporative cooler (acceptable):** Lower capital cost, heats in winter, evaporative section can drop summer supply air ~15–20°F below outdoor dry-bulb — but adds humidity, which is already abundant in Austin.`
`- **DOAS (dedicated outdoor air system):** Highest comfort, full humidity control year-round, best for fine dining where dining-room comfort matters.`
`- **Avoid:** "Untempered" or "passive louver" MUA (a hole in the wall with a damper). This is technically code-compliant for the 400-CFM threshold, but on a 6,000+ CFM solid-fuel hood it produces an unworkable kitchen 8 months a year in Austin.`

`**Tell-tale signs of an undersized MUA system, operationally:**`
`- Front door is hard to pull open when the hood runs.`
`- Smoke "rolls out" from under the hood capture area onto the cook line — this is loss of capture and containment, the central failure mode.`
`- Pilot lights on gas appliances blow out.`
`- The grill chimney back-drafts smoke into the kitchen.`
`- Dining room doors slam.`
`- HVAC bills are 30%+ higher than expected because conditioned dining-room air is being sucked out the kitchen exhaust.`

`---`

`### 6. Exhaust Fan Requirements for Solid Fuel`

`**Listing — what to demand on the spec sheet:**`
`- **UL 705 Supplement SC** (formerly UL 762, merged into UL 705 in June 2021). This is the listing for "Power Ventilator for Restaurant Exhaust Appliances." Vendors may still write "UL 762" — that's fine; it means the same thing. NFPA 96 §8.1.1 requires this listing on any fan in a commercial kitchen exhaust path.`
`- The fan must be **upblast type** with the **motor located outside the airstream** (NFPA 96 §8.1.1.1) — the airstream over a solid-fuel hood routinely exceeds 400°F intermittently, plus carries embers. Motors in the airstream fail prematurely and become an ignition source.`
`- The fan must be **hinged with a hold-open retainer and weatherproof flexible cable** (NFPA 96 §8.1.1.1) for cleaning access — you will be cleaning monthly.`
`- Fan must include a **1-gallon (max) grease drain receptacle** (NFPA 96 §8.1.1.3), readily visible.`

`**Why inline (cabinet/utility-set) fans are problematic for solid fuel:**`
`- An "inline" fan sits inside the building, in the duct line between the hood and the roof. For solid fuel, this means: (a) burning embers, (b) creosote-coated duct, and (c) potential 700°F+ exhaust gases pass through a fan inside the building envelope. If the fan ever ignites or fails mechanically, the failure point is *inside* your kitchen ceiling. NFPA 96 doesn't outright prohibit inline fans, but every solid-fuel best-practice document (CaptiveAire TB20-1020, Halton, Accurex) explicitly says **"inline fans should be avoided"** for solid fuel; some manufacturers will only approve them on solid fuel with engineering sign-off.`
`- Inline fans also typically use aluminum or composite fan wheels. **Aluminum melts at ~1,220°F**, and a solid-fuel duct fire routinely hits 1,800–2,000°F. The wheel becomes a projectile.`

`**Why a steel-wheel upblast fan is the right answer:**`
`- **Steel fan wheel** withstands the heat and ember exposure typical of solid-fuel exhaust without warping, melting, or losing balance during a fire event (CaptiveAire TB20-1020 specifically calls out steel wheels for solid fuel).`
`- **Belt-drive** preferred over direct-drive for this duty: motor sits in a separate ventilated compartment outside the airstream, and bearings/belts are field-serviceable.`
`- **Located on the roof, upblast configuration**, discharging up and away from the roof surface.`
`- **Variable Frequency Drive (VFD)** is optional but useful — lets you tune the fan to actual measured CFM at startup (factory CFM ratings rarely match field conditions due to duct pressure losses).`

`**What to specify, in vendor-friendly language:**`
`> "Roof-mounted upblast centrifugal exhaust fan, UL 705 Supplement SC listed for restaurant exhaust appliances and **rated for solid fuel / 700°F continuous duty**, steel fan wheel, belt drive, motor isolated from airstream, hinged base with hold-open retainer, factory-installed grease drain to a 1-gallon receptacle, and provided with a hinged grease containment/diverter system listed under UL 710A."`

`---`

`### 7. Duct Construction for Solid Fuel — Why "Mechanical Duct" Fails Code`

`**Material and gauge (NFPA 96 §7.5.1, IMC §506.3.1, UMC §510.5):**`
`- **Carbon steel ≥ 0.054"–0.060" (16 gauge)**, OR **stainless steel ≥ 0.043"–0.048" (18 gauge)**.`
`- **Aluminum, galvanized steel, and FRP are PROHIBITED.** Galvanized duct (the silver shiny stuff used for HVAC) is what an unscrupulous mechanical contractor will try to install because it's cheaper and easier — galvanized coating off-gasses zinc fumes at high temperature and the duct itself isn't rated for grease/heat.`
`- **Factory-built grease duct** listed under UL 1978 is acceptable (round, double-wall, often stainless) and is sometimes preferred for solid fuel because it's tested, has integrated cleanouts, and can be listed for reduced clearance to combustibles (often down to 0").`

`**Welding (NFPA 96 §7.5.2.1):**`
`- **All seams, joints, penetrations, and the duct-to-hood-collar connection shall have a liquid-tight continuous external weld.** No riveting, no S-cleats, no mastic, no pop screws penetrating the duct wall. Internal access fasteners must NOT penetrate the duct.`
`- **Butt joints on field-fabricated duct are prohibited** (NFPA 96 §7.5.5.2 and UMC §510.5.2). Joints must be lapped and welded.`
`- The IMC requires a **light test** — a 100-watt light is passed through the entire duct and any leak is visible to an inspector outside. Listed UL 1978 duct is exempt.`

`**Slope (NFPA 96 §7.1.4 / IMC §506.3.7):**`
`- **Horizontal duct: 2% slope (¼" per foot) toward the hood or to a grease drain.** If horizontal run exceeds 75 ft, **slope increases to 8% (1" per foot)** — an issue you don't want, which is why you keep horizontal runs short.`
`- No dips, traps, or low points; if a low point is unavoidable, it must have a welded grease drain to a non-combustible, closed, rainproof container.`

`**Clearance to combustibles (NFPA 96 §4.2 / IMC §506.3.6):**`
`- **18 inches minimum to combustible construction** (wood framing, paper-faced gypsum on wood studs, insulation).`
`- **3 inches minimum to limited-combustible construction.**`
`- **0 inches to non-combustible construction** (metal studs with non-paper gypsum, masonry, concrete).`
`- Clearance can be reduced with a **listed field-applied wrap (ASTM E2336)** or a **listed factory-built grease duct enclosure (UL 2221)** — but these are engineered systems with strict installation conditions, not improvisations.`

`**Access panels (NFPA 96 §7.4):**`
`- **20" × 20" personnel access** on horizontal ducts where size permits (§7.4.1.1).`
`- Where 20" × 20" is not feasible: **smaller cleanout panels at intervals not exceeding 12 ft and at every change of direction** (§7.4.1.2, §7.4.2.1).`
`- Panels: **same gauge and material as the duct**, gasketed/sealed to **1500°F**, fasteners must NOT penetrate duct wall, listed UL grease duct access doors (e.g., Ductmate ULtimate) are the standard.`
`- Panels must be physically reachable — if a panel is buried behind drywall or a fire wrap with no access, the duct fails inspection.`

`**Enclosure / shaft (NFPA 96 §7.7):**`
`- For your one-story building this likely doesn't apply directly, but: any duct passing through a fire-rated assembly above the kitchen ceiling needs either (a) a 1-hour rated shaft enclosure, or (b) a UL 2221 listed factory-built grease duct, or (c) a listed field-wrap (ASTM E2336, e.g., 3M Fire Barrier Duct Wrap 615+).`

`**How to spot duct shortcuts in a bid:**`

`| Red Flag in Bid | Why It's a Problem |`
`|---|---|`
`| "Galvanized spiral duct" or any galvanized | Not allowed for grease duct (NFPA 96 §7.5.1) |`
`| "S-cleat" or "drive-cleat" joints | Not liquid-tight; not welded (§7.5.2.1) |`
`| "Mechanical seal duct" / "TDC flange" | Same — not a continuous weld |`
`| Unstated gauge | Default assumption is they're using the wrong one |`
`| "Aluminum ductwork" | Prohibited |`
`| No mention of clearance to combustibles | They haven't planned for the 18" or for wrap |`
`| No access panel locations shown | Will not pass inspection |`
`| Duct routed flat with no slope | Violates §7.1.4 |`
`| "Field-fabricated, no UL listing" with butt joints | Prohibited (§7.5.5.2) |`
`| Duct wrap brand not specified | The wrap must be a specific listed product (ASTM E2336) |`

`The right answer for your application: **all-welded 16-gauge black/carbon steel rectangular duct, externally welded continuous seams, 2% slope back to hood, gasketed UL-listed access panels at 12 ft and at every elbow,** with either 18" clearance maintained or a **listed wrap (3M Fire Barrier 615+ or equal, ASTM E2336)** if clearance can't be maintained. A round factory-built UL 1978 stainless system is a defensible upgrade and is often easier to clean.`

`---`

`### 8. Rooftop Termination & Grease Containment`

`**Rooftop termination requirements (NFPA 96 §7.8.2 / IMC §506.3.13):**`

`- **Discharge ≥ 40 inches above the roof surface** (NFPA 96 §7.8.2.1, IMC §506.3.13.1). This is the most commonly missed requirement. The fan's discharge opening — not the curb, not the fan housing top — must be 40" above the roof. On an upblast fan that means the curb height + fan height + any extension must total ≥40".`
`- **Horizontal clearances:**`
`- **≥10 ft** from adjacent buildings, property lines, and outdoor air intakes.`
`- **≥10 ft horizontal + 3 ft vertical above** any operable door, window, or fresh air intake within 10 ft (NFPA 96 §7.8.3 / Figure 7.8.3).`
`- **≥5 ft** from any combustible construction (fan housing).`
`- **Wall termination is NOT permitted for solid fuel exhaust systems** (Accurex/industry guidance under NFPA 96; the fan must terminate through the roof). For your project this aligns with the landlord's TPO/corrugated metal roof anyway.`

`**Grease containment (NFPA 96 §7.8.2.1 (4)–(6)):**`

`The fan and rooftop termination must include the means to **drain grease out of any traps or low points** into a **non-combustible, closed, rainproof, structurally sound container that will not sustain combustion.** In practice this means:`

`- A **rooftop grease containment device** (e.g., Grease Lock, Facilitec Rooftop Grease Containment, Grease Guard, Mr. Greasebag) installed under the fan's drain spout, listed under **UL 710A** (Exhaust Hoods for Commercial Cooking Equipment with Integral Fire Suppression System / grease collection accessories).`
`- The fan itself has a 1-gallon (max) drain receptacle (NFPA 96 §8.1.1.3).`
`- A **rooftop grease containment "filter pillow" or absorbent pad** in a steel pan around the fan base to catch fan-cap dripping. Required by many AHJs and explicitly addressed in NFPA 96 2025 updates.`
`- Some jurisdictions also require **a non-combustible grease curb / pan extending several feet around the fan curb** to protect the membrane.`

`**Why this matters specifically for your TPO roof:**`

`- **TPO membrane is a thermoplastic.** It is not rated for direct grease contact — grease degrades the plasticizers, causes shrinkage, and voids the membrane manufacturer's warranty. Any grease that escapes the containment device onto the TPO will void the warranty and can cause leaks within months.`
`- **Solid-fuel exhaust produces 5–10× more grease/creosote than gas/electric** — your rooftop grease loading will be heavy.`
`- The landlord's preferred roofer is the only party who should be cutting and flashing the curb. **Plan the sequence:** hood vendor specs the curb size and location, structural engineer reviews roof framing for the curb load (a steel-wheel upblast fan + curb + grease containment can run 400–700 lbs concentrated), landlord's roofer cuts and flashes, hood vendor sets the fan, electrical contractor wires it. Pay the roof penetration vendor at tenant's cost — but verify the flashing detail includes a grease-resistant cant strip / target patch and that the roofer warrants the penetration to match the TPO warranty.`

`**Coordination responsibility — who owns it:**`

`- **Tenant (you)** owns the design intent, fan/curb selection, location coordination, and ultimate fitness for purpose.`
`- **Hood vendor / kitchen ventilation contractor** owns the curb specification, the structural load the curb will impose, and the fan installation onto the curb.`
`- **Landlord's roofer** owns the roof opening, flashing, membrane termination, and warranty.`
`- **Tenant's MEP engineer** (or hood vendor's licensed engineer) owns the stamped drawings showing the penetration location, structural review confirmation, and rooftop equipment loads on the building's structural drawings.`

`Get a **written sequence of operations** from your GC tying these four parties together in advance. Roof penetrations done out of sequence or without the right cant/target patch are the single most common source of post-occupancy leaks in restaurant fit-outs.`

`---`

`### 9. The Right Questions to Ask a Hood Vendor (Before Signing)`

`Use this list verbatim. A competent solid-fuel hood vendor will answer all of them quickly and in writing. A vendor who hedges, deflects, or asks "why are you asking?" is not the right vendor.`

`1. **"Is the hood UL 710 listed and rated Extra-Heavy-Duty / 700°F for solid fuel cooking? Please provide the listing number and cut sheet."**`
`2. **"What is your design exhaust CFM, in CFM per linear foot, and what is that number based on — the manufacturer's listed minimum, ASHRAE 154, or the IMC/UMC prescriptive table?"** (You want a listed-hood number, not a 550 CFM/ft prescriptive default unless the listing requires it.)`
`3. **"Show me on the drawings: hood length, front overhang, side overhangs, mounting height above the cooking surface, and filter height above the cooking surface. Confirm filters are ≥48" above the charcoal/wood cooking surface per NFPA 96 §14.5.3."**`
`4. **"What spark-arrester filters are you specifying? UL 1046 listing number? Provide the cut sheet."**`
`5. **"Confirm in writing that this hood and its duct system are entirely separate from any other hood or exhaust path in the building, per NFPA 96 §14.3.3."**`
`6. **"What is the duct material, gauge, joint method, and slope? Are all seams continuously externally welded liquid-tight per NFPA 96 §7.5.2.1?"**`
`7. **"How are you maintaining clearance to combustibles — 18", listed wrap (which one, ASTM E2336?), or listed factory-built duct (UL 1978 / UL 2221)?"**`
`8. **"Where are the grease duct access panels located? Please show all panel locations on the duct riser drawing and confirm they are UL-listed gasketed panels rated to 1500°F."**`
`9. **"What is the exhaust fan's UL listing — UL 705 Supplement SC? Steel fan wheel? Belt drive? Motor outside the airstream? Provide cut sheet."**`
`10. **"What is the makeup air strategy? CFM, type (DOAS / direct gas-fired / DX-cooled), interlock with the exhaust fan, and how are you handling Austin summer humidity?"** Do NOT accept "the landlord's RTU will handle it" — it won't.`
`11. **"What rooftop grease containment system are you specifying, what is its UL 710A listing, and have you coordinated curb size, structural load, and the 40" discharge height above the TPO roof?"**`
`12. **"What fire suppression system are you specifying — manufacturer, model, UL 300 listed for solid fuel hazard area? How many flow points / nozzles per appliance, and is solid fuel covered explicitly in the listing?"**`
`13. **"Is the system designed for monthly cleaning per NFPA 96 §11.4 / Table 14.8 — i.e., are access panels, fan hinge, and fuel-storage rooms designed for monthly service?"**`
`14. **"Will you provide stamped engineering drawings for Austin DSD plan review under the 2024 UMC, and have you done a solid-fuel project in Austin before? Please name two."**`
`15. **"What is your scope vs. excluded scope? Specifically — who provides the MUA unit, the fire suppression system, the gas piping to the suppression solenoid, the roof curb, the roof penetration, the electrical disconnect, the hood lighting circuit, and the fire alarm interface?"**`

`---`

`### 10. Red Flags — Things to Reject Outright`

`| # | Vendor Says / Proposes | Why It's Wrong |`
`|---|---|---|`
`| 1 | "We can put your wood grill and your gas range under one hood to save you money." | Direct violation of NFPA 96 §14.3.3 / IMC §507.2.2 / UMC §517.3.1. Will fail plan review, will void insurance. |`
`| 2 | "Standard galvanized HVAC ductwork" or "spiral duct" | Galvanized is prohibited for grease duct (NFPA 96 §7.5.1). Spiral, if not UL 1978 listed, is not acceptable. |`
`| 3 | "S-cleat / TDC / mastic / mechanical seal joints" | Not a liquid-tight continuous external weld (§7.5.2.1). |`
`| 4 | "We'll use baffle filters — no need for spark arresters." | Direct violation of §14.1.6 / §14.5.2. |`
`| 5 | "Inline fan in the ceiling" or "cabinet fan" for solid fuel | Allowed only with engineering approval and not best practice for solid fuel; ember/creosote risk inside the building envelope. |`
`| 6 | "Aluminum fan wheel" | Aluminum melts well below solid-fuel duct fire temperature; steel wheel is required for solid-fuel duty. |`
`| 7 | "UL 762" listing only, with no UL 705 SC reference | UL 762 was merged into UL 705 Supplement SC in June 2021 — vendor's product literature should reflect this. Old-stock fans are common; verify a current SC listing. |`
`| 8 | "The landlord's 10-ton RTU will handle makeup air." | Categorically false at 6,000–9,000 CFM exhaust. The RTU supplies ~4,000 CFM total for the entire space and is not interlocked with the hood. |`
`| 9 | "Untempered louver MUA" or "we'll just leave the back door open." | Operationally unworkable in Austin summer; also fails NFPA 96 §14.6.3 interlock requirement and IECC C403.7.5. |`
`| 10 | "Fan discharge can sit on the curb — no extension needed." | NFPA 96 §7.8.2.1 requires discharge ≥40" above roof surface. Most curbs aren't tall enough alone. |`
`| 11 | "We don't need a rooftop grease containment box — the fan has a drain." | NFPA 96 §7.8.2.1(4)–(6) requires a non-combustible, rainproof grease collection device beyond the fan's 1-gallon receptacle. TPO roof + solid fuel grease without containment = warranty void in months. |`
`| 12 | "UL 300 wet chemical system, standard package." | UL 300 covers Type I cooking; the system must be specifically **listed for solid-fuel cooking equipment** per NFPA 96 §14.7.1. Solid-fuel listings often require additional water-spray nozzles or a different agent strategy. |`
`| 13 | "Filters can sit 24" above the charcoal." | Wrong height — solid fuel requires **48" minimum** filter height above cooking surface (§14.5.3). |`
`| 14 | "We can clean it quarterly like a normal hood." | NFPA 96 Table 14.8 / §11.4 require **monthly** cleaning for solid fuel. Vendor not knowing this signals they don't understand the application. |`
`| 15 | No stamped engineer drawings, no Austin permit history, no NFPA 96 §14 references in the submittal. | Bid not technically responsive to the application. |`
`| 16 | "We'll wrap the duct with regular fiberglass insulation for clearance." | Clearance reduction requires a specific listed product tested to ASTM E2336 (e.g., 3M Fire Barrier 615+, Thermal Ceramics FireMaster). Generic insulation is not allowed. |`
`| 17 | "Suppression is the fire-protection contractor's problem — not in my scope." | Hood vendor and suppression contractor must coordinate nozzle placement, fusible link locations, and gas/electric shutoff. Lack of coordination = failed inspection. Demand a coordinated submittal. |`

`---`

`## Details`

`### How NFPA 96 Chapter 14 Maps to the Austin Building Code`

`Austin is one of a small handful of Texas cities that adopts the **Uniform Mechanical Code (UMC)** rather than the IMC. Austin's currently-effective adoption is the **2024 UMC** (Ordinance 20250410-044, effective July 10, 2025), preceded by the 2021 UMC effective September 1, 2021. The UMC's solid-fuel provisions live in **Section 517**, which extracts directly from NFPA 96 Chapter 14:`

`- **UMC §517.1** — Venting application (mirrors NFPA 96 §14.1)`
`- **UMC §517.3** — Hoods for solid fuel (NFPA 96 §14.3); §517.3.1 is the separation rule`
`- **UMC §517.5** — Grease removal devices (NFPA 96 §14.5)`
`- **UMC §517.6** — Air movement (NFPA 96 §14.6) — **MUA interlock required**`
`- **UMC §517.7** — Fire-extinguishing equipment (NFPA 96 §14.7)`
`- **UMC §517.8** — Inspection / cleaning`
`- **UMC §517.9** — Fuel storage`

`Most national hood manufacturers and most chain restaurant builders cite the IMC (because most of Texas is IMC). The IMC equivalents for your reference when reading vendor cut sheets:`

`- **IMC §506** — Ducts (construction, slope, clearance, access)`
`- **IMC §507** — Hoods (§507.2.2 = Type I Extra-Heavy-Duty separation rule)`
`- **IMC §508** — Makeup air`

`The substantive content is the same — both UMC §517 and IMC §507.2.2 reference NFPA 96 Chapter 14. **Vendors should be writing both UMC and NFPA 96 references on Austin submittals.** Vendors who only cite IMC may be unfamiliar with Austin's plan review process.`

`### Korean Live-Fire Style — Specific Notes`

`Korean fine dining live-fire typically involves **binchotan / oak charcoal** in a fixed grill (jikbul/sumibiyaki style) or in tabletop guests grills with a back-of-house prep grill. A few application-specific points:`

`- **If the live fire is exclusively back-of-house** (i.e., a chef-controlled wood/charcoal grill on the cook line), this knowledge base applies straightforwardly: one solid-fuel wall canopy hood over the cook line, one solid-fuel duct riser, one upblast fan.`
`- **If the live fire is also at the table** (downdraft Korean BBQ at each table), that's a fundamentally different ventilation problem governed by NFPA 96 Chapter 16 (Downdraft Appliance Ventilation Systems) and is outside the scope of this Domain 1 document. If your concept includes both, the back-of-house grill is its own NFPA 96 Chapter 14 system, and the dining-room downdraft is its own Chapter 16 system. They cannot share. Talk to a kitchen ventilation engineer who has done Korean BBQ in Texas before — JC Enterprises (Gardena CA) and similar manufacturers make purpose-built downdraft systems. **Do not let one vendor pretend a single hood/exhaust solves both.**`
`- **Fuel storage** for charcoal is a real consideration: NFPA 96 §14.9 requires non-combustible enclosure with walls/floor/ceiling extending ≥3 ft past the appliance footprint, and if interior, sprinklered. For a ~563 SF kitchen, the charcoal storage room should be planned early and located where it doesn't compete with prep space. Many operators put it in a lockable metal cabinet at the back of the kitchen with daily replenishment from outdoor bulk storage.`

`### What 6,000–9,000 CFM Means for Other Trades`

`Once you lock the hood CFM, several tenant-scope items follow that vendors often miss:`

`- **Electrical service:** A 7.5–10 HP exhaust fan is a 30–50 amp 208/230V 3Φ load. The MUA unit (DX-cooled) can be another 80–100 amps. Make sure the building electrical service has capacity, and that you have a fire-alarm-interlocked shunt trip on the cooking equipment circuit (NFPA 96 §10.5 requires fuel/electrical shutoff on suppression activation).`
`- **Gas service:** Solid-fuel itself doesn't use gas, but the suppression system needs a gas-shutoff valve in series with all gas appliances under or near the hood (even auxiliary gas — §14.7.11). The MUA unit, if direct gas-fired, is itself a significant gas load (~250,000–500,000 BTU/hr).`
`- **Roof structure:** A 7.5–10 HP upblast fan, an 8,000-CFM MUA unit, and the curbs total ~2,500–4,000 lbs concentrated on the roof. The landlord's structural engineer should confirm capacity in writing before the curb is cut. Especially relevant on a corrugated metal roof.`
`- **Sound:** A 7.5 HP fan on the roof is ~85 dBA at 5 ft. If the building is in a mixed-use area with residential nearby (parts of South Austin around St. Elmo Rd. are mixed-use), check the City of Austin noise ordinance (Title 9-2) and consider a sound attenuator or silencer in the duct, or specify a high-efficiency low-sone fan.`
`- **Water service for fire suppression and any continuous-mist hood:** A continuous-mist or water-wash hood will need a 3/4" cold-water supply, a hot-water connection (for wash cycle), a drain, and a backflow preventer (RPZ).`

`---`

`## Recommendations`

`### Stage 1 — Before You Solicit Bids (Now)`
`1. **Lock the cook-line layout in writing.** Final LF, appliance positions (especially charbroiler at the end of line vs. middle), and whether any non-solid-fuel equipment will be near the line. This drives every downstream number.`
`2. **Decide tableside vs. back-of-house live fire.** If both, commit early to two separate ventilation systems (Chapter 14 + Chapter 16).`
`3. **Engage a Texas-licensed mechanical engineer (MEP)** with restaurant solid-fuel experience to do a preliminary load calc. Expect to spend $3,500–$8,000 on a stamped MEP design. Do not skip this — Austin DSD will require stamped drawings for solid-fuel cooking.`
`4. **Get the landlord's structural engineer to pre-review** roof capacity for the anticipated fan + MUA + curb loads. Get this in writing before signing the lease addendum on roof penetrations.`

`### Stage 2 — Soliciting Bids`
`5. **Issue an RFP, not a price-only request.** Include the 15 questions in §9 above as required deliverables.`
`6. **Get at least three bids** from solid-fuel-capable vendors. CaptiveAire, Halton, Accurex, Greenheck, and Streivor all make qualified solid-fuel hood packages; local Austin installers should be able to quote any of these.`
`7. **Reject any bid that contains red flags from §10.** Don't try to negotiate them out — the vendor's willingness to propose them is itself the disqualifier.`

`### Stage 3 — Bid Evaluation Thresholds`
`- **Reject if exhaust CFM < 350 CFM/ft of cookline** (without manufacturer's listed minimum to support a lower number).`
`- **Reject if MUA < 80% of exhaust** or if MUA is "the landlord's RTU."`
`- **Reject if duct is anything other than 16ga carbon or 18ga stainless welded, or UL 1978 listed factory-built.**`
`- **Reject if fan is not UL 705 SC listed, steel wheel, with motor out of airstream.**`
`- **Reject if fire suppression isn't specifically listed for solid fuel.**`

`### Stage 4 — Construction`
`8. **Sequence the roof penetrations:** structural sign-off → curb delivery → landlord's roofer cuts/flashes → vendor sets fan/MUA → electrical/gas hookup. In writing, in your GC's CPM schedule.`
`9. **Witness the duct light test** before any insulation, wrap, or ceiling closes. NFPA 96 / IMC require the duct to be light-tight; you (or your MEP) should be there to confirm.`
`10. **Witness the fan startup and air balance.** The TAB (testing, adjusting, balancing) contractor should measure actual exhaust CFM at the hood, actual MUA CFM, and the kitchen-to-dining pressure differential. Pressure target: kitchen 0.01–0.02 in. w.c. negative to dining; building NOT exceeding 0.02 in. w.c. negative to outside.`

`### Stage 5 — Operations`
`11. **Sign a monthly hood-cleaning contract** with an IKECA-certified vendor before you open. NFPA 96 §11.4 / Table 14.8 requires monthly for solid fuel; your insurance will require documentation.`
`12. **Train the head cook on the daily/weekly maintenance:** scrape combustion chamber to bare metal weekly (§14.8); empty ash daily into a metal can stored ≥10 ft from the building; clean filters daily.`
`13. **Plan annual recommissioning** of the MUA unit and fan: belts, bearings, motor amperage, suppression nozzle inspection, fusible link replacement per UL listing.`

`### Benchmarks That Would Change the Recommendation`
`- **If the cook-line shrinks below 8 LF:** A smaller (3,500–5,000 CFM) hood may permit a less-elaborate MUA strategy — possibly belt-driven indirect-gas MUA without DX cooling.`
`- **If the live fire is gas-only with wood smoker boxes for flavoring:** NFPA 96 §14.3.4 exception may apply and the system may not need full Chapter 14 separation. Still requires spark arresters and listed suppression. Have a code official confirm in writing.`
`- **If you add a dining-room downdraft system:** Re-scope under NFPA 96 Chapter 16 entirely; the back-of-house Chapter 14 system stays separate.`
`- **If you change the kitchen layout to put the live fire near a property line or under a residence:** Re-check the 10 ft rooftop separation rules; you may need to reroute the fan or invest in a Pollution Control Unit (electrostatic precipitator with HEPA + UV/carbon for odor) to mitigate neighbor complaints. Halton PolluStop, CaptiveAire PCU, and Cadexair are the major players.`

`---`

`## Caveats`

`- **Code edition specifics:** Austin's currently-adopted UMC is the 2024 edition (effective July 10, 2025). NFPA 96 references in this document are to the 2021 edition with awareness of 2024/2025 update language; section numbers can shift slightly between editions (older 2014–2017 NFPA 96 editions used Chapter 15 instead of Chapter 14 for solid fuel — the question explicitly cites Chapter 14, which matches 2021/2024). Always have the engineer of record cite the edition Austin DSD will use on your specific permit.`
`- **NFPA 96 is incorporated by reference** into Austin's UMC §517 and into IMC §506.3 (in IMC jurisdictions). The UMC and NFPA 96 are *not always identical* — when they conflict, the UMC controls in Austin. Differences are usually in section numbering, not substantive content.`
`- **CFM ranges given here are typical industry numbers** from ASHRAE 154, IMC Table 507.5, and CaptiveAire / Halton / Accurex design guidance. Your specific listed hood may permit lower numbers, and your specific Austin plan reviewer may insist on higher numbers — neither is unusual. Your MEP engineer's stamped calc is what controls.`
`- **The 10-ton RTU sizing assumption** (≈4,000 CFM total supply) is a typical commercial RTU rule of thumb (~400 CFM/ton). Your specific RTU model may deliver 350–450 CFM/ton — get the actual nameplate. Either way, no single 10-ton RTU is large enough to be the makeup air source for a 6,000+ CFM solid-fuel hood.`
`- **Roof penetrations on a TPO/corrugated metal hybrid roof** are non-trivial. The landlord's preferred-vendor requirement is normal in Austin commercial leases and protects the landlord's TPO warranty. Budget for it as a meaningful tenant cost ($8,000–$25,000 for a fan curb + MUA curb + flashing on a hybrid roof). Get a written quote from the landlord's roofer through the lease landlord-improvement-allowance process before signing the suite-specific work letter.`
`- **Pollution Control Units (PCUs) and odor mitigation** were not asked about in detail but bear watching: if neighbors complain about wood-fire smoke (a very real risk in dense Austin commercial corridors), the City Health Department or AFD can require retrofit of a PCU at considerable cost ($40,000–$120,000). For a solid-fuel concept it's worth pricing a double-pass ESP + UV/carbon module up front, even if you decide not to install it on opening day, so you know the path-to-compliance cost.`
`- **Insurance:** Your commercial property carrier will likely require NFPA 96 compliance, monthly cleaning records, annual fire-suppression service, and may charge a solid-fuel surcharge on your premium. Get an insurance quote *before* signing the construction contract — solid-fuel premiums in Texas can be 25–60% higher than gas/electric. If a carrier refuses to bind, that's a signal to revisit the design.`
`- **This document is a vendor-conversation knowledge base, not engineering design.** It will let you read a hood submittal critically, ask the right questions, and reject obvious shortcuts. It is not a substitute for a stamped MEP design by a Texas-licensed Professional Engineer, which Austin DSD will require at permit submission.`

`# Fire Suppression (Solid Fuel) & Fire Alarm Knowledge Base`
`## 207 E St Elmo Rd, Austin, TX — Korean Live-Fire Restaurant (2,310 SF / 563 SF Kitchen)`

`This document is a companion reference to the existing Solid Fuel Exhaust Ventilation Compliance Guide. It is written for the owner — not the designer — so that proposals from fire suppression contractors and fire alarm contractors can be evaluated, challenged, and approved with confidence. Two domains are covered: (1) solid-fuel fire suppression under NFPA 96 Chapter 14, and (2) the building fire alarm system under IFC Chapter 9 and NFPA 72. They are separate scopes, separate trades, and separate permits, but they must be designed as one integrated life-safety package. The cross-reference matrix at the end of the document shows exactly where they touch.`

`Code citations throughout reference the 2021 International Fire Code (IFC) and 2021 International Mechanical Code (IMC) as adopted by the City of Austin with local amendments (Austin Land Development Code Chapter 25-12, Article 7), the 2021 edition of NFPA 96, NFPA 17A, NFPA 72, and NFPA 101. Austin's transition to the 2024 IFC was in process as of early 2026; the substantive provisions referenced below are unchanged in the 2024 cycle.`

`---`

`# SECTION 1 — DOMAIN 2: FIRE SUPPRESSION (SOLID FUEL)`

`## 1.1 Why a Standard UL 300 Wet Chemical System Alone Is Not Sufficient for Solid Fuel`

`UL 300 ("Standard for Fire Testing of Fire Extinguishing Systems for Protection of Commercial Cooking Equipment") was published in 1994 to address the higher autoignition temperatures of vegetable oils and the better insulation of modern cooking equipment. It is the listing standard cited by NFPA 96 and the IFC for protection of grease-laden vapor cooking. **Every commercial kitchen suppression system you will be quoted — Ansul R-102, Pyro-Chem PCL/Kitchen Knight II, Buckeye Kitchen Mister, Amerex KP, CaptiveAire CORE — is listed to UL 300.** That checks the box for grease-laden vapor protection over fryers, ranges, and griddles. It does **not** by itself satisfy NFPA 96 Chapter 14 for solid-fuel cooking.`

`The reason is that NFPA 96 imposes **additional, parallel requirements** on solid fuel that go beyond a UL 300 listing:`

`- **§14.3.3 — Separate exhaust system.** Solid-fuel cooking equipment served by a hood and duct must be on a duct system separate from all other exhaust systems. You cannot share a hood with gas/electric appliances.`
`- **§14.7.5 — Water-based agents required.** "Listed fire-extinguishing equipment for solid-fuel-burning cooking appliances, where required, shall be in accordance with [the suppression chapter] and shall use water-based agents." A standard wet chemical agent (potassium acetate, potassium carbonate, etc.) is not water-based in the sense Chapter 14 requires; the agent must include water capacity for cooling and char extinguishment.`
`- **§14.7.6 / §14.7.7 — Sufficient size to "totally extinguish."** The system must "be of sufficient size to totally extinguish fire in the entire hazard area and prevent reignition of the fuel." Wet chemical cylinders sized for grease-vapor knockdown cannot meet this for a wood/charcoal bed (more in §1.2 below).`
`- **§14.7.8 / §14.7.9 — Firebox volume thresholds.** Fireboxes of 5 cubic feet or less require a portable water-spray or Class K extinguisher; fireboxes exceeding 5 cubic feet require a **fixed water pipe system with a hose** (more in §1.4 and §1.5).`
`- **§14.1.6 — Spark arresters.** Required ahead of the grease-removal device.`
`- **§11.4 — Cleaning frequency.** Solid-fuel exhaust cleaning is monthly, not quarterly or semiannually.`

`A vendor who quotes a single Ansul R-102 cylinder over a wood-fired grill with no water pipe, no separate hood, standard 360°F links, and quarterly cleaning is selling a noncompliant package. That vendor will fail Austin Fire Department plan review and will fail acceptance test.`

`The most relevant insurance industry guidance — State Auto Bulletin TB-P29-0619 (Commercial Cooking with Solid Fuels) — explicitly states that "conventional wet-chemical agent extinguishing systems with limited volume capacity may not be as effective" and recommends "a UL-300 listed (or equivalent) water-based or wet chemical water-assist type of extinguishing system that uses water mist with surfactants."`

`## 1.2 The "Totally Extinguish" Standard — NFPA 96 §14.7.6 and §14.7.7`

`In standard cooking suppression (deep fryer, range), the suppression event is fast: a wet chemical agent saponifies hot oil, knocks down flame, cools the surface, and holds for two-to-three minutes against re-ignition. The fuel — oil in a fry pot — is finite and contained.`

`In solid-fuel cooking, the fuel is the burning **bed of wood and charcoal itself**. Knocking down flame is not extinguishment. Embers continue to burn at 1,000°F+ inside the fuel bed and in creosote deposits in the duct, and they will re-ignite the moment chemical agent dissipates. NFPA 96 §14.7.6 demands the suppression system be "rated and designed to extinguish solid-fuel cooking fires" and §14.7.7 requires it "be of sufficient size to totally extinguish fire in the entire hazard area and prevent reignition of the fuel."`

`In plain language: the system must put the fire **all the way out, including embers**, not merely knock down flame. That requires:`

`- **Significant water volume**, not a fixed cylinder of finite agent.`
`- **Sustained discharge** that continues long enough to soak embers — a wet-chem cylinder discharges in roughly 60 seconds; a water-based system can run continuously off the building water main.`
`- **Coverage of the entire hazard area** — the appliance, the plenum, the duct, and any creosote deposits that have formed in the duct riser.`

`This is why CaptiveAire — the largest U.S. manufacturer of commercial kitchen ventilation — explicitly recommends only its CORE Protection system (water + surfactant) for solid-fuel applications, and not its tank-based TANK system (wet chemical), even though both are UL 300 listed. The recommendation is technical, not marketing: a fixed-volume agent cylinder cannot meet the "totally extinguish" test for a 50-pound bed of charcoal.`

`## 1.3 Solid-Fuel Suppression Options on the Market`

`Five system architectures are realistically available in the U.S. market in 2026. Each has tradeoffs.`

`### A. CaptiveAire CORE Protection (water + surfactant)`
`- **Manufacturer:** CaptiveAire Systems, Inc.`
`- **What it is:** A factory-integrated water-based fire suppression system built into the hood. Uses an unlimited domestic water supply mixed with a liquid surfactant agent to suppress fires; the same plumbing also runs a daily wash cycle that flushes the duct/plenum with hot water and surfactant to reduce grease and creosote buildup.`
`- **Listing:** ETL Listed to UL 300 and ULC/ORD-C1254.6.`
`- **Detection:** Electric thermal "Firestats" with 360°F default and rate-of-rise; for solid fuel, **600°F firestats are required** (CaptiveAire Tech Bulletin TB20-1020).`
`- **When it applies:** This is the system most likely to be specified for the St Elmo Rd project, and the system most code officials in Austin are familiar with for solid fuel. CaptiveAire states CORE is its **only recommended** suppression for solid-fuel applications.`
`- **Tradeoffs:** Requires a dedicated, supervised water supply line tapped immediately downstream of the building main (or sprinkler riser). Drain provisions required. Installed only as part of a CaptiveAire hood package — you cannot retrofit CORE under a non-CaptiveAire hood.`

`### B. Water mist systems`
`- **Manufacturers:** Marioff HI-FOG (Carrier), Fogtec, Tyco AquaMist, several others.`
`- **What it is:** A high-pressure (or intermediate-pressure) system that atomizes water into very fine droplets to absorb heat and displace oxygen. Can use less total water than a deluge but at higher pressures (typically 175 psi to 1,400+ psi).`
`- **Listing:** NFPA 750 governs water mist; some products are UL 300 listed.`
`- **When it applies:** Better suited to industrial/marine/data center applications. Used in solid-fuel kitchens occasionally but rare in U.S. restaurants because of cost and limited servicing network.`

`### C. Wet chemical with water-assist / hybrid`
`- **Manufacturers:** Buckeye Kitchen Mister with water-assist, Amerex KP with water-assist, Pyro-Chem PCL hybrid configurations.`
`- **What it is:** A traditional UL 300 wet-chemical system supplemented by a tied-in water flush to address creosote and embers.`
`- **When it applies:** A retrofit option when the hood is already in place and a CORE-style integrated system isn't feasible. Acceptable to many AHJs when paired with a fixed water pipe per §14.7.9, but watch the listing — some configurations are listed for solid fuel and some are not. Verify the UL listing card explicitly says "solid fuel" or "extra-heavy-duty cooking" before accepting.`

`### D. Standard wet chemical (Ansul R-102, Pyro-Chem PCL/Kitchen Knight II, Buckeye Kitchen Mister, Amerex KP)`
`- **Solid-fuel coverage is limited.** The Ansul R-102 manual lists a 3N nozzle for "mesquite char-broiler protection" and for ceramic/natural charcoal char-broilers, but only within a narrow envelope of broiler dimensions. The R-102 is not generally suitable as the sole system for a wood-fired pit, smoker, or large solid-fuel grill.`
`- **When it applies:** Adjacent gas-fired equipment under a separate hood, or a small solid-fuel charbroiler that fits within the listing. Not as primary protection for the live-fire station that will define this restaurant.`

`### E. Solid masonry exception (rare)`
`- NFPA 96 §14.7.2 provides that solid-fuel cooking appliances "constructed of solid masonry or reinforced portland or refractory cement concrete and vented in accordance with NFPA 211" are **not required** to have fixed automatic fire-extinguishing equipment, where acceptable to the AHJ. This is the route for some traditional pizza ovens. It is unlikely to apply to a Korean live-fire grill, but it is worth confirming with the AHJ if any masonry hearth is in the design.`

`**Recommendation for the St Elmo Rd project:** the default specification should be a CaptiveAire hood with CORE Protection, 600°F firestats, supervised water supply, plus a fixed water pipe and hose under §14.7.9 if any firebox exceeds 5 cubic feet. This is the path of least resistance with the Austin Fire Department.`

`## 1.4 The 5 Cubic Foot Firebox Threshold — NFPA 96 §14.7.8 and §14.7.9`

`NFPA 96 splits solid-fuel appliances into two regulatory classes by **firebox volume**:`

`**Below 5 cubic feet (NFPA 96 §14.7.8):**`
`- A listed 2-A rated water-spray fire extinguisher, **or**`
`- A 1.6-gallon wet chemical fire extinguisher listed for Class K fires per NFPA 10`
`- Travel distance to the appliance not more than 20 feet`

`**Above 5 cubic feet (NFPA 96 §14.7.9):**`
`- A **fixed water pipe system** with a hose in the kitchen capable of reaching the firebox`
`- The hose must be equipped with an adjustable nozzle capable of producing a fine to medium spray or mist`
`- The system must deliver water at sufficient pressure and volume — commonly cited as **40 psi minimum at 5 GPM minimum** at the nozzle, though the code text references §14.7.9 sub-sections for the specific performance criteria; verify the current edition with the AHJ.`

`### Calculating firebox volume on a 4-6 foot commercial cook setup`

`Firebox volume is the **internal cubic volume of the combustion chamber** — the space where wood/charcoal actually burns, not the overall appliance footprint or the cook surface above it.`

`A typical 4-foot commercial wood-burning charbroiler with an 18" wide × 24" deep × 6" deep ash/fuel pan has an internal firebox of:`
`- 1.5 ft × 2.0 ft × 0.5 ft = **1.5 cubic feet** → below threshold`

`A 5-foot Korean BBQ-style live-fire grill with an internal coal bed of 24" wide × 48" deep × 8" deep:`
`- 2.0 ft × 4.0 ft × 0.67 ft = **5.36 cubic feet** → above threshold; fixed water pipe required`

`A 6-foot smoker pit with an internal firebox of 30" × 60" × 12":`
`- 2.5 ft × 5.0 ft × 1.0 ft = **12.5 cubic feet** → well above threshold`

`**The threshold is easy to cross.** Any wood-fired cooking equipment larger than a residential-scale grill is likely to require a fixed water pipe. The owner should ask the kitchen equipment supplier for the manufacturer's published firebox volume in cubic feet, in writing, and provide it to the suppression vendor before quoting.`

`### What changes once the threshold is crossed`

`Once a firebox is above 5 cu ft:`
`- The portable extinguisher allowance (§14.7.8) **no longer satisfies** the code. A fixed water pipe is required in addition to the automatic suppression system.`
`- The fixed water pipe is not the automatic system; it is a **secondary, manually operated hose** for staff to use during a working fire to soak the fuel bed.`
`- A Class K portable extinguisher (§14.7.8 Note / NFPA 10 §5.5.5.1) is still required for the kitchen regardless.`

`## 1.5 The Fixed Water Pipe System — Plumbing Coordination`

`The fixed water pipe required by §14.7.9 is a small but critical scope item that frequently falls between trades. Here is what the system must deliver and how it must be coordinated.`

`**Performance:**`
`- Capable of reaching the firebox with a hose long enough to operate without entering the hot zone (typically 25-50 feet of 1" hose).`
`- Adjustable nozzle producing fine to medium spray or mist (a straight-stream firefighting nozzle is not appropriate — straight stream onto burning charcoal can spread embers).`
`- Minimum flow and pressure as specified in NFPA 96 §14.7.9. The widely-cited values used by AHJs are **40 psi minimum operating pressure and 5 GPM minimum flow** at the nozzle, but verify the current edition language with the AHJ during plan review.`

`**Plumbing integration:**`
`- Tapped from the building's domestic cold water main — typically a dedicated 1" line.`
`- Equipped with a backflow preventer (RPZ assembly per Austin Water Utility cross-connection requirements) since the line crosses from potable water into a fire-extinguishment use.`
`- A control valve and quarter-turn ball valve at the hose station.`
`- Drain provisions to prevent freezing in shoulder-season conditions.`

`**Who installs what:**`
`- The **plumber** runs the line, installs the backflow preventer, provides the tee and shutoff at the hose station.`
`- The **suppression vendor** (or kitchen equipment vendor) provides and mounts the hose reel, nozzle, and signage. Some CaptiveAire integrated packages include the hose reel as part of the CORE assembly; verify on the submittal.`
`- The **GC** is responsible for closing the gap between the two scopes in writing — this is a documented source of change orders on solid-fuel projects.`

`**Austin-specific note:** Austin Water requires testable backflow preventers on commercial connections. The annual backflow test will become an ongoing operational obligation.`

`## 1.6 Detection — 600°F Fire Stats vs. 360°F/450°F`

`A "fire stat" or "thermostat" in this context is a heat-actuated detector — a fusible-link assembly or an electronic thermal sensor — that triggers the suppression system when it reaches a calibrated temperature.`

`**Standard cooking suppression** uses fusible links rated **360°F or 450°F** placed in the hood plenum and at the duct collar above each appliance. These work for grease-vapor fires, where flame temperatures over the fryer reach the link quickly.`

`**Solid-fuel cooking** runs much hotter at steady state. Wood-fired grills routinely show plenum temperatures of 400-500°F during normal heavy operation. A 360°F link in a wood-fired plenum will discharge the suppression system every dinner service. A 450°F link will discharge frequently. **Solid fuel applications require 600°F fire stats** — both at the duct collar and at downstream detection points in the duct riser (CaptiveAire Tech Bulletin TB20-1020; reflected in current AHJ practice).`

`Recent industry data, summarized in Risk Management Magazine and in CaptiveAire's bulletins, also shows that fusible-link assemblies in solid-fuel duct applications **fail to activate reliably** when fires start in the upper duct above the detector. For this reason, electronic thermal detection (rate-of-rise plus fixed-temperature, supervised by a control board with battery backup) is preferred over mechanical fusible links for solid fuel. CaptiveAire's CORE system uses electronic firestats by default. Where mechanical fusible links are used, **multiple detection points in the duct riser** — preferably under each exhaust fan — are needed to catch upper-duct fires.`

`If a vendor quotes 360°F or 450°F links over the wood/charcoal station, that is a definitive sign the vendor does not understand solid-fuel detection. The system will either nuisance-trip in service or fail to detect a real upper-duct creosote fire.`

`## 1.7 Self-Cleaning Manifolds and Continuous Wash-Down`

`Solid-fuel cooking generates **carbon, creosote, and grease-laden vapors** at higher rates than gas/electric cooking (NFPA 96 §A.4.1.6). Creosote is highly combustible, deposits unevenly inside the duct riser, and is the primary cause of catastrophic kitchen-fire spread in steakhouses and BBQ restaurants.`

`A **self-cleaning hood** (sometimes called a wash-down hood or water-wash hood) injects hot water and detergent through a manifold of spray nozzles inside the plenum and behind the filters at the end of each cooking shift. The wash cycle removes deposits before they can accumulate to dangerous thickness.`

`In the CaptiveAire CORE system, the same plumbing that delivers water-and-surfactant for fire suppression also runs the daily wash cycle. This is intentional — the wash cycle keeps the plumbing primed and tested, and the surfactant tank is monitored continuously.`

`**What to look for in a spec:**`
`- A wash manifold that sprays the **full length of the plenum and into the duct collar**, not just the front filter face.`
`- **Hot water supply** — a dedicated hot water heater or a heat recovery coil in the hood plenum (CaptiveAire offers a heat recovery coil option; this also reduces the restaurant's hot water energy cost).`
`- **Surfactant injection** during the wash cycle, with a low-level alarm on the surfactant reservoir.`
`- A documented wash cycle of **at least 3 minutes**, typical of NFPA 96 Annex guidance.`
`- **Drain provisions** sized for the wash discharge plus solids; a grease interceptor downstream is required by Austin plumbing code.`

`A vendor selling a non-self-cleaning hood for solid-fuel cooking is asking the owner to accept an ongoing monthly hot-pressure-wash service contract for the duct ($300-$800 per visit), plus the elevated risk that comes with manual cleaning of a solid-fuel duct.`

`## 1.8 Indoor and Outdoor Stations — Is a Separate Suppression System Required Outside?`

`If the project includes an **outdoor BBQ pit or smoker under a covered structure** (overhang, awning, pergola with roof, partial enclosure), NFPA 96 Chapter 14 still applies. The triggering language is in NFPA 96 §1.1.1 and §4.1: the standard governs commercial cooking operations regardless of whether they are inside the main building, provided they produce smoke or grease-laden vapors and are under any form of "roofed enclosure" that captures effluent.`

`The practical questions for an outdoor pit are:`

`1. **Is there a roof or overhang above the pit?** If yes, NFPA 96 generally requires a Type I hood and exhaust system, just as if the pit were indoors. The hood requires its own suppression system.`
`2. **Is the pit fully open to the sky (no overhead structure)?** If yes, the suppression and ventilation requirements of NFPA 96 do not apply, but Austin's outdoor cooking and life-safety provisions (clearances to combustibles, spark arresters, fuel storage) still do, and the AHJ can require additional measures under NFPA 96 §14.4 (location and application restrictions) and the Austin Fire Code Special Events / Open Flame provisions.`
`3. **Is the outdoor station "covered" but with significant open sides?** This is the gray area. Austin AFD has historically treated covered outdoor cook structures as requiring NFPA 96 compliance once the roof captures any meaningful effluent. Get a written interpretation from AFD plan review before committing to an outdoor pit design.`

`**If a covered outdoor pit is in the project:**`
`- It needs its **own dedicated Type I hood, separate duct, separate suppression system** (a single suppression system cannot serve both indoor and outdoor stations — §14.3.3).`
`- It needs its **own fire stats, manual pull station, and gas/fuel shutoff** (if it has any gas component).`
`- The suppression cylinder/control panel must be located in a conditioned enclosure (32-130°F per CORE specs; similar for wet chemical). This typically means a small mechanical closet adjacent to the patio.`
`- A separate fuel storage area for cordwood / charcoal must comply with NFPA 96 §14.9.2 (noncombustible enclosure, sprinklers if pile exceeds 5 cu ft, spark arresters).`

`The owner should expect **two separate suppression contracts** if both an indoor live-fire station and a covered outdoor pit are in the program. The vendor must price both, with separate cylinders, separate detection lines, and separate manual pull stations.`

`## 1.9 Required Interlocks on Suppression Activation`

`NFPA 96 §10.4 and §8.2/8.3 dictate what must happen automatically when the suppression system discharges. These interlocks are mechanical and electrical and they are the primary place where the **fire suppression scope and the fire alarm scope intersect**.`

`**On suppression activation, the system must:**`

`| Action | Code basis | Notes |`
`|---|---|---|`
`| Shut off all sources of fuel and electric power that produce heat to all equipment under the protected hood | NFPA 96 §10.4.1 | Includes adjacent gas appliances under the same hood that are not themselves protected (§10.4.3) |`
`| Shut off auxiliary fuel (gas, oil, electric ignition) for solid-fuel appliances with auxiliary heat | NFPA 96 §14.7.11 | Applies to gas-assist wood ovens, electric-ignition wood broilers |`
`| Shut off makeup air **supplied internally to the hood** | NFPA 96 §8.3.2 | External MAU need not shut off — this is widely misunderstood |`
`| **Continue running the exhaust fan** unless the listing requires otherwise | NFPA 96 §8.2.3.1 | Exhaust must keep pulling smoke/agent up the duct |`
`| Require manual reset before fuel/power is restored | NFPA 96 §10.4.4 | Resets via a manual-reset relay; auto-restart is prohibited |`
`| Send a signal to the building fire alarm panel | IFC §904.3.5; NFPA 72 §17.13 | This is the bridge to Section 2 |`

`**Important nuance for solid fuel (NFPA 96 §10.4.5):** "Solid fuel cooking operations shall not be required to be shut down." Code recognizes you cannot turn off burning wood. The shutoff requirement applies to electric ignition, gas-assist burners, and rotisserie motors — not to the burning fuel bed itself. This is why the fixed water pipe system exists: someone must manually wet the fuel bed after suppression discharge.`

`**The gas shutoff valve** is a mechanical or solenoid valve installed on the gas supply line to the cooking equipment. Mechanical valves (Asco, Maxitrol) are held open by a tensioned cable connected to the suppression release; when the release fires, the cable goes slack, the valve closes, and the only way to reopen it is manually. Solenoid valves are held open by a 24V or 120V signal that drops on suppression activation. Either is acceptable; mechanical is more robust and has no power dependency, which is why it remains the default.`

`**The shunt-trip breaker** disconnects electric heat-producing appliances (electric griddles, electric salamanders) on activation. It is wired by the electrician based on a panel schedule provided by the suppression vendor. Lighting and refrigeration under the hood are typically not shunted (those are not heat-producing).`

`**The signal to the fire alarm panel** is a dry contact (a Form C relay, normally open or normally closed, on the suppression control board) wired to a supervised input on the fire alarm control panel. This is the connection that turns a kitchen suppression discharge into a building-wide alarm with central station notification. Without this connection, only the people standing in the kitchen know the system has fired.`

`## 1.10 Inspection and Maintenance for Solid-Fuel Suppression`

`NFPA 17A (Wet Chemical Extinguishing Systems) and NFPA 96 Chapter 11 set the maintenance schedule. Solid-fuel applications carry the strictest schedule.`

`| Frequency | Activity | Performed by | Code basis |`
`|---|---|---|---|`
`| Daily (end of cooking shift) | Run the wash cycle (self-cleaning systems); visual check of fuel storage | Owner/staff | Manufacturer; NFPA 96 §11.4 |`
`| Monthly | Visual inspection of pull stations, gauge pressure, nozzle blow-off caps in place, pipe/cable condition | Owner/staff per NFPA 17A §7.2 | NFPA 17A §7.2 |`
`| Monthly | **Exhaust system cleaning** (solid fuel) | Licensed kitchen exhaust cleaner | NFPA 96 Table 11.4 |`
`| Semiannually (every 6 months) | Full professional inspection of all components — detection, releasing devices, agent containers, piping, nozzles, signals, auxiliary equipment; replacement of fusible-link metal-alloy elements; functional test of gas valve, shunt trip, fan interlocks, fire alarm panel signal | Licensed suppression contractor (TDI-SFMO licensed in Texas) | NFPA 17A §7.3; NFPA 96 §11.2 |`
`| Annually | Combustion chamber inspection; bare-metal duct cleaning verification; fire alarm interconnect switch test; Class K extinguisher inspection | Suppression contractor + KEC | NFPA 96 §11.4; NFPA 10 |`
`| Every 12 years | **Hydrostatic pressure test** of agent containers and hose assemblies | Suppression contractor or recharge facility | NFPA 17A §7.5.1 |`

`**Compared to standard kitchen suppression:** the only schedule item unique to solid fuel is the **monthly exhaust cleaning** — a standard kitchen typically goes quarterly or semiannually depending on volume. Everything else is the same schedule, but performed against more demanding hardware (water lines, surfactant tanks, 600°F detection, fixed water pipe).`

`**Realistic ongoing cost in the Austin market (2026):**`
`- Semiannual professional suppression inspection: **$300-$500 per visit, $600-$1,000/year**`
`- Monthly exhaust hood cleaning (solid fuel): **$400-$700 per visit, $4,800-$8,400/year** — this is the single largest ongoing fire-protection line item for a solid-fuel restaurant`
`- Annual fire alarm inspection: **$300-$600/year** (covered in Section 2)`
`- Annual fire alarm monitoring: **$420-$1,200/year** (covered in Section 2)`
`- 12-year hydrostatic test on suppression cylinders: **$200-$500 amortized**, typically bundled with a recharge after any discharge event`
`- Class K extinguisher annual service: **$25-$40 per extinguisher**`
`- Backflow preventer annual test (Austin Water): **$75-$150**`

`**Total realistic annual fire-protection operating budget for this restaurant: $7,000-$12,000/year**, dominated by the monthly exhaust cleaning. This is the number the owner should put into the proforma — it is roughly double what a non-solid-fuel restaurant of the same size would spend.`

`## 1.11 Twelve Questions to Ask Every Fire Suppression Vendor`

`These are the questions that distinguish a vendor with real solid-fuel experience from a vendor selling a stock R-102 system. Insist on written answers.`

`1. **"List five solid-fuel cooking restaurants you have installed suppression in within the past three years, with owner contact references."** A vendor who cannot name five recent solid-fuel jobs in Texas is learning on yours.`
`2. **"What UL listing covers your proposed system specifically for solid fuel? Provide the listing card and the appliance-specific listing for our equipment."** Generic UL 300 is not enough; the listing must address solid fuel and the specific appliance type.`
`3. **"What is the firebox volume in cubic feet of each solid-fuel appliance, and which appliances are above the 5 cubic foot threshold under NFPA 96 §14.7.8?"** They should know this already, in writing, before quoting.`
`4. **"For appliances above the 5 cubic foot threshold, what is your scope for the fixed water pipe system per §14.7.9? Does your scope include the plumber, or does that fall to a separate trade?"** Get the trade boundary in writing.`
`5. **"What is the activation temperature of every fire stat / fusible link in your design, and where is each one located?"** Anything below 600°F over a wood-fired station is wrong.`
`6. **"How does your system 'totally extinguish' embers in the fuel bed per §14.7.7? What is the agent volume, discharge duration, and water source?"** A 6-gallon wet chemical cylinder discharging in 60 seconds does not meet this. They should describe a continuous water supply or equivalent.`
`7. **"What is the wash cycle frequency, duration, and surfactant capacity? Is the surfactant level monitored with low-level alarm?"** For self-cleaning hoods.`
`8. **"What dry contact signal will you provide to the fire alarm panel? Is it supervised? What is the signal type — alarm, supervisory, or trouble?"** This is the integration point with Section 2. The correct answer is a supervised alarm signal on suppression discharge plus a supervisory signal on system trouble.`
`9. **"What is your scope for the gas shutoff valve — mechanical or solenoid, who provides it, who installs it?"** And: "Do you coordinate with the plumber on gas line routing?"`
`10. **"What is your scope for the shunt-trip breaker, and what panel schedule do you provide to the electrician?"** They should be able to hand you a one-page panel schedule.`
`11. **"What is your inspection contract — semiannual price, what's included, what's extra (e.g., recharge, fusible link replacement, hydro test)?"** Put the line items on paper.`
`12. **"Are you TDI-SFMO Texas State Fire Marshal licensed for fixed extinguishing systems? Provide the license number and the technician's certification."** Texas requires it; some vendors operate without it. Verify on the SFMO website.`

`## 1.12 Red Flags in a Solid-Fuel Suppression Proposal`

`Any one of these is a stop-the-presses item:`

`- **A single Ansul R-102 or Pyro-Chem PCL cylinder** quoted as the sole suppression system over a wood-fired or charcoal-fired station with a firebox above 1-2 cubic feet.`
`- **No mention of NFPA 96 Chapter 14**, §14.7.6, §14.7.7, §14.7.8, or §14.7.9 in the scope narrative.`
`- **No fixed water pipe** quoted for fireboxes that will obviously exceed 5 cubic feet.`
`- **360°F or 450°F fusible links** specified over the solid-fuel station.`
`- **Shared duct or hood** between solid-fuel appliances and gas/electric appliances. This is a code violation per §14.3.3 and a sign the vendor is treating the project like a generic restaurant.`
`- **No spark arrester** in the filter / grease-removal scope.`
`- **Quarterly or semiannual exhaust cleaning** in the maintenance scope (it must be monthly for solid fuel).`
`- **No interlock to the fire alarm panel** — the vendor says "we don't tie into fire alarm; that's their scope." Wrong. The dry contact is suppression scope; the input module is fire alarm scope. The vendor must specify the contact.`
`- **No surfactant tank or wash cycle** for an integrated water-based system, or no daily wash schedule for a self-cleaning system.`
`- **The vendor cannot produce solid-fuel references** in Texas or cites only one-off pizza ovens (not the same hazard class).`
`- **The vendor does not hold a TDI-SFMO Fixed Fire Extinguishing System license**, or the cited technician is not certified.`
`- **The price is "too good"** — a compliant solid-fuel suppression package for a single 4-6 ft live-fire station typically runs $18,000-$35,000 installed, plus the fixed water pipe and plumbing tie-in, plus integration work. A bid significantly under that range is buying the job by leaving scope out.`
`- **No commissioning / acceptance test plan**, no offer to attend AFD acceptance, no documentation deliverable list.`
`- **Extended discharge time** is not addressed. Wet-chem cylinders discharge in roughly 60 seconds; for solid fuel, the suppression event needs sustained or repeatable discharge to soak embers. The vendor must explain how this happens.`
