`# SECTION 2 — DOMAIN 3: FIRE ALARM SYSTEM`

`## 2.1 Fire Alarm vs. Fire Suppression — Why They Are Separate`

`A **fire suppression system** puts fires out. It is a kitchen-hood-specific system governed by NFPA 96 / NFPA 17A, listed to UL 300, installed by a TDI-SFMO licensed fixed-extinguishing-system contractor, permitted as part of the kitchen hood / mechanical scope.`

`A **fire alarm system** does not put fires out. It detects fire (smoke, heat, manual pull, sprinkler flow), notifies occupants (horns, strobes, voice), and notifies the fire department (central station). It is a building-wide life-safety system governed by IFC §907 and NFPA 72, with control equipment listed to UL 864, installed by a different contractor — a TDI-SFMO licensed fire alarm planning superintendent and licensed fire alarm technicians, on a separate permit.`

`**The two systems must be integrated** so that a kitchen suppression discharge produces a building fire alarm, but they are not the same scope. They are bid separately, designed separately, permitted separately, and inspected separately. A fire alarm contractor will not install your kitchen suppression. A kitchen suppression vendor will not install your building fire alarm system.`

`**Where confusion costs money:** GCs and owners regularly assume "the Ansul guy will hook up the fire alarm." He won't. He provides one dry contact on his control board. The fire alarm contractor must be on site, with the panel powered, to land that contact on a supervised input module, program it, and acceptance-test it with the AFD inspector. If the trades are not coordinated, the AFD acceptance test fails, the Certificate of Occupancy is delayed, and the owner pays $1,500-$4,000 in re-inspection and re-test fees plus rent for an empty restaurant.`

`The single most important coordination meeting on the entire build is a 30-minute conference call between the GC, the suppression vendor, the fire alarm contractor, the electrician, and the plumber, scheduled before any of them rough in.`

`## 2.2 Code Basis — When a Fire Alarm Is Required`

`The applicable codes for this project:`

`- **2021 IFC as adopted by the City of Austin** (LDC Ch. 25-12, Art. 7), with local amendments. (Austin was transitioning to the 2024 IFC in 2025-2026; substantive provisions on §907 and §903 are unchanged.)`
`- **2021 IBC** for occupancy classification and occupant load (Table 1004.5).`
`- **NFPA 72 (2022)** — National Fire Alarm and Signaling Code — for fire alarm system design and installation. Referenced by IFC §907.`
`- **NFPA 101 (Life Safety Code)** — referenced where occupancy-driven life-safety provisions apply (egress, occupant notification).`
`- **2021 IMC §606** — duct smoke detector requirements.`
`- **City of Austin Fire Protection Criteria Manual** (2012 edition; in revision).`
`- **Texas Administrative Code Title 28, Part 1, Chapter 34** — TDI State Fire Marshal's Office rules for fire alarm contractor licensing.`

`**Occupancy classification:** A restaurant primarily for food and drink consumption is **Group A-2** under IBC §303.3 (assembly use, food/drink). If the calculated occupant load is fewer than 50, the occupancy can be reclassified as Group B (business). For this project, given a 2,310 SF total area and a Korean fine-dining program, A-2 is almost certainly the correct classification.`

`### Occupant load calculation for this project`

`Using IBC Table 1004.5 (occupant load factors):`
`- **Kitchen (commercial)**: 200 SF/person (gross). 563 SF kitchen → 563 / 200 ≈ **3 occupants**.`
`- **Dining area, tables and chairs (unconcentrated)**: 15 SF/person (net). Assuming the remaining 1,747 SF is split roughly 1,400 SF dining + 347 SF support (restrooms, host, storage), the dining floor at 15 SF/person → 1,400 / 15 ≈ **93 occupants**.`
`- **Standing/bar area** (if the program includes a bar): 5 SF/person (net) — this drives the number up quickly. A 200 SF bar standing area → 40 occupants.`

`**Realistic occupant load range for this restaurant: 90 to 140 persons.**`

`### IFC §907 fire alarm trigger`

`IFC §907.2.1 (Group A occupancies): a manual fire alarm system is required when the occupant load **due to the assembly use is 300 or more**. **At ~100-140 occupants, a fire alarm is not strictly triggered by §907.2.1 alone.**`

`However, **the fire alarm requirement is also triggered indirectly** by the sprinkler requirement (next paragraph) and by Austin local amendments. Specifically, IFC §903.4 requires automatic sprinkler systems to be electrically supervised by a fire alarm system; if sprinklers are required, a fire alarm system to monitor them is required.`

`### IFC §903.2.1.2 sprinkler trigger (Group A-2)`

`An automatic sprinkler system is required for Group A-2 occupancies where any of the following exists:`
`1. The fire area exceeds **5,000 SF**, or`
`2. The fire area has an occupant load of **100 or more**, or`
`3. The fire area is on a floor other than the level of exit discharge.`

`**At an occupant load of 100 or more, sprinklers are required.** For this 2,310 SF project, the occupant load is at or near the 100-person threshold. If the bar program pushes it over 100 — likely — **sprinklers are required**, and therefore **a fire alarm system to supervise the sprinklers is required**.`

`If the occupant load can be held below 100 (no bar / very tight seating count), sprinklers may not be triggered, and a basic fire alarm system may not be triggered either. But two other triggers commonly catch this kind of restaurant in Austin:`

`- **Duct smoke detection (IMC §606.2.1)** is required on any HVAC return air system over 2,000 CFM. Where a duct smoke detector is required, it must be supervised — which in practice means a fire alarm panel must exist.`
`- **Austin local amendments and AFD interpretations** — the AFD plan reviewer can require a fire alarm system based on a hazard finding (live-fire cooking is one such hazard). The landlord's LOI explicitly anticipates this by stating no fire alarm is provided and any required system is tenant scope.`

`**Conclusion:** Plan on a fire alarm system being required. The cost of designing and budgeting for it is small; the cost of finding out at AFD plan review that you need one and didn't budget it is large.`

`## 2.3 System Type — Addressable vs. Conventional`

`**Conventional** fire alarm systems are zoned. Each circuit (zone) reports as a single point — when a smoke detector activates, the panel says "Zone 3 alarm" but cannot say which detector in Zone 3. Cheaper hardware; harder to troubleshoot; more false alarms because there is no point-level diagnostic.`

`**Addressable** fire alarm systems assign each device a unique digital address. The panel reports "Detector D-12, Kitchen, alarm" rather than "Zone 3 alarm." Easier to commission, easier to inspect, far easier to troubleshoot, fewer nuisance alarms because individual detectors can be sensitivity-adjusted.`

`For a 2,310 SF single-story restaurant, **addressable is the correct choice**, for three reasons:`

`1. **Most modern Austin commercial fire alarm work is addressable.** Common panels in this size range: Honeywell/Notifier NFS-320, Honeywell Silent Knight 6700-series, Edwards EST3 (overkill for this size), Potter PFC-6200, Fire-Lite ES-50X. Any reputable Austin fire alarm contractor will quote one of these by default.`
`2. **Future expansion / changes are simpler.** A restaurant kitchen will be modified — equipment added, hood reconfigured, BOH walls moved. Addressable systems handle moves/adds/changes without rewiring.`
`3. **AFD inspectors are familiar with addressable troubleshooting.** A trouble signal that says "Detector D-7 supervisory: dust accumulation" is something a tech can address in 15 minutes; a conventional "Zone 2 trouble" can mean a 90-minute search.`

`**Cost delta:** an addressable system for this size restaurant typically runs **15-25% more than a conventional system at the panel and device level** ($2,000-$5,000 more on a $12,000-$20,000 install) and is offset within 3-5 years by lower service costs.`

`## 2.4 Required Components`

`A 2,310 SF Group A-2 restaurant fire alarm system, designed properly, will include:`

`**Fire Alarm Control Panel (FACP):**`
`- Listed to **UL 864** (Standard for Control Units and Accessories for Fire Alarm Systems), 11th edition.`
`- Located in a back-of-house area accessible to AFD personnel — typically the office or a dedicated mechanical/electrical room.`
`- Equipped with battery backup sized for **24 hours of standby plus 5 minutes of alarm** per NFPA 72 §10.6.7.`
`- Dedicated 120V circuit from the building electrical panel, breaker locked in the on position and labeled red ("Fire Alarm — Do Not Disconnect") per NFPA 72.`
`- A **remote annunciator** at the main entrance is required by IFC §907.2.13 in some configurations; AFD typically requires an annunciator at the front door for first-responder access. This is also where the **Knox Box** lives (see §2.7).`

`**Initiating devices:**`
`- **Smoke detectors** listed to **UL 268** (Smoke Detectors for Fire Alarm Systems, 7th edition). Locations:`
`- Above the FACP.`
`- In any electrical room.`
`- In any "back-of-house" area where fire detection is needed for early warning (office, server closet).`
`- Smoke detectors are generally **not placed in the kitchen** because of nuisance-alarm risk from cooking smoke; heat detectors are used in kitchen areas instead.`
`- **Heat detectors** listed to **UL 521** (Heat Detectors for Fire Protective Signaling Systems). Locations:`
`- Throughout the kitchen (typically 135°F or 194°F fixed-temperature, plus rate-of-rise).`
`- Storage rooms, dish rooms.`
`- Any location where smoke detection would nuisance-trip.`
`- **Manual pull stations** at each required exit per IFC §907.4. Mounted 42-48 inches above finished floor; ADA compliant.`
`- **Duct smoke detectors** (UL 268A) on any HVAC return air system over 2,000 CFM (IMC §606.2.1). Programmed to **shut down the HVAC unit** on activation (to prevent smoke spread) and to send a supervisory signal to the FACP. Most rooftop package units serving a restaurant of this size are 4-7 tons (1,600-2,800 CFM); units near or above 2,000 CFM trigger this.`
`- **Sprinkler flow switch and tamper switch** (if the building is sprinklered). The flow switch sends an alarm signal when water flows; the tamper switch sends a supervisory signal if a sprinkler valve is closed.`
`- **Kitchen suppression interlock** — a supervised input from the dry contact provided by the suppression vendor. This is the bridge described in §1.9.`

`**Notification appliances:**`
`- **Horn/strobes** (combined audible/visible) listed to UL 1971 / UL 464. Placed throughout occupied spaces such that:`
`- Audibility: 15 dBA above ambient or 5 dBA above maximum sound level for 60 seconds, per NFPA 72 §18.4.`
`- Visibility: candela rating sufficient for room geometry per NFPA 72 Table 18.5.5.5.1 — typically 75-110 cd in dining areas, 15-30 cd in restrooms.`
`- **ADA compliance**: visible appliances required in all public-use spaces and toilet rooms; the synchronized-strobe rule applies if more than one strobe is visible from a single point.`

`**Other:**`
`- **Power supply / battery cabinet** sized per NFPA 72 §10.6 calculations (standby + alarm).`
`- **Communicator(s)** for central station monitoring — see §2.7.`

`**Where each device goes and why:**`
`- The FACP and annunciator are placed where AFD can find them quickly, near the main entrance or in a visible BOH location.`
`- Heat detectors (not smoke) in the kitchen — cooking smoke nuisance-trips smoke detectors.`
`- Duct smoke detectors are placed in the return air duct **upstream of any filter** per IMC §606.2.1, so smoke from the dining area is detected before it recirculates.`
`- Pulls at exits — if a person is leaving because of a fire, pulling the alarm on the way out is the normal use.`
`- Strobes in restrooms — required because someone in a restroom may not hear a horn over running water.`

`## 2.5 Sprinkler vs. No Sprinkler — Interaction with the Fire Alarm Scope`

`**If sprinklers are required** (most likely, per §2.2 above):`
`- IFC §903.4 requires sprinkler systems to be electrically supervised. The fire alarm system performs that supervision via:`
`- **Waterflow switch** at each riser → alarm signal at the FACP`
`- **Tamper switch** at each control valve → supervisory signal at the FACP`
`- **Low-air pressure** (if dry-pipe; not applicable in a typical restaurant)`
`- IFC §903.4.2 requires an **exterior alarm bell** or horn/strobe activated by waterflow.`
`- In a 2nd-generation tenant space, **verify with the landlord whether sprinkler infrastructure already exists** to the demising walls. If yes, the tenant scope is the interior sprinkler distribution and tie-ins. If no, the tenant scope includes a full system from the underground tap forward, which is a major scope item ($12,000-$30,000 for this size).`

`**If sprinklers are not required** (tight occupant load, no bar, all triggers avoided):`
`- The fire alarm scope is simpler — no flow/tamper inputs, no sprinkler supervision. But duct detectors, kitchen suppression interlock, and notification still apply, so the system still exists.`

`**What to verify with the landlord — get in writing before signing the lease, or as an LOI amendment:**`
`1. Is there an existing sprinkler riser to the space, and what is its size and pressure?`
`2. Is there an existing sprinkler main with available capacity for the tenant build-out?`
`3. Where is the nearest waterflow / tamper supervision point, and is it currently monitored?`
`4. Is there an existing fire alarm panel for the building, and if so, is the tenant required to tie into it or install a stand-alone panel? (The LOI states no fire alarm is provided, suggesting stand-alone.)`
`5. What is the location and capacity of the fire department connection (FDC) serving the space?`

`A 2nd-gen restaurant space at 207 E St Elmo Rd that previously housed a non-restaurant or a smaller-occupant-load tenant may have **no existing sprinkler system** — the landlord's LOI implies as much by stating fire alarm is tenant scope. Confirm sprinkler infrastructure status separately.`

`## 2.6 Required Interlocks and Integrations — Where Section 1 and Section 2 Connect`

`| System / Event | What happens | Code basis |`
`|---|---|---|`
`| Kitchen suppression discharges | Suppression dry contact closes → FACP sees alarm input → building horn/strobes activate → central station notified → AFD dispatched | IFC §904.3.5; NFPA 72 §17.13; NFPA 96 §10.4 |`
`| Gas shutoff on suppression activation | Mechanical or solenoid valve closes on the gas main feeding the protected hood. Some installations also tie this to a 24V relay driven by the FACP for redundancy | NFPA 96 §10.4.1 |`
`| Fire alarm general activation | Optionally trigger gas shutoff via a building-wide gas solenoid (best practice in solid-fuel restaurants) | IFC §605.1; AFD discretion |`
`| Smoke detection in HVAC duct | HVAC unit shuts down (supply fan, return fan) to prevent smoke spread; supervisory signal at FACP | IMC §606.4 |`
`| Sprinkler flow | FACP sees alarm; horns/strobes activate; central station notified | IFC §903.4 |`
`| Sprinkler tamper | FACP sees supervisory signal; central station notified | IFC §903.4 |`
`| Elevator recall | Not applicable — single story | IFC §607; ASME A17.1 |`
`| Access control unlock on alarm | If the front door uses electromagnetic locks for after-hours, those must release on FACP alarm. Most fine-dining restaurants don't use mag locks; if they do, this is a coordination item with the security/access vendor | IBC §1010.2.10 |`
`| Exhaust fan continues running on suppression | Exhaust fan stays on; only internal makeup air shuts off | NFPA 96 §8.2.3.1, §8.3.2 |`
`| Manual reset required | Suppression release, FACP, gas valve, shunt-trip breaker — none auto-reset | NFPA 96 §10.4.4; NFPA 72 |`

`This is the integration map. The fire alarm contractor's submittal must show **every one of these signals** in a riser diagram and an input/output matrix. If they don't, the submittal is incomplete.`

`## 2.7 Monitoring`

`**Central station monitoring** is a 24/7 service by a remote facility (central station) that receives signals from your fire alarm panel via cellular communicator, IP communicator, or both, and dispatches the fire department on alarm. NFPA 72 Chapter 26 governs the service.`

`**Is monitoring required?** For Group A-2 restaurants in Austin:`
`- IFC §907.6.6 generally requires fire alarm monitoring "in accordance with NFPA 72" for required systems.`
`- If sprinklers are required, monitoring of the sprinkler supervisory and waterflow signals is required (IFC §903.4).`
`- Austin's Operational Permit 105.6.16 (Fire Protection Systems) requires annual inspection of monitored systems.`
`- **Practically, yes — plan on monitoring.** The exception (where a system is "required by code" but not required to be monitored) is rare and not worth pursuing for a restaurant.`

`**What monitoring costs in the Austin market (2026):**`
`- **Stand-alone monitoring** (no other services): **$30-$60/month** ($360-$720/year)`
`- **Monitoring bundled with annual inspection**: **$60-$100/month** ($720-$1,200/year)`
`- **Setup / activation fee**: $150-$400 one-time`
`- **Cellular communicator hardware**: $500-$1,500 one-time (typically included in install scope)`

`**How to evaluate a monitoring provider:**`
`1. **UL Listed central station** — look for **UL 827** listing (Standard for Central Station Alarm Services). Ask for the UL listing number; verify on UL Product iQ.`
`2. **Five-Diamond designation** from The Monitoring Association (TMA) — voluntary certification indicating the station has met training, audit, and operational standards.`
`3. **Redundancy** — at least two geographically separated central stations (in case one loses power/internet).`
`4. **Response time** — NFPA 72 §26.3.7 requires alarm signals to be retransmitted to the AHJ within 90 seconds of receipt. Ask the provider to commit to this in writing.`
`5. **Communication path** — single cellular path is acceptable per NFPA 72 §26.6.3.2 for many applications; dual path (cellular + IP) is more robust and increasingly the standard.`
`6. **Local presence** — Austin-based providers (FireTron, Impact Fire, Koorsen, Tech Systems, ABC Fire Systems) are easier to coordinate with than out-of-state national providers.`

`**Watch the contract terms.** Monitoring contracts have historically locked owners into 3-5 year terms with auto-renewal. In a tenant build-out, the owner should negotiate:`
`- **Initial term no longer than 3 years**, or month-to-month after the first year.`
`- **No auto-renewal** beyond a 1-year term.`
`- **30-day cancellation** with no termination fee after the initial term.`
`- **Price escalation cap** (e.g., no more than 5% annually).`
`- **Right to assign** if the restaurant is sold.`

`## 2.8 City of Austin Permit and Inspection Process`

`Austin Fire Department (AFD) Plan Review and the Development Services Department (DSD) handle fire alarm permits. The high-level process:`

`1. **Pre-design** — confirm occupant load and sprinkler trigger with AFD plan reviewer (informally; saves rework later).`
`2. **Construction documents** — the fire alarm contractor (must hold a TDI-SFMO Fire Alarm Planning Superintendent license) prepares stamped drawings: floor plan with device locations, riser diagram, battery calculations, voltage drop calculations, sequence of operations / input-output matrix, equipment cut sheets, and NFPA 72 compliance narrative.`
`3. **Plan submittal** — submitted via the Austin Build + Connect (AB+C) portal as part of the tenant build-out permit. Fee schedule per AFD; typical fire alarm plan review fee for this size is **$300-$700**.`
`4. **AFD Plan Review** — AFD engineers review for IFC §907 / NFPA 72 compliance. Typical timeline in 2025-2026 is **3-6 weeks** for first review; comments returned; revisions; second review **1-3 weeks**.`
`5. **Construction installation** — fire alarm contractor installs after rough-in coordination with electrician, mechanical, plumbing, and suppression vendor.`
`6. **Pre-test** — fire alarm contractor conducts a documented 100% pre-test of every device per NFPA 72 §14.4. This is internal; not witnessed by AFD.`
`7. **AFD Acceptance Test** — AFD inspector witnesses a full system test. Every device activated; every notification appliance verified; every interlock tested (kitchen suppression discharge → FACP → horn/strobe → central station → AFD dispatch confirmation). Typical scheduling lead time **1-3 weeks**.`
`8. **Knox Box installation** — required for any monitored fire alarm or sprinkler system (Austin LDC 25-12 Article 7 Section 506). Ordered through` [`KnoxBox.com/austinfire-boxes`](http://KnoxBox.com/austinfire-boxes)`, mounted per AFD spec, keys provided to AFD.`
`9. **Alarm Permit (Austin Police Department / DSD Alarm Administration)** — separate from the construction permit; required for the alarm to be enabled. Apply through the Alarm Administration Portal or 3-1-1. Annual renewal.`
`10. **Operational Permit** — Austin LDC §25-12 Section 105.6.16 requires an **annual operational permit** for all fixed fire protection systems including the fire alarm. Renewed annually with documentation of the third-party annual inspection submitted via The Compliance Engine (TCE).`
`11. **Certificate of Occupancy** — depends on **all** of the above. AFD will not sign off on a CO until: fire alarm acceptance test passes, sprinkler acceptance test passes (if applicable), kitchen suppression acceptance test passes, Knox Box is installed and keyed, operational permit is paid.`

`**The fire alarm acceptance test is typically the last AFD inspection before CO.** A failed acceptance test pushes the CO out 1-3 weeks for the re-test. **Plan for this in the construction schedule.** Have the fire alarm contractor's pre-test documentation in hand a week before the AFD acceptance test is scheduled.`

`## 2.9 Coordination Dependencies`

`The fire alarm contractor depends on every other trade. The owner's job is to make sure the GC has these coordination items on the schedule.`

`| Coordination | What the fire alarm contractor needs | When |`
`|---|---|---|`
`| **Mechanical contractor** | HVAC unit CFM ratings, return-air duct routing, location of return-air filter for each unit (so duct detectors can be located upstream of filters per IMC §606.2.1) | At mechanical rough-in — usually 30 days before fire alarm rough-in |`
`| **Plumbing contractor** | Sprinkler riser location, waterflow/tamper switch locations, fire department connection location | At sprinkler rough-in |`
`| **Suppression vendor** | Number, location, and signal type of dry contacts from the suppression control board; manual pull station locations | At suppression submittal stage |`
`| **Electrician** | Dedicated 120V circuit to FACP from a labeled breaker; low-voltage conduit routing if hard-pipe is required (often required by AFD over open ceilings); shunt-trip breaker for kitchen heat-producing equipment per panel schedule from suppression vendor | At electrical rough-in |`
`| **General contractor** | Wall types and locations, ceiling type and height, finish schedule (devices need to be plumb and aligned with ceiling tile grid), wall blocking for FACP and pull stations, rough-in coordination meetings | Throughout construction |`
`| **Access control / security vendor** | Door hardware schedule for any electromagnetic locks; FACP must release locks on alarm | At access control submittal |`
`| **Landlord** | Sprinkler tie-in approval; building communications path (if cellular signal is poor, may need to use building IP); roof access for any rooftop annunciator or monitor | Before lease signing if possible |`

`**The most common coordination failure** is the kitchen suppression interlock being missed at rough-in. The suppression vendor doesn't run wire; the fire alarm contractor doesn't install the suppression cylinder. Both expect the other to handle "the wire between us." Specify in writing: **the fire alarm contractor runs the low-voltage conductor from the suppression control board to a fire alarm input module**, terminates both ends, and tests. The suppression vendor provides the dry contact and the input/output specification.`

`## 2.10 Realistic Cost Ranges (Austin Market, 2026)`

`For a 2,310 SF Group A-2 restaurant, addressable system, with:`
`- 1 FACP (Notifier, Silent Knight, Fire-Lite, or equivalent)`
`- 1 remote annunciator`
`- ~6-10 smoke detectors`
`- ~4-8 heat detectors`
`- 2-3 manual pull stations`
`- 2-3 duct smoke detectors`
`- 8-15 horn/strobes`
`- Sprinkler flow/tamper inputs (if sprinklered)`
`- Kitchen suppression interlock`
`- HVAC shutdown relays`
`- Cellular dual-path communicator`
`- Battery backup, equipment cabinet, conduit, wire, programming, pre-test`

`| Item | Low-bid range | Quality-bid range |`
`|---|---|---|`
`| Equipment + installation | $9,000-$12,000 | $14,000-$22,000 |`
`| Plan review + AFD permit fees | $400-$800 | $400-$800 |`
`| Acceptance test labor | $500-$1,000 | $1,000-$2,000 |`
`| Knox Box (purchase + install) | $300-$500 | $400-$700 |`
`| Cellular communicator + setup | $600-$1,200 | $1,200-$1,800 |`
`| Year 1 monitoring (12 months) | $360-$600 | $720-$1,200 |`
`| **Year-1 total installed + monitored** | **$11,160-$16,100** | **$17,720-$28,500** |`

`**Typical reasonable target for this project: $18,000-$22,000 installed and active, with first-year monitoring included.**`

`**What the cost difference reflects:**`
`- **Low-bid systems** typically use entry-level equipment (Fire-Lite ES-50X, Silent Knight 6700) with minimum device counts, conventional or limited-addressable architecture, single-path cellular, and a small monitoring company. Often work, but service after the install can be slow; firmware updates and parts may lag.`
`- **Quality bids** use better-supported equipment families (Notifier NFS-320, Edwards), full addressable architecture, dual-path communication, larger UL 827-certified central stations, and a contractor with a full service department. The premium buys faster service response, fewer false alarms, easier expansion when the kitchen reconfigures, and a panel that will still be supported in 10 years.`

`For a fine-dining concept the owner expects to operate for 10+ years, the quality bid is the better economic choice. The annual savings on false-alarm fees alone (Austin charges escalating fees for repeat false alarms from the same address) typically recover the premium within 3 years.`

`## 2.11 Ten Questions to Ask Every Fire Alarm Contractor`

`1. **"Do you hold a current Texas Department of Insurance State Fire Marshal's Office (TDI-SFMO) Fire Alarm Planning Superintendent license? What is the license number? Who is the technician of record on this project, and what is their license?"** Verify on the TDI-SFMO website. Operating without this license is a violation, and your project cannot legally pass acceptance.`
`2. **"Is your proposed Fire Alarm Control Panel listed to UL 864 11th edition? Provide the listing card."** Older panels may still be listed to 10th edition; this is acceptable but check that the panel is currently supported by the manufacturer.`
`3. **"Provide a complete input/output matrix and sequence of operations document with your bid."** Every input → every output, listed. If they can't, they are designing on the fly.`
`4. **"How will you handle the kitchen suppression interlock? Specifically: who runs the wire between the suppression control board and the FACP input module, who terminates both ends, and who is responsible if it fails the AFD acceptance test?"** The correct answer is them, them, and them — the fire alarm contractor.`
`5. **"Who pulls the fire alarm permit, and is the permit fee included in your bid?"** Should be the fire alarm contractor, included in bid.`
`6. **"What monitoring options do you offer? Is the central station UL 827 listed? Is it Five Diamond designated by TMA? Provide the contract terms in writing — initial term, auto-renewal, cancellation, escalation."** Negotiate the contract before signing.`
`7. **"What is your standard warranty on parts, on labor, and on programming? What is your service response time during business hours and after hours?"** 1 year parts/labor is minimum; 2 years is better. After-hours response in Austin should be ≤ 4 hours for fire alarm trouble.`
`8. **"What is the panel's spare capacity for future expansion? If we add 10 devices in 18 months, will the panel handle them, or will we need a new panel?"** Sized for 25-50% spare capacity is correct for a restaurant.`
`9. **"What is your annual inspection contract — price, scope, what's included, what's billed extra?"** NFPA 72 Chapter 14 inspection is annual. Price should include the test report submitted to The Compliance Engine on behalf of the City of Austin.`
`10. **"Provide three Austin-area restaurant fire alarm references with owner contacts, all installed in the past 24 months."** Call them. Ask about communication, schedule reliability, AFD acceptance pass rate, and post-install service.`

`## 2.12 Red Flags in a Fire Alarm Proposal`

`- **No license number cited.** Texas requires TDI-SFMO licensing. If the bid doesn't show a license number, walk.`
`- **Conventional system proposed for a 2,310 SF restaurant.** Possible but inferior; ask why and demand a written justification.`
`- **No input/output matrix or sequence of operations.** This is the design document; without it, the bid is an estimate, not a scope.`
`- **Kitchen suppression interlock listed as "by others" or unclear.** This is the integration that fails most often. The fire alarm contractor must own this scope end-to-end.`
`- **Single-path cellular communicator only**, in a building with marginal cellular signal. Field-test cellular signal at the FACP location before accepting; if iffy, require dual-path.`
`- **No duct smoke detection budgeted** despite an HVAC system over 2,000 CFM. IMC §606.2.1 violation; AFD will catch this at plan review and the owner pays for the change order.`
`- **Monitoring contract longer than 3 years** with auto-renewal and termination penalty. Negotiate down.`
`- **Panel sized to bare minimum** with no spare capacity. Future kitchen reconfigurations will require a panel replacement.`
`- **No remote annunciator at the front door** in a configuration where AFD requires one. AFD will require this; better to budget for it now.`
`- **No Knox Box in the bid.** It's required. Roughly $300-$700 line item.`
`- **The acceptance-test fee is "billed separately" or "T&M".** Should be a fixed fee, included in bid.`
`- **The contractor cannot name a recent A-2 restaurant project in Austin** with AFD acceptance.`
`- **Wholly subcontracted monitoring** to a non-UL 827 central station, or a station not Five Diamond. Acceptable in some cases but verify what you're getting.`
`- **No mention of NFPA 72 §10.6 battery calculations** in the submittal. Required deliverable.`
`- **No mention of duct detector HVAC shutdown sequence** (per IMC §606.4). Required.`

`# 3. CROSS-REFERENCES — INTERLOCKS THAT BRIDGE SECTION 1 AND SECTION 2`

`The two systems are not independent. The following interlocks make them function as one life-safety package. Each one must appear in **both** the suppression vendor's submittal **and** the fire alarm contractor's input/output matrix. If either submittal is missing one of these, the package is incomplete.`

`| # | Interlock / Signal | Originates In (Section 1) | Terminates In (Section 2) | Code Basis | Whose Scope |`
`|---|---|---|---|---|---|`
`| 1 | Kitchen suppression discharge → building alarm | Suppression control board, Form C dry contact on activation | Fire alarm input module, supervised, programmed as alarm | IFC §904.3.5; NFPA 72 §17.13; NFPA 96 | Suppression provides contact; fire alarm provides input module and wiring |`
`| 2 | Kitchen suppression trouble → supervisory | Suppression control board trouble contact | Fire alarm input, programmed as supervisory | NFPA 72; manufacturer | Suppression provides contact; fire alarm provides input module |`
`| 3 | Kitchen suppression discharge → gas shutoff | Mechanical cable release or 24V solenoid command | Mechanical gas valve or solenoid valve on gas main | NFPA 96 §10.4.1 | Suppression scope (mechanical valve); plumber installs valve in gas line |`
`| 4 | Kitchen suppression discharge → shunt trip breaker | Suppression control board electrical output | Shunt-trip breaker in electrical panel for kitchen heat-producing circuits | NFPA 96 §10.4.1 | Suppression provides spec; electrician installs breaker and wires |`
`| 5 | Kitchen suppression discharge → makeup air shutoff (internal MAU only) | Suppression control board output | Internal makeup air damper / fan disconnect | NFPA 96 §8.3.2 | Suppression + mechanical |`
`| 6 | Kitchen suppression discharge → exhaust fan stays on | No action — exhaust continues to run | (No fire alarm action) | NFPA 96 §8.2.3.1 | Suppression scope to verify; electrician to verify fan circuit |`
`| 7 | Manual pull at kitchen suppression pull station → suppression discharge → all of the above | Suppression manual pull (independent of fire alarm pull) | All of #1-#5 above | NFPA 96 §10.5 | Suppression scope |`
`| 8 | Building fire alarm activation (any cause) → optional gas shutoff | (None — originates in fire alarm) | Building gas solenoid valve on incoming gas main (best practice; not always required by code) | IFC §605.1; AFD discretion | Fire alarm + plumber |`
`| 9 | HVAC duct smoke detector activation → HVAC shutdown + supervisory at FACP | (None — originates in fire alarm) | HVAC unit fan disconnect; supervisory signal at FACP | IMC §606.4 | Fire alarm scope; mechanical provides contactor |`
`| 10 | Sprinkler waterflow → fire alarm activation → central station → AFD | (None — sprinkler is third subsystem) | Fire alarm input → notification → communicator | IFC §903.4 | Sprinkler contractor provides flow switch; fire alarm wires it |`
`| 11 | Sprinkler tamper → supervisory at FACP → central station | (None — sprinkler) | Fire alarm supervisory input → communicator | IFC §903.4 | Sprinkler + fire alarm |`
`| 12 | Manual reset required after any of the above | Suppression manual reset; FACP reset | FACP reset; gas valve manual reset; shunt-trip breaker manual reset | NFPA 96 §10.4.4; NFPA 72 | Both — owner trains staff on the reset sequence |`

`**The single document that captures all of this is the fire alarm contractor's Input/Output Matrix, signed and submitted to AFD as part of the construction documents.** When the owner reviews the fire alarm submittal, the question is simple: are all 12 of the above rows in the matrix? If yes, the design is complete. If not, send it back.`

`# RECOMMENDATIONS`

`**Before signing the GC contract:**`
`1. Get firebox dimensions in cubic feet, in writing, from the kitchen equipment supplier for every solid-fuel appliance. Determine whether any cross the 5 cu ft threshold under NFPA 96 §14.7.8.`
`2. Confirm with the landlord in writing: existing sprinkler infrastructure status, water service capacity at the meter, available electrical service to the FACP location, whether there is existing fire alarm wiring or a building panel.`
`3. Schedule a pre-design meeting with AFD plan review (free, informal) to confirm: sprinkler trigger interpretation given the planned occupant load, any AFD-specific solid-fuel requirements, Knox Box requirements, monitoring requirements.`

`**During design:**`
`4. Specify a CaptiveAire hood with CORE Protection (or equivalent integrated water-based system) for any solid-fuel station. Specify 600°F firestats. Specify a fixed water pipe per §14.7.9 if any firebox exceeds 5 cu ft.`
`5. Specify an addressable fire alarm system listed to UL 864 with dual-path cellular/IP communication and at least 25% spare device capacity.`
`6. Require both vendors to submit a coordinated input/output matrix covering the 12 interlocks listed in Section 3.`
`7. Require a documented coordination meeting (suppression + fire alarm + electrician + plumber + mechanical + GC) before any rough-in.`

`**Bid evaluation thresholds:**`
`8. Disqualify any suppression vendor that proposes a single wet-chemical cylinder as the sole solid-fuel suppression, or that uses 360°F/450°F links over a wood/charcoal station, or that lacks 5+ recent solid-fuel references in Texas, or that lacks TDI-SFMO licensing.`
`9. Disqualify any fire alarm contractor that cannot produce a TDI-SFMO Planning Superintendent license number, that proposes a conventional system without justification, that does not include the kitchen suppression interlock end-to-end in their scope, or that quotes a monitoring contract longer than 3 years with auto-renewal.`

`**Budget targets:**`
`10. Solid-fuel suppression installed: **$25,000-$45,000** (system + fixed water pipe coordination + commissioning), depending on number of stations and outdoor scope.`
`11. Fire alarm system installed and active: **$18,000-$25,000** (panel, devices, communicator, Knox Box, year-1 monitoring).`
`12. Annual ongoing fire-protection operating cost (suppression service + monthly hood cleaning + alarm monitoring + alarm inspection + permit renewals + extinguisher service): **$8,000-$12,000/year**.`

`**Thresholds that would change these recommendations:**`
`- If the occupant load can be definitively held below 100 (no bar program, tight seating count, written confirmation from the architect) **and** all HVAC units stay below 2,000 CFM return capacity, the fire alarm system requirement may not be triggered. This is unlikely for a fine-dining concept but worth checking.`
`- If no firebox exceeds 5 cu ft (small charbroiler, no smoker pit, no large grill), the fixed water pipe is not required and the suppression scope simplifies meaningfully.`
`- If the AHJ accepts a written CaptiveAire CORE Protection submittal as fully satisfying NFPA 96 Chapter 14 without a separate fixed water pipe (some AHJs do this when the integrated system has sufficient continuous water capacity), the project saves the plumbing tie-in scope. Get the AHJ position in writing before relying on it.`

`# CAVEATS`

`This document is a knowledge base for vendor evaluation, not a design document. It does not substitute for engineered drawings stamped by a Texas-licensed engineer or by a TDI-SFMO Planning Superintendent. Code citations refer to the editions of NFPA 96, NFPA 17A, NFPA 72, NFPA 101, IFC, and IMC currently adopted by the City of Austin (predominantly the 2021 editions with local amendments under Austin LDC Ch. 25-12 Art. 7); Austin's transition to the 2024 IFC was in process as of the date of this document. The owner should verify current adopted editions and any new local amendments with AFD plan review at project initiation.`

`Specific numerical thresholds (e.g., "40 psi at 5 GPM" for the §14.7.9 fixed water pipe, "24-hour standby plus 5 minutes alarm" for FACP batteries) reflect widely-cited values used by AHJs and equipment manufacturers; verify the precise current code language with the AHJ at plan review.`

`Cost ranges are 2026 Austin-market estimates derived from multiple Austin-area fire protection contractor public price guidance (FireTron, Impact Fire, Spectrum, ABC Fire Systems) and national industry averages (Koorsen, Buyerzone, Forbel). Actual quotes will vary with hood size, number of solid-fuel stations, building condition, and market timing. Always obtain three competitive bids; reject the lowest if it cannot answer the questions in §1.11 and §2.11.`

`Where vendor recommendations are made (e.g., CaptiveAire CORE for solid-fuel suppression), they reflect current industry consensus and the manufacturer's own published guidance, not an exclusive recommendation. Equivalent water-based systems from other manufacturers may be acceptable provided they are listed for solid fuel and accepted by the Austin AHJ.`

`The single point most likely to be contested at AFD plan review is whether a covered outdoor BBQ pit (if included in the program) requires its own NFPA 96-compliant hood and suppression. Resolve this with AFD in writing before construction begins.`
