pages.content:
`# Korean Fine Dining Restaurant — Plumbing, Grease Interceptor & Roof Penetration Knowledge Base`
`**Project: 207 E St Elmo Rd, Austin TX 78745**`
`**Companion Reference to: Solid Fuel Exhaust Ventilation Compliance Guide & Fire Suppression / Fire Alarm Compliance Guide**`

`---`

`## How to Use This Document`

`This is a single reference covering three interconnected scopes that will define the technical and financial backbone of the restaurant buildout: the City of Austin grease interceptor approval process (Section 1), the plumbing fixture rough-in and finish for kitchen, bar, and restrooms (Section 2), and the roof penetration coordination required by the LOI (Section 3). It is written for the owner — not a designer — so that you can read a vendor proposal, sit in a coordination meeting, and confidently push back when something is wrong.`

`A short cross-reference at the end identifies the decisions that bridge multiple sections (the dishwasher, the hood/MAU, restroom vent stacks) so you do not approve them in isolation.`

`---`

`# SECTION 1 — DOMAIN 3: GREASE INTERCEPTOR (AUSTIN WATER INDUSTRIAL WASTE)`

`## 1.1 Why This Section Comes First`

`Under Austin City Code Chapter 15-10 (Wastewater Regulations) and the Austin Water Industrial Waste (IW) program, **no commercial food preparation business may operate without a grease interceptor approved by Austin Water**. The approval process — administered by the IW Office under §15-10 and the IW grease interceptor design criteria last modified in March/April 2021 — is now embedded inside the City's Commercial Plan Review (CPR) process and must run **before** a plumber buys a tank, before the slab is poured around stub-outs, and before the kitchen equipment list is locked. Austin Water states this in unambiguous capital letters on its sizing page: **"Do not purchase a grease trap/interceptor without obtaining a building plan approval including an Industrial Waste approval letter."** Buying first exposes the owner to rejection and full replacement cost.`

`For a Korean fine dining restaurant with a commercial dishwasher, the rule is even more specific: **a minimum 500-gallon liquid-holding-capacity gravity grease interceptor (GGI) is mandatory**, and in most real-world cases the fixture-unit math will push the required size to 1,000–1,500 gallons.`

`## 1.2 The Austin Industrial Waste Approval Process — Step by Step`

`The IW process is no longer a separate appointment-driven track. As of the current configuration of the Austin Build + Connect (AB+C) portal, IW review is a parallel reviewer attached to the Commercial Plan Review submittal. The practical sequence:`

`1. **(Optional but recommended) Pre-application appointment.** Schedule a virtual or in-person appointment with IW through the Permitting and Development Center (PDC) appointments page. Use this to confirm sizing methodology, sample-port location, and whether the existing landlord stub-outs are in the right place. Walk-ins are no longer accepted.`
`2. **CPR submittal through AB+C.** Your architect/MEP submits the building plan set through the Commercial Plan Review intake. **Tell the intake staff to add Industrial Waste to the reviewer list** — this is a known failure point. The AB+C portal becomes the document-of-record for IW Approval Letters.`
`3. **IW plan review.** A Pretreatment Specialist (assigned by zip code; 78745 has a designated specialist) reviews the plumbing layout, fixture schedule, GI sizing calc, sample manhole location, vent layout, and manufacturer/model. They will issue plan review comments back through CPR.`
`4. **IW Approval Letter issued.** Once plans are clean, IW drafts and posts the IW Approval Letter to the project's AB+C record. **This letter — not a verbal sign-off — is the document the plumber uses to order the tank.** Austin Water explicitly warns that plans often change between cycles, so the plumber must download the final approved letter from AB+C.`
`5. **Building permit & plumbing trade permit issuance.** IW approval is a precondition; the plumbing permit cannot finalize without it.`
`6. **Excavation, set, and underground rough-in.** The tank is set, plumbed (waste in, vent, sample manhole on the effluent side), and prepared for inspection.`
`7. **Installation inspection.** The City's plumbing inspector verifies the installation; an IW Pretreatment Specialist may also inspect, particularly for first-time food-service tenants and for any non-standard configuration.`
`8. **Backfill, riser to grade, traffic-rated cover.**`
`9. **Pre-occupancy.** The owner must establish a service contract with a **City of Austin–permitted Liquid Waste Hauler** before the Certificate of Occupancy. Austin Water now expects a hauler relationship documented at opening.`
`10. **Operational compliance forever after.** Pumping every ≤90 days, manifests retained 3 years, FOG ≤200 mg/L at the sample port.`

`**Consequence of skipping IW pre-approval:** plan rejection, equipment rejection, re-excavation, full replacement, retroactive penalties, and — for an interceptor purchased that does not meet the new April 2021 GGI design criteria — the contractor and tank are simply turned away on inspection. There is no negotiating around it.`

``**IW contact:** `IndustrialWaste@austintexas.gov` / 512-974-7293. The mailing/physical address for IW correspondence is 6310 Wilhelmina Delco Dr., 3rd Floor, Austin, TX 78752.``

`## 1.3 Sizing — The Three-Step Formula and the 500-Gallon Floor`

`Austin Water uses a **three-step fixture-unit method** documented at` [`austintexas.gov/water/grease-trap-sizing-design-criteria`](http://austintexas.gov/water/grease-trap-sizing-design-criteria)`.`

`**Step 1 — Total Fixture Units (FU).** Each grease-bearing or potentially grease-bearing fixture is assigned an FU value based on the trap-arm (drain) size. For indirectly connected fixtures (those draining through a floor sink or hub drain — the standard configuration for commercial kitchen equipment):`

`| Fixture | 2" arm | 3" arm | 4" arm |`
`|---|---|---|---|`
`| 3-compartment sink | 4 | 6 | 8 |`
`| Dishwasher | — | 6 | 8 |`
`| Wok stove | 4 | 6 | 8 |`
`| Hand sink | 2 | 3 | 4 |`
`| Mop sink | 2 | 3 | 4 |`
`| Floor sink (cold/clear) | 2 | 3 | 4 |`

`Directly connected floor drains carry 2/3/4 FU at 2"/3"/4". **Garbage disposals/grinders have been prohibited in commercial kitchens in Austin since January 2008** — there is no FU value because they cannot be installed at all.`

`**Step 2 — Minimum flow rating in GPM.** Multiply total FU × 3 GPM. This is the Austin-specific multiplier (other Texas jurisdictions vary).`

`**Step 3 — Minimum liquid holding capacity.** Multiply GPM × 12 minutes (the total retention time = 7 minutes in compartment 1 + 5 minutes in compartment 2). Result is required tank volume in gallons.`

`**Worked sizing example for this restaurant (typical Korean fine dining kitchen, 563 SF):**`

`Assume the following fixtures plumbed to the GI through floor sinks/hub drains, with 3" trap arms unless noted:`

`| Fixture | Qty | FU each | FU total |`
`|---|---|---|---|`
`| 3-comp sink (3" arm) | 1 | 6 | 6 |`
`| Pre-rinse / scrap sink at dish (2" arm, indirect) | 1 | 4 | 4 |`
`| Commercial dishwasher (3" arm) | 1 | 6 | 6 |`
`| Wok / range / griddle floor sink (3" arm) | 2 | 6 | 12 |`
`| Prep sinks (2" arm each, indirect) | 2 | 4 | 8 |`
`| Mop sink (3" arm, direct) | 1 | 3 | 3 |`
`| Floor drains in kitchen (3" arm, direct) | 2 | 3 | 6 |`
`| Hand sinks — *not required to be plumbed to GI per Austin general design notes* | 2 | 0 | 0 |`

`**Total FU ≈ 45.** (A real fixture schedule may push this to 50–60 once every floor sink under refrigeration condensate, walk-in floor pan, ice machine, and beverage station is counted; cold/clear-water-only floor sinks count for sizing only when not 1"-lipped condensate-only.)`

`- Step 2: 45 × 3 = **135 GPM minimum flow rating**`
`- Step 3: 135 × 12 = **1,620 gallons minimum liquid capacity**`

`That math — without overriding judgment from the IW reviewer — points to a **1,500-gallon GGI** as the practical minimum for this kitchen, with 2,000 gallons a defensible upsize given live-fire cooking volume and the dishwasher load. **The 500-gallon "minimum-with-dishwasher" rule is a floor, not a target.** Austin Water explicitly reserves the right to require larger if peak loads warrant.`

`The 60/40 split means the first compartment is roughly 60% of the volume (delivering the 7-minute retention) and the second is 40% (5-minute retention). On a 1,500-gallon tank, that is approximately 900/600.`

`## 1.4 GGI vs. HGI — Why This Restaurant Gets a GGI`

`- **Gravity Grease Interceptor (GGI):** large, in-ground (or above-grade), two-compartment tank built per Austin's April 2021 criteria. Concrete or non-corrodible (HDPE/fiberglass/stainless) construction. Required for any food-service operation with a dishwasher or wok stove and for full-service restaurants generally.`
`- **Hydromechanical Grease Interceptor (HGI):** smaller, single-compartment device with vented flow control, ASME A112.14.3-compliant, flow-rated ≥75 GPM. Austin allows HGIs for **low-FOG operations** — coffee shops, sandwich shops, bakeries — and only where a dishwasher is not used. HGIs >500 gallons must also have the 60/40 split.`

`A Korean fine dining restaurant with a commercial dishwasher, wok, and live-fire cooking is unambiguously a GGI project. An HGI proposal from a plumber for this site is a red flag that the plumber has not read the Austin IW criteria.`

`## 1.5 GGI Design Requirements (Austin Water, March/April 2021 Criteria)`

`The IW criteria for GGI design are mandatory and not negotiable on a typical project:`

`1. Two compartments (extremely large units may have three).`
`2. **60/40 split** between compartments.`
`3. Compartment 1 retention ≥ 7 minutes at rated flow; compartment 2 retention ≥ 5 minutes.`
`4. **Inverts and vents external to the compartments.**`
`5. The inlet flowline must be ≥ 3" above the static water level.`
`6. The vent must be ≥ 3" above the static water level.`
`7. The inlet must enter near the half-height of the static water level; the outlet must be ≥ 12" above the tank floor.`
`8. Flow-diffusion features (diverter plate or "tee" piping) on inlet and between compartments and at outlet.`
`9. Concrete or non-corrodible material (lifespan 15–20+ years).`
`10. **Each compartment must be accessible for cleaning and inspection — no exceptions.** Manholes/risers must extend to grade.`
`11. **A sample manhole/sample port is required at end-of-pipe** — downstream of where the GI effluent and all sanitary waste lines combine, *before* connection to the City main. It must be accessible at all times (not in a drive lane, not in a creek, not buried). This is how Austin Water grab-samples for the 200 mg/L FOG limit.`

`**Engineered GGIs** (factory-built HDPE/fiberglass tanks) are allowed if they meet the 60/40 split, are non-corrodible, and may have internal or external inverts. This is a design accommodation for sites where a precast concrete tank cannot be set.`

`**Approved manufacturers** are listed in Austin Water's *Manufacturers List of Grease Trap or Grease Interceptor* (current revision dated 2024). Common approved suppliers familiar with Austin's criteria include **Schier (Big Foot GGI, GB-500-B specifically called out for the Austin market), Park-USA, Highland Tank, Watts, Mifab, Thermaco/Big Dipper (HGI applications only — not for this project), and Affordable Concrete Products**. Austin Water explicitly does not endorse manufacturers; the list confirms only that the company knows the criteria. **Do not order without confirming the specific model number against the IW Approval Letter.**`

`## 1.6 What "Stub-outs Provided" in the LOI Actually Means`

`The LOI states: "*Grease trap location is marked on plans, stub-outs provided, but final type and capacity are determined by City of Austin — provided and installed by tenant.*"`

`That sentence is doing a lot of work. Translated:`

`- **Landlord delivers:** a stubbed sanitary waste line, a vent connection, and (typically) a marked rough location for the GI on the site plan. That stub may be a capped pipe terminating at the demising wall, at the exterior slab edge, or in a marked area outside the building footprint.`
`- **Landlord does NOT deliver:** the tank, the excavation, the riser, the sample manhole, the cover, the connection from kitchen fixtures into the tank, or any sizing decision.`
`- **Tenant scope:** everything from fixture trap arms through the floor sinks/hub drains, through the in-slab waste piping, through the GI, through the sample manhole, to the connection point at the landlord's stub.`

`**Clarify in writing with the landlord before the GC mobilizes:**`

`1. Exact location and elevation (invert) of the sanitary stub.`
`2. Exact location and elevation of the vent stub (and whether it is independent or shared).`
`3. Pipe material and diameter of each stub.`
`4. Whether the slab area between the GI location and the stub is the landlord's pour or the tenant's pour.`
`5. Whether the depressed slab for the walk-in cooler conflicts with any underground GI piping route.`
`6. Confirmation that the marked GI location can accept the size IW will require (a 1,500-gallon precast concrete tank typically has a footprint near 5'×10' and 6'+ depth — verify the location can physically accept this).`

`If any of those answers are unclear, the GC cannot price the underground plumbing accurately and your bids will diverge wildly.`

`## 1.7 Installation Scope — What a Real GGI Bid Should Look Like`

`A complete commercial-plumber bid for the GI scope will line-item:`

`- Excavation (including any rock or saw-cutting of the existing slab if the GI is sited within the building footprint, which is rare in Austin restaurant projects but does happen; almost always exterior here).`
`- Bedding sand / pea gravel.`
`- Tank delivery and setting (typically requires a crane or large excavator; coordination with delivery access).`
`- Inlet/outlet piping and connections.`
`- Inlet flow-diffusion details and inter-compartment "tee" piping per Austin spec.`
`- External venting (to grade or through-roof — see Section 3 cross-reference).`
`- Sample manhole construction (precast structure, marked, accessible).`
`- Risers to grade with cast-iron or composite traffic-rated cover (H-20 rated if any vehicular traffic possible).`
`- Cleanouts upstream and at sample manhole.`
`- Backfill compaction in lifts.`
`- As-built drawing, hydrostatic test, IW inspection coordination.`
`- Final grade and surface restoration.`

`**Typical Austin-market 2026 cost range** for an exterior 1,000–1,500 gallon precast concrete GGI installed: **$15,000–$30,000 all-in** (tank $4,500–$10,000; excavation/labor/connections/sample manhole $8,000–$18,000; permits/coordination $500–$2,000). HDPE engineered units (Schier Big Foot 1500) trend $2,000–$5,000 higher on the tank side but can save on installation in tight or rocky sites. Plan for the higher end ($25,000–$35,000) if the IW Approval Letter requires 2,000+ gallons or if the marked location requires demolition of existing paving.`

`A bid below $12,000 for a 1,000-gallon-plus install in Austin in 2026 is almost certainly missing scope.`

`## 1.8 Inspection — When Austin Water Must Be Onsite`

`Austin Water IW staff are present at two points where their absence will void the work:`

`1. **Installation inspection** before backfill. The inspector verifies inlet/outlet inverts, flow diffusion, vent compliance, sample manhole location and depth, structural integrity, and whether the manufacturer/model matches the IW Approval Letter. **Do not let the GC backfill before this inspection** — re-excavation to verify is extraordinarily expensive and on the GC.`
`2. **First and ongoing pumping/cleaning inspection.** Per Austin's pretreatment FAQ, "an Industrial Waste staff member must be present at the time of service to perform the grease trap inspection while it is empty." The owner coordinates the IW staff appointment to align with the licensed hauler's pump-out. This continues forever — the IW inspector periodically attends pump-outs throughout the life of the business.`

`**Failure modes** at installation inspection include: inverts wrong, no sample manhole, vent missing or internal to compartments, undersized tank vs. IW letter, manufacturer/model substitution, riser not to grade, cleanouts missing. Each of these triggers a re-inspection fee and typically 2–4 weeks of schedule slip.`

`## 1.9 Operational Compliance — The Forever Rules`

`Once open, the owner inherits a permanent set of obligations under Austin City Code §15-10:`

`| Rule | Citation | Detail |`
`|---|---|---|`
`| **Pump every ≤90 days** | §15-10-197 | Or sooner if FOG + solids in the final compartment reach 50% of the wetted height |`
`| **50% wetted-height trigger** | §15-10-197 | Measured from tank floor to invert of outlet pipe — this is the **current** rule. Some legacy or third-party literature still cites a 25% rule; for Austin specifically, the City Code and IW guidance reference the 50% threshold. The 25% number appears in some other Texas jurisdictions and in older industry materials — do not let a service vendor invoice you for "early" pumps based on the wrong threshold. |`
`| **Manifest retention** | §15-10-165(B) | All hauler manifest records must be retained on-site for 3 years and produced on inspection |`
`| **Permitted hauler only** | §15-10-197 | Only haulers holding a current City of Austin Liquid Waste Hauler permit may pump and transport |`
`| **FOG discharge limit** | §15-10-23 | Instantaneous max 200 mg/L at the sample port |`
`| **Penalty** | §15-10-22 / Class C misdemeanor | Up to **$2,000 per day per violation**; cost recovery for sanitary sewer overflows |`
`| **No enzymes/microbial additives in the GI** | §15-10-22(23) | The direct addition of enzymes, chemicals, or microbial agents to a grease trap is prohibited in Austin. **This differs from Houston**, which permits certain approved additives. Limited use in upstream floor drains is allowed only if it does not interfere with GI separation. |`
`| **No food grinders/disposals** | January 2008 prohibition | Garbage disposals are flatly prohibited in Austin commercial kitchens — design around food scrap collection systems and a make-up flow ≤1.28 GPM if a food digestor is added later |`

`**Inspection failures** typically take the form of: trap >50% full, no manifests on file, manifests not from a permitted hauler, FOG sample >200 mg/L, evidence of additive use, or a non-functioning sample port. Each is enforceable as a daily violation.`

`## 1.10 The 12 Questions to Ask a Commercial Plumber About the Grease Interceptor`

`1. How many Austin Water IW approval letters have you obtained in the last two years, and can you share two recent project addresses?`
`2. Walk me through your sizing calc: what FU did you assign each fixture, what is the GPM, and what is the resulting minimum gallons?`
`3. Are you proposing a GGI or HGI, and why? (Correct answer for this project: GGI.)`
`4. Which manufacturer and model number, and is it on Austin Water's current Manufacturers List?`
`5. How does your design meet the April 2021 GGI criteria — specifically the 60/40 split, 7+5 retention, external inverts and vents, and inlet flow diffusion?`
`6. Where will the sample manhole sit, and is it downstream of where GI effluent and sanitary lines combine?`
`7. How is the GI vent routed — through the roof, and have you coordinated with the roofer on the penetration? (Cross-references Section 3.)`
`8. What is your riser-to-grade approach, and will the cover be H-20 traffic-rated?`
`9. How will you sequence inspection scheduling so the City inspector arrives before backfill?`
`10. What is included vs. excluded — excavation, slab cut, sample manhole, traffic cover, backfill compaction, surface restoration, hydrostatic test?`
`11. Will you download the IW Approval Letter from the AB+C portal yourself, or rely on the GC to forward it? (Correct answer: the plumber should pull it directly.)`
`12. What is your re-inspection / re-work guarantee if the installation fails IW or City plumbing inspection due to your work?`

`## 1.11 What to Bring to the Industrial Waste Submittal — Owner's Checklist`

`When the architect submits to CPR with IW on the reviewer list, the package should include:`

`- Cover sheet with a signature line for IW`
`- Site plan showing GI location, water meter, water/wastewater service connections, and sample port location`
`- Plumbing floor plan to scale with all fixtures labeled, pipe diameters and materials called out, and the GI shown`
`- GI sizing calculation (the three-step calc) with all FU shown`
`- GI manufacturer cut sheet matching a model on the Manufacturers List`
`- Menu (or for fine dining, a representative menu describing cooking processes — IW uses this to confirm GI is required and to assess FOG load)`
`- Equipment schedule including the dishwasher (high-temp vs. low-temp), three-comp, prep sinks, wok station, and any food-waste collection or digestor system (which requires a separate Preliminary Request for Food Digestor Installation Form)`
`- Confirmation that no garbage disposal is included`
`- If proposing a variance from any criterion: engineering justification sealed by a Texas P.E.`

`## 1.12 Cost & Bid Red Flags`

`| Red flag | What it means |`
`|---|---|`
`| Plumber proposes a 100–500 gallon HGI | Has not read Austin's criteria; will be rejected |`
`| No mention of IW Approval Letter in scope | Will buy a tank before approval; replacement risk |`
`| Total bid <$12,000 for a 1,000+ gallon installed GGI | Underscoping; expect change orders |`
`| Tank manufacturer/model not specified | Unable to verify against Manufacturers List |`
`| No sample manhole line item | Will fail IW inspection |`
`| Vent routed internal to compartments | Violates April 2021 criteria |`
`| "We'll figure out the size after we're under construction" | Wrong sequence; IW approval must precede purchase |`
`| Pumping contract bundled with installation, with the same vendor | Acceptable, but confirm hauler holds a current City of Austin Liquid Waste Hauler permit |`
`| Install bid does not include hydrostatic test | Common failure point; insist on it |`

`The cost of getting it wrong: re-excavation and tank replacement on a 1,500-gallon GGI in Austin runs **$25,000–$50,000+** plus 6–10 weeks of schedule loss, and the City may issue penalties for unpermitted work.`

`# SECTION 2 — DOMAIN 4: PLUMBING FIXTURES (KITCHEN, BAR, RESTROOMS)`

`## 2.1 The Code Backdrop for Austin`

`Austin's plumbing code is layered. As of mid-2026 you should expect the project to be reviewed under:`

`- **Austin's adopted plumbing code:** Effective July 10, 2025, the City of Austin adopted the **2024 Uniform Plumbing Code (UPC) with Local Amendments** (Ordinance 20250410-042). The 2024 UPC replaces the 2021 UPC that had been in effect since September 1, 2021. **Austin uses the UPC, not the IPC** — confirm with your plumber and architect because they sometimes default to IPC habits from other Texas markets. The 2021 IPC remains a useful reference but is not the governing code.`
`- **Mechanical:** 2024 Uniform Mechanical Code (UMC) with local amendments, effective July 10, 2025.`
`- **Building/Energy/Fire:** 2021 IBC/IECC/IFC (adopted September 1, 2021); the 2024 IBC/IECC was also adopted under Ordinance 20250410-045 effective July 10, 2025 — verify with DSD which edition applies to your permit submittal date.`
`- **Electrical:** 2023 NEC (NFPA 70), effective September 11, 2023.`
`- **Texas Food Establishment Rules (TFER)**, 25 TAC Chapter 228, which adopt the 2017 FDA Food Code by reference.`
`- **Texas Accessibility Standards (TAS)** administered by TDLR — closely tracks 2010 ADA Standards.`
`- **Austin City Code Chapter 15-10** (wastewater) for grease and indirect-waste connections.`

`## 2.2 Kitchen — 563 SF, Live Fire Cooking`

`### 2.2.1 Three-Compartment Sink`

`TFER/§228 (adopting FDA Food Code) requires a 3-compartment sink in any establishment that washes, rinses, and sanitizes utensils and equipment manually. **The presence of a commercial dishwasher does not eliminate the 3-comp requirement** — this is a frequent owner misconception. The 3-comp is the backup and the primary for items that cannot run through a dish machine (sheet pans, large pots, knives, sharpening tools, blender pitchers).`

`A compliant spec for a fine dining Korean kitchen:`

`- Stainless steel, 16-gauge or heavier (14-gauge for the heaviest service); NSF-listed`
`- Each compartment large enough to accept the largest piece of equipment to be washed (size to your largest stockpot, jeotgal containers, or banchan bins)`
`- **Two integral drainboards, one at each end** — soiled side and clean side. TFER requires this; a single drainboard is non-compliant unless adjacent to the warewashing machine`
`- Faucet: 8" wall-mount, swing spout reaching all three compartments; commercial grade (T&S Brass B-0231 series, Fisher 8030 series, Chicago Faucets, Encore are typical)`
`- Pre-rinse arm sometimes mounted at the 3-comp — separate from the dishwasher pre-rinse if dish room is distinct`
`- **Indirect waste**: each compartment drains through an air gap to a floor sink, then to the grease interceptor. Direct connection to the sanitary line is prohibited under UPC for this fixture.`
`- Hot water at the faucet ≥110°F per TFER (most operations design to 120°F supply)`

`What to verify on submittal: manufacturer cut sheet, gauge, dimension of each compartment, drainboard length, NSF mark, faucet model, and indirect-waste detail showing air gap to floor sink.`

`### 2.2.2 Pre-Rinse Spray Valve`

`The federal energy conservation standard (10 CFR 431.266, effective January 28, 2019) caps pre-rinse spray valves at flow rates between 1.00 and 1.28 GPM at 60 psi depending on spray force class. **EPA's WaterSense voluntary 1.28 GPM specification was sunset January 1, 2019** because DOE adopted the threshold as the federal floor. Practical spec:`

`- 1.07–1.28 GPM (T&S Brass B-0107/B-0108, Fisher 2949, Krowne Royal Series are common)`
`- Hose length: 36–44" stainless flex`
`- Trigger or push-button handle with auto-shutoff`
`- Mounted on the soiled-dish side of the dishwasher rack`
`- Separate cold and hot supply lines stubbed at 1/2" with shut-offs`

`The plumber roughs in: hot supply, cold supply, vacuum breaker, mounting (deck or wall), and indirect drain to the same floor sink that serves the dish station.`

`### 2.2.3 Handwashing Sinks`

`TFER §228.147 / §228.181 requires **handwash sinks conveniently located in the food preparation area**, used **only for handwashing**. Rule of thumb (and Dallas/most Texas city interpretations): one handwash sink within 25 linear feet of any food prep area, plus one in or adjacent to the dish room. For a 563 SF kitchen with a cookline, prep, and dish, plan **two dedicated handwash sinks minimum** (one at the cookline, one at prep/dish).`

`- Faucet must deliver **water at ≥100°F (TFER); 110°F per local Dallas-style amendments and Austin's UPC defaults** through a mixing valve or combination faucet. Steam-mixing valves are not permitted.`
`- Activation: knee valve, foot pedal, wrist blade, or sensor — sensor is most common in fine dining for hygiene and aesthetics. Manual single-handle is acceptable but staff-training-dependent.`
`- Soap dispenser and disposable towel dispenser must be coordinated with the plumber (mounting), the GC (blocking), and the millwork team`
`- Handwash sinks are **not required to be plumbed to the grease interceptor** under Austin's general design notes — they may drain directly to sanitary`
`- Each must have a sign reminding employees to wash hands`

`### 2.2.4 Floor Drains and Floor Sinks`

`A live-fire Korean kitchen needs aggressive floor drainage. Plan locations:`

`- Under or adjacent to the 3-comp sink (floor sink receiving indirect waste)`
`- Under or adjacent to the dishwasher (floor sink with air gap to dish drain)`
`- At the cookline — a floor drain or floor trough is essential given wash-down practice with live-fire cooking; coordinate with the hood manufacturer for integrated floor-trough options`
`- Inside or just outside the walk-in cooler (consider waterproofing of slab depression)`
`- At the mop sink/janitor closet`
`- Under any ice machine or large condensate-producing equipment (indirect waste, "clear waste" floor sink with 1" lip)`
`- Under prep sinks`

`Slope: **1/4" per foot to drain** (UPC and TFER both reference). Cast iron is preferred over PVC for kitchens because of grease, hot water, and durability — and because PVC under live-fire and grease loads can fail prematurely. Trap primers are required on every floor drain that may go dry; without them, sewer gas backflows are guaranteed (and a TFER violation).`

`**Connection routing — the critical decision:**`
`- Floor sinks/floor drains receiving grease-bearing wastewater (3-comp, dishwasher, prep sinks, cookline floor sink, mop sink under TFER reading) **route to the grease interceptor**`
`- Floor drains under ice machines, beverage condensate, walk-in cooler condensate (cold/clear) may drain to sanitary, but per Austin design notes can be routed through the GI without counting against sizing **provided they have a 1" lip** indicating cold/clear-only`
`- Restroom floor drains: sanitary only (never GI)`

`### 2.2.5 Commercial Dishwasher Rough-In`

`The restaurant uses a commercial dishwasher; for fine dining, this should be a **high-temperature sanitizing machine** (final rinse 180°F at the manifold delivering 160°F at the dish surface, per FDA Food Code and NSF/ANSI 3). Low-temperature chemical sanitizing machines exist but are not preferred for fine dining because of chemical residue concerns and reduced grease-cutting performance.`

`Plumbing rough-in:`
`- **Dedicated hot water line** — typically 3/4" supply, 140–180°F to the booster heater (or the building hot water at 140°F if the booster is internal to the machine)`
`- **Booster heater connection** — internal boosters require a 208/240V electrical feed; external boosters (Hatco, Champion) are typical for door-type and conveyor machines and require their own water and power`
`- **Drain to grease interceptor via air gap or air break** — UPC requires indirect waste; the dishwasher discharge falls into a floor sink that routes to the GI`
`- **Vent** — the dishwasher hood vent (if fitted) is exhaust, not plumbing; the drain vent is plumbing scope`
`- **Backflow prevention** at the supply`
`- **Confirm building hot water capacity** — a 50-gallon storage water heater is the floor; the 2017 FDA Food Code (adopted by TFER) and Austin amendments require hot water generation sufficient for peak demand, which for this kitchen plus dishwasher plus prep sinks plus three handwashes likely means **80–120 gallon storage with a recovery rate matching dish machine GPH consumption**`

`If the dishwasher discharge water exceeds 150°F entering the GI, a **drain tempering valve** is required (Schier specifically calls this out). Dishwasher waste enters the GI hot, and without tempering it impairs FOG separation and shortens tank life.`

`### 2.2.6 Mop Sink / Janitor Closet`

`Required by TFER and by Austin code as a "service sink" — the only sink permitted for disposal of mop water and janitorial liquid waste. Specifications:`

`- Floor-mounted, 24"×24" or 24"×36" terrazzo or molded composite (Fiat MSB-2424, Mustee, Florestone)`
`- Hot and cold mixing faucet with hose-thread spout, vacuum breaker, integral wall brace`
`- 3" drain to floor sink, then to GI (mop sinks count as grease-bearing for IW sizing)`
`- Located out of the food path, often near the back-of-house`

`Why it matters: TFER violation if missing or used as a hand sink; health code citation if dirty mop water is dumped in the 3-comp or hand sink.`

`### 2.2.7 Indirect vs. Direct Waste — The Concept That Matters Most`

`**Direct waste**: a fixture's drain runs hard-piped through a trap to the sanitary system.`
`**Indirect waste**: a fixture's drain terminates above a receptor (floor sink, hub drain) with an air gap or air break — there is no direct connection to the sanitary system.`

`UPC and Austin local amendments require **indirect waste for**:`
`- Three-compartment sinks`
`- Prep sinks`
`- Commercial dishwashers`
`- Ice machines`
`- Walk-in cooler condensate`
`- Refrigeration drip pans`
`- Beverage station condensate / soda gun drains`

`**Direct waste is allowed for**:`
`- Hand sinks`
`- Mop sinks`
`- Floor drains (themselves)`
`- Toilets, urinals, lavatories`

`The reason: indirect waste prevents sanitary backflow from contaminating food-contact equipment. A plumber who proposes direct connection of a 3-comp or dishwasher to sanitary in Austin has either misread the code or is cutting corners.`

`## 2.3 Bar — Within the 605 SF Bar/Entry/Circulation Zone`

`### 2.3.1 Back Bar Ice Bin Drain`

`**Connects to sanitary, NOT to the grease interceptor.** The ice bin is a "clear waste" fixture — melted ice and beverage residue are not grease-bearing. Compliant install:`

`- Bar sink waste runs through a trap and indirect-waste line (air gap)`
`- Terminates over a floor sink or hub drain in the back bar slab area`
`- That floor sink ties to sanitary`

`If a plumber routes the ice bin to the GI, you are paying to oversize the GI for water that does not need treatment, and you may get a violation for routing non-grease-bearing waste through pretreatment without authorization.`

`### 2.3.2 Glass Wash Sink and Bar Hand Sink`

`Texas health code reading and most AHJs (Austin DSD's interpretation aligns) require a **3-compartment sink at the bar** for manual glass washing **even if an automatic glass washer is present**, unless the AHJ accepts a glass washer plus a single bar dump sink as equivalent. The conservative spec is 3-compartment plus glass washer.`

`**Each bar must have its own dedicated handwash sink**, separate from the glass-wash sink. This is a frequent and costly miss in fine dining bar design where the bartender's "sink" is assumed to count for everything. Spec:`

`- Dedicated bar handwash with hot/cold mixing faucet, ≥100°F hot water`
`- Soap and towel dispenser`
`- Drains to sanitary (not GI)`

`### 2.3.3 Beer / Beverage / Soda Plumbing`

`**Plumbing scope:**`
`- Cold water supply to the glycol chiller (if used) — typically 1/2" supply`
`- Floor drain or floor sink near the keg cooler / draft tower base`
`- Drain for the soda BIB room (Coca-Cola or Pepsi typically requires a floor drain, water supply for carbonator, electrical, and sometimes a dedicated floor sink for any condensate)`

`**Equipment scope (NOT plumbing):**`
`- Beer lines themselves, glycol lines, FOBs, towers, taps, regulators`
`- Soda lines (BIB to gun), CO2 plumbing, syrup pumps`

`**Boundary**: the plumber stubs water, drain, and provides the floor sink or floor drain. Beverage line scope belongs to the beverage equipment installer (Micro Matic, Perlick service, or the beverage distributor's tech). Coordinate the locations during rough-in or the beverage installer will be drilling concrete after the slab is finished.`

`## 2.4 Restrooms — 154 SF Total Bathroom Footprint, Slab Leave-Out`

`The LOI delivers a rough slab opening only; the tenant builds out from slab up. With 154 SF total, the realistic footprint allocations are:`

`- **Two ADA-compliant single-user (unisex) restrooms**, ~70–77 SF each, OR`
`- **One ADA-compliant unisex + one standard (still TAS-compliant) restroom**`

`For a fine dining Korean restaurant where the restrooms are a design touchpoint and where occupant load (calculated from dining + bar area) likely lands in the 50–100 person range, **two single-user unisex rooms is almost always the right answer** — both ADA-accessible. This avoids gendered-restroom conflicts, simplifies the plan, allows higher-end finish detailing, and aligns with current Austin and national fine dining design trends.`

`**Occupant load and fixture count** are governed by the IPC table referenced in IBC Chapter 29 / UPC Chapter 4 as adopted by Austin. For an A-2 occupancy (restaurant) at this size, the minimum fixture count typically lands at 1 water closet + 1 lavatory per gender at this occupant load, or 2 unisex single-user toilet rooms (which IBC §1109.2.1/§1108.2.1 expressly permits and which most jurisdictions accept as equivalent).`

`### 2.4.1 Floor-Mounted vs. Wall-Hung Toilets`

`| | Floor-mounted | Wall-hung |`
`|---|---|---|`
`| Aesthetic for fine dining | Standard, conservative | Cleaner lines, contemporary, preferred for high-end Korean fine dining |`
`| Plumbing rough-in | 12" rough from finished wall; floor flange | **In-wall carrier system required** — Geberit Duofix, Sloan, Zurn Z1201/Z1202, Jay R. Smith 0211Y series; needs 2×6 (minimum) framing depth, often 2×8 |`
`| Cleaning | Hard to clean around base | Floor below is open — easier wash-down |`
`| Cost (fixture + carrier + labor) | $400–$900 fixture; $200–$400 install labor | $700–$2,500 fixture; **$500–$1,200 carrier**; $400–$700 install labor; net premium $800–$1,800/fixture |`
`| Maintenance | Direct access to flush valve and trap | Carrier access through behind-wall panel; harder for in-place repair |`
`| ADA | Standard | Carrier height adjustable to ADA 17–19" seat height |`

`**Recommendation for this project:** wall-hung toilets in both restrooms, with a Geberit Duofix or Sloan in-wall carrier. Pair with **Duravit, Toto Aquia or Toto Carlyle II, Kohler Veil, or Villeroy & Boch Subway 2.0** for fine dining design language. The carrier premium is a known cost; the design payoff is significant in a guest-facing bathroom.`

`Verify with the GC that the demising/restroom walls will be framed with ≥2×6 (preferably 2×8) at all carrier locations and that solid blocking is installed before drywall — retrofitting a carrier into a 2×4 wall is impossible and will require demolition.`

`### 2.4.2 Commercial vs. Residential Fixtures — Flush Valves vs. Tank Toilets`

`**Common misconception**: that Austin's plumbing code requires flushometer (commercial flush-valve) toilets in every restaurant. It does not. The UPC and Austin amendments classify fixtures as "public" or "private" by use. A small fine dining single-user toilet room is acceptable with either:`

`- A **flushometer-type wall-hung toilet** (Sloan Royal, Zurn Z6000) — high-traffic, durable, no tank`
`- A **dual-flush tank-type wall-hung** (Toto Aquia, Duravit DuraStyle, Kohler Veil) — quieter, more residential aesthetic, 1.28/1.6 GPF or lower`

`For a 50–100 occupant fine dining restaurant with two unisex single-user rooms, **tank-type or in-wall-cistern wall-hung toilets are appropriate and common**. They look better, are quieter (a meaningful consideration in a small-footprint restaurant where the bathroom is adjacent to the dining room), and code-compliant. Reserve flushometer toilets for higher-volume operations (fast casual, multi-stall public restrooms).`

`### 2.4.3 ADA / Texas Accessibility Standards Compliance`

`For each unisex single-user restroom:`

`- **60" diameter clear turning space** (or T-shape within 60"×60") that does not overlap fixtures`
`- **30"×48" clear floor space** at lavatory (forward approach) and at toilet`
`- **Toilet centerline 16–18" from the side wall**; seat height 17–19" above finished floor`
`- **Side grab bar** 42" minimum, mounted 33–36" above finished floor, located 12" max from rear wall, extending 54" minimum from rear wall`
`- **Rear grab bar** 36" minimum, 33–36" above floor, extending 12" on one side and 24" on the other from the toilet centerline`
`- **Mirror**: bottom edge ≤40" above finished floor`
`- **Lavatory rim** ≤34" above floor; knee clearance 27" min, 11–25" depth; pipes insulated or guarded`
`- **Faucet**: lever, push, electronic, or other operable without tight grasping/pinching/twisting and ≤5 lbs operating force`
`- **Door**: 32" minimum clear width when open 90°; lever or other compliant hardware operable with closed fist`
`- **Door swing must not encroach on the 60" turning space** — this is the #1 ADA failure in small commercial restrooms; if the door must swing in, the room footprint must enlarge`
`- **Tactile and Braille signage** mounted 48–60" to baseline of highest character, on the latch side of the door, on the wall (not the door)`

`154 SF total split into two ~77 SF rooms is tight but feasible. The architect must size each room with door-swing geometry verified before the layout is locked. If the math does not work, the choices are: outward-swinging doors, a single larger ADA unisex plus a smaller non-ADA second room (legal only in limited scenarios — verify with TAS RAS), or expanding the bathroom footprint.`

`### 2.4.4 Lavatory / Restroom Sink`

`For a fine dining design tier, choices in order of design impact and complexity:`

`- **Vessel sink on a console or floating counter**: highest design impact; trap and supplies must be detailed for a clean look (often chrome P-traps, supplied with offset extensions); ADA compliance requires careful counter/knee-clearance design`
`- **Undermount in stone or solid-surface counter**: classic fine dining look; easier ADA compliance; trap concealed`
`- **Wall-hung lavatory** (Duravit Vero Air, Kohler Purist): minimalist, easiest ADA compliance; trap exposed (specify chrome P-trap and insulated drain/supply per ADA)`
`- **Wall-mount faucet** (deck mount also fine): sensor or single-lever; for fine dining, lever style is more design-forward than sensor`

`Hot water delivery: a small **point-of-use water heater** (2.5–6 gallon, electric) under each lavatory is preferred over running a long hot-water loop from the kitchen heater — faster delivery, reduced energy waste, simpler design.`

`### 2.4.5 Bidet Seats / Smart Toilets`

`If the design calls for a bidet seat (Toto Washlet, Kohler C³ — increasingly common in Korean fine dining for cultural alignment):`

`- Requires a **GFCI electrical outlet within 1 ft of the toilet**, behind or beside the unit`
`- Requires a **cold water tee at the toilet supply** (most bidet seats run off cold water; some have internal heaters)`
`- **Plan this from day one** — adding a bidet seat after the wall is closed means cutting tile to install the outlet and tap the supply, a $600–$1,500 retrofit that should be a $100 rough-in if planned`

`### 2.4.6 Floor Drain in Restroom`

`**Restroom floor drains are not required** for restaurant restrooms in Austin under UPC, but they are commonly installed for cleaning. If included:`

`- Slope finish floor 1/4" per foot to drain`
`- Trap primer required (otherwise sewer gas)`
`- Waterproof membrane on the slab leave-out before tile`
`- Sanitary connection only — never to GI`

`For 154 SF total, a single floor drain in each restroom is a reasonable inclusion; some fine dining operators omit them in favor of fully sealed, no-drain restrooms cleaned with damp mop only.`

`### 2.4.7 Restroom Ventilation — Plumbing Coordination`

`Each restroom requires mechanical exhaust per UMC (75 CFM minimum continuous or 50 CFM intermittent for single-user). The exhaust fan is mechanical scope, not plumbing. **The plumbing vent stack** for the toilets and lavatories is plumbing scope and **terminates through the roof** — coordinate location with the roofer (Section 3) and with the architect to avoid the vent stack landing in a soffit or aesthetically prominent location.`

`Vent stacks for two restrooms can typically be combined to a single 2"–3" vent through the roof, depending on the 2024 UPC venting tables and the layout. Confirm with the plumber.`

`## 2.5 The 12 Questions to Ask Your Commercial Plumber Before Awarding the Plumbing Contract`

`1. How many Austin restaurant projects have you completed in the last 24 months, with what AHJ outcomes? (Looking for: clean track record, first-time pass on IW and DSD plumbing inspections.)`
`2. Are you bidding to UPC 2024 with current Austin local amendments?`
`3. How are you handling indirect waste — show me the air-gap detail at the dishwasher and at each prep/3-comp sink.`
`4. Where are floor sinks and floor drains located, and which route to the GI vs. sanitary?`
`5. What is your handwash sink count, and where are they located relative to food prep areas? (Confirm 25-ft rule.)`
`6. What is your specification for the dishwasher booster heater — internal or external, GPH, kW, and is the electrical capacity adequate?`
`7. For the restrooms, are you specifying floor-mounted or wall-hung toilets, and which carrier system? Is wall framing depth confirmed with the GC?`
`8. How are restroom plumbing vent stacks routed to the roof, and have you coordinated with the roofer's preferred vendor on penetrations?`
`9. What is your trap-primer schedule for floor drains?`
`10. What is your pre-rinse spray valve specification (GPM)?`
`11. How are you handling the 2" domestic water service from the building tap to fixtures — material (Type L copper, PEX, CPVC), sizing, isolation valves at each fixture group?`
`12. Provide a separate line for the bar's dedicated handwash sink, glass-wash sink, ice bin drain (sanitary), and beverage room rough-in.`

`## 2.6 Realistic 2026 Austin Cost Ranges`

`For a 2,310 SF Korean fine dining restaurant of this configuration:`

`| Scope | Range |`
`|---|---|`
`| **Plumbing rough-in** (in-slab waste/vent, water distribution, no fixtures, no GI) | $30,000–$55,000 |`
`| **Fixtures and trim** (kitchen sinks, faucets, pre-rinse, hand sinks, mop sink, floor drains, bar fixtures) | $18,000–$32,000 |`
`| **Restroom fixtures + carriers** (2 unisex, wall-hung, lavatory, accessories) | $8,000–$18,000 |`
`| **Dishwasher rough-in + booster heater** | $4,000–$9,000 |`
`| **Water heater(s) + recirc** | $5,000–$12,000 |`
`| **Grease interceptor (1,500 gal GGI installed, see §1.7)** | $20,000–$30,000 |`
`| **TOTAL plumbing scope (incl. GI, excl. kitchen equipment cost)** | **$85,000–$150,000+** |`

`The wider Austin restaurant buildout market data (TM International / EB3 Construction / industry estimating) puts fine dining buildouts at $300–$600/SF; for a 2,310 SF project that is $700,000–$1,400,000 all-in. Plumbing is typically 8–15% of that, which lines up with the table above.`

`# SECTION 3 — DOMAIN 13: ROOF PENETRATIONS`

`## 3.1 The LOI Mechanism and Why It Matters`

`The LOI is explicit: **"Any roof penetrations required by tenant must be patched using landlord's preferred vendor at tenant's cost."** This single clause does several things at once:`

`- It protects the **roof manufacturer warranty** (Carlisle, GAF, Firestone/Holcim Elevate, Versico, Johns Manville) on the new combination corrugated metal + TPO roof — most TPO manufacturer warranties (10–30 year NDL) require that all penetrations and repairs be performed by **manufacturer-certified contractors**, often a specific shortlist.`
`- It transfers cost responsibility to the tenant for every cut, every flashing detail, every patch.`
`- It puts the tenant in a **single-source pricing position** — you have no leverage to bid the work because the landlord has named the vendor.`
`- It shifts the coordination burden to the GC, who must sequence the hood contractor, plumber, electrician, mechanical contractor, and the landlord's roofer in the right order.`

`This is a normal commercial-lease provision. It is not predatory. But it requires active management or you will pay 2× and still get callbacks.`

`## 3.2 Inventory of Penetrations Required for This Restaurant`

`| Penetration | Approximate size | Approximate weight | Structural support | Code basis |`
`|---|---|---|---|---|`
`| Solid-fuel exhaust fan curb (upblast, hinged, listed UL 762, with grease containment) | 36"×36" to 48"×48" curb opening | Curb + fan + grease box: 250–500 lb | Engineered curb with structural framing tied to roof structure; load review by structural engineer | NFPA 96 §7.8, Ch. 14; IMC/UMC §510, §517 |`
`| Make-up Air Unit (MAU) curb | 48"×72" to 60"×96" depending on CFM | 600–1,500 lb | Engineered curb tied to roof structure; structural review essential | NFPA 96 §8.4 / UMC §511 |`
`| Existing landlord-delivered 10-ton RTU | Already installed by landlord | — | Existing | — |`
`| Additional RTUs if required | 36"×72" | 400–800 lb | Engineered curb | UMC |`
`| Plumbing vent stacks (1.5"–4" diameter) | 4–8 stacks for kitchen, bar, restrooms | <20 lb each | Pipe support; pipe boots/Dektites | UPC §906, §907 |`
`| HVAC condensate and refrigerant line penetrations | 1"–3" | <10 lb | Pipe boot/penetration pocket | UMC |`
`| Gas line through roof (if natural gas to MAU heater or rooftop equipment) | 1.5"–3" | — | Pipe boot, dielectric isolation | IFGC |`
`| Electrical conduit (rooftop equipment whips) | 1"–2" | — | Pipe boot | NEC |`
`| Low voltage / data (POS, security cameras, rooftop sensors) | 1"–2" | — | Pipe boot | NEC |`

`A well-coordinated solid-fuel restaurant project with this footprint typically lands at **8–14 separate roof penetrations**. Each one is a leak risk and a warranty trigger.`

`## 3.3 The Solid-Fuel Exhaust Fan Curb — The Highest-Stakes Penetration`

`NFPA 96 Chapter 14 (solid-fuel cooking) layered on top of Chapter 7 (rooftop terminations) and Chapter 8 (fan installation) drives the curb design.`

`**Curb construction requirements:**`
`- Curb **height above roof surface**: NFPA 96 §7.8.2.1 requires the duct-to-fan attachment point to be **≥ 18" above the roof surface**, and the fan discharge to be **≥ 40" above the roof surface**. Many AHJs (including Austin's interpretation of NFPA 96 as referenced through the UMC §517 solid-fuel provisions) enforce these literally.`
`- Curb constructed from minimum 18-gauge galvanized steel, internally insulated to maintain duct exterior surface clearances to combustibles`
`- Engineered curb with internal counterflashing details, designed for the dead load + wind load on the fan + grease box`
`- **Welded to or mechanically fastened** to the duct riser inside the curb`
`- Sloped top to drain water away from the fan base`
`- **Listed for solid-fuel applications** if used with wood/charcoal cooking (NFPA 96 §14.5.1 — grease removal devices and adjacent components must be steel/stainless or specifically approved for solid fuel)`

`**Why curb height matters:** A short curb concentrates grease and water pooling at the roof membrane around the fan, which is the #1 source of rooftop grease leaks and roof warranty callbacks. Short curbs also fail the 40" fan-discharge clearance and the 18" duct attachment clearance — a routine NFPA 96 inspection citation.`

`**Spark arrestor:** NFPA 96 §14.5.2 requires a spark arrestor between the cooking equipment and the grease removal device for any solid-fuel operation that can generate airborne sparks/embers (which any wood or charcoal grill can). This is often integrated into the hood; the rooftop fan is downstream of the spark arrestor but the AHJ will verify the arrestor exists.`

`## 3.4 Grease Containment per NFPA 96 §7.8.2.1`

`The rooftop termination must be arranged with:`

`- **(4)** Drainage of grease out of low points/traps in the fan or duct into a **noncombustible, closed, rainproof, structurally sound collection container** that will not sustain combustion`
`- **(5)** A grease collection device that does not inhibit fan performance`
`- **(6)** Listed grease collection systems per UL 710A`

`Practically, this means a **continuous welded grease containment box** ringing the upblast fan, sloped to drain, with a 1-gallon-maximum readily accessible and visible grease receptacle that can be removed for cleaning (per §8.1.2.3). Common systems: **Grease Lock, Facilitec, Rooftop Solutions** retrofit boxes; or fan-integrated containment from **Captive-Aire, Greenheck, Loren Cook, Penn Barry**.`

`**Clearances per §7.8 / IMC §510.9:**`
`- ≥ 10 ft horizontal clearance from outlet to adjacent buildings, property lines, and air intakes`
`- ≥ 5 ft horizontal clearance from outlet to combustible structures`
`- ≥ 3 ft vertical separation below an exhaust outlet for any air intake within 10 ft (with additional separation for intakes above the exhaust plane: 10 ft + 0.25 ft per degree above horizontal)`
`- The MAU must be located to honor these clearances — a frequent design problem on small rooftops where the fan and MAU end up too close`

`**Who installs the grease containment:** typically the hood contractor / kitchen equipment vendor specifies it, the mechanical contractor or hood contractor installs the fan and box, and the **landlord's roofer integrates the curb flashing into the existing roof membrane**. This is the handoff most often blown.`

`## 3.5 Construction Sequencing — Where This Goes Wrong`

`The right sequence:`

`1. **Pre-construction coordination meeting** with the GC, hood contractor, mechanical contractor, plumber, electrician, structural engineer, and the landlord's roofer. Walk the roof. Mark every intended penetration on a roof plan. Get sign-off in writing.`
`2. **Structural review** of the roof framing at each penetration location. Solid-fuel curbs and MAU curbs add significant point loads; the existing structure may need reinforcement.`
`3. **Curb fabrication** (curbs are typically fabricated and shipped before the hood contractor mobilizes).`
`4. **Roof opening cut by the landlord's roofer** (NOT by the hood contractor) — this is the critical handoff point.`
`5. **Curb set** by the hood contractor or mechanical contractor on top of the cut and reinforced opening.`
`6. **Roofer flashes the curb** to the existing TPO/metal roof — base flashing, membrane terminations, counterflashing.`
`7. Hood contractor sets the fan / grease box / fire suppression duct components on the curb.`
`8. Plumbing vents, condensate, gas, electrical penetrations cut and flashed by the roofer in coordination with each trade.`
`9. **Final roof inspection** by the manufacturer's certified rep before warranty issuance.`

`**What goes wrong:**`
`- The hood contractor cuts the roof opening with a Sawzall before the roofer arrives — voids the warranty and damages the membrane. Almost always results in a callback and an extra patching charge.`
`- The roofer is brought in too late, after the curb is set incorrectly — re-work, extra flashing, paid twice.`
`- The MAU and exhaust fan curbs are installed in clearance violation of NFPA 96 §7.8 — fan must be relocated, new curb cut, and the original opening patched.`
`- Plumbing vent stacks are cut by the plumber instead of the roofer — same warranty problem.`
`- No one thinks about the gas penetration until the inspector calls it out post-completion.`

`The GC's contract should explicitly assign **roof penetration cutting and flashing to the landlord's preferred roofer**, and explicitly prohibit other trades from cutting the roof under any circumstances. Make this a contractual line.`

`## 3.6 The "Landlord's Preferred Vendor" — What to Negotiate`

`Before the GC mobilizes, the owner (or the GC on the owner's behalf) must obtain in writing from the landlord:`

`1. **Vendor name and contact.**`
`2. **Scope they cover** (e.g., do they only cut/patch, or do they also flash curbs that other trades supply?).`
`3. **Pricing structure** — flat fee per penetration size, T&M with rate schedule, or bundled. Typical Austin-market 2026 pricing: **$800–$2,500 per small penetration** (vent stacks, pipe boots), **$2,500–$6,000 per medium curb** (RTU, MAU base), **$5,000–$12,000 per large solid-fuel exhaust curb with grease containment integration.**`
`4. **Turnaround time** — how many business days between scheduling and execution. Insist on ≤5 business days.`
`5. **Warranty terms** — what does the vendor warrant on their patch (typical: 1–5 year workmanship), and is the landlord's roof manufacturer warranty preserved?`
`6. **Insurance** — the vendor's certificate of insurance must list the tenant and GC as additional insured for the duration of the work.`
`7. **Coordination expectation** — will they attend the pre-roof coordination meeting? Insist yes.`
`8. **Whether the vendor is the manufacturer's certified installer** for the specific TPO membrane (Carlisle Sure-Weld, GAF EverGuard, Firestone/Elevate UltraPly, Versico, Johns Manville). If not, the warranty is at risk.`

`**Negotiation leverage points:**`
`- Cap the pricing per penetration with a not-to-exceed schedule.`
`- Require itemized invoices, not lump-sum.`
`- Require advance written quote for any penetration before work starts.`
`- Require photo documentation of each completed penetration.`

`## 3.7 Roof Warranty Implications`

`TPO membrane warranties from major manufacturers run **10, 15, 20, or 30 years**, with NDL (No Dollar Limit) options available on full-system warranties. All of them require:`

`- Installation by a manufacturer-certified contractor`
`- Use of manufacturer-approved flashings, adhesives, primers, and accessory materials`
`- Penetrations and repairs performed by certified contractors using manufacturer details`
`- Annual or bi-annual inspections in some cases`
`- No alterations or repairs by unapproved parties`

`**If a non-certified contractor cuts the roof, the warranty for that roof area — and potentially the entire roof — is voided.** This is why the LOI pushes all penetration work to the landlord's preferred vendor.`

`**Documents the owner should obtain before any roof work begins:**`
`- Copy of the manufacturer warranty certificate (from landlord)`
`- Manufacturer name, system, membrane thickness (typically 60-mil reinforced TPO)`
`- Warranty duration and start date`
`- Confirmation in writing from the landlord that the preferred vendor is the manufacturer's certified installer`
`- Photo and as-built documentation of each completed penetration`
`- Updated warranty certificate (if required) post-completion`

`## 3.8 TPO + Corrugated Metal Interface — The Tricky Part`

`The roof is described in the LOI as a **combination corrugated metal and TPO** roof. This is unusual and creates specific detailing challenges:`

`**Penetrations through TPO field membrane:**`
`- Heat-welded TPO pipe boots (manufacturer-supplied prefab — Carlisle, GAF, Elevate all make them) for round penetrations 1"–6"`
`- Custom-welded TPO target patches over field seams when a penetration crosses one`
`- TPO penetration pockets (filled with pourable sealer) for irregular or grouped penetrations`
`- Curb base flashing: 60-mil reinforced TPO curb wrap, heat-welded to field membrane and mechanically terminated at the top of the curb with a termination bar and counterflashing`

`**Penetrations through corrugated metal:**`
`- EPDM/silicone pipe boots (Dektite, Master Flash, Aztec) compressed and screwed to the metal panel with butyl tape sealant beneath`
`- Closure strips at the corrugation profile to maintain the seal`
`- Boot must match the corrugation profile (which varies by panel) — mis-sized boots leak`

`**The transition between TPO and metal at a curb that crosses both materials:**`
`- This is where leaks live. The detail typically requires a **TPO-coated metal counterflashing** that bridges the membrane systems with butyl-taped overlap onto the metal panel, mechanically fastened with neoprene-washered screws, then sealed with manufacturer-approved sealant`
`- The detail must be drawn by the roofer and approved by the manufacturer's tech rep before installation`
`- **Caulk-only flashing is unacceptable** — any vendor proposing it should be replaced`

`**Common TPO membrane manufacturers and their approved detail libraries:**`
`- Carlisle SynTec (Sure-Weld TPO) — extensive online detail library, Carlisle-certified contractors only`
`- GAF EverGuard — GAF Master Select certified contractors`
`- Holcim Elevate (formerly Firestone) UltraPly TPO — Red Shield Licensed Applicators`
`- Versico VersiWeld — Versico Authorized Roofing Contractors`
`- Johns Manville (JM TPO) — JM Peak Advantage contractors`

`## 3.9 The 10 Questions to Ask Before Penetration Work Begins (In Writing)`

`To the **landlord**:`
`1. Who is the preferred roofing vendor, and are they manufacturer-certified for the installed TPO system?`
`2. Will any tenant penetration work void any portion of the manufacturer warranty?`
`3. Will the preferred vendor attend the pre-construction roof coordination meeting?`

`To the **GC**:`
`4. How is your contract written to ensure no trade other than the landlord's roofer cuts or patches the roof?`
`5. What is your sequencing plan — show me the schedule line items for each penetration with the responsible trade.`
`6. What is your contingency line for change orders to the landlord's roofer?`

`To the **landlord's roofer**:`
`7. Provide a per-penetration quote or rate schedule, including the solid-fuel exhaust curb integration, MAU curb, vent stacks, and miscellaneous.`
`8. What is your workmanship warranty and how does it interact with the manufacturer warranty?`
`9. Provide your manufacturer certification number and a current certificate of insurance.`
`10. What is your typical lead time from scheduling to onsite execution?`

`## 3.10 2026 Austin Cost Expectations`

`Budget the following on the LHI (Leasehold Improvement) line:`

`| Item | Range |`
`|---|---|`
`| Solid-fuel exhaust curb cut, structural reinforcement, and flashing integration | $5,000–$12,000 |`
`| MAU curb cut and flashing | $3,000–$7,000 |`
`| Plumbing vent stacks (each) | $400–$1,200 |`
`| HVAC condensate / refrigerant penetrations (each) | $400–$900 |`
`| Gas line penetration (if needed) | $600–$1,500 |`
`| Electrical / low voltage penetrations (each) | $300–$800 |`
`| **Total roof penetration scope (typical for this restaurant)** | **$15,000–$35,000** |`

`Add a **15–20% contingency** because actual penetration count typically exceeds initial planning by 1–3 penetrations.`

`## 3.11 Red Flags`

`| Red flag | What it signals |`
`|---|---|`
`| GC proposes hood contractor cutting the roof "to keep the schedule" | Will void warranty; inevitable callback |`
`| No roof coordination meeting on the schedule | Sequence will fail |`
`| Landlord won't name the preferred vendor in writing | Pricing will be untestable |`
`| Vendor pricing is T&M only with no rate cap | Open-ended exposure |`
`| Vendor is not manufacturer-certified for the installed TPO | Warranty voided |`
`| MAU and exhaust fan placed within 10 ft of each other | NFPA 96 §7.8 violation; fan or MAU will need to move |`
`| Caulk-only flashing detail | Will leak within 1–3 years; not warranty-compliant |`
`| Curb height under 18" duct attachment / 40" fan discharge | NFPA 96 violation; AHJ will fail it |`
`| No grease containment box specified | NFPA 96 §7.8.2.1(4)/(5) violation |`
`| Plumber says "we'll cut our own vent stacks" | Voids warranty; LOI violation; immediate red flag for the GC contract |`

`---`

`# CROSS-REFERENCES — Decisions That Bridge Multiple Sections`

`The following decisions or scope items appear in more than one section of this guide and should not be made in isolation:`

`1. **The commercial dishwasher** drives both the **grease interceptor sizing** (Section 1.3 — adds 6–8 fixture units, triggers the 500-gallon GGI minimum) and the **plumbing rough-in** (Section 2.2.5 — booster heater, 180°F final rinse, indirect waste to floor sink, drain temperature ≤150°F entering GI). Confirm the dishwasher model is locked before the GC submits to CPR; a model change after IW Approval may force a re-submittal.`

`2. **Roof penetrations bridge the Solid Fuel Exhaust Ventilation Compliance Guide and Section 2 of this guide.** The hood exhaust fan curb (covered in the prior compliance guide and Section 3 here), the makeup air unit (prior guide and Section 3), and the **plumbing vent stacks** (Section 2.4.7 and Section 3) all penetrate the roof and all must be patched by the landlord's preferred vendor at tenant cost. Plan for the cost as a single line item with the GC, not as separate trade costs.`

`3. **The grease interceptor vent** (Section 1.5, item 6) is itself a roof penetration. Verify with the plumber whether the GI vent terminates through-roof (most common) or to grade with a vent cap — and if through-roof, add it to the penetration count in Section 3.2.`

`4. **Restroom ventilation interlock** (Section 2.4.7) requires a mechanical exhaust fan terminating through the roof — add this penetration to the inventory in Section 3.2.`

`5. **Sample manhole location** (Section 1.5) interacts with the site plan's surface finish. If sited in a paved area, specify H-20 traffic-rated cover (Section 1.7); if sited in a landscape area, confirm it cannot be obscured or buried — Austin Water rejects inaccessible sample ports.`

`6. **Hand sinks** (Section 2.2.3) are not plumbed to the GI per Austin design notes (Section 1.3). This affects fixture-unit count downward — confirm the plumber's sizing calc excludes hand sinks.`

`7. **Gas service** for the live-fire cooking and any rooftop MAU heater interacts with **roof penetrations** (Section 3.2) and with the IFGC adopted under Austin's 2024 code package; confirm gas routing in the same coordination meeting that locks roof penetrations.`

`8. **The 50% wetted-height rule** under §15-10-197 (Section 1.9) is the operational trigger for pump-outs and supersedes any 25% rule cited in older or out-of-jurisdiction literature. Confirm this with the licensed hauler at contract signing.`

`---`

`## Sources for Verification`

`The owner can verify the technical claims in this document at the following primary sources:`

`- **Austin Water Industrial Waste sizing & design criteria:**` [`austintexas.gov/water/grease-trap-sizing-design-criteria`](http://austintexas.gov/water/grease-trap-sizing-design-criteria)
`- **Austin Water Pretreatment FAQ:**` [`austintexas.gov/department/pretreatment-frequently-asked-questions`](http://austintexas.gov/department/pretreatment-frequently-asked-questions)
`- **Industrial Waste Plan Review (now part of CPR):**` [`austintexas.gov/department/industrial-waste-plan-review-pretreatment-plan-review`](http://austintexas.gov/department/industrial-waste-plan-review-pretreatment-plan-review)
`- **Austin Water Manufacturers List of Grease Trap or Grease Interceptor:**` [`austintexas.gov/sites/default/files/files/Water/SSD/`](http://austintexas.gov/sites/default/files/files/Water/SSD/) `(current revision PDF)`
`- **Austin City Code Chapter 15-10 (Wastewater Regulations):**` [`library.municode.com/tx/austin`](http://library.municode.com/tx/austin)
`- **Austin Build + Connect (AB+C) Portal:**` [`austintexas.gov/development-services/austin-build-connect-abc`](http://austintexas.gov/development-services/austin-build-connect-abc)
`- **Austin Building Technical Codes (Chapter 25-12 amendments to UPC/UMC/IBC etc.):**` [`austintexas.gov/page/building-technical-codes`](http://austintexas.gov/page/building-technical-codes)
`- **Texas Food Establishment Rules (TFER), 25 TAC Chapter 228:**` [`dshs.texas.gov`](http://dshs.texas.gov) `/ Texas Secretary of State Texas Administrative Code`
`- **NFPA 96 — Standard for Ventilation Control and Fire Protection of Commercial Cooking Operations:**` [`nfpa.org/codes-and-standards/96`](http://nfpa.org/codes-and-standards/96)
`- **EPA / DOE pre-rinse spray valve standards:**` [`epa.gov/watersense/pre-rinse-spray-valves;`](http://epa.gov/watersense/pre-rinse-spray-valves;) `10 CFR 431.266`
`- **U.S. Access Board Toilet Rooms Guidance:**` [`access-board.gov/ada/guides/chapter-6-toilet-rooms`](http://access-board.gov/ada/guides/chapter-6-toilet-rooms)
`- **TPO membrane manufacturer detail libraries:** Carlisle SynTec, GAF EverGuard, Holcim Elevate UltraPly, Versico, Johns Manville (each maintains an online flashing details and certified contractor lookup)`
`- **Industrial Waste contact:**` [`IndustrialWaste@austintexas.gov`](mailto:IndustrialWaste@austintexas.gov) `/ 512-974-7293`

`This document should be re-reviewed if the project crosses an adoption boundary (e.g., if Austin updates to the 2027 UPC) or if Austin Water issues revised IW criteria, which historically happens every 3–5 years.`
