`# Domain 5: FLOORING — Compliance & Specification Knowledge Base`
`**Project:** Korean Fine Dining Restaurant, 207 E St Elmo Rd, Austin, TX`
`**Document Series:** Reference Document #4 (companion to Solid Fuel Exhaust Ventilation, Fire Suppression & Alarm, and Plumbing/Grease Interceptor/Roof Penetration guides)`
`**Audience:** Restaurant owner — sophisticated non-engineer evaluating commercial flooring vendor proposals`
`**Total Interior:** 2,310 SF | **Zones:** Dining 988 SF · Kitchen/BOH ~700 SF · Restrooms 154 SF · Bar/Entry/Circulation ~605 SF`

`---`

`## TL;DR — The Three Things That Will Make or Break This Floor Package`

`- **Slab moisture testing per ASTM F2170 (in-situ relative humidity probes) is the gating decision for every zone.** No reputable engineered hardwood, urethane mortar, or epoxy resinous system warranty survives a slab that wasn't tested. If the slab reads >75% RH for hardwood or >80–85% RH for resinous, you either pay for vapor mitigation ($3–$8/SF adder) or your floor fails. A bid without a moisture testing line item is incomplete on its face.`
`- **For each zone, there is one "right" answer that matches Sŏn's quality target and live-fire kitchen reality:** engineered white oak with a ≥4 mm wear layer, glue-down with a urethane or silane-modified-polymer adhesive in the dining room; cementitious **urethane mortar** (Stonhard Stonclad UT, Dur-A-Flex Poly-Crete MDB, BASF MasterTop, or Florock urethane mortar) at 1/4″ thickness with **integral cove base and hopper'd floor drains** in the kitchen; **large-format porcelain with epoxy grout** (Laticrete SpectraLOCK or Mapei Kerapoxy) over a **Schluter Kerdi or Laticrete Hydro Ban** waterproof membrane in the restrooms; and a continuous slip-rated hard surface (urethane mortar or polished concrete) behind the bar.`
`- **Three integration points bridge flooring to other trades and must be drawn and sequenced before any contract is signed:** (1) floor drain rims must be set flush with the finished floor *before* the urethane mortar pour, with a hopper detail and 1/4″/foot slope coordinated with the plumber; (2) integral cove base height must be coordinated with drywall and FRP (fiber-reinforced plastic) wall panel termination — drywall stops above the cove, FRP overlaps the top of the cove; (3) all transitions across thresholds must comply with ADA / Texas Accessibility Standards §404.2.5 — 1/4″ vertical max, 1/4″ to 1/2″ requires a 1:2 bevel, anything over 1/2″ requires a ramp.`

`---`

`## KEY FINDINGS`

`| Zone | Recommended System | DCOF (wet) target | Approx. Installed Cost (Austin 2026) |`
`|---|---|---|---|`
`| Dining (988 SF) | Engineered white oak, ≥4 mm wear layer, glue-down with Bostik BEST or Mapei Ultrabond ECO 980 | n/a (dry) | $20,000–$45,000 |`
`| Kitchen/BOH (~700 SF) | Urethane mortar (Stonclad UT / Poly-Crete MDB) at 1/4″, broadcast aggregate, integral 4–6″ cove base | ≥0.50, target 0.55+ at cookline (ANSI A326.3 "Oils/Greases") | $10,000–$22,000 |`
`| Restrooms (154 SF) | Large-format porcelain + epoxy grout + Schluter Kerdi / Laticrete Hydro Ban membrane | ≥0.42 minimum, ≥0.50 at fixtures | $4,000–$10,000 |`
`| Bar/Entry/Circulation (~605 SF) | Urethane mortar behind bar; large-format porcelain or polished concrete in entry; recessed walk-off mat well | ≥0.42 (entry/circulation) ; ≥0.50 behind bar | $9,000–$25,000 |`

`**Total flooring package range:** ~$43,000–$102,000 installed, depending on slab condition, moisture mitigation needs, hardwood selection, and design ambition.`

`---`

`# SECTION 1 — DINING ROOM (HARDWOOD, 988 SF)`

`## 1.1 Solid vs. Engineered Hardwood — Why Engineered Wins on Slab-on-Grade`

`Solid hardwood (3/4″ tongue-and-groove milled from a single piece of wood) and engineered hardwood (a hardwood "wear layer" or "veneer" laminated to a multi-ply plywood, HDF, or SPC core) look identical when finished. The difference is dimensional behavior:`

`- **Solid hardwood expands and contracts across its full thickness** with humidity changes. Austin's annual humidity cycle (RH swings from ~30% in January to ~70%+ during summer monsoon weeks, plus indoor HVAC cycles) is exactly the condition that makes solid wood cup, crown, and gap. Solid wood also cannot be glued or floated over a concrete slab without a sleeper system (a wood subframe) — it must be nailed.`
`- **Engineered hardwood's cross-laminated core resists dimensional change** because the plies run perpendicular to one another. It is purpose-built for slab-on-grade installation. The National Wood Flooring Association (NWFA) explicitly approves engineered for above-, on-, and below-grade installation; solid is approved on- and above-grade only, and over wood subfloors only.`

`**For this project, engineered hardwood is the correct specification.** A vendor proposing solid hardwood over the landlord's concrete slab is either proposing a sleeper system (raises the floor 1–1.5″, eats into ceiling height and creates ADA transition problems) or making a mistake.`

`### Engineered Hardwood Spec Cheat Sheet`

`| Spec line | What to ask for | Why |`
`|---|---|---|`
`| **Total thickness** | 1/2″ (12.7 mm) to 5/8″ (15 mm) minimum | Thinner (3/8″) products have insufficient core and short wear layer; thicker can create transition problems |`
`| **Core construction** | Multi-ply Baltic birch or poplar **or** HDF (high-density fiberboard) | Plywood cores are most stable for restaurant FOH; SPC (stone-plastic composite) cores are aggressive vinyl/wood hybrids — fine for retail but read as "luxury vinyl" to design-savvy guests |`
`| **Number of plies** | 7-ply or more for premium wide plank; 3-ply minimum | More plies = more dimensional stability |`
`| **Wear layer (top veneer of real hardwood)** | **3 mm minimum, 4 mm strongly preferred, 6 mm for premium fine dining** | NWFA's Refinishable Program threshold is 2.5 mm for distressed/factory-finished, 3.2 mm for unfinished smooth. A 4 mm wear layer can be sanded and refinished 3–4 times and lasts 50+ years; a 2 mm wear layer can be sanded once and lasts 30–40 years |`
`| **Top veneer species** | White oak, hickory, walnut, hard maple, or ash | These are commercially proven |`

`**Brands appropriate to fine dining commercial use (in rough order of price/prestige):** Carlisle Wide Plank Floors, DuChâteau (Chateau, Riverstone, Vernal Collections — typically 4 mm wear layer, 5/8″ total, European white oak, oil finish, lifetime structural / 3-year commercial finish warranty), Stuga, Mirage Engineered (Canadian), Hallmark Floors, Mannington Restoration Collection, Mohawk TecWood. Expect Carlisle and DuChâteau to spec at $14–$22/SF material; Mirage and Mannington at $9–$14/SF; Mohawk at $7–$10/SF.`

`## 1.2 Species and Finish for Korean Fine Dining`

`The Janka hardness test measures the force (in pounds-force, lbf) required to embed an 11.28 mm steel ball halfway into a wood sample. Higher = more dent resistance.`

`| Species | Janka (lbf) | Restaurant FOH verdict |`
`|---|---|---|`
`| **White oak (Quercus alba)** | 1,360 | **Preferred.** Hard, tannic (rot/insect-resistant), takes stain and fuming beautifully. The default for contemporary fine dining. |`
`| **Hickory** | 1,820 | Excellent. Pronounced grain variation reads "rustic" — works for some Korean concepts, less so for refined modernist design. |`
`| **Hard maple** | 1,450 | Excellent for durability; can read cold/clinical and accepts stain unevenly. |`
`| **Walnut (American black)** | 1,010 | **Acceptable for fine dining if traffic is managed.** Softer than oak — will dent under chairs without floor protectors — but its warm, dark tone is highly prized for upscale dining. |`
`| **Ash** | 1,320 | Good alternative to oak; lighter, more linear grain. |`
`| **Red oak** | 1,290 | Avoid for fine dining. Pinker undertone, more grain variation, and turns greenish under water-based finishes. |`
`| **Soft maple, pine, douglas fir** | 950 / 690 / 660 | Avoid. Soft species dent under heels and chair legs almost immediately. |`

`**Korean fine dining design language** typically gravitates to warm-toned, low-contrast woods with a quiet matte finish — most often natural-fumed white oak, smoke-stained or oiled white oak, or American walnut. Wide planks (7″–10″) with a wire-brushed surface and matte UV-cured oil/urethane finish are the contemporary default.`

`### Visual Finish Vocabulary`

`- **Wire-brushed** (light mechanical brushing of the soft grain) — masks micro-scratches, reads "natural," excellent for restaurants. **Recommended.**`
`- **Hand-scraped** — pronounced texture; reads "rustic farmhouse." Generally not aligned with a Korean fine dining aesthetic.`
`- **Smooth** — modern, clean, but every scratch shows. Acceptable only with the hardest finishes.`
`- **Matte / low-sheen (5–15 sheen units)** — hides wear and scratches, reads contemporary. **Recommended.**`
`- **Satin (25–35 sheen)** — acceptable.`
`- **Semi-gloss / gloss** — every fingerprint, every scratch is visible. Not appropriate for restaurant FOH.`
`- **Color treatments** — natural, white-washed, smoked/fumed (ammonia process that reacts with white oak's tannin to darken without surface dye), reactive stains. Discuss with the designer; the technical point is that **factory-applied UV-cured finishes outperform any site-applied finish** for commercial wear.`

`## 1.3 Glue-Down vs. Floating vs. Nail-Down Over Concrete Slab`

`| Method | Restaurant FOH verdict |`
`|---|---|`
`| **Glue-down** | **The correct method for fine dining commercial over slab-on-grade.** The plank is bonded directly to the concrete with a urethane, MS (silane-modified polymer), or hybrid adhesive. Result: solid underfoot feel, no hollow sound, no creep at the edges, longest service life. |`
`| **Floating** | Acceptable for budget retail; produces an audible hollow "tap" underfoot that is unmistakable to fine dining guests. Foam underlayment also voids glue-down warranty if mistakenly added. **Not recommended for Sŏn.** |`
`| **Nail-down** | Requires a plywood subfloor or sleeper system over the slab. Adds 1–1.5″ of floor height (creates ADA transition issues, eats ceiling height, complicates door swings). Rarely cost-effective in a 988 SF dining room over an existing slab. **Not recommended.** |`

`### Concrete Prep for Glue-Down`

`Glue-down requires the slab to meet all of the following before adhesive is troweled:`

`1. **Flatness**: the industry rule is no more than 3/16″ deviation in a 10-foot run (equivalent to ASTM E1155 floor flatness FF35, floor levelness FL25). Slabs that fail flatness are corrected with a self-leveling underlayment such as **Ardex K-15** (Portland-cement-based, 1/4″–1.5″ neat, 5500 psi, walkable in 2–3 hours) or **Mapei Novoplan 2**.`
`2. **Surface profile**: CSP-2 to CSP-3 (Concrete Surface Profile, ICRI scale) — achieved by mechanical grinding or shotblasting. This removes laitance, curing compounds, and old adhesive residue and gives the new adhesive something to grip.`
`3. **Cleanliness**: no oil, paint overspray, dust, or efflorescence. The slab must be vacuumed (HEPA) immediately before adhesive application.`
`4. **Moisture**: see Section 1.5.`

`### Adhesive Conversation`

`Three classes of adhesive are appropriate for engineered hardwood glue-down over concrete:`

`- **Moisture-cure urethane** (e.g., **Bostik BEST**, **Bostik Pro-Cure**, **Sika SikaBond**, **Mapei Ultrabond ECO 980**, **Mapei Ultrabond ECO 990**, **Stauf PUM-950**) — the workhorse. Bostik BEST claims it serves as both adhesive and moisture-vapor membrane (waiving moisture testing if the slab is "properly prepared, dry to the touch, and fully cured"); **do not rely on this loophole for a fine dining build — get the ASTM F2170 test anyway**. Bostik's own data sheet says solid hardwood and slabs >3 lb MVER or >75% RH require Bostik MVP4 or equivalent prior application.`
`- **Silane-modified polymer (MS Polymer / SPUR)** — newer chemistry, lower VOC, easier cleanup; Mapei Ultrabond ECO 980 and Stauf SMP-960 are typical examples.`
`- **Acrylic / PVA** — appropriate only for thin engineered or budget retail. Not appropriate for premium wide plank. **Reject any bid using a water-based acrylic for 7″+ wide plank.**`

`The trowel notch (typically 1/4″ × 1/4″ V or square notch for engineered up to 5/8″ thick) and coverage (30–40 SF/gallon) are stated on the adhesive technical data sheet (TDS). Ask the contractor to confirm.`

`## 1.4 Commercial-Grade Finish Requirements`

`- **Wear layer 3 mm minimum, 4 mm preferred, 6 mm for premium.** Below 3 mm, the engineered product is essentially a "lifetime laminate" that cannot survive a single sanding; it has no place in fine dining FOH.`
`- **Factory-finished beats site-finished for commercial use.** Factory UV-cured urethane finishes are typically formulated with aluminum oxide nanoparticles that significantly improve abrasion resistance vs. any site-applied polyurethane. Site finishing also requires 5–7 days of off-gassing and floor protection that's incompatible with a tight commercial schedule.`
`- **Low-gloss / matte hides scratches.** A high-gloss finish will telegraph every micro-scratch within 90 days of opening.`
`- **Look for these performance indicators on the TDS:**`
`- **Taber abrasion test** (ASTM D4060, CS-17 wheel, 1000-cycle) — a residential floor will show 50–100 mg loss; commercial-grade should show ≤25 mg loss.`
`- **NWFA Engineered Wood Flooring Refinishable Certification** — confirms the product can be refinished (i.e., wear layer ≥2.5 mm factory-finished or ≥3.2 mm unfinished).`
`- **AC rating** — borrowed from laminate, occasionally cited; AC4 is the commercial threshold.`
`- **Manufacturer's warranty must include "light commercial" or "commercial" use.** DuChâteau, for example, offers a Lifetime Structural / 25-Year Residential Surface / **3-Year Commercial Surface** warranty on its Chateau Collection — that 3-year commercial line is what protects the restaurant-use claim. A residential-only warranty in a restaurant is voided on day one.`

`## 1.5 Moisture Testing — The Single Most Important Line Item in the Bid`

`Excess moisture from the slab will destroy a glue-down hardwood floor — adhesive failure (cupping, lifting), microbial growth, finish blistering. The two ASTM-recognized tests:`

`- **ASTM F1869 — Calcium Chloride MVER (Moisture Vapor Emission Rate)** — a sealed dish of anhydrous calcium chloride is weighed before and after a 60–72-hour exposure on the slab; result is reported in **lb of water per 1,000 SF per 24 hours**. **For hardwood, the threshold is ≤3 lb/1,000 SF/24 hr.** This test only measures the surface vapor emission, not the slab interior.`
`- **ASTM F2170 — In-situ Relative Humidity Probes** — calibrated RH sensors are placed in drilled sleeves at 40% of slab depth (one-sided drying) for a minimum 24-hour equilibration. Result is reported in **% RH at probe depth**. **For hardwood, the threshold is ≤75% RH per NWFA Installation Guidelines and most major hardwood manufacturers (Mannington, Mirage, Mohawk, DuChâteau).** For most resinous flooring, the threshold is ≤80–85% RH. This test is the more accurate of the two for predicting long-term performance and is now what most flooring manufacturers actually require for warranty.`

`**Conditions for valid F2170 testing:** building must be enclosed and at occupancy temperature/humidity for at least 48 hours before probe insertion, and the probe must equilibrate at least 24 hours after sleeve install (newer ASTM F2170-23 says 24 hr; some manufacturers require 72 hr).`

`**One probe per 1,000 SF for the first 1,000 SF, plus one per additional 1,000 SF** is the ASTM minimum. For 988 SF dining + 605 SF circulation, plan on 2–3 probes; for the kitchen, plan on 2 more. Total testing cost: $400–$1,200.`

`### What Happens If the Slab Fails Moisture Testing`

`The vendor applies a **vapor mitigation primer** before the adhesive — a two-part epoxy or polyurethane membrane that drops effective vapor transmission to near zero. Common products:`

`- **Aquafin VRS** (epoxy) — handles up to 25 lb MVER / 100% RH`
`- **Mapei Planiseal VS / VS Fast** (epoxy) — no MVER limit if no standing water`
`- **Mapei Planiseal MB** (epoxy)`
`- **Mapei Planiseal MSP** (polymer-based, up to 99% RH)`
`- **Bostik D-200** / **Bostik MVP4** (epoxy)`
`- **Sika MB** (epoxy)`
`- **Koster VAP I 2000** (epoxy)`

`Typical cost adder: **$3–$8/SF** depending on system and slab condition. For 988 SF, that is $3,000–$8,000 of additional cost — and it is the single biggest budget swing factor in the dining room flooring package. **The LOI's "exposed concrete slab" delivery means you cannot price the hardwood reliably until the slab is moisture-tested.**`

`## 1.6 Concrete Subfloor Preparation — What "Surface Imperfections" Really Means`

`In a new-construction or 2nd-gen Austin space, the LOI phrase "exposed concrete slab, may have surface imperfections" typically conceals one or more of the following:`

`- **Control joints and saw cuts** (intentional cracks every 12–15 ft to manage shrinkage) — these need to be filled with semi-rigid epoxy or polyurea joint filler before any flooring goes down.`
`- **Surface roughness from broom or float finish** — must be ground to CSP-2/3.`
`- **Birdbaths / low spots** (areas where a 10-ft straightedge shows >3/16″ deviation) — patched with self-leveler.`
`- **Curing compounds, sealers, or densifiers** applied by the slab contractor — these are bond-breakers and must be mechanically removed.`
`- **Old adhesive residue, paint overspray, drywall mud splatters** — common in tenant turnover spaces.`
`- **Cracks** — non-moving cracks <1/8″ are bridged by good urethane adhesive (Bostik BEST claims 1/8″ crack-bridging); larger cracks need crack isolation membrane (Schluter DITRA, Laticrete 125 Sound & Crack Adhesive).`

`**Proper prep involves:**`
`1. Mechanical grinding or shotblasting to CSP-2/3 (think coarse sandpaper texture).`
`2. Patching low spots and feathering high spots with cementitious self-leveling underlayment (Ardex K-15, Mapei Novoplan 2, Mapei Ultraplan 1 Plus).`
`3. Vacuum cleaning (HEPA) immediately before adhesive.`
`4. Achieving overall flatness of FF35/FL25 minimum (3/16″ in 10 ft).`

`**Who scopes prep:** typically the flooring contractor. Sometimes the GC handles initial grinding and the flooring contractor handles patching. **The bid must spell out which.**`

`**Cost range for full prep:** $2–$8/SF. For a slab in unknown condition, ask vendors to bid prep as a separately priced unit with a per-bag self-leveler line item, or as a "prep allowance" with a clear scope of what's included and a unit price for change orders.`

`### 12 Questions to Ask the Hardwood Vendor`

`1. What manufacturer, collection, and SKU are you specifying? Provide a cut sheet.`
`2. What is the **wear-layer thickness** in mm and the **total plank thickness** in mm? Is the product NWFA-certified Refinishable?`
`3. What does the manufacturer's **commercial** warranty cover and for how long?`
`4. Walk me through your **ASTM F2170 in-situ RH testing** protocol — number of probes for ~1,600 SF (dining + circulation), equilibration time, action thresholds, and cost.`
`5. If the slab fails RH testing, what vapor mitigation primer do you propose and what is the cost adder per SF?`
`6. What **adhesive** are you using (manufacturer/SKU), what trowel notch, and what is the coverage rate?`
`7. What is your scope for **slab prep** — is grinding, patching, self-leveling, and crack treatment all included or carved out as allowance?`
`8. Provide three Austin-area fine dining or upscale commercial references with owner contact info and addresses I can drive to.`
`9. Are your installers **NWFA-certified** (Certified Installer, Craftsman, or Master Craftsman level)?`
`10. What is your construction sequence — do you install before or after millwork, casework, and FF&E? Who is responsible for floor protection during the rest of the build?`
`11. What expansion gap detail are you using at walls and at columns? How will the perimeter be finished — base shoe, integral cove, or millwork-bonded base?`
`12. Have you visited the slab in person, or is this bid based on plans only?`

`### Red Flags in a Hardwood Bid`

`- No ASTM F2170 test line item, or "moisture testing as needed" with no cost.`
`- Wear layer <3 mm proposed for restaurant use.`
`- Solid hardwood proposed over the slab without a sleeper system.`
`- Site-finished hardwood proposed (off-gassing time, schedule risk, inferior finish).`
`- Floating installation proposed for fine dining FOH.`
`- Acrylic adhesive proposed for 7″+ wide plank.`
`- Single $/SF blended price covering "everything."`
`- Residential-only warranty from manufacturer.`

`# SECTION 2 — KITCHEN / BOH / SERVICE AREAS (~700 SF)`

`## 2.1 Commercial Kitchen Flooring Options — and Why Urethane Mortar Is Right for Live-Fire Korean`

`| System | What it is | Where it fits |`
`|---|---|---|`
`| **Cementitious urethane mortar (urethane cement)** | A 3- or 4-component poured-in-place system: urethane-urea binder + Portland cement + graded quartz/silica aggregates + pigments. Troweled at 3/16″ to 3/8″ thickness. Examples: **Stonhard Stonclad UT** (5 mm / ~3/16″, the reference standard for commercial kitchens, HACCP-certified), **Stonhard Stonclad UR**, **Dur-A-Flex Poly-Crete MDB** (1/4″) and Poly-Crete SLB (3/16″), **BASF MasterTop UR**, **Sherwin-Williams FasTop M** (3/8″ trowel mortar) and FasTop S (3/16″ slurry), **Sika Sikafloor PurCem**, **Florock Florock-PUMA / FloroCrete**. | **Recommended.** Resists thermal shock from hot grease, steam cleaning, and ice water — a non-negotiable property in a live-fire Korean kitchen with charcoal grills, induction, and walk-in coolers in close proximity. Seamless, NSF/ANSI 51 listed for food-zone surfaces, USDA/FDA compliant, naturally resistant to organic acids and harsh detergents. |`
`| **Epoxy resinous flooring** | Multi-coat 100%-solids epoxy with broadcast quartz or aluminum-oxide aggregate, typically 60–125 mil total thickness. Examples: **Stonhard Stonshield**, **Sherwin-Williams General Polymers / Resuflor**, **Dur-A-Flex Dur-A-Quartz / Hybriflex**, **Florock decorative epoxy**. | Acceptable secondary option for non-cookline BOH (prep, dish, pastry). Less thermal-shock resistant than urethane mortar; epoxy can yellow under UV, becomes brittle, and is prone to delamination when subjected to hot grease spills or steam from a charcoal cookline. |`
`| **Quarry tile + epoxy grout** | 6×6 or 8×8 unglazed natural-clay tile with abrasive grit embedded in surface (Daltile Quarry Tile, Daltile Quarry Textures, Metropolitan Ceramics QuarryBasics, American Olean) set with ANSI A118.4 modified thinset and grouted with 100%-solids epoxy grout. | The traditional commercial-kitchen standard. Durable, slip-resistant, time-tested. Drawbacks: hard and cold underfoot (fatigue), grout joints concentrate maintenance and harbor grease over decades, edges chip on dropped pans, and the system is no longer cheaper than urethane mortar. |`
`| **Sealed concrete** | Densifier (Prosoco LS, Ameripolish) + dye/stain + topcoat sealer. | **Not appropriate at the cookline.** Cannot be cleaned to commercial sanitation standard, will not pass ANSI A326.3 wet DCOF for greasy areas, and is not approved by most AHJs as a food-prep floor. Acceptable only in dry storage or an office. |`
`| **Single-ply commercial vinyl / SVT** | Roll vinyl or LVT plank with welded seams. | Used in some QSR kitchens. **Not appropriate for a fine-dining live-fire kitchen** — wood/charcoal embers, hot grease, and steam cleaning will destroy it. |`
`| **Porcelain or natural stone tile** | Large-format porcelain. | Acceptable for non-cookline service areas; not used at cookline because grout maintenance is impractical and slip rating typically inadequate. |`

`**Recommendation: 1/4″ cementitious urethane mortar** (Stonhard Stonclad UT or Dur-A-Flex Poly-Crete MDB) **with broadcast quartz aggregate, integral 4–6″ cove base, hopper'd floor drains, and a urethane topcoat (Stonseal UT7 / Poly-Crete TF Plus / Armor Top).** Spec the heaviest available standard texture for the cookline area and the lighter texture for prep/dish (where staff need easy mopping). The system is NSF/ANSI 51 listed, HACCP-certified, FDA/USDA compliant, and meets Texas Food Establishment Rules (TFER, 25 TAC §228) requirements for "smooth, durable, easily cleanable" floors with coved floor/wall junctures.`

`## 2.2 Slip-Resistance Standards — What Actually Applies`

`The retired ASTM D2047 / James Machine static-friction test (target 0.5 SCOF) is **obsolete** and should not appear in a modern bid. The current standard is:`

`**ANSI A326.3 — Test Method for Measuring Dynamic Coefficient of Friction (DCOF) of Hard Surface Flooring Materials** (revised February 2022 as ANSI A326.3-2021), measured with the **BOT-3000E tribometer** using SBR test foot and SLS solution. ANSI A326.3-2021 introduced **five Product Use Categories** with category-specific thresholds:`

`| Category | Threshold (wet, unless noted) | Typical applications |`
`|---|---|---|`
`| **Interior, Dry (ID)** | ≥0.42 dry | Hotel lobbies, dry showrooms |`
`| **Interior, Wet (IW)** | ≥0.42 wet | Entry foyers, public restrooms, FOH dining, grocery |`
`| **Interior, Wet Plus (IW+)** | ≥0.50 wet | Public showers, pool decks, locker rooms |`
`| **Exterior, Wet (EW)** | ≥0.55 wet | Patios, walkways |`
`| **Oils/Greases (O/G)** | ≥0.55 wet (typical mfr-declared) | **Commercial kitchen cookline, fryer/grill areas, food prep** |`

`For **Sŏn's kitchen and cookline, the target spec is DCOF ≥0.55 wet under the ANSI A326.3 Oils/Greases category.** The dining room and bar fall under Interior, Wet (≥0.42 wet); the entry, where wet shoes track in, should target ≥0.42 wet at minimum and ≥0.50 if budget allows. **Note:** ANSI A326.3 explicitly states the test is for "comparing surfaces" and is not by itself a determination of slip safety; prudent practice is to spec a system that achieves 0.55+ at the cookline rather than the 0.42 floor.`

`OSHA does not publish a binding slip-resistance number but cites ANSI standards; commercial general-liability insurers and franchise concepts often impose a higher threshold (commonly 0.50 or 0.60 wet) — review your policy.`

`**Slip resistance comes from the broadcast aggregate, not the resin.** Finer aggregate (e.g., Dur-A-Flex F60 fine) cleans easily but yields lower DCOF; coarser aggregate (e.g., Q-Rok Quartz, Flintshot) yields higher DCOF but is harder to mop. The standard spec is "medium texture" at the cookline and "light texture" in prep zones. The contractor's TDS or independent third-party DCOF report on the **specified system** (not just the resin) is what verifies the number.`

`**Ask the vendor for:** a third-party DCOF test report on the specific Stonclad UT (or equivalent) build with the specific aggregate broadcast and topcoat, demonstrating wet DCOF ≥0.55.`

`## 2.3 Cove Base — Required, Not Optional`

`Texas Food Establishment Rules (TFER, 25 TAC §228), most local AHJs, and the FDA Food Code require: *"Floors in food prep areas, food storage areas, utensil-washing areas, walk-in refrigeration units, dressing rooms, locker rooms and toilet rooms shall be designed, constructed, and installed so they are smooth and easily cleanable, with floor and wall junctures coved, and enclosed or sealed, and shall be maintained in good repair."*`

`**Integral cove base** is the only correct interpretation in a urethane mortar / epoxy cookline:`

`- **Integral** = the cove material is the same urethane/epoxy system as the floor, troweled up the wall to a defined height with no joint at the floor/wall transition. Stonhard, Dur-A-Flex, Sherwin-Williams, Florock, and Sika all sell formulated cove mortars (Stonhard Stonshield 980 Coving Resin, Dur-A-Flex E903UCB Cove Base Urethane Mortar, Resinwerks Cove Resin) for this purpose.`
`- **Height**: 4″ standard, 6″ preferred behind the cookline and dishwasher; 4″ acceptable elsewhere. Some AHJs accept 2″.`
`- **Radius**: 3/4″ to 1″ minimum at the floor/wall transition (the curved profile that lets a squeegee or mop reach into the corner). A few specs call for a 2″ radius in healthcare/pharma; 1″ is the right call for restaurants. Avoid the 45° "cant" cove style — it's primarily for cart impact protection in food-processing plants and is not typically called for in a restaurant kitchen.`

`**Coordination with wall trades is critical:**`
`- Drywall must terminate **above** the cove top (typically 4–6″ above slab).`
`- FRP (fiber-reinforced plastic) wall panel **overlaps** the top edge of the cove — never the other way around. The lap is sealed with NSF-listed silicone.`
`- Stainless steel wall panels (cookline splash zone) similarly terminate above the cove.`

`**Vinyl cove base** (4″ Roppe, Johnsonite, Burke) is **acceptable in non-cookline BOH areas** — dry storage, office, employee restroom, dry hallway — but **never at the cookline, near a floor drain, in the dish room, or anywhere subject to wet washdown**. Vinyl cove fails at adhesive seam over time, peeling and harboring grease; it's also not approved by most health departments at wet/cookline locations.`

`## 2.4 Floor Drain Integration — the Highest-Risk Detail in the Build`

`Get this wrong and the kitchen has a permanent puddle and an annual health-department flag.`

`**Sequencing rules:**`
`1. **Drains must be set BEFORE the urethane mortar is poured.** Drain bodies are roughed-in by the plumber per the Plumbing/Grease Interceptor Compliance Guide, with the drain rim set so that after the 1/4″ urethane pour the rim sits flush or 1/16″ below the finished floor surface — never proud.`
`2. **Slope to drain: 1/4″ per foot toward the drain (UPC 2024 §708.0; also IPC §704.1).** This is also the slope target for finished kitchen floors per virtually every AHJ. The slope can be built into the slab at the time the landlord pours the structural slab, or — more commonly — built up during the urethane mortar installation using a sloped underlayment of polymer-modified cementitious grout (e.g., **PumaCRETE/EPF slope-to-drain underlayment** or **Stonhard Stonset TG6** as the substrate, with the urethane mortar at uniform 1/4″ thickness over the slope). Slope-to-drain underlayment typically adds 75–100% to the urethane mortar cost in the affected area.`
`3. **Hopper detail at each drain.** The urethane mortar is troweled into a "hopper" — a beveled depression that flows down to the drain rim, tying the floor system mechanically and chemically into the rim. Without a hopper, the edge cracks within 12 months. Stonhard specs Stonflex MP7 around drains; Dur-A-Flex calls for a primer collar; the Schluter Kerdi-Drain has an integrated bonding flange that performs a similar function for tile.`
`4. **Membrane around the drain.** Even in urethane mortar (which is inherently waterproof), a waterproofing collar (Stonhard ME7, Laticrete Hydro Ban) extends 12–18″ around the drain to handle minor differential movement.`

`**Common failure modes (red flags during install observation):**`
`- Flooring poured before drains are set → drain inevitably ends up proud or recessed, water pools.`
`- Slab finished flat with no slope, no underlayment slope built in → permanent standing water, fails health inspection.`
`- Drain rim set above finished floor → trip hazard plus standing water all around.`
`- No hopper detail → edges crack within a year, harboring grease and bacteria.`
`- Plumber and flooring contractor not coordinated on sequencing → finger-pointing, change orders.`

`This is the single most important coordination meeting in the project. **Hold a drain-coordination preconstruction meeting between the GC, plumber, and flooring contractor before any drain is roughed-in.**`

`## 2.5 Waterproofing and Moisture Management Under the Kitchen Floor`

`- **Urethane mortar systems are inherently waterproof** when installed with integral cove and proper drain hoppers. No separate sheet membrane is needed under the body of the floor.`
`- **Quarry tile installations require a waterproof membrane** beneath the mortar bed — Schluter Kerdi, Laticrete Hydro Ban, Mapei Mapelastic AquaDefense — particularly around drains.`
`- **Slab moisture testing per ASTM F1869 and F2170 is required before any resinous floor**: Dur-A-Flex Poly-Crete data sheet specifically references F-2170; Stonhard requires moisture content <5% before installing Stonclad UT. Resinous flooring is somewhat more tolerant of slab moisture than hardwood (typical threshold 80–85% RH), but exceeding the limit is the leading cause of resinous floor delamination.`
`- **Vapor mitigation for resinous flooring:** Dur-A-Flex MVP primer is specified above 75% RH; Stonhard Stonproof RH7 handles high-RH slabs; Mapei Planiseal VS handles unlimited RH if no standing water.`

`### 12 Questions to Ask the Kitchen Flooring Vendor`

`1. What specific urethane mortar system are you specifying (manufacturer, product line, thickness, topcoat)? Provide the TDS.`
`2. Are you on the **manufacturer's certified installer list** (Stonhard certified, Dur-A-Flex certified, Sherwin-Williams certified)? Provide proof.`
`3. What **wet DCOF per ANSI A326.3** does your system achieve under the Oils/Greases category, with the specific aggregate and topcoat I'm getting? Provide a third-party report.`
`4. What is your **integral cove base** spec — height, radius, material continuity?`
`5. What is your **drain hopper detail** — show me the section drawing.`
`6. Has the slope-to-drain been verified or quoted? If the slab is flat, what is your slope underlayment system and cost adder?`
`7. What ASTM F2170 testing protocol are you using and what is your action threshold for resinous flooring?`
`8. What is your sequence relative to the plumber, the equipment installer, and the FRP/wall panel installer? Provide a Gantt-style sequence.`
`9. Provide three Austin-area commercial-kitchen references — restaurants, ideally with live-fire cooking — with phone numbers.`
`10. What is your **manufacturer warranty** on the system and your **labor warranty**? Are they single-source (one company stands behind the whole assembly) or split?`
`11. What is your touch-up and repair protocol if a section fails? How long is the kitchen out of service for a repair?`
`12. What floor protection are you installing during the rest of the buildout, and who owns damage from other trades after your pour?`

`### Red Flags in a Kitchen Bid`

`- Sealed concrete proposed at the cookline.`
`- Vinyl cove proposed at any wet area, cookline, or floor-drain location.`
`- Single $/SF rate covering the entire ~700 SF without differentiating cookline vs. dry-storage.`
`- No moisture testing line item.`
`- No DCOF report on the actual specified system (just resin marketing literature).`
`- No drain hopper detail or no coordination with the plumber.`
`- Contractor not on the manufacturer's certified installer list.`
`- Epoxy proposed at the cookline (acceptable only if owner has chosen it knowingly with full understanding of thermal-shock vulnerability).`
`- No integral cove base on the urethane mortar system.`
`- Bid does not address slope-to-drain — assumes the slab is already sloped.`

`---`

`# SECTION 3 — RESTROOMS (154 SF)`

`## 3.1 Tile Options for a Fine Dining Restroom`

`| Tile | Verdict |`
`|---|---|`
`| **Porcelain (≤0.5% absorption per ANSI A137.1)** | **Recommended.** Frost-proof, durable, lowest maintenance, available in large format (24×48, 24×24, 12×24) for a contemporary look with minimal grout. Brands: Daltile, Crossville (Crossville EW / IW+ ratings explicitly published), Florida Tile, MSI, Emser, Mirage, Atlas Concorde. |`
`| **Natural stone (marble, limestone, travertine)** | Acceptable for design impact but requires sealing every 6–12 months, etches from acidic cleaners (citrus, urine residue, many disinfectants), and is the highest-maintenance option in any restroom — at restaurant cleaning frequency, etching is essentially unavoidable on calcite-bearing stone. If used, restrict to feature wall or vanity tops, not the floor. |`
`| **Ceramic** | Cheaper than porcelain, higher absorption (typically 3–7%), softer surface — acceptable for low-traffic residential, **inferior to porcelain for commercial.** |`
`| **Mosaic / small-format** | Often used as accent on shower or feature wall; the increased grout joint density actually improves slip resistance, so mosaic on the floor in front of urinals/toilets is a design-and-safety move. |`

`## 3.2 Slip Resistance for Restroom Wet Areas`

`Same ANSI A326.3 standard as the rest of the project:`

`- **Floor field tile:** wet DCOF ≥0.42 minimum (Interior Wet category).`
`- **In front of urinals, toilet, lavatory:** target ≥0.50 wet — these zones see frequent water on the floor.`
`- **Smaller tile = more grout joints = better slip resistance.** This is why you'll see designers spec 12×12 or 6×6 (or even 2×2 mosaic) at restroom floors despite the larger format trend on walls.`
`- **Anti-slip surface treatments** (post-installation chemical etching from SlipNOT, Sure Step, Slip Doctors) are available for natural stone if you go that direction; verify the treatment doesn't void the tile's appearance warranty.`

`Verify by asking the supplier for the **manufacturer-declared Product Use Classification** (per ANSI A326.3-2021's classification system) — a Crossville, Daltile, Florida Tile, or MSI product will be classified IW (Interior Wet) or IW+ on the technical data sheet.`

`## 3.3 Restroom Floor Drains`

`- **Austin code does not require a floor drain in a restaurant restroom**, but one is commonly included for cleaning purposes (see the Plumbing Compliance Guide).`
`- If included, slope tile to drain at 1/4″ per foot.`
`- **Linear drains** (Schluter Kerdi-Line, QuickDrain, Infinity Drain) preferred over center-point drains for design quality and ease of slope (only one direction of slope needed instead of four).`
`- **Waterproof membrane is mandatory** under any tile floor with a drain or in a wet zone: Schluter Kerdi (PEVA sheet, 8-mil), Laticrete Hydro Ban (liquid-applied), Mapei Mapelastic AquaDefense (liquid-applied), Custom Building Products RedGard. Membrane must turn up the wall a minimum of 6″ and integrate with the drain flange.`

`## 3.4 Tile Setting and Grout for Fine Dining Restrooms`

`- **Thinset:** ANSI A118.4 (modified) or A118.11 thinset for porcelain ≤0.5% absorption. Brand examples: Mapei Ultraflex 2 / Ultraflex LFT (large format tile), Laticrete 254 Platinum, Custom Building Products MegaLite.`
`- **Grout: epoxy, not cement.** Laticrete SpectraLOCK PRO Premium (ANSI A118.3, <0.5% absorption — comparable to porcelain itself; antimicrobial Microban additive) and Mapei Kerapoxy CQ are the two primary specs. Epoxy grout in a restaurant restroom **never needs sealing, resists mildew, doesn't etch from cleaners, doesn't pick up dye from black grout color, and lasts the life of the tile.** The cost premium over cement grout (~$2–$4/SF added) is paid back in a single year of reduced re-sealing and re-grouting.`
`- **Grout color strategy:** dark grout hides mildew and shoe scuffs and is the universal choice for restaurant restrooms; light grout looks high-design but will look bad within 6 months without epoxy chemistry. Pick dark grout with dark or light tile; dark grout with light tile creates strong visual rhythm; light grout only with epoxy, never with cement.`

`## 3.5 Restroom Cost Stack — 154 SF`

`| Line | $/SF | Total |`
`|---|---|---|`
`| Porcelain field tile (designer-grade, large format) | $8–$25 | $1,200–$3,850 |`
`| Modified thinset, epoxy grout, waterproof membrane (Kerdi/Hydro Ban) | $4–$10 | $620–$1,540 |`
`| Setting labor | $8–$18 | $1,230–$2,770 |`
`| Linear drain (if included) | lump sum | $400–$1,200 |`
`| Trim, transitions, Schluter profiles | lump | $300–$700 |`
`| **Total installed** | | **~$4,000–$10,000** |`

`### Restroom Vendor Questions`

`1. Manufacturer's declared Product Use Classification per ANSI A326.3-2021 for the specified floor tile? Provide TDS.`
`2. Modified thinset ANSI rating (A118.4 or A118.11)?`
`3. Epoxy grout brand and ANSI A118.3 compliance?`
`4. Waterproof membrane brand, type, and how it integrates with the drain (if installed) and turns up the wall?`
`5. Tile layout drawing showing slope to drain (if applicable) and field/accent transitions?`

`---`

`# SECTION 4 — BAR + ENTRY + CIRCULATION (~605 SF)`

`## 4.1 Behind the Bar`

`**Bar staff stand on this floor for 8–12 hour shifts.** Comfort, slip resistance, and durability matter more than aesthetics — most of this floor is hidden by the bar die and the back-bar millwork.`

`| Option | Verdict |`
`|---|---|`
`| **Continuous urethane mortar** (Stonclad UT or Poly-Crete MDB) extended from the kitchen | **Recommended.** Provides ≥0.55 DCOF, seamless to the kitchen, integrates with floor drains behind the bar. |`
`| **Epoxy resinous with high DCOF** | Acceptable second choice. |`
`| Sealed concrete with rubber bar mats | Mats are tripping hazards, hygiene problem (grease and beverage spillage rots beneath them within months), inconsistent surface for staff. |`
`| Tile | Grout failure under continuous wet conditions; cold underfoot. |`

`**Floor drains behind the bar** are typical — coordinate location with the plumber (typically near the ice well, dump sink, and beer tap manifold). Same hopper detail as kitchen.`

`**Anti-fatigue management:** spec quality bar mats (Notrax, Andersen Comfort Flow, San Jamar) on top of the urethane mortar where staff stand most. Mats are easy to lift and clean nightly; the urethane mortar underneath is washable and slip-rated.`

`## 4.2 Entry / Circulation`

`The entry is the single dirtiest patch of floor in the restaurant — wet shoes, gravel, parking-lot grit, the occasional spilled latte. It is also the first impression. Three viable design-quality finishes:`

`| Option | Notes |`
`|---|---|`
`| **Large-format porcelain** (24×24, 24×48) | Excellent. Slip-rated IW+ if the right tile is chosen. Pairs visually with restroom porcelain. |`
`| **Terrazzo (poured-in-place or precast)** | Highest-end design statement; expensive ($25–$60/SF installed) but extremely durable. |`
`| **Polished concrete** | Design-forward, durable, no transitions to the slab. See §4.3. |`
`| **Hardwood continuation from dining** | Acceptable only if a generous walk-off mat well is recessed into the slab at the entry to catch water before it reaches the wood. Hardwood at the entry without a mat well is a maintenance failure waiting to happen. |`

`**Recessed walk-off mat well** — a depression in the slab (1/2″ to 3/4″ deep, sized to receive a roll-out coir, rubber, or carpet walk-off mat) at the entry vestibule. Standard fine-dining detail; protects the rest of the FOH floor. Coordinate with GC if the slab is being topped/leveled — the well should be cast or saw-cut and chipped before flooring trades arrive.`

`## 4.3 Polished Concrete as a Design Option`

`**Polish levels** (per Concrete Polishing Council / CPC nomenclature):`
`- **Level 1 (~100–200 grit)**: ground concrete, flat-matte, no shine. Industrial.`
`- **Level 2 (~400 grit)**: honed, low sheen.`
`- **Level 3 (~800 grit)**: satin polish — **the minimum for fine dining FOH**.`
`- **Level 4 (~1500–3000 grit)**: high polish, mirror-like.`

`Process: aggressive grind (CSP-3) → multiple progressive grit passes → densifier (lithium silicate; Prosoco Consolideck LS, Ameripolish 3DHS, Solomon Grind-Chem) → optional dye or acid stain → topcoat sealer (Ameripolish SR², Prosoco Consolideck Stain & Wear, Surecrete EcoPolish) → buff.`

`**Cost:** $7–$18/SF depending on level, dye/stain work, and slab condition.`

`**Pros:** extremely durable, easy clean, design-forward, no transitions if continued from the kitchen pour — though obviously the kitchen will not be polished concrete, so the boundary is at the kitchen pass.`

`**Cons:** cold and hard underfoot, acoustically reflective (loud), shows every imperfection in the slab — including the surface imperfections the LOI flagged. **The slab quality limits the polished-concrete result.** If the existing slab is broom-finished and pitted, polished concrete will telegraph it. Mock up a 4×4 ft test patch before committing.`

`## 4.4 Transitions Between Flooring Types`

`Fine dining guests notice transitions instantly — a sloppy threshold reads as unprofessional regardless of how nice the dining room hardwood is. Plan and detail every boundary.`

`**Common transitions in this project:**`
`- Hardwood (dining) → urethane mortar (kitchen pass)`
`- Hardwood (dining) → porcelain or polished concrete (entry)`
`- Hardwood (dining) → urethane mortar (bar floor)`
`- Porcelain (restroom) → hardwood (corridor)`
`- Walk-off mat well → entry tile`

`**ADA / Texas Accessibility Standards (TAS) §404.2.5 thresholds for changes in level:**`
`- **0 to 1/4″**: vertical, no edge treatment required.`
`- **1/4″ to 1/2″**: must be beveled at 1:2 maximum slope (rise:run).`
`- **>1/2″**: requires a ramp meeting §405 (1:12 max slope, handrails per length).`
`- **At doorways**: maximum threshold height 1/2″ in new construction (3/4″ for sliding exterior doors), with bevel above 1/4″.`

`**Transition products to know:**`
`- **Schluter Reno-T** (T-shape, equal flooring heights) — bronze, brushed aluminum, anodized aluminum, brass, stainless.`
`- **Schluter Reno-U** (U-shape, edge protection where one floor terminates without a continuation).`
`- **Schluter Reno-V** (V-shape, ramped transition between unequal heights).`
`- **Schluter Schiene** (L-shape edge profile for tile-to-other).`
`- **Schluter Dilex** (movement joint profile — important at long hardwood runs).`
`- **Wood reducer strips** (matched to the hardwood — beveled solid wood transition from hardwood down to tile/concrete).`
`- **Brass or bronze T-bars** for hardwood-to-hardwood at room boundaries on long runs.`

`**Why this matters at Sŏn's quality level:** a 1/2″-thick stone threshold dropped between dining hardwood and a porcelain entry, with no bevel and no profile, is the first thing a designer-conscious guest's eye locks onto when they walk in. Specify each transition by drawing — don't leave it to the trim carpenter to figure out on installation day.`

`## 4.5 Bar/Entry/Circulation Cost Stack — ~605 SF`

`| Scenario | $/SF | Total |`
`|---|---|---|`
`| Urethane mortar behind bar (~150 SF) + porcelain entry/circulation (~455 SF) | $14–$25 blended | $8,500–$15,000 |`
`| Urethane mortar bar + polished concrete entry/circulation | $10–$22 blended | $6,000–$13,500 |`
`| Hardwood continuation through entry (with mat well) + urethane mortar bar | $14–$28 blended | $8,500–$17,000 |`

`---`

`# SECTION 5 — GENERAL / CROSS-CUTTING TOPICS`

`## 5.1 Slab Moisture Testing — The Single Decision That Affects Every Zone`

`| Test | What it measures | Threshold for hardwood | Threshold for resinous |`
`|---|---|---|---|`
`| **ASTM F1869** Calcium Chloride MVER | Surface moisture vapor emission rate (lb/1,000 SF/24 hr) | ≤3 lb | ≤5 lb (system-dependent) |`
`| **ASTM F2170** In-situ Relative Humidity probes (the modern gold standard) | Internal RH at 40% slab depth | ≤75% RH | ≤80–85% RH (system-dependent) |`
`| **ASTM F2420** Surface RH | Surface RH only (less accurate; rarely used alone) | n/a as primary | n/a as primary |`

`**Test protocols (both):** building enclosed, HVAC running at occupancy temperature/humidity for 48 hours before testing; F2170 probes equilibrate 24+ hours after sleeve install (manufacturer-dependent — some require 72 hours).`

`**Number of probes/tests:** ASTM F2170 calls for 3 probes for the first 1,000 SF, plus 1 per additional 1,000 SF. For 2,310 SF total interior, plan on 5–6 probes.`

`**Cost:** $400–$1,200 total, typically performed by the flooring contractor as a line item.`

`**Failure to test voids the warranty** for every major hardwood manufacturer (Mannington, Mirage, Mohawk, DuChâteau, Hallmark, Stuga, Carlisle), every major adhesive manufacturer (Bostik, Mapei, Sika, Stauf), and every major resinous flooring manufacturer (Stonhard, Dur-A-Flex, Sherwin-Williams, Florock).`

`**Action thresholds and remediation:**`
`- Pass (≤75% RH): proceed normally.`
`- Fail (>75% RH): apply vapor mitigation primer (Aquafin VRS, Mapei Planiseal VS / VS Fast / MB / MSP, Bostik MVP4, Sika MB, Koster VAP I 2000) at $3–$8/SF before proceeding.`

`## 5.2 The Cross-Trade Coordination Map`

`Five integration points where flooring touches another trade. **A buildout that gets these wrong creates back-charges, change orders, and rework.**`

`1. **Slab (landlord/GC) ↔ Flooring contractor** — flatness, cleanliness, moisture, and any topping/slope work. Hold a slab-handover walk-through with the GC and flooring contractor before the LL hands over.`
`2. **Plumber ↔ Flooring contractor** — floor drains roughed in, finished elevation, hopper detail, slope. Hold a drain coordination meeting before any plumbing rough.`
`3. **Drywall/wall trade ↔ Flooring contractor** — drywall must terminate above cove top; FRP/SS panels must lap over cove top. Spec the wall section on the construction drawings.`
`4. **Millwork/casework ↔ Flooring contractor** — does the FOH base run on top of the hardwood (more expensive, prettier joints) or does the hardwood run under the millwork (cheaper, hides cut edges)? Either is acceptable; pick one per zone and document.`
`5. **Equipment installer ↔ Flooring contractor** — hood pedestals, walk-in cooler thresholds, floor-mounted equipment legs all generate point loads and sequencing constraints. Walk-in cooler floors typically extend the urethane mortar inside the box; coordinate.`

`## 5.3 NSF / Food-Zone Surface References`

`- **NSF/ANSI 51 — Food Equipment Materials** governs surfaces in contact with food, but is also referenced for floors in food prep areas. Stonhard Stonclad UT, Dur-A-Flex Poly-Crete MDB, BASF MasterTop, and Florock urethane mortar all carry NSF/ANSI 51 listings for food-zone use.`
`- **HACCP International certification** is the higher-tier food-safety certification; Stonclad UT and several Dur-A-Flex systems carry it.`
`- **TFER (25 TAC §228)** language: floors in food prep, storage, dishwashing, walk-ins, dressing, and toilet rooms must be "smooth and easily cleanable, with floor and wall junctures coved." This is the line that mandates integral cove base.`

`## 5.4 The Master 12-Question Vendor Questionnaire (Apply to Every Bid)`

`1. Provide three Austin-area fine dining or commercial restaurant references with owner contacts.`
`2. What ASTM moisture testing protocol (F1869, F2170, or both) do you use, where in this building, with how many probes, and what are your action thresholds for hardwood and for resinous flooring?`
`3. What slab prep is included in your bid — grinding/shotblasting (to what CSP), self-leveling, patching, crack treatment, moisture mitigation? List as separate line items.`
`4. What wet DCOF (per ANSI A326.3-2021, with manufacturer-declared Product Use Classification) does your specified kitchen flooring system achieve? Provide a third-party report on the specific build (resin + aggregate + topcoat).`
`5. What is your wear-layer thickness on the dining room engineered hardwood, and what manufacturer/series? Provide TDS.`
`6. What adhesive system are you using for hardwood glue-down (manufacturer, SKU, trowel notch, coverage)?`
`7. What is your scope for cove base — integral, vinyl, or tile? Height, radius, and wall-trade coordination?`
`8. How are floor drains integrated, and have you coordinated with the plumber? Show me the hopper section detail.`
`9. What is your warranty on materials (manufacturer) and labor (installer)? Single-source or split?`
`10. Are you on the manufacturer's certified installer list for the resinous flooring system? Provide proof.`
`11. What is your construction sequence — does flooring go in before or after millwork, casework, equipment, FRP wall panel? Provide a sequence schedule.`
`12. Have you reviewed the slab condition in person, or is your bid based on plans only?`

`## 5.5 The Master Red-Flags List`

`- **No moisture testing line item** or no testing protocol cited.`
`- **No prep allowance** — flat per-SF price with no slab condition assumptions.`
`- Wear layer **under 3 mm** on engineered hardwood for commercial.`
`- **Site-finished hardwood** proposed for restaurant FOH.`
`- **Vinyl cove base** proposed for the cookline area.`
`- **Sealed concrete** proposed as the kitchen finish.`
`- **No DCOF documentation** on the kitchen flooring system, or DCOF cited for resin only without aggregate broadcast.`
`- **No mention of integral cove base** on the urethane mortar system.`
`- Bid **doesn't differentiate by zone** — single per-SF rate for the whole project.`
`- Contractor **not on manufacturer's certified installer list** for the resinous system.`
`- **No drain hopper detail or sequencing** with the plumber.`
`- **Solid hardwood proposed** over the slab without a sleeper system.`
`- **Floating hardwood proposed** for a fine-dining FOH.`
`- Manufacturer warranty cited is **residential-only.**`

`---`

`# RECOMMENDATIONS`

`## Stage 1 — Before You Sign Any Flooring Contract (next 2–4 weeks)`

`1. **Get the landlord's construction documents for the slab** — pour date, mix design, vapor-barrier specification beneath the slab, and any curing compounds applied. If the slab was poured within 90 days of LL handover, plan on extended dry time before any flooring goes down (concrete typically requires 30 days/inch of slab thickness to dry to <75% RH under ideal conditions).`
`2. **Hire one flooring contractor (not the GC) to perform an ASTM F2170 in-situ RH test on the slab as soon as the building is enclosed and HVAC is running.** Cost: ~$600–$1,200. This single test will tell you whether the dining room engineered hardwood comes in at $20K or $35K. This decision drives the whole budget. **This test is mandatory before any flooring vendor's bid is reliable.**`
`3. **Specify by zone, not by total area.** Issue a flooring RFP with four zone scopes (dining hardwood, kitchen urethane mortar, restroom porcelain, bar/entry/circulation) and require pricing line-by-line, including separated slab prep and moisture mitigation allowances.`

`## Stage 2 — During Vendor Selection (next 4–8 weeks)`

`4. **Get three bids per zone**, and require all three to use the same baseline scope (same product spec, same ANSI A326.3 DCOF target, same cove and drain detail, same prep assumptions). Identical scope is the only way to compare bids.`
`5. **For the kitchen, require certified installer status from the manufacturer.** Stonhard, Dur-A-Flex, and Sherwin-Williams all maintain certified installer programs; an uncertified contractor on Stonclad UT voids the manufacturer warranty.`
`6. **Visit one current Austin restaurant with each top-finalist's work installed.** Walk the floor, talk to the owner about how it has held up, especially around drains and cove base.`
`7. **Hold a coordination meeting between the GC, plumber, and chosen flooring contractor before drains are roughed-in.** This is the most important pre-construction meeting in the project for flooring.`

`## Stage 3 — During Construction`

`8. **Witness or document the moisture test** (date, probe locations, equilibration time, readings). Keep this with the project records — it's your warranty backup for the next 25 years.`
`9. **Witness the first cove-base pour** in the kitchen. Use the "glove test" — run a gloved hand along the cove; if the glove snags on anything, that section needs to be re-sanded before it cures. The cove is what will most likely fail a health inspection if installed sloppily.`
`10. **Photograph every floor drain hopper detail before it's covered**, and confirm slope by pouring a cup of water at the farthest point of the kitchen and watching it find the drain.`

`## Benchmarks That Would Change These Recommendations`

`- **If the slab fails F2170 dramatically (>90% RH)**, reconsider whether glue-down hardwood is the right play in the dining room — at that point you're paying $7–$8/SF for vapor mitigation on top of $15+/SF for material; large-format porcelain at 24×48 may deliver the design intent at lower total cost and less risk.`
`- **If the kitchen square footage grows beyond 700 SF** (e.g., banquet kitchen added later), urethane mortar has scaling labor advantages; reconsider quarry tile if the area gets to ~1,500 SF.`
`- **If the project schedule compresses to <6 weeks from slab handover to opening**, urethane mortar (which can be poured and walked on overnight) becomes more attractive than tile (which requires 24-hour cure on thinset before grouting).`
`- **If insurance carrier mandates a higher DCOF** (some carriers want 0.60 wet at cookline), step up the broadcast aggregate texture and/or add a secondary anti-slip topcoat.`

`---`

`# CAVEATS`

`- **Cost figures are 2026 Austin commercial estimates** and assume normal market conditions. They do not account for compressed schedules, unusual slab repair scope, or tariff-driven changes in imported European white oak pricing (DuChâteau, Stuga, and similar brands source heavily from European mills).`
`- **ANSI A326.3 itself states that the DCOF test is for "comparing surfaces" and is not by itself an assessment of slip risk.** A 0.42 or 0.55 reading is a floor, not a ceiling; high-quality operators target 0.55–0.60 wet at the cookline regardless of code minimum. Ongoing cleaning practices, footwear policy for staff, and prompt spill response do more for actual slip safety than any DCOF number.`
`- **Texas Food Establishment Rules (TFER, 25 TAC §228)** is the governing state regulation, but **the Austin/Travis County Health Department is the Authority Having Jurisdiction (AHJ) for plan review and inspection at 207 E St Elmo Rd.** Local interpretation can be stricter than state minimum on issues like cove base height (some inspectors want 6″ behind dishwashers), drain spacing, and material approval. Submit floor finish samples and a wall-section detail to the Austin Health Department during the plan review phase to confirm acceptability.`
`- **The "Bostik BEST waives moisture testing" claim** appears in Bostik's own marketing literature and TDS but should not be relied on for a fine dining buildout. Independent moisture testing is cheap insurance against a $30,000 floor failure.`
`- **Manufacturer warranties exclude commercial misuse.** A spec sheet may list a "lifetime structural warranty" but will exclude commercial wear, water damage, and improper maintenance. Read the actual warranty document, not the marketing summary.`
`- **Site conditions discovered during demo or after slab inspection can change scope dramatically.** The most common surprise is a slab pour with high residual moisture (a "young" or "wet" slab) — this can add $5,000–$15,000 to the project.`
`- **This document does not replace a licensed Texas architect or interior designer's specification work** for the actual permit drawings. It is a knowledge base for evaluating proposals from those professionals and from the flooring contractors who execute them.`
`- **Sources informing this document include:** ANSI A326.3-2021, ASTM F1869-23, ASTM F2170-23, NWFA Installation Guidelines and Refinishable Program (2022), Texas Food Establishment Rules (25 TAC §228), Texas Accessibility Standards / 2010 ADA Standards §404.2.5 and §405, Uniform Plumbing Code 2024 §708.0, manufacturer technical data sheets from Stonhard, Dur-A-Flex, BASF/MasterBuilders, Sherwin-Williams, Florock, Sika, Bostik, Mapei, Laticrete, Schluter, Daltile, Crossville, DuChâteau, Stuga, Mirage, and Ardex. Verify any specific compliance claim against the current published version of the cited standard before using it in a contract document.`

pages.content:
`# Sŏn — HVAC Distribution, Walk-In Cooler & Acoustics Compliance Guide`
`## Reference Document #5 in the 207 E St Elmo Rd Build Series`

`---`

`## TL;DR`

`- **The 10-ton landlord RTU is almost certainly undersized for a Korean live-fire restaurant of 2,310 SF; demand a Manual N (ACCA commercial load calculation) before signing any mechanical contract, and budget for either supplemental rooftop tonnage or zone-specific mini-splits in the kitchen and bar before the GMP is finalized.**`
`- **The depressed slab for the walk-in is a single-shot construction sequence — get the panel manufacturer, GC, plumber, electrician, and flooring sub coordinated on a written sequence of operations *before* the box arrives, because re-pouring a topping slab to fix a depth or vapor-barrier mistake will cost more than the entire walk-in.**`
`- **Acoustic risk to office neighbors is the most likely source of a landlord-triggered remediation order; lock in (a) a written STC/dB(A) threshold from the landlord, (b) a baseline pre-occupancy sound test, and (c) spring-isolated rooftop curbs and a sound-rated demising wall *before* drywall closes — retrofitting any of these post-opening costs 4–10× the upfront premium.**`

`---`

`## Key Findings`

`1. **HVAC sizing math doesn't work at face value.** Restaurant rule-of-thumb cooling load is 200–300 SF/ton (live-fire pushes the lower end); 2,310 SF at 250 SF/ton implies ~9.2 tons *just for the dining/bar/circulation envelope* before kitchen heat-of-rejection from refrigeration and dishwashing. With a live-fire kitchen exhaust hood removing 4,000–6,000 CFM and a Make-Up Air Unit (MAU) replacing 80–90% of that, the building HVAC must supply the 10–20% transfer-air gap *and* condition the dining room *and* offset solar gain on a Climate Zone 2A (Austin) summer afternoon. The 10-ton RTU will run flat-out and still lose ground in July and August unless supplemented.`

`2. **The "main trunk line" is a starting point, not a system.** What the landlord delivers is a sized supply duct from the rooftop unit's curb dropping into the tenant space — typically rectangular galvanized sheet metal terminating at a transition fitting near the demising wall or above a ceiling chase, with one return drop or a simple return plenum tap. Everything downstream — branches, takeoffs, dampers, diffusers, returns, insulation, sealing, and balancing — is tenant scope. A mechanical contractor's bid that doesn't itemize each of these is incomplete.`

`3. **Kitchen pressurization is the single most-overlooked design parameter in restaurants.** Per ASHRAE Standard 154 (Ventilation for Commercial Cooking Operations), the kitchen must run *slightly negative* relative to the dining room so that grease-laden, garlic-laden, gochujang-laden cooking air stays in the kitchen instead of migrating to where the guests are eating. Hitting that pressure relationship requires the mechanical contractor and the hood/MAU contractor to share design CFMs and agree to a single set of numbers, in writing, before either submits shop drawings.`

`4. **A walk-in cooler installed into a depressed slab is a six-trade choreography.** GC pours topping slab → walk-in vendor sets panels and floor system → plumber roughs in condensate drains → electrician pulls dedicated circuits → refrigeration tech runs lines and starts up → flooring sub installs finished floor inside the box flush with the kitchen finished floor. The most common failure mode in this LOI configuration is **wrong slab depression depth** — the depression must equal the walk-in floor system thickness *plus* the topping slab thickness *plus* the finished kitchen floor thickness, all coordinated *before* the landlord pours.`

`5. **Refrigerant choice has a 2026 expiration date.** Under EPA's AIM Act and Technology Transitions Rule, R-404A is effectively gone for new equipment; current standard for new commercial refrigeration is R-448A or R-449A (HFO-blend HFCs at GWP ~1,280–1,390). EPA's October 2025 reconsideration extended the 1,400-GWP ceiling for remote condensing units to 2032, preserving R-448A/R-449A as compliant choices for this build. The next transition (to A2L lower-GWP refrigerants like R-454A/R-454C) is on the horizon — specify equipment now that ships with R-448A or R-449A and is *retrofittable* to lower-GWP options.`

`6. **Acoustic risk in the LOI sits with the tenant entirely.** The landlord retains "reasonable discretion" to require sound or vibration mitigation if neighboring office tenants complain. Without a written threshold (e.g., NC 35 in the office; STC 50 at the demising wall; ≤ 45 dB(A) at the property line for rooftop equipment) the tenant is exposed to an open-ended remediation obligation. Establish the threshold *now*, in writing, before construction documents are stamped.`

`7. **A minimalist design language is acoustically unforgiving.** A Korean fine-dining aesthetic of polished concrete, hardwood, exposed steel, and stone — without any acoustic treatment — will reliably hit 85–90 dB(A) at full house. That's the "have to shout" zone; published research (Whitlock & Dodd 2008; Kang 2007; restaurant industry reverberation surveys) and Acoustical Society of America data indicate fine-dining target is RT60 = 0.6–0.9 seconds and occupied levels 70–78 dB(A). Plan absorptive treatment from day one as a design element, not as remediation.`
