`## SECTION 1 — DOMAIN 6: HVAC DUCT DISTRIBUTION`
`==============================================`

`### 1.1 What "Main Trunk Line into Building" Actually Means`

`The landlord's scope ends at a defined hand-off point. For a 10-ton packaged rooftop unit (RTU) such as a Trane Voyager, Carrier WeatherMaker 48TC, Daikin Applied Rebel, or Lennox Energence, the typical delivery is:`

`- **Supply trunk:** A rectangular galvanized sheet metal supply duct, sized for the RTU's nominal 4,000 CFM (10 tons × 400 CFM/ton industry rule), dropping vertically through the roof curb and transitioning to a horizontal trunk above the ceiling. Trunk sizing typically 24"×16" or 30"×14", reducing as branches take off. The landlord usually terminates this at a transition collar at the tenant demising line or above a ceiling chase.`
`- **Return:** Either (a) a single return air drop from the RTU into a return plenum (the entire ceiling cavity acts as a low-pressure return), or (b) a ducted return trunk paralleling the supply. Plenum return is cheaper but limits placement of combustible materials in the cavity per IMC §602; ducted return is preferred for restaurants because it allows precise return-grille placement and avoids drawing kitchen-adjacent ceiling air into the system.`
`- **Power and controls:** Disconnect at the unit, low-voltage thermostat wiring stubbed to a designated thermostat location.`
`- **Outdoor air:** The RTU's economizer hood and outdoor-air damper provide the building's ventilation per ASHRAE 62.1 and the 2024 Austin Mechanical Code (UMC 2024 with local amendments, effective July 10, 2025, per Ordinance 20250410-044).`

`**What the tenant scope picks up from there:**`
`- All branch ducts off the trunk (supply takeoffs with manual volume dampers, transitions, elbows, end caps)`
`- Return air ducts/grilles or return plenum boots (depending on configuration)`
`- All diffusers, registers, grilles`
`- Insulation (exterior wrap or interior liner)`
`- Duct sealing per SMACNA Class A`
`- Zoning hardware (zone dampers, bypass dampers if VAV)`
`- Thermostats and zone control panels`
`- Test, Adjust, and Balance (TAB) by independent agency`
`- Duct smoke detectors (IMC §606.2.1) — required because a 10-ton RTU at 4,000 CFM exceeds the 2,000 CFM threshold`

`**Code basis:** Austin adopted the 2024 Uniform Mechanical Code (UMC) with local amendments, effective July 10, 2025, alongside the 2024 IBC and 2024 IECC. The 2024 UMC governs duct construction (Chapter 6), insulation (Chapter 6), and ventilation rates (Chapter 4). For commercial kitchen ventilation, NFPA 96 governs (cross-reference Compliance Guide #1) and the 2024 IMC §507/§508 are commonly cited by Austin DSD even where UMC is the adopted code, because Austin's IMC equivalents are referenced in the Building Code for the kitchen exhaust system.`

`### 1.2 Zone Design — Why One Thermostat Will Fail`

`A restaurant has wildly different thermal loads in adjacent rooms. A single thermostat sized to keep the dining room comfortable will leave the kitchen at 90°F+ and the bar humid; sized to cool the kitchen, it will freeze the dining room to 65°F.`

`**Zoning recommendations for Sŏn:**`

`| Zone | SF | Drivers | Suggested Approach |`
`|---|---|---|---|`
`| Kitchen | 563 | Live fire, dishwasher exhaust, refrigeration condenser rejection if any indoor units, cookline radiant heat | **Dedicated supply** from RTU + dedicated MAU. Kitchen treated as exhaust-driven zone; HVAC supplies tempered air, does not return through kitchen. |`
`| Dining | 988 | Occupant load (50–80 guests at peak), lighting, glazing if any, transfer air for kitchen pressurization | Primary zone served by RTU; absorbs return-air function for the building. Single thermostat. |`
`| Bar | 605 (incl. entry/circ.) | Occupant density, beverage-fridge condenser rejection, door-opening losses at entry | **Separate zone**, ideally its own thermostat with zone damper, or a supplementary mini-split (e.g., Mitsubishi Mr. Slim, Daikin Aurora, LG Multi-V) to handle peak bar loads independently. |`
`| Bathrooms | 154 | Exhaust-only; transfer air | No HVAC supply needed beyond transfer; exhaust per UMC §403 and IMC §403 (50 CFM intermittent or 20 CFM continuous per fixture). |`

`**VAV vs. CAV:** A true Variable Air Volume system on a 10-ton RTU is over-engineered for a 2,310 SF tenant — VAV economics start to make sense above 20–25 tons. The right answer for Sŏn is **constant-volume, multi-zone**: the RTU runs at constant supply CFM, and zone dampers (with a bypass damper to prevent fan back-pressure) modulate flow to dining vs. bar based on individual thermostat calls. Honeywell TrueZONE HZ432, EWC Controls Ultra-Zone, or Arzel zoning panels are the typical hardware for this scale.`

`If the load calculation shows the 10-ton RTU is genuinely undersized (see §1.4), the better answer is the RTU as primary + one or two ductless mini-splits as supplemental for the bar and any chronically hot spot near the kitchen pass.`

`### 1.3 Kitchen Exhaust Offset and Pressurization`

`This is where Compliance Guide #1 (Solid Fuel Exhaust) and this document interlock. The kitchen exhaust hood, sized for a solid-fuel cookline, will pull approximately 4,000–6,000 CFM (depending on hood length and ASHRAE 154 cooking-duty classification — solid fuel/wood/charcoal is "extra heavy" per ASHRAE 154 §4.4, requiring 300–400+ CFM per linear foot of hood).`

`**The math that must be reconciled:**`

`- **Hood exhaust CFM:** Set by NFPA 96, IMC §507, ASHRAE 154 — the hood vendor specifies.`
`- **MAU (Make-Up Air Unit) CFM:** Per ASHRAE 154 §6.1, replacement air shall equal exhaust CFM minus net exfiltration; in practice, MAU replaces 80–90% of exhaust to keep the kitchen slightly negative.`
`- **Transfer air from dining room:** The remaining 10–20% comes from the dining room or bar via under-cut doors, transfer grilles, or building HVAC over-supply. This is what creates the **pressure differential** that keeps cooking smells in the kitchen.`
`- **Building HVAC supply to dining:** Must equal dining ventilation requirement (ASHRAE 62.1 Table 6.1: 7.5 CFM/person + 0.18 CFM/SF for restaurant dining; 7.5 CFM/person + 0.06 CFM/SF for bar/lounge, with a 70 occupants/1,000 SF default) **plus** the transfer-air contribution to the kitchen.`

`**Worked example for Sŏn (illustrative, not a substitute for engineering):**`
`- Hood exhaust assumption: 5,000 CFM (e.g., 14-foot hood at 350 CFM/ft for solid fuel)`
`- MAU at 85%: 4,250 CFM`
`- Transfer air required: 750 CFM from dining → kitchen`
`- Dining ventilation per ASHRAE 62.1: 988 SF × 0.18 + (50 occupants × 7.5) = 178 + 375 = 553 CFM minimum outdoor air`
`- Bar ventilation: 605 SF × 0.06 + (40 occupants × 7.5) = 36 + 300 = 336 CFM minimum`
`- Total dining-side outdoor air requirement: ~890 CFM, which the 10-ton RTU's economizer can provide (typical economizer minimum OA is 15–25% of supply = 600–1,000 CFM at 4,000 CFM total).`

`The pressure relationship target is **kitchen –0.02 to –0.05 inches w.c. relative to dining**. Hitting this target requires the TAB agent (see §1.8) to measure and adjust at startup, with the hood, MAU, and dining HVAC all running.`

`### 1.4 Sizing — Is 10 Tons Adequate?`

`**Short answer: probably not, and you must verify with a Manual N.**`

`- 10 tons = 120,000 BTU/hr cooling capacity.`
`- 2,310 SF interior — but the kitchen (563 SF) is largely an exhaust-driven zone with its own MAU; the HVAC effectively conditions ~1,747 SF (dining + bar + circulation + entry).`
`- Austin Climate Zone 2A: 1% summer design temperature ~99°F dry bulb / 74°F coincident wet bulb (per ASHRAE Climatic Design Conditions for Austin/Camp Mabry).`
`- Restaurant rule-of-thumb: 200–300 SF/ton with live-fire cooking; 250 SF/ton is a defensible mid-range.`
`- 1,747 SF ÷ 250 = ~7 tons just for dining/bar/circulation envelope.`
`- Plus: kitchen residual sensible load (heat that the hood doesn't capture and the MAU doesn't carry — typically 10–15% of equipment heat gain); refrigeration condenser rejection if any indoor walk-in condensers (which we are advising against — see §2); occupant latent load (Korean BBQ tableside grills increase this); solar gain on west-facing glazing if any.`

`**This is why a Manual N is mandatory.** ACCA's Manual N — Commercial Load Calculations (5th edition) is the ANSI-recognized standard for small/midsize commercial buildings. It uses CLTD/CLF methodology to calculate room-by-room sensible and latent loads from:`

`- Occupant count and activity level by zone`
`- Lighting power density (W/SF)`
`- Kitchen equipment heat gain (BTU/hr) — the cookline manufacturer publishes these`
`- Glazing area, orientation, U-factor, SHGC`
`- Wall and roof U-values (the corrugated metal/TPO assembly)`
`- Infiltration rate (door openings, hood pressurization losses)`
`- Outdoor design conditions for Austin`

`**What to do if Manual N shows the 10-ton RTU is undersized:**`

`1. Ask the landlord in writing whether they will upsize the RTU at their cost. (LOI says "10-ton RTU and main HVAC trunk line" — if the load calc proves 10 tons is insufficient for the permitted use, this is a negotiation point.)`
`2. If the landlord won't upsize, plan supplementary cooling:`
`- **Bar mini-split:** 18,000–24,000 BTU/hr ductless (Mitsubishi MSZ-FH, Daikin Quaternity, LG Art Cool) — $4,000–$8,000 installed including line-set and electrical.`
`- **Kitchen pre-rinse / dish area:** 12,000–18,000 BTU/hr spot cooling — $3,500–$6,500 installed.`
`- **Host stand / private dining if any:** 12,000 BTU/hr — $3,000–$5,000.`
`3. Verify the 800-amp 120/208V service can carry supplementary equipment without panel upgrade.`

`### 1.5 Duct Material Options`

`Per UMC 2024 §603 (Austin's adopted code), the following are permitted with restrictions:`

`| Material | Application | Pros | Cons / Caveats |`
`|---|---|---|---|`
`| **Galvanized sheet metal (G60/G90), rectangular** | Standard supply trunk and large branches | Rigid, durable, low leakage when sealed properly, supports SMACNA Class A sealing | Higher labor cost; aesthetic if exposed |`
`| **Spiral round galvanized** | Branches, exposed-ceiling design feature | Lower friction loss than rectangular (round is the most efficient duct shape), aesthetic when exposed and powder-coated, lower leakage class achievable | Requires more ceiling height; harder to fit through tight cavities |`
`| **Flex duct, UL 181 Class 1 listed** | **Limited to short connections from branch to diffuser** | Cheap, fast install | UMC §603.4.1 (and Austin's adopted version) limits factory-made flexible air ducts/connectors to **5 feet maximum length in commercial construction** and prohibits use in lieu of rigid elbows/fittings. The 2021 IMC and many AHJs allow up to 14 feet for "flexible air connectors" but Austin under UMC is the more restrictive 5-foot limit. **Misuse of flex duct is the #1 cause of restaurant HVAC failures.** |`
`| **Fiber duct board / fiberglass-lined** | Code-permissible per UMC §603 | Low cost; built-in acoustic absorption | **Avoid in restaurants** — fiberglass interior is impossible to clean if grease or kitchen-air contamination occurs; not appropriate for any duct downstream of an air path that touches kitchen. |`

`**Sealing class:** UMC §603 and SMACNA HVAC Duct Construction Standards classify duct sealing as Class A (all transverse joints, longitudinal seams, and wall penetrations sealed), Class B (transverse joints + longitudinal seams), or Class C (transverse joints only). ASHRAE 90.1-2022 — and ASHRAE 90.1-2019, which is the basis for Austin's adopted IECC — now requires **Class A for all HVAC duct systems** regardless of pressure class. **Specify Class A in the contract.** Cost premium over Class C is minimal (~5%) and energy savings plus pressurization control are substantial.`

`**Insulation:** Per UMC §605 and ASHRAE 90.1, supply ducts in unconditioned space (above ceiling outside the building envelope, or in mechanical chases) require R-6 minimum (Climate Zone 2); supply ducts inside conditioned space typically R-4.2. Use external duct wrap (1.5" or 2" fiberglass with FSK vapor barrier, e.g., Johns Manville Microlite or Owens Corning SoftR) sealed at all seams.`

`### 1.6 Return Air Design — Restaurants Are Different`

`**The cardinal rule:** Returns are not located in the kitchen. The building HVAC system supplies tempered air to the kitchen for makeup air offset, but it does not pull air back through the kitchen — that air goes out the hood. Pulling kitchen air back through the building HVAC contaminates coils with grease, fouls filters, and shortens equipment life by years.`

`**Where returns go in Sŏn:**`
`- Primary return(s) in the **dining room ceiling**, at the rear of the room (away from the kitchen pass to avoid drawing kitchen-side air toward the return)`
`- Secondary return in the **bar** if bar is a separate zone`
`- Return-air path from circulation/entry via transfer grilles into the dining return`
`- **Bathroom exhaust** is a separate, dedicated exhaust system (not connected to the return)`

`**ASHRAE 62.1 minimum outdoor air for this occupancy mix:**`
`- Restaurant dining room: 7.5 CFM/person + 0.18 CFM/SF (Class 2 air — Table 6.1)`
`- Bar/lounge: 7.5 CFM/person + 0.06 CFM/SF`
`- Default occupant density restaurant dining: 70 per 1,000 SF; bar/cocktail: 100 per 1,000 SF (use design occupant load if known)`

`The MAU is 100% outdoor air for the kitchen by definition. The RTU economizer provides outdoor air for the dining/bar/circulation zone. The TAB agent must verify both at startup.`

`### 1.7 Diffuser and Grille Selection`

`For a Korean fine-dining ceiling, "office grille" plastic eggcrate is a design failure. Specify from manufacturers like **Titus, Krueger, Price Industries, METALAIRE, Nailor**. The architect's reflected ceiling plan (RCP) drives placement.`

`**Recommendations:**`
`- **Linear slot diffusers** (Titus ML-39, Krueger LMT, Price SDS) — 1-, 2-, or 3-slot. Excellent throw control, clean aesthetic, available in matte black for dark-ceiling Korean design language. NC 25–30 typical at design CFM. Ideal for dining room.`
`- **Square plaque diffusers** (Titus PAS, Krueger 1900 series) — for general supply in flat ceilings.`
`- **Drum jet / nozzle diffusers** — for high open-ceiling spaces over the dining room or bar; longer throw, exposed-aesthetic.`
`- **Return grilles** — perforated face return (Titus 350PR) or eggcrate stamped from steel and powder-coated, not plastic.`

`**Acoustic target:** NC 30–35 in dining room, NC 35–40 at bar, NC 40 at kitchen (per ASHRAE Handbook — HVAC Applications, Chapter 49: Noise and Vibration Control). Diffuser selection at design CFM determines whether you hit this — verify the manufacturer's NC rating in the cut sheet at the actual CFM you'll deliver.`

`### 1.8 Test, Adjust, and Balance (TAB)`

`TAB is a separate scope from the mechanical contractor. A TAB agent is an independent third party certified by **NEBB** (National Environmental Balancing Bureau), **AABC** (Associated Air Balance Council), or **TABB** (Testing, Adjusting and Balancing Bureau, ANSI-accredited). They:`

`1. Measure CFM at every supply diffuser, return grille, and exhaust point.`
`2. Adjust manual volume dampers and zone dampers to achieve design CFM ±10%.`
`3. Verify the kitchen-to-dining pressure relationship (slightly negative kitchen).`
`4. Verify outdoor air rates at the RTU and MAU.`
`5. Issue a sealed TAB report with measured-vs.-design values for every air terminal, suitable for permit closeout and code inspection.`

`**Why this matters for Sŏn specifically:** The interaction of (RTU + MAU + hood exhaust + transfer air + bathroom exhaust) is a four-system pressure puzzle. Without TAB, the kitchen will end up either positive (smells migrate to dining — guest complaints) or excessively negative (front door slams shut, hood loses capture, gas appliances backdraft).`

`**Cost for a 2,310 SF restaurant in Austin 2026:** $1,500–$3,500 lump sum, or $0.50–$1.50/SF. **AABC certification provides the strongest independence guarantee** — AABC firms cannot be affiliated with mechanical contractors, eliminating the "self-test" conflict. NEBB allows affiliation; if you select a NEBB firm, ensure it is *not* the same entity that installed the ductwork.`

`**Hire the TAB agent directly**, not as a sub of the mechanical contractor. This is the single highest-leverage move you can make to ensure the system works.`

`### 1.9 Controls and Thermostats`

`Specify **commercial-grade** programmable thermostats:`
`- **Honeywell T7350** or Honeywell Commercial TB7980 — proven, Austin-vendor-supported.`
`- **Pro1 IAQ T955WH** — restaurant industry favorite, durable, simple.`
`- **Ecobee Commercial (SmartBuildings)** — cloud-monitored, BACnet integration, energy reporting.`
`- **Google Nest Pro** — only the Pro version; the residential Nest is not appropriate.`

`Avoid residential-only thermostats (basic Nest, Honeywell Home, Sensi residential). They lack 7-day commercial scheduling, multi-stage compatibility, occupancy-based setback, and BMS integration.`

`**Zone control panel:** Honeywell TrueZONE HZ432 (4-zone) or EWC Controls Ultra-Zone is appropriate scale for Sŏn.`

`**Demand-controlled ventilation (DCV):** ASHRAE 90.1 and the IECC require DCV for spaces with occupancy >25 people/1,000 SF and design OA >3,000 CFM. Sŏn likely doesn't trigger this threshold but DCV with CO₂ sensors in dining and bar can save material energy in low-occupancy hours.`

`### 1.10 Coordination Dependencies`

`The mechanical contractor must coordinate with:`

`1. **Hood / MAU contractor (Compliance Guide #1):** Agree on hood CFM, MAU CFM, kitchen pressure target. Single set of numbers, signed off by both.`
`2. **Electrician:** RTU power (already at the unit from landlord), MAU power, mini-split power if used, control wiring, duct smoke detector wiring to fire alarm panel (Compliance Guide #2).`
`3. **TAB agent:** Pre-balance walk-through, post-balance report.`
`4. **Fire alarm contractor (Compliance Guide #2):** Duct smoke detector per IMC §606.2.1 — required for any system >2,000 CFM (the 10-ton RTU at 4,000 CFM is well over). Detector shuts down RTU on smoke detection and signals the fire alarm panel. UL 268A listed (not UL 268).`
`5. **GC:** Rough-in coordination, ceiling height confirmation, structural support for hung ductwork (per SMACNA hanger spacing tables — typically 8–10 ft for trunks, 4 ft for branches).`
`6. **Architect:** RCP alignment, lighting clearance, supply/return location relative to kitchen pass.`
`7. **Plumber (Compliance Guide #3):** Condensate drain from the RTU and from any indoor coil — must drain to an indirect waste, not a fixture.`

`### 1.12 Twelve Questions to Ask a Mechanical Contractor Before Accepting a Bid`

`1. Have you performed (or will you provide) an ACCA Manual N load calculation for this tenant? Will you provide the calculation as part of the deliverable?`
`2. What is your design kitchen-to-dining pressure differential, and how will you verify it at startup?`
`3. What is your specified SMACNA seal class — A, B, or C?`
`4. How many zones are you proposing, and where is the zone breakdown? What is the zone control panel manufacturer and model?`
`5. What is the maximum length of flex duct in your design? (Should be ≤5 ft per UMC; insist on it in writing.)`
`6. Who is your TAB agent, are they independent (AABC) or affiliated (NEBB), and is TAB included in your bid or a separate line?`
`7. What return-air configuration are you proposing — ducted return or plenum return — and why?`
`8. What R-value of duct insulation are you specifying, and where?`
`9. What thermostat make/model are you specifying? (Reject any residential-only model.)`
`10. Have you coordinated CFM with the kitchen hood contractor and the MAU contractor? Provide the joint coordination sheet.`
`11. What is your duct smoke detector model and tie-in path to the fire alarm panel?`
`12. What is your warranty on workmanship and equipment, and what is your service response time for emergency calls?`

`### 1.13 Red Flags in a Mechanical Bid`

`- **No Manual N referenced.** Sized "by rule of thumb" or "by SF." Reject.`
`- **Flex duct >5 ft anywhere in commercial design.** Code violation under Austin's UMC.`
`- **Single thermostat for the whole space.** Will fail.`
`- **TAB bundled with mechanical scope, by mechanical's own employees.** Self-testing eliminates the value of TAB.`
`- **Plenum return with kitchen ceiling included in plenum.** Will contaminate equipment.`
`- **Residential thermostat (Nest, Sensi, Honeywell Home).** Inadequate.`
`- **No duct smoke detector line item.** Code-required and will catch you at inspection.`
`- **Sealing Class C or unspecified.** Wastes 10–20% of supply air to leakage.`
`- **Return air intake within 10 ft of kitchen pass.** Will draw cooking smells into HVAC.`
`- **No insulation specified, or "as required by code."** Demand R-value in writing.`
`- **No coordination with hood contractor mentioned.** Will produce a pressurization failure.`
`- **Lump-sum bid without itemization.** You can't compare bids; you can't change order intelligently.`

`## SECTION 2 — DOMAIN 8: WALK-IN COOLER`
`==============================================`

`### 2.1 Cooler vs. Freezer Configuration for Korean Fine Dining`

`A Korean fine-dining kitchen at 50–100 covers/night needs:`
`- **Cold storage at 33–39°F:** Banchan prep, daily protein, dairy, cut produce, in-process kimchi at active fermentation stage. This is the *workhorse* — typically used 30–50 times per service.`
`- **Cold storage at 32–34°F:** Long-fermented kimchi at storage stage (kimchi is best held just above freezing to slow fermentation), aging beef if dry-aging program, cold-chain proteins.`
`- **Frozen storage at 0°F or below:** Bulk proteins (galbi, brisket, pork belly), seafood, ice cream/desserts, ice for service.`

`**Recommended configuration for Sŏn:** A combo box with **walk-in cooler ~80–100 SF + walk-in freezer ~30–50 SF as one unit** with a shared wall — typical foodservice "cooler-with-freezer-inside" or side-by-side configuration. This is more efficient than two independent boxes (shared wall reduces panel cost and refrigeration load) and fits the 563 SF kitchen footprint.`

`**Sizing rule of thumb:** 1.5 cubic feet of cold storage per cover per day, plus 30–50% headroom for Korean banchan/kimchi inventory which runs higher than typical Western menus. For 75 covers: 75 × 1.5 × 1.4 (Korean factor) = ~158 cu ft → about 80–100 SF of cooler floor at 8 ft ceiling. Freezer ~30–50 SF.`

`### 2.2 Walk-In Panel System Construction`

`**Standard manufacturers (specify by name in the bid):**`
`- **Kolpak** (a Welbilt brand) — broad availability, good Texas dealer network.`
`- **Master-Bilt / Norlake** (Standex) — long-standing foodservice industry standard.`
`- **Polar King** — fiberglass exterior, popular for outdoor; for indoor steel-skin box, Polar King Industries or Polar King International.`
`- **Thermo-Kool** — heavy-duty commercial, often specified for higher-end.`
`- **Imperial Brown** — long-life panels, good warranty.`
`- **U.S. Cooler** — value-engineered, broadly available.`

`**Panel specs to require:**`
`- 4" thick polyurethane foamed-in-place insulation for cooler (R-32 nominal, though urethane R-value degrades over years — extruded polystyrene retains insulation value better but is less common in walk-in panels).`
`- 4–6" thick for freezer (R-32 to R-48 nominal); the federal Energy Independence and Security Act (EISA) mandates R-28 minimum for freezer floor.`
`- 26-gauge stainless steel interior skin (food contact); stainless or painted galvanized exterior; specify stainless if the exterior is visible in the kitchen.`
`- Cam-action locking system (industry standard) for field assembly.`
`- NSF/ANSI Standard 7 certification (commercial refrigerator and freezer construction) — this is the food-zone listing required by health code.`

`### 2.3 The Topping Slab Pour-Back — Critical Detail for the LOI`

`**This is the defining detail of the Sŏn walk-in installation, because the landlord is delivering a depressed slab.**`

`The depression is sized so that, after the walk-in floor system is installed and a topping slab is poured back inside the box, the **finished kitchen floor is flush with the finished walk-in floor** — no threshold, no transition.`

`**Coordination math (must be verified before landlord pours base slab):**`

`Depression depth = (walk-in floor panel or insulated screed thickness) + (vapor barrier thickness, negligible) + (topping slab thickness — typically 4") + (interior finish floor thickness — typically tile or quarry tile, ~5/8" + thinset)`

`For a 4" walk-in floor system + 4" topping slab + 5/8" quarry tile = **~8-5/8" depression depth required**. For a "floorless" walk-in (insulated screed only, with topping slab providing the floor): vinyl screed ~1/2" + 4" topping + 5/8" quarry tile = **~5-1/8" depression**.`

`The walk-in vendor's floor system thickness must be confirmed in writing before the landlord pours.`

`**Sequence of operations (insist on in writing in the GC's schedule):**`

`1. **Landlord:** Pour base slab with depression to coordinated depth.`
`2. **Tenant rough-in:** Plumber sets condensate drain to an indirect waste (Compliance Guide #3); electrician roughs in conduit for refrigeration unit power, evaporator power, lighting, door alarm, and temperature monitoring.`
`3. **Walk-in panel install:** Vendor sets perimeter wall panels on continuous closed-cell gasket; installs floor system or insulated screed (PVC vinyl screed or aluminum thermal break with foam insert).`
`4. **Vapor barrier:** Continuous polyethylene vapor barrier (≥6 mil) under the topping slab.`
`5. **Topping slab pour:** GC's concrete sub pours 4" reinforced concrete (typically 3,500 psi mix with welded-wire mesh or fiber reinforcement) inside the box, screeded flush with the surrounding rough kitchen slab. Smooth steel-troweled finish if quarry tile is going down; broom finish only if a sealed-concrete or epoxy floor is the final surface.`
`6. **Cure:** 7 days minimum before kitchen flooring is installed.`
`7. **Kitchen flooring (Compliance Guide #4):** Quarry tile or specified system installed continuously across the threshold, flush into the box.`
`8. **Walk-in ceiling panels and door:** Set after flooring (or before, depending on panel system; coordinate with vendor).`
`9. **Refrigeration:** Evaporator coils set, refrigerant lines run to remote condenser, controls wired, system started up.`
`10. **Sanitary cove:** NSF-listed cove base or coved tile at the floor/wall junction inside the box (required for sanitation per TFER and FDA Food Code).`

`**Common failure modes:**`
`- **Depression too shallow:** Topping slab pours proud of kitchen floor — threshold required, ADA non-compliance, trip hazard, sanitation seam.`
`- **Depression too deep:** Topping slab is recessed below kitchen floor — water pools at the threshold, freezer experiences frost heave at the perimeter.`
`- **No vapor barrier under topping slab:** Moisture migrates upward, condensation on the cold side, floor failure within 2–5 years.`
`- **No insulation under topping slab in freezer:** Frost heave cracks the slab from below; federal EISA requires R-28 minimum.`
`- **Wrong concrete mix:** Standard 2,500 psi mix is inadequate for the point loads of loaded carts and pallet jacks; specify 3,500 psi minimum.`
`- **Topping slab poured too late, after kitchen tile is set:** Forced threshold or expensive tile rework.`

`### 2.4 Refrigeration System — Remote vs. Self-Contained`

`**Specify remote condenser. Period.**`

`| Configuration | Remote (recommended) | Self-Contained |`
`|---|---|---|`
`| Where the condenser sits | On the roof or at a remote pad outside; refrigerant lines run to the box | On top of or beside the walk-in box, inside the kitchen |`
`| Heat rejection | Outside | Into the kitchen, adding ~10,000–20,000 BTU/hr to kitchen cooling load |`
`| Noise inside box | Quiet (only evaporator fan) | Loud (compressor + condenser fan + evaporator) |`
`| Service | Easier — tech doesn't need to enter kitchen | Requires kitchen access for any service |`
`| Capital cost | Higher (line set, structural support for roof unit) | Lower |`
`| Adjacency to office tenants (acoustics) | Must coordinate with rooftop equipment placement and vibration isolation | Less roof noise — but loses the indoor-noise tradeoff |`

`For Sŏn, with adjacent office tenants and the LOI's vibration-suppression clause, **remote condenser on the roof with spring vibration isolators (Mason Industries, Vibro-Acoustics, Kinetics Noise Control) is the only correct answer.**`

`**Refrigerant choice (2026):**`
`- Default for new install: **R-448A** (Honeywell Solstice N40) or **R-449A** (Chemours Opteon XP40). Both are HFO/HFC blends, GWP ~1,280–1,390, ASHRAE A1 (non-flammable, non-toxic).`
`- These comply with EPA SNAP and the 1,400 GWP ceiling that EPA's October 2025 Reconsideration rule extended to January 1, 2032 for remote condensing units.`
`- Avoid R-404A (GWP ~3,920 — being phased out, prices rising under AIM Act phasedown).`
`- A2L refrigerants (R-454A, R-454C) are emerging but have mild flammability classification; only specify A2L if the local code (Austin's IBC/IMC) and the equipment OEM list it.`
`- Specify **POE (polyolester)** lubricant in the compressor.`

`**Compressor / condensing unit manufacturers:** Heatcraft (Beacon II controls), Russell (Genesis controls), Bohn, Hussmann, Bally, Larkin. For a 1.5–3 HP cooler condensing unit + 1–1.5 HP freezer condensing unit (typical Sŏn sizing), all are appropriate.`

`**Evaporator coil:** TXV (thermostatic expansion valve) or EEV (electronic expansion valve) — EEV is more efficient and ~$300–$600 premium per coil; worth it for energy savings over 10-year life. Defrost by electric heater for freezer; off-cycle defrost (no heater needed) for cooler.`

`**Condensate management:** Cooler evaporator condensate routes to indirect waste (floor sink, hub drain) per UPC §807 / Austin's adopted UPC 2024. Freezer evaporator condensate line must be heat-traced where it passes through freezer space and through unconditioned space, to prevent freeze-up and back-blockage into the box.`

`### 2.5 Electrical and Controls Coordination`

`Per typical sizing for Sŏn:`

`| Circuit | Voltage / Amps |`
`|---|---|`
`| Cooler condensing unit | 208V single or three-phase, 20–30A |`
`| Freezer condensing unit | 208V single or three-phase, 30–40A (defrost adds load) |`
`| Cooler evaporator fan(s) | 120V, 15A |`
`| Freezer evaporator fan(s) + defrost heater | 208V, 20–30A |`
`| Interior LED lighting | 120V, 15A (vapor-tight, NSF-listed fixtures, e.g., Kason 1810 LED) |`
`| Door alarm + temperature monitoring | 120V, 15A (or low-voltage) |`

`The 800-amp 120/208V landlord service is more than adequate for total walk-in load (~50–80A combined including starting amps).`

`**Controls:**`
`- **Stand-alone box controllers:** Heatcraft Beacon II Smart Defrost (excellent diagnostics), Russell Genesis, KE2 Therm controllers — set point, defrost timing, alarms.`
`- **Centralized monitoring:** Optional but increasingly standard. Cloud-based temperature monitoring with audible local alarm + remote alerting via cellular/Wi-Fi: **CAS DataLoggers, MarCELL, Monnit, Therma, SensorPush** — $300–$1,500 installed. **This is essentially required** for HACCP / TFER compliance documentation; manual paper temperature logs are increasingly unacceptable to Austin Public Health inspectors.`
`- **Door alarms:** Audible alarm if door open >3 minutes (not code-required but strongly recommended; prevents a $5,000 product loss from someone leaving the door propped open).`

`### 2.6 Health Code Requirements`

`Per **Texas Food Establishment Rules (TFER, 25 TAC §228)** and the **FDA Food Code** as adopted by Texas:`

`- **Cooler temperature:** ≤41°F for TCS (Time/Temperature Control for Safety) foods. (Texas establishments permitted after September 11, 1999 are subject to the 41°F rule — Sŏn is new construction, so 41°F applies absolutely.)`
`- **Freezer temperature:** Foods must remain frozen ("hard to the touch"); industry practice is 0°F or below.`
`- **Temperature documentation:** Inspectors expect temperature logs (digital monitoring is preferred and increasingly the inspection norm).`
`- **Interior materials:** NSF/ANSI 7 listed; smooth, non-absorbent, easily cleanable.`
`- **Lighting:** Commercial LED, shielded, NSF-listed (e.g., Kason 1810 LED, MaxLite vapor-tight). Foot-candle minimum at the working surface per TFER.`
`- **Cove base:** Continuous coved transition at floor/wall juncture inside the box (built into the walk-in panel system or formed in the topping slab and tile).`
`- **Shelving:** NSF-listed (Metro Super Erecta, Cambro Camshelving Elements, InterMetro). Bottom shelf minimum 6" off floor per TFER §228.114 to allow cleaning beneath.`
`- **Drain:** Floor drain inside the cooler is permitted but not required; if installed, must be a sanitary floor drain with deep-seal trap and indirect waste connection (Compliance Guide #3).`

`### 2.7 Twelve Questions to Ask a Walk-In Cooler Vendor`

`1. What is your floor system thickness, and have you coordinated with the GC and architect to verify the depression depth in the landlord's slab?`
`2. What is the topping slab thickness you require, who is pouring it, and at what point in the schedule?`
`3. Is the refrigeration system remote (rooftop condenser) or self-contained? If self-contained, why?`
`4. What refrigerant are you supplying — R-448A, R-449A, or A2L? Confirm the equipment is shipped pre-charged.`
`5. What is the panel R-value for the cooler and the freezer? Is it polyurethane or extruded polystyrene?`
`6. Are the panels NSF/ANSI 7 certified? Provide the listing.`
`7. What controls are you supplying — stand-alone (Heatcraft Beacon II / Russell Genesis) or BMS-integrated?`
`8. Is door alarm + temperature monitoring with remote alerting included, or is that a tenant-furnished add?`
`9. What is the warranty on panels (typically 10 years), refrigeration (typically 1 year on parts and labor, with extended optional), and door (5 years)?`
`10. Who is your refrigeration installer in Austin, and are they EPA Section 608 certified for the refrigerant you're specifying?`
`11. What is your delivery lead time? (Custom boxes: 6–10 weeks; quick-ship: 2–4 weeks.)`
`12. Do you provide installation, or do I need a separate installer? If you provide it, who does the topping slab pour-back, and is that in your scope?`

`### 2.8 Red Flags in a Walk-In Cooler Bid`

`- **Self-contained refrigeration proposed for Sŏn.** Wrong call given adjacent tenant context.`
`- **No remote condenser vibration isolation specified.** Will trigger a landlord noise complaint within months.`
`- **R-404A refrigerant.** Not legal for new equipment under EPA Technology Transitions Rule.`
`- **No NSF/ANSI 7 certification on panels.** Won't pass health inspection.`
`- **Topping slab "by others" with no detail.** Will fall through the cracks unless someone owns it.`
`- **No floor system thickness coordinated with depression.** Wait until panel arrives to discover the problem? Don't.`
`- **No temperature monitoring proposed.** Modern Austin Public Health inspectors expect it.`
`- **No defrost heater on freezer evaporator coils.** Will ice up within weeks.`
`- **3-year-old or "refurbished" refrigeration unit.** Shorter remaining life, possibly using legacy refrigerants.`
`- **No door alarm.** Operational risk; cheap to add up front.`

`==============================================`
`## SECTION 3 — DOMAIN 9: ACOUSTICS & SOUND ATTENUATION`
`==============================================`

`### 3.1 The LOI Language — "Landlord's Reasonable Discretion"`

`The LOI gives the landlord open-ended discretion to require sound or vibration mitigation at the tenant's sole cost. This is a meaningful exposure. Without a written threshold, the tenant is at the mercy of:`
`- A neighboring tenant complaint (subjective)`
`- A landlord-driven sound test (timing and method unspecified)`
`- Post-opening operational changes (live performance schedule, kitchen volume) that retrigger the clause`

`**Before construction documents are stamped, get the following from the landlord in writing (a side letter or lease amendment is sufficient):**`

`(a) **Specific threshold and test method.** Examples that are defensible: "Background sound level in the adjacent office tenant space (with Sŏn operating at peak business hours) shall not exceed NC 40 measured per ANSI S12.2." Or: "Vibration at the demising wall shall not exceed VC-A per ASHRAE/ASA standards." Or: "Sound pressure level at the property line shall not exceed 60 dB(A) daytime / 55 dB(A) nighttime per City of Austin Noise Ordinance." Choose one, and write it down.`

`(b) **Baseline test before opening.** A pre-occupancy sound test conducted jointly by an acoustic consultant of the tenant's choosing (or an agreed third party). Establishes a documented starting condition, against which any later complaint can be compared.`

`(c) **Remediation timeline.** If a complaint is raised, the tenant has a defined notice and cure period (e.g., 60 days to investigate, 90 days to implement a fix, with reasonable extensions).`

`(d) **Specific construction requirements, if any.** Some landlords have a standard tenant-improvement specification (e.g., "demising wall shall achieve STC 50 minimum, full-height to deck, with no penetrations within 12" of deck"). If they have one, get it now and design to it.`

`### 3.2 Sound Transmission Basics`

`| Metric | Standard | What It Measures | Typical Restaurant Use |`
`|---|---|---|---|`
`| **STC (Sound Transmission Class)** | ASTM E90 (lab) / ASTM E336 (field) / ASTM E413 (rating) | Airborne sound transmission through a partition | Demising walls — target STC 50–55 to office |`
`| **IIC (Impact Insulation Class)** | ASTM E492 / ASTM E989 | Structure-borne impact noise through floor/ceiling | Less applicable here — Sŏn is at-grade, not above another tenant |`
`| **NC (Noise Criteria)** | ANSI S12.2 / ASHRAE Handbook | Background interior sound from mechanical systems | NC 30–35 in dining, NC 40 in office at demising wall |`
`| **NRC (Noise Reduction Coefficient)** | ASTM C423 | Sound absorption of a surface (0 = reflective, 1 = perfectly absorbent) | Specify NRC 0.85+ for ceiling treatment |`
`| **RT60 (Reverberation Time)** | ISO 3382-1 | Time for sound to decay 60 dB after source stops | 0.6–0.9 s for fine dining |`
`| **Lp(A)** | A-weighted dB | Sound pressure level weighted to human hearing | Operational target 70–78 dB(A) at peak |`

`**STC reference levels (ASTM E413):**`
`- STC 25–30: Normal speech audible and intelligible.`
`- STC 35: Loud speech audible, partly intelligible.`
`- STC 40: Loud speech faintly audible, not intelligible.`
`- STC 45: Loud speech not audible; raised voices barely heard.`
`- STC 50: Loud music faintly heard; loud speech inaudible. **Code minimum for multi-family dwelling unit demising walls per IBC.**`
`- STC 55: Loud music heard only as a low rumble. **Common high-end commercial demising standard.**`
`- STC 60+: Most music not perceptible. Performance/theater partition.`

`**For Sŏn adjacent to office tenants: target STC 50–55 minimum at the demising wall.**`

`### 3.3 Wall Assembly Options — Demising Wall to Office`

`| Assembly | Construction | STC | Approx. Cost (LF, 10-ft tall) |`
`|---|---|---|---|`
`| Standard partition | 5/8" gyp + 3-5/8" 25-gauge steel stud + 5/8" gyp, batt insulation | 38–42 | $80–$120 |`
`| Sound-rated partition | 5/8" gyp + 3-5/8" 25-gauge stud at 24" o.c. + RC-1 resilient channel + 2× 5/8" gyp on tenant side, R-13 mineral wool, acoustic sealant all joints | 50–55 | $180–$250 |`
`| Decoupled / staggered stud | 2× 2-1/2" steel studs offset on 6" plates, 5/8" gyp each side, mineral wool | 55–60 | $300–$400 |`
`| Double-wall (independent studs) | Two separate stud walls with 1–2" airspace, mineral wool in both cavities, double-layer gyp on at least one side | 60–65 | $450–$600 |`

`**Construction details that make or break STC performance:**`
`- Acoustic sealant (Tremco Acoustical Sealant, USG SHEETROCK Acoustical Sealant) at top, bottom, and all penetrations — every electrical outlet has a putty pad (Specified Technologies, 3M Fire Barrier).`
`- Wall extends **full height to the underside of the structural deck** — not just to the suspended ceiling. This is critical and frequently violated. A demising wall stopped at the ceiling allows sound to flank over the top of the wall through the shared ceiling cavity.`
`- No back-to-back electrical boxes; stagger by minimum 24".`
`- 25-gauge studs at 24" on center outperform 20-gauge at 16" by about 7 STC points (lighter, more flexible studs decouple better).`

`**Recommendation for Sŏn:** Sound-rated partition (STC 50–55), full-height to deck, with putty-padded outlet boxes and acoustic sealant. Verify by field test (ASTM E336) post-construction if the landlord requires it. **Do not rely on the standard partition unless the landlord explicitly accepts STC 38–42 in writing, which they almost certainly will not.**`

`### 3.4 Ceiling Assembly and Flanking`

`If Sŏn and the adjacent office tenant share the same roof structure, sound can flank over the demising wall through the ceiling cavity. The most effective remediation is the demising wall extending full-height to deck (above) — that physically blocks the flanking path.`

`If full-height demising is not feasible, alternatives:`
`- Hard-lid gypsum ceiling on the tenant side with R-19 batt insulation in the ceiling cavity above the demising wall.`
`- Decoupled ceiling on resilient channels or hat channels; mineral wool batt insulation.`
`- Acoustic ceiling tile (ACT) with high CAC (Ceiling Attenuation Class) rating — Armstrong Ultima, USG Mars High-NRC — CAC 35–40. CAC measures the ceiling's contribution to room-to-room sound transmission via the ceiling plenum.`

`**Cost:** Insulation + sealing in cavity: minimal, ~$2–$5/SF. Decoupled hard-lid ceiling: $15–$30/SF.`

`### 3.5 Mechanical Noise — The Most Overlooked Issue`

`This is where the LOI's vibration-suppression clause is most likely to bite. Adjacent office tenants are sensitive to:`

`**Rooftop equipment vibration (transmitted through roof structure into shared building elements):**`
`- 10-ton RTU on a curb above Sŏn.`
`- MAU on a curb (Compliance Guide #1).`
`- Solid-fuel exhaust fan on a curb (Compliance Guide #1).`
`- Walk-in cooler condenser(s) on the roof.`

`**Solution:** Spring-isolated rooftop curbs under all rooftop equipment ≥3 tons. Specify by manufacturer:`
`- **Mason Industries RSC-dB** (rooftop spring curb, dB designation for low frequency control)`
`- **Mason Industries CMAB** (curb-mounted aluminum base, integrated spring, 1" deflection)`
`- **Vibro-Acoustics RSI / RSC** spring isolation curbs`
`- **Kinetics Noise Control KSCR / RIC** spring curbs`

`Specify minimum 1" static deflection (low frequency) for spring isolators, with neoprene pad in series for high-frequency isolation. For smaller equipment (<3 tons, e.g., walk-in condensers), neoprene pads (Mason ND, Kinetics NPS) are sufficient at $50–$200 per unit.`

`**Cost premium:** Spring-isolated curb adds $1,500–$4,000 per unit over a standard rigid curb. For Sŏn's full rooftop fleet (RTU + MAU + exhaust fan + condensers), budget $8,000–$15,000 in curb upgrades. **This is the single best-spent acoustic dollar in the entire build.**`

`**Exhaust fan noise (the single loudest rooftop source on a solid-fuel system):**`
`- Specify low-sound exhaust fan (Greenheck GB upblast roof exhaust, Loren Cook GC, CaptiveAire DR).`
`- Add a duct silencer downstream if a baseline test or model shows the noise exceeds the threshold.`
`- For solid-fuel exhaust, the silencer must be **media-free** (Helmholtz resonator type) because grease will accumulate in fiberglass-media silencers and become a fire hazard. Specify Vibro-Acoustics RNM/CNM "no-media" silencer or equivalent. Verify with the local AHJ that the silencer is acceptable in the grease duct path — most AHJs accept media-free silencers, but get it in writing.`

`**MAU noise:** Same approach — specify low-sound MAU (RuppAir, AccuRex, CaptiveAire MAU lines all offer sound-rated configurations). Duct silencer in the supply path if needed.`

`**Refrigeration condenser noise:** Spring-isolated curb or pad; consider acoustic enclosure if the condenser sits over the office side of the building. Bohn / Heatcraft offer factory low-noise condenser packages.`

`**Reference:** ASHRAE Handbook — HVAC Applications, Chapter 49 (Noise and Vibration Control) is the authoritative engineering guide. The acoustic consultant will use it.`

`### 3.6 HVAC Duct-Borne Noise`

`Supply and return ducts can carry noise from the kitchen/dining/bar into adjacent space if they share return plenums or pass through demising walls.`

`**Solutions:**`
`- Internal duct liner (1" or 2" fiberglass acoustic liner — Owens Corning QuietR, Knauf Atmosphere) on the first 10–20 ft of supply downstream of the RTU, and on returns near the unit. **Note:** Duct liner is acceptable in supply/return ducts but **not in any duct that touches kitchen exhaust** — same grease/cleanability issue.`
`- External duct wrap with mass-loaded vinyl (Audimute, Acoustiblok) for ducts crossing demising walls.`
`- Duct silencers at critical locations.`
`- Avoid shared return plenums between Sŏn and adjacent tenant ceiling cavities — verify that the ceiling cavity above Sŏn does not connect to the office tenant ceiling cavity.`

`**NC criteria for restaurant occupied spaces (per ASHRAE Handbook Chapter 49 Table 1):**`
`- Fine dining: NC 30–35 (background, mechanical only)`
`- Casual dining: NC 35–40`
`- Bar/lounge: NC 40–45 acceptable`

`### 3.7 Fine-Dining Acoustic Target — The Guest Experience`

`This is the design problem, distinct from the landlord-compliance problem.`

`**Reverberation time (RT60):**`
`- Target: **0.6–0.9 seconds** at 500–1,000 Hz octave bands.`
`- >1.0 s: Conversational difficulty, Lombard effect (guests raise voices, which cascades into 85+ dB(A) at full house).`
`- <0.5 s: "Dead" feeling, music lacks warmth, room feels uncomfortable and exposed.`

`**Background sound level (HVAC running, no occupants):**`
`- NC 30–35 / 40–45 dB(A) — quiet enough to support conversation, ambient enough to mask service-area noise.`

`**Occupied sound level (full house at peak):**`
`- 70–78 dB(A): The fine-dining sweet spot — energetic but conversational.`
`- 80–85 dB(A): Restaurant industry average; perceived as "loud."`
`- 85–90 dB(A): "Have to shout"; published research shows guest dwell time and per-cover spend decrease, especially for older guests.`
`- <65 dB(A): Feels empty, awkward, every conversation overheard.`

`**The minimalism problem:** Korean fine-dining design language often emphasizes polished concrete, exposed structure, hardwood, and stone. These materials all reflect sound (NRC 0.05–0.15). A 988 SF dining room with 12-ft ceiling (~12,000 cu ft) and only hard surfaces will have RT60 in the 1.5–2.0 second range — well into the "shout zone." At full occupancy of ~50 guests, the room will hit 85–90 dB(A) without mechanical or music noise contribution.`

`**Treatment tools (NRC values approximate):**`
`- **Kvadrat Soft Cells** — fabric-tensioned absorber panels, design-grade, NRC 0.85–1.0. Premium aesthetic; $30–$60/SF.`
`- **Armstrong Tectum** — wood-fiber acoustic panels, exposed-mount or ceiling clouds, NRC 0.60–0.85. $5–$10/SF.`
`- **USG Acoustical (Mars, Halcyon)** — high-performance ceiling tile, NRC 0.85–0.95.`
`- **Decoustics Claro** — perforated wood veneer with absorber backing, NRC 0.70–0.85. $20–$40/SF.`
`- **Pinta Acoustic / BAUX** — wood wool or felt panels, design-driven; varies.`
`- **Perforated wood panels with mineral wool backing** — millwork-integrated, NRC 0.60–0.80, custom-fabricated by GC's millworker. $15–$30/SF.`
`- **Heavy upholstered banquettes** — significant absorption (NRC 0.5–0.7), and FF&E rather than construction scope.`
`- **Area rugs in dining** — FF&E scope, but contribute meaningfully to RT60.`

`**Strategy for Sŏn:** Treat the ceiling as the primary absorption plane (largest unbroken surface; sound travels upward and reflects). 60–70% ceiling coverage with NRC 0.85+ material brings RT60 from 1.5–2.0 s down to the 0.7–0.9 s target. Combine with banquette upholstery and area rugs in design language. This is a design-from-day-one decision; retrofitting acoustic panels onto a finished ceiling is expensive and rarely as elegant.`

`### 3.8 The Acoustic Consultant — When and Why`

`**Engage early.** The acoustic consultant should be on the team before construction documents are 50% complete, so that wall assemblies, ceiling configuration, and rooftop equipment placement can be designed acoustically rather than remediated.`

`**Typical scope of work:**`
`1. Acoustic design narrative (the "why" behind specifications).`
`2. Demising wall and ceiling specification (STC, CAC).`
`3. Mechanical noise specification (NC targets, vibration isolator selection, silencer placement).`
`4. Room acoustics — RT60 modeling, treatment selection and quantity.`
`5. Optional: Live performance system review if music is amplified.`
`6. Post-construction verification testing (ASTM E336 for STC field test; ANSI S12.2 for NC; balloon-pop or impulse-response RT60 measurement).`

`**Typical fee for a 2,310 SF restaurant in Austin 2026:** $5,000–$15,000 depending on scope. For a fine-dining restaurant with a possible live-performance program adjacent to office tenants, $10,000–$15,000 is appropriate and a small fraction of total project cost.`

`- **BAi** (Austin, TX — acoustics and A/V consulting)`

`### 3.10 Twelve Questions to Ask an Acoustic Consultant`

`1. What restaurants have you consulted on, and what was the operational sound level achieved (dB(A) at full occupancy)?`
`2. What is your proposed RT60 target for our dining room, and what is your modeling basis (Sabine, Eyring, or measured)?`
`3. What demising wall STC do you recommend for our office adjacency, and what is the assembly?`
`4. What rooftop vibration isolation specification do you recommend (deflection in inches, manufacturer)?`
`5. Will you specify the kitchen exhaust fan silencer? Are you familiar with the media-free silencer requirement for grease ducts?`
`6. What NC criteria do you specify for dining, bar, kitchen?`
`7. What is your scope of post-construction verification testing, and is it included in your fee?`
`8. Who is the engineer of record for your specifications — you, or the mechanical engineer? (Important for constructibility and liability.)`
`9. Will you attend the pre-construction meeting and the rough-in walk-through?`
`10. What is your escalation path if the GC or sub deviates from your specification?`
`11. Have you worked with the City of Austin DSD on similar projects?`
`12. What is your fee structure — fixed, hourly with cap, or percentage of construction?`

`### 3.11 Red Flags If the Consultant Route Is Bypassed`

`- Demising wall designed by the GC's drywall sub at "STC 45 typical." Won't pass an honest field test.`
`- Rooftop equipment placed without vibration isolation or with neoprene pads only on equipment ≥3 tons.`
`- Ceiling acoustic treatment "value-engineered out" late in design to save $8,000. Will require $40,000 retrofit post-opening.`
`- Kitchen exhaust silencer with fiberglass media in the grease path. Fire hazard; will be flagged on health/fire inspection.`
`- Demising wall stopped at the suspended ceiling rather than extending to deck. Sound flanks over.`
`- No pre-occupancy baseline test. You have no defense if the office tenant complains in month 3.`
`- "We'll add panels later if it's a problem." Aesthetic and operational disruption is materially worse than designing it in.`
`- No acoustic spec for HVAC diffuser noise (NC rating). Diffusers selected on price, not performance.`

`---`

`## CROSS-REFERENCES: How These Three Domains Bridge to the Prior Compliance Guides`

`The four prior compliance guides and this fifth document do not stand alone — many decisions made in one domain constrain or trigger requirements in others. The most important integration points:`

`### Kitchen Exhaust CFM (Guide #1) → HVAC Sizing (this Guide §1.3) → Acoustics (this Guide §3.5)`

`The hood CFM, set by the cookline equipment and ASHRAE 154, drives the MAU CFM, which drives the building HVAC make-up offset, which drives the dining ventilation rate per ASHRAE 62.1, which drives the RTU economizer setpoint, which drives the kitchen-to-dining pressure differential, which drives whether smells migrate. **The hood CFM is also the primary acoustic source on the roof** — and the larger it is, the more isolation is required. Lock in the hood CFM in writing at one number, signed off by the hood vendor, MAU vendor, and mechanical contractor jointly, before any of these systems are released for fabrication.`

`### Rooftop Equipment Placement (Guide #3 roof penetrations + this Guide §3.5)`

`Each rooftop curb is a roof penetration (Compliance Guide #3) AND a structural load AND an acoustic source. Coordinate placement so:`
`- Curbs are over Sŏn's space, not over the demising line into the adjacent office tenant.`
`- Spring-isolated curbs are specified for all equipment ≥3 tons.`
`- Roof structural reinforcement (if any) is identified before the landlord's roof is in place (or before tenant penetrations are cut).`
`- The TPO/corrugated combination roof is detailed at each curb per the manufacturer's standard detail.`

`### Depressed Slab (this Guide §2.3) → Plumbing Rough-In (Guide #3) → Kitchen Flooring (Guide #4)`

`The slab depression is sized on the basis of the walk-in floor system + topping slab + finished kitchen floor. If the kitchen floor changes (e.g., from quarry tile to epoxy), the topping slab thickness must change. **The kitchen flooring decision must be locked before the depression depth is finalized.** Plumbing rough-ins inside the depressed area (condensate to indirect waste) must be coordinated with the walk-in vendor's panel layout — if a drain ends up under a panel, it's blocked.`

`### Demising Wall Acoustic Spec (this Guide §3.3) → Drywall Schedule (GC scope)`

`The acoustic spec must be confirmed and detailed in the construction documents *before drywall closes*. Once a wall is finished and painted, opening it to add resilient channel or a second layer is destructive and expensive. The acoustic consultant should walk the site at rough-in and again at pre-rock to verify.`

`### Fire Alarm (Guide #2) → Duct Smoke Detector (this Guide §1.10) → HVAC Shutdown`

`The duct smoke detector required by IMC §606.2.1 ties into the fire alarm panel and shuts down the RTU on activation. This is one device, but it sits at the intersection of three trades: mechanical (duct mount), electrical (power), and fire alarm (signal). Identify the responsible party in writing before rough-in.`

`### Refrigerant (this Guide §2.4) → Refrigerant Leak Detection (future regulatory)`

`EPA's AIM Act and Section 608 regulations are tightening on refrigerant leak detection and reporting. Specify equipment that supports leak detection from day one (most modern condensing units do); maintain refrigerant logs from day of charging.`

`---`

`## Recommendations`

`**Stage 1 — Before Permit Application (next 30 days):**`

`1. **Commission a Manual N load calculation** for the tenant space at $800–$2,000 from a licensed mechanical engineer or ACCA-certified contractor. Use the result to confirm or refute the 10-ton landlord RTU. **Threshold to escalate:** if Manual N shows >12 tons total cooling load, demand RTU upsize from landlord in writing or budget supplementary mini-splits.`
`2. **Get the landlord's acoustic threshold in writing.** Specific number, specific test method, specific cure period. **Threshold to escalate:** if landlord refuses to specify, escalate to lease counsel before signing the construction amendment.`
`3. **Confirm depressed slab depth** with the chosen walk-in vendor before the landlord pours the base slab. **Threshold to escalate:** any disagreement >1/2" between vendor's required floor system and slab depression — pause until reconciled.`

`**Stage 2 — During Construction Documents (next 60 days):**`

`4. **Engage an acoustic consultant** at $5,000–$15,000 fee. Design demising walls, rooftop isolation, ceiling treatment, and HVAC noise concurrently. **Threshold to escalate:** if the GC or mechanical sub pushes back on isolation curbs as "value-engineering," hold the line — this is the highest-leverage acoustic spend.`
`5. **Lock the hood CFM** with hood vendor, MAU vendor, and mechanical contractor in a single signed coordination sheet. **Threshold to escalate:** any single number changes after the sheet is signed without all three parties re-signing.`
`6. **Specify Sealing Class A, R-6 duct insulation, ≤5 ft flex duct, and AABC-independent TAB** in the mechanical contract. Reject any deviation.`
`7. **Specify R-448A or R-449A refrigerant**, remote condenser with spring isolation, and stand-alone walk-in controls with cloud temperature monitoring.`

`**Stage 3 — During Construction (next 90–120 days):**`

`8. **Pre-construction coordination meeting** with all six trades touching the walk-in (GC, walk-in vendor, plumber, electrician, refrigeration, flooring sub). Document the sequence of operations.`
`9. **Rough-in walk-through with acoustic consultant** before drywall closes. Verify resilient channels, sealant, and outlet box treatments.`
`10. **TAB mid-construction visit** to verify duct rough-in matches design before insulation.`

`**Stage 4 — Pre-Opening (final 30 days):**`

`11. **TAB report issuance** with measured kitchen-to-dining pressure differential and CFM at every diffuser. Reject any zone outside ±10% of design.`
`12. **Acoustic baseline test** by acoustic consultant — establish documented pre-opening sound levels for landlord/tenant record.`
`13. **Walk-in temperature monitoring activation** with 7-day data log before first product loaded.`

`**Thresholds That Change the Recommendations:**`

`- If Manual N shows the 10-ton RTU is *adequate* (i.e., total load ≤9 tons): proceed with single-RTU + zoning approach; skip mini-splits.`
`- If the landlord agrees in writing to an STC 50 demising wall and includes vibration-isolated curbs in their base-building scope: tenant acoustic budget shrinks by ~$10,000–$15,000.`
`- If the live-performance program is dropped: demising wall can be STC 50 rather than STC 55+; saves ~$3,000.`
`- If the kitchen exhaust CFM comes in below 4,500 CFM (smaller hood, less heavy-duty cooking duty): MAU and HVAC interaction simplifies; supplementary cooling may not be needed.`

`---`

`## Caveats`

`1. **All cost ranges are Austin 2026 estimates** based on market conditions through Q1 2026. Refrigerant prices, steel/copper commodity volatility, and labor availability can shift these by 15–25% in either direction within 12 months.`

`2. **Code adoption status:** Austin adopted the 2024 UMC and 2024 UPC effective July 10, 2025 (Ordinances 20250410-044 and -042). The 2024 IBC, IECC, IRC, IPMC, and IWUIC also took effect July 10, 2025. The 2024 IMC is not separately adopted by Austin (UMC governs mechanical), but IMC sections cited in this document are referenced by industry practice and by the IBC/Fire Code for kitchen exhaust and fire alarm interfaces. Verify current status with Austin DSD before permit submission.`

`3. **EPA refrigerant regulations are actively evolving.** EPA's October 2025 Reconsideration Rule extended the 1,400 GWP ceiling for some refrigerated equipment subsectors to January 1, 2032, which preserves R-448A/R-449A as compliant. However, additional rules (including the next AIM Act phasedown step in 2029) will further tighten supply. Specify equipment that is **A2L-ready** for future retrofit.`

`4. **The Manual N must be performed by a qualified engineer or ACCA-certified contractor.** Online calculators give rule-of-thumb estimates only and are not accepted by Austin DSD for permit review of commercial restaurants with kitchen loads.`

`5. **STC field test results typically run 5 points lower than lab ratings** (ASTM E336 field STC vs. ASTM E90 lab STC) due to flanking, workmanship, and penetrations. Specify STC 55 lab if you need STC 50 field.`

`6. **The ASHRAE 62.1 ventilation rates cited are from the 2019/2022 editions.** Standards are updated on a 3-year cycle; verify which edition is referenced by Austin's adopted IECC/UMC at time of permit.`

`7. **The acoustic consultant firms listed are illustrative**, not endorsements. Solicit at least two competing scopes and check references with restaurant clients of similar profile.`

`8. **The walk-in cooler vendor recommendations are widely available brands**, not endorsements. Local Austin foodservice equipment dealers (such as those serving the Texas Restaurant Association) will have established relationships with subset of these manufacturers and can quote competitively.`

`9. **The "live performance" possibility in the operational profile changes the acoustic risk profile materially.** If amplified live music is in scope at any time, demising wall STC requirement rises to 55–60 and the acoustic consultant scope expands to include sound-reinforcement system design. Decide this before construction documents lock.`

`10. **Rooftop equipment vibration isolation effectiveness depends on installation quality.** Spring isolators that are not properly leveled, that have shipping blocks left in place, or that are short-circuited by rigid conduit/piping connections will provide little or no isolation. The acoustic consultant or commissioning agent should verify installation before the roof is closed up.`

`11. **Health code requirements (TFER, FDA Food Code) cited are accurate as of the document date** but are subject to revision by the Texas Department of State Health Services and by Austin Public Health (the local AHJ for retail food). Verify with Austin Public Health Environmental Services Division (EHSD) at plan review.`

`12. **This document is a knowledge-base reference for vendor evaluation, not engineering documentation.** Any installation, refrigerant handling, or structural decision must be made by a licensed engineer, certified contractor, or licensed technician with project-specific responsibility. Owner's reliance on this document in lieu of professional design or specification is not appropriate.`
