`# Reference Document 6 — Sŏn / 207 E St Elmo Rd, Austin TX`
`## Electrical Distribution, Low-Voltage Rough-In, Architectural Lighting (Tunable White + Smart Glass), and High-Fidelity Audio`

`---`

`## TL;DR`

`- **The 800-amp 120/208V three-phase service is correctly sized for an all-electric Korean fine-dining concept of this footprint, but the *real* design battle is in the four invisible systems that ride underneath it: a fully zoned panel architecture with 25% spare; a low-voltage room and conduit grid that has to be poured before slabs and closed before ceilings; a Lutron HomeWorks QS + Ketra (or equivalent dual-channel tunable white) lighting backbone integrated with electrochromic glass via BACnet/dry-contact; and a DSP-corrected, point-source/architectural audio system that respects the vaulted, hard-surfaced room.** Get those four right and the rest of the build serves the design.`
`- **Specify, do not delegate.** Insist on CRI 95+ / R9 80+ for every interior fixture, IP65 for every outdoor speaker, PoE+ Cat6A wired access points (not mesh), a dedicated PCI-segregated POS VLAN per Toast's published requirements, and electrochromic glass (View / SageGlass) for solar-control glazing — *not* PDLC, which is a privacy film and does nothing for Austin's 2A heat load. Reject any electrician, AV "guy," or lighting showroom rep who proposes residential-grade dimmers on tunable white, ceiling speakers blanket-distributed in a vaulted room, or who can't produce a load schedule, photometric study, RT60 measurement, and scene programming spec as deliverables.`
`- **Austin 2026 rough budget for the scope in this document:** electrical distribution $9–14/SF (interior) + $25–60K hardscape/exterior rough-in; low-voltage/structured cabling + network + cameras $45–95K; architectural lighting (Lutron HWQS + Ketra-tier fixtures + smart glass controls integration, fixtures excluded from electrical) $120–280K for the interior package, smart glass another $75–150/SF of treated glazing; audio (Meyer/B&W-tier interior + B&W AM-1 patio + DSP/amp rack + outdoor infrastructure) $65–140K. Total infrastructure-and-systems envelope to protect design integrity: **~$350–650K** beyond shell electrical, depending on smart-glass scope and audio tier.`

`---`

`## SECTION 1 — ELECTRICAL DISTRIBUTION (Domain 7)`

`### What 800A / 120/208V three-phase actually means`

`Your landlord is delivering a wye-configured three-phase service with three "hot" legs (120V each to the neutral) and a shared neutral. Phase-to-neutral = 120V (every standard receptacle, lighting circuit, POS); phase-to-phase = 208V (most three-phase kitchen equipment, larger motors, the MAU). A balanced 800A service at 208V three-phase yields a theoretical capacity of roughly **288 kVA** (800 × 208 × √3 ÷ 1000), which is comfortably above the typical demand load for an all-electric restaurant of this size calculated under NEC Table 220.88 (the optional restaurant method). For a 2,310 SF interior with live-fire Korean cooking, a connected load in the 300–400 kVA range will demand-factor down to roughly 170–215 kVA — fitting cleanly inside 800A with the mandated NEC 215.2/220 spare. **800A is the right service. Don't let it get clipped.**`

`What the tenant gets to work with: the landlord's scope ends at a main distribution panel (MDP) location, code-minimum receptacles, and conduit infrastructure to a designated low-voltage point of connection. Everything past the MDP — sub-panels, branch circuits, equipment connections, lighting control panels, exterior circuits — is tenant work.`

`### Load inventory for Sŏn`

`Build a line-item load schedule covering at minimum:`

`**Kitchen (563 SF — the heaviest load center):**`
`- Walk-in cooler/freezer compressor (typically 208V/3-phase, 15–25A each)`
`- Live-fire Korean grill exhaust (Type I hood) — exhaust fan 208V 3-phase motor, 5–15 HP depending on CFM; MAU motor 208V 3-phase 3–10 HP`
`- Commercial dishwasher (typically 208V/3-phase booster heater, 40–60A)`
`- Reach-ins, prep refrigeration, undercounter refrigeration (120V dedicated)`
`- Induction ranges / electric griddles / salamanders / rice cookers / banchan warmers (mix of 208V and 120V)`
`- Hood fire suppression (low draw, but dedicated)`

`**Bar (within the 605 SF bar/entry/circulation):**`
`- Ice machine — 120V/15A or 20A dedicated, typically 5–8A draw`
`- Back-bar refrigeration (bottle coolers, kegerator) — 120V each, dedicated`
`- Glasswasher — typically 208V single-phase or 120V depending on model`
`- Blenders, espresso machine (espresso commonly 208V/30A dedicated for two-group)`
`- Soda system pump`

`**HVAC:**`
`- Rooftop unit (RTU) — 208V/3-phase, will dominate the non-kitchen load; size dictated by Climate Zone 2A cooling load on the vaulted/skylit volume`
`- Bathroom exhaust fans (120V)`

`**Lighting (tunable white drives circuit count up):**`
`- Interior tunable white zones — **two 120V circuits per zone** if using dual-driver/two-channel architecture, or one 120V circuit feeding a dual-channel driver per zone`
`- Exterior architectural / string / path lighting on dedicated circuits`
`- Emergency egress / exit signs`

`**Tech and controls:**`
`- Lutron HomeWorks QS panel(s) — dedicated 120V/20A`
`- Smart glass controllers (View, SageGlass) — dedicated 120V; very low draw but never share with motors or kitchen equipment`
`- Audio amplifier rack — typically a dedicated 30A circuit, 120V or 208V depending on amplifier choice`
`- POS / network rack — dedicated isolated-ground "clean" circuits, on UPS`

`**Outdoor (the part most contractors underbuild):**`
`- Bromic Tungsten Smart-Heat electric heaters — Bromic's 2000W/3000W/4000W single-element units run on 208V or 240V; their 6000W double-element units pull up to **two 15A elements** per unit (often a 30A 240V circuit recommended; consult unit-specific sheet — the 120V/15A figure circulating online applies only to the smaller Tungsten 2000W). Plan one dedicated circuit per heater, fed from an exterior sub-panel and switched through a Bromic on/off or dimmer controller installed in conditioned space.`
`- Outdoor string/festoon lighting (120V, dimmable but not tunable)`
`- Architectural uplighting / path / grade lights (120V or low-voltage from a remote magnetic transformer)`
`- Misting system pump (120V, dedicated, GFCI)`
`- Outdoor audio — amplifier in conditioned rack; speaker wire (low-voltage) only outside`
`- Outdoor POS tablets (120V GFCI under counter at outdoor service stations)`
`- Security cameras (PoE — supplied from interior switch, but conduit must be roughed)`

`### Panel architecture`

`**Main Distribution Panel (MDP):** 800A main, located per landlord's delivery point. Feeds:`

`1. **Kitchen sub-panel** — sized for connected kitchen load + 25% spare per NEC 220 best practice. Typically 200–400A, 120/208V three-phase, 42-space minimum. Locate inside or immediately adjacent to kitchen, behind a serviceable panel door. **Every cord-and-plug appliance and every fixed appliance in the kitchen with a sink or food/beverage prep adjacency must be GFCI-protected per NEC 210.8(B) (2023)** — this means GFCI breakers in the panel, not plug-level GFCIs hidden under equipment. Use UL-Listed Class A GFCI breakers (Bender, Littelfuse Shock-Block, Eaton SureTest) sized appropriately for 208V three-phase loads where required.`
`2. **Bar / dining sub-panel** — 100–200A, 120/208V, serves bar equipment, dining receptacles, dining lighting circuits (separately metered or sub-metered loads if needed).`
`3. **Exterior sub-panel** — 100–200A, located in a serviceable but weather-protected location, dedicated to all patio circuits: heaters, lighting, audio, misting, POS, cameras, exterior signage. **Every outdoor outlet falls under NEC 210.8(F) (2023) GFCI requirements.**`
`4. **Lighting control panel feed** — dedicated breakers feeding the Lutron HomeWorks QS panel; the HWQS panel then home-runs out to each zone driver.`
`5. **Mechanical/HVAC** — RTU, MAU, exhaust fan, bathroom exhaust.`
`6. **Tech / clean power** — POS/network rack on UPS, lighting controls processor, smart glass controller.`

`**25% spare capacity** is non-negotiable. Code minimum is one thing; restaurants add equipment for a decade after opening (extra reach-in, sake warmer, espresso upgrade, patio heater additions). The cheap part of a panel is the empty space.`

`### Tunable white circuits — *why this is not a normal lighting circuit*`

`A tunable white fixture has **two LED engines** (typically 2700K warm and 5000K or 6500K cool) that must be independently controlled in intensity and then mixed to produce any CCT in between. There are three legitimate ways to power and control this; only two work for Sŏn:`

`1. **Two 120V circuits per zone**, each feeding one channel through a dedicated dimming driver, controlled by a dual-channel control output (DALI Type 8, DMX, or Lutron's proprietary EcoSystem/HWQS protocol). Robust, the standard for high-end installations.`
`2. **One 120V circuit feeding a dual-channel driver** that does the mixing internally and is controlled by a single multi-channel control input (DALI Type 8, Casambi, or — for Ketra — its own Clear Connect Type X wireless protocol). Lower wire count, more expensive driver.`
`3. **A standard wall dimmer on a single channel.** This does not produce tunable white. **If a contractor proposes this, fire them.**`

`**Lutron HomeWorks QS with Ketra is the canonical specification** for this caliber of project. Ketra's S30/S38 lamps and D2/D3/D4 downlights deliver 90+ CRI with R9 >90 across a 1400K–10,000K range with proprietary "Vibrancy" control, and they communicate wirelessly via Clear Connect Type X — eliminating control wire pulls in some zones (still need 120V for line voltage, but the second control channel is over the air). For coves, linear, and tape light, Lutron's own Lumaris RGB+TW driver integrates natively. HWQS supports 10,000 zones across 50,000 SF, easily sufficient for Sŏn.`

`Allocate dedicated wall space for the **Lutron HomeWorks QS panel** in the low-voltage room or a dedicated controls closet — minimum 24"W × 36"H clear, with dedicated 120V/20A power and home-run conduit to each zone.`

`### POS & technology circuits`

`Toast's published network requirements (and sound PCI-DSS practice) call for dedicated ethernet drops on a segregated VLAN. From an electrical perspective:`

`- **Dedicated isolated-ground (IG) circuits** for POS terminals, KDS, network rack, server. These prevent the POS from sharing a ground path with kitchen equipment, eliminating ground-loop noise and brownout-related crashes.`
`- **UPS for the network rack and at minimum one POS terminal at the host stand**, sized for graceful shutdown and 15+ minutes of credit-card processing during a flicker.`
`- Minimum 4–6 dedicated 20A circuits for tech/POS/network across the building, on the bar/dining sub-panel.`

`### Outdoor circuits — what must be roughed before hardscape pours`

`**This is the single biggest mistake on patio-heavy concepts.** Once the slab is poured and pavers are set, every conduit run becomes saw-cutting and trenching at multiples of the original cost. Before hardscape:`

`- Conduit to every Bromic heater location (one circuit per unit; oversize the conduit one trade size for future)`
`- Conduit to every patio audio speaker location (low-voltage in dedicated conduit, **never sharing with line-voltage**)`
`- Conduit to every architectural uplight, path light, bollard`
`- Conduit for festoon/string light power and switching`
`- Misting system pump power + GFCI`
`- Outdoor POS tablet power at every outdoor service station (GFCI WP receptacle in cast box)`
`- Camera conduit (PoE — 1" conduit minimum for pull capacity to each camera location, including the trellis 861 SF, covered 1,186 SF, and enclosed 821 SF patios)`
`- Two empty 1" "future" conduits to each major patio zone — cheapest insurance you'll ever buy`

`### Code, permitting, inspection`

`The **City of Austin adopted the 2023 NEC effective late 2023**, with local amendments published under City Code Chapter 25-12-4. Texas TDLR adopted the 2023 NEC statewide effective September 1, 2023. Key 2023 NEC sections for this scope:`

`- **210.8(B) GFCI in non-dwelling kitchens** — applies to every receptacle 125–250V supplied by single-phase ≤50A or three-phase ≤100A in the kitchen and any area with a sink and food/beverage prep`
`- **210.8(D) GFCI for fixed/cord-and-plug appliances** (ranges, dishwashers, microwaves) regardless of receptacle location`
`- **210.8(F) GFCI for outdoor outlets** ≤150V to ground, ≤50A — covers the patio`
`- **220.88 optional restaurant load calculation** (Table)`
`- **240.4(B) / 240.6(A)** for rounding to next standard breaker size`
`- **300.5** for buried low-voltage in conduit (12" minimum cover with rigid PVC; 6" with concrete encasement)`
`- **725 / 800** for low-voltage/communications cabling routing and separation`

`Austin Energy commercial inspection is sequenced: rough-in inspection (before walls close), service inspection (before energization), and final. Your electrician must coordinate with Austin Energy's Service Planning group for the meter base and any utility coordination. Build at least 2 weeks of inspection buffer into the schedule.`

`### 12 Questions to Ask an Electrical Contractor`

`1. Show me a complete Sŏn-specific load schedule with NEC 220.88 calculation and 25% spare per panel.`
`2. Where exactly will the kitchen, bar/dining, and exterior sub-panels go, and why?`
`3. Walk me through how every kitchen receptacle and fixed appliance complies with NEC 210.8(B) and (D) — GFCI breakers in panel, or device-level?`
`4. How are tunable white lighting zones being circuited — two channels per zone or dual-channel driver per zone? Show me the one-line.`
`5. What's your sequence with the lighting designer, AV designer, and low-voltage contractor before walls close?`
`6. Show me the outdoor circuit plan: every Bromic heater, every speaker, every uplight, every camera, every outlet — on one drawing, before hardscape.`
`7. What conduit are you running for low-voltage tech, and how is it separated from line voltage? (NEC 725.136)`
`8. What's your isolated-ground / clean-power approach for POS and network rack?`
`9. How are you sizing the audio amp rack circuit and the lighting control panel feed?`
`10. What's your AIC/SCCR rating strategy at the MDP given the available fault current at this site?`
`11. What spare conduits are you running to the patio zones and to ceiling-accessible chases for future work?`
`12. How many Austin commercial restaurants have you wired in the last 24 months — references with addresses.`

`### Red Flags`

`- No load schedule offered, just a per-square-foot quote`
`- "We'll run the lighting on standard dimmers" — wrong for tunable white`
`- Outdoor scope deferred to "after the patio is built" — too late`
`- Single sub-panel feeding both kitchen and dining — guarantees nuisance trips`
`- No conduit allocation for low-voltage, AV, lighting controls in writing`
`- Refusal to coordinate with Lutron programmer / AV integrator before rough-in`
`- GFCI plan that relies on plug-in GFCI receptacles instead of GFCI breakers in the kitchen`
`- No spare circuits or conduit budgeted`

`### Austin 2026 Cost Range — Electrical Distribution`

`For a fit-out of this size (2,310 SF interior + 2,868 SF patio, all-electric kitchen, full outdoor scope):`
`- **Service distribution (MDP, sub-panels, feeders): $35–55K**`
`- **Interior branch circuits, devices, kitchen rough-in: $55–95K**`
`- **Outdoor sub-panel + full patio rough-in (heaters, lighting, audio, misting, POS, cameras, future conduit): $40–70K**`
`- **Lighting control infrastructure (line-voltage feeds to drivers and HWQS panel — fixtures and controls *not* included): $15–25K**`
`- **Permits, inspections, coordination: $5–10K**`
`- **All-in electrical scope: $150–255K**, or roughly **$9–14/SF interior plus the discrete patio number**. EB3 Construction's Austin restaurant data ($4–9/SF for "electrical work") understates this kind of spec — that range is for a generic concept, not a vaulted, all-electric, smart-glass, tunable white, outdoor-heated Korean fine-dining build. Plan high.`

`---`

`## SECTION 2 — LOW VOLTAGE & TECHNOLOGY ROUGH-IN (Domain 10)`

`### What the landlord delivers vs. what the tenant builds`

`Landlord conduit infrastructure in your delivery covers raceway from the building's telecom service entrance to your designated **low-voltage point of connection** (LV POC) inside the tenant space. The ISP (typically Google Fiber, AT&T Fiber, Spectrum Business, or Astound depending on the address) terminates at the LV POC. **Everything beyond is tenant scope.**`

`The low-voltage room — separate from the electrical room, ideally adjacent — needs:`
`- Minimum 4'×6' clear floor, ideally 6'×8' for service access`
`- One 24U–42U wall-mount or floor-standing rack (Middle Atlantic, Lowell, Chatsworth)`
`- Dedicated 120V/20A circuit (two recommended for redundancy, on UPS)`
`- Active ventilation — equipment generates real heat; install at minimum a thermostat-controlled exhaust fan, ideally a small ductless mini-split or integration into the main HVAC return at +1 ton allocation`
`- Dedicated grounding bus bonded to building ground`
`- A fire-rated wall penetration sleeve to pull future cable`
`- Clean, dry, locked`

`### Structured cabling`

`- **Cat6A** is the right interior backbone for 2026 — supports 10GBASE-T to 100m, runs PoE++ (90W) to current and future APs and cameras. Use Cat6A throughout for new construction; the cost delta vs. Cat6 is negligible at this scale.`
`- **Single-mode fiber (OS2)** between the LV room and any remote IDF (none required at this footprint, but pull a 6-strand to the bar location for future).`
`- **Drop count** for Sŏn (planning estimate):`
`- 6 POS terminals × 1 = 6 drops`
`- 4 KDS screens (kitchen line, expo, bar, prep) × 1 = 4 drops`
`- 4 receipt printers × 1 = 4 drops`
`- Host stand iPad / SevenRooms station × 2 = 2 drops`
`- Handheld charging dock × 2 = 2 drops`
`- Wireless APs (interior + patio) × 6–8 = 6–8 drops`
`- IP cameras × 10 = 10 drops`
`- Smart glass controller × 1 = 1 drop`
`- Lutron HWQS processor × 2 = 2 drops (one primary, one for keypad/integration redundancy)`
`- DSP / audio control × 2 = 2 drops`
`- Music streaming source × 1 = 1 drop`
`- Building management / HVAC interface × 1 = 1 drop`
`- **Spares (always pull at least 25% extra): minimum 12**`
`- **Total ~50–60 Cat6A drops**`

`### Toast POS infrastructure — exactly what's required`

`Toast's published network spec (Toast Network Requirements, current revision):`
`- **Dedicated VLAN for POS, separate from all other traffic**`
`- All POS equipment on Cat5e or higher (Cat6A is overkill but correct), EIA/TIA-568B termination`
`- A PoE+ switch on the POS VLAN (Toast handhelds, KDS, and some printers benefit from PoE)`
`- WiFi for handhelds on the **same VLAN** as wired POS, **5GHz only**, on the "least utilized channel," signal not below −65 dBm in service areas, **client isolation disabled**, mDNS/Bonjour enabled`
`- 15 Mbps down / 5 Mbps up dedicated to Toast minimum (in practice, plan 50/20 or better)`
`- Outbound URLs/ports per Toast firewall allowlist`
`- Toast subnet: 192.168.192.0/24 with .1 gateway (their default)`

`Per **PCI-DSS**, the POS VLAN is logically segmented from the staff/admin VLAN and the guest WiFi VLAN. Three minimum:`
`- **VLAN 10 — POS** (PCI scope; restricted firewall rules; only Toast-allowlisted destinations)`
`- **VLAN 20 — Staff/Admin** (back-office laptop, manager iPad, security NVR, BMS)`
`- **VLAN 30 — Guest WiFi** (captive portal, rate-limited, completely isolated from VLANs 10/20)`
`- Optional **VLAN 40 — IoT/AV** (Lutron, smart glass, Sonos/streamer, cameras if not on staff)`

`### Hardware locations & rough-in`

`For each POS terminal: **a Cat6A drop AND a 120V receptacle within 18" of the terminal location.** The receipt printer at the same station typically has its own drop and outlet. Handheld charging docks need power + drop. The host stand needs power + drop for the SevenRooms iPad and the reservation printer. Outdoor POS terminals require IP-rated enclosures and weather-rated boxes; pull Cat6A in conduit to outdoor service stations now.`

`### Enterprise WiFi — *which tier is right*`

`Three serious options for a hospitality space at this scale:`

`- **Ubiquiti UniFi** (U6 Pro, U6 Enterprise; outdoor U6-Mesh / UAP-AC-M-Pro): The pragmatic sweet spot for 2026. Strong hardware, no licensing fees, capable controller, robust VLAN/firewall, integrates with UniFi Protect for cameras if you want a single-vendor ecosystem. Recommended for Sŏn.`
`- **Cisco Meraki**: Polished cloud dashboard, world-class support, mandatory annual licensing — typical TCO is 2–3× UniFi over 5 years. Right answer if you're a multi-location group with no on-site IT.`
`- **TP-Link Omada**: 15–30% cheaper than UniFi, performance comparable, fine for a single-location operator. Fewer outdoor model options.`

`**Skip consumer mesh (Eero, Google Nest Wifi, etc.).** They cannot do enterprise VLAN segmentation, will not survive PCI scrutiny, and degrade under restaurant-density device counts.`

`**AP count for Sŏn (Cat6A wired PoE+, never mesh-backhauled in a commercial space):**`
`- Interior 2,310 SF, vaulted ceiling, hard surfaces: **3 APs** (one over dining, one over bar/entry, one near kitchen/back-of-house) — vaulted ceiling makes one centered AP insufficient because high-mounted APs have less effective dwell at table height`

`Speaker wire and AV control runs are **a separate cabling system** from data:`

`## SECTION 3 — ARCHITECTURAL LIGHTING: TUNABLE WHITE & SMART GLASS (Domain 11)`

`### Tunable white fundamentals`

`Tunable white is the ability to set any **correlated color temperature (CCT)** between two endpoints — typically 2700K (warm, candlelight, incandescent halogen) and 5000K or 6500K (cool, daylight, north-sky) — and to set any intensity from ~0.1% to 100% **independently** of the CCT. It's achieved with **dual-channel LED engines**: one warm string, one cool string, mixed by the driver based on a dual control signal (DALI Type 8, two DMX addresses, two 0–10V channels, or proprietary like Ketra's Clear Connect Type X).`

`A single-channel "full-spectrum" LED (like Soraa's Vivid series) is *not* tunable white — it's a fixed CCT with very high CRI/R9. A "dim-to-warm" fixture is *also* not tunable white — it's a single-channel LED that mimics an incandescent's amber shift as it dims (typically from 3000K at full to 1800–2200K near zero), but it cannot decouple CCT from intensity.`

`**For Sŏn, true tunable white is the right answer**, because the operating arc demands independent control: morning coffee daypart wants higher CCT (3500–4000K) at moderate intensity to feel awake and clean; dinner warmth wants 2700–3000K at moderate-low intensity; late-night intimacy wants 2200–2700K at very low intensity but still requires task light at the bar that shouldn't get warmer than 2700K. Dim-to-warm couples those values. True tunable white separates them.`

`### What CCT looks like on Korean fine-dining presentations`

`- **2700K**: Galbi marbling reads rich and rendered; gochujang reads deep, complex red; banchan ceramics warm into hospitality; skin tones (especially Asian skin) appear flattering with warmth in cheek and lip; broth reads amber-translucent. **The dinner anchor.**`
`- **3000K**: Slightly more clarity — reads "elegant restaurant"; food still warm but a touch crisper. Good for early dinner/transition.`
`- **3500K**: Neutral-warm; banchan colors discriminate well (yellow daikon vs. white radish), but the room loses intimacy. **Daypart/coffee.**`
`- **4000K**: Office light. Murders mood. Useful only for kitchen line task lighting.`
`- **5000K**: Daylight. Skin pallid, food washed out, dessert berries lose saturation. Never use this in dining; it exists in the tunable system only as the cool endpoint that mixes downward.`

`### CRI and R9 — *the spec that protects food integrity*`

`**CRI (Ra)** is an averaged measure of how accurately a source renders 8 standardized pastel test colors compared to a black-body reference at the same CCT. **CRI 90+** is the floor for fine dining. **CRI 95+ is what you specify.**`

`**R9 is a 9th, supplemental test color — saturated red.** R9 is not included in the average Ra. A fixture can have CRI 90 and R9 of 20 and look terrible on red foods. Galbi, gochujang, kimchi, red pepper, dessert berries, marbled tuna at the bar — every one of these is an R9 test. **Specify R9 80+ minimum.**`

`How to verify on a manufacturer datasheet: look for a published CRI value AND a separately published R9 value. If R9 isn't published, the fixture is hiding it. The Ketra D2/D3/D4 datasheets explicitly list "CRI ≥ 90 (R9 > 90)" — that's the spec language to demand from every fixture in the package.`

`**Brands that consistently deliver CRI 95+ / R9 80+:**`
`- **Ketra/Lutron** — the hospitality benchmark; 90+ R9 across the entire CCT range`
`- **USAI Lighting** (BeveLED Mini, BeveLED Trimless Adjustable) — performance + value`
`- **Soraa** (Vivid series) — extremely high CRI/R9 in single-CCT MR16 format`
`- **Erco** — museum-grade German engineering, tunable white available across Quintessence and Compar lines`
`- **Selux** — museum/cultural specialist`
`- **Lumenpulse** — large-scale architectural, Lumencove Nano TW for coves`
`- **Acuity Brands** (Mark Architectural, Juno) at the value end with credible specs`

`### Dim-to-warm vs. tunable white — *when each is appropriate*`

`- **Dim-to-warm** (single-channel, mimics incandescent dimming arc): perfect for fully residential luxury hospitality (a Beverly Hills hotel suite, a single-CCT cove behind a banquette) where the only setting variable is intensity, and the warmth-as-it-dims is the whole point. Brands: USAI Color Select, Lumenwerx Warm Glow, DMF Lighting.`
`- **True tunable white** (dual-channel, decoupled CCT and intensity): correct for any space with a daypart arc (Sŏn), any space integrated with daylight harvesting via smart glass (Sŏn), any space where the same fixture must serve coffee at 3500K and late-night at 2400K (Sŏn).`

`**Decision for Sŏn: true tunable white throughout interior. No dim-to-warm.**`

`Control implications: every tunable white fixture is **two addresses, two channels** (or one dual-channel address in DALI Type 8 / Ketra). Plan twice the channel count of a static system. The HWQS panel sizing accommodates this; the budget does too.`

`### Smart glass technologies — *one is right, two are wrong*`

`| Technology | How it works | Transition | VLT range | Solar control | Right for Sŏn? |`
`|---|---|---|---|---|---|`
`| **Electrochromic (EC)** — View, SageGlass | Lithium-ion intercalation in metal-oxide nano-layer with low-voltage DC | 1–10 minutes | 60% clear → 1–2% tinted | **Yes — primary purpose, blocks up to 93% solar heat** | **YES** |`
`| **PDLC** — Smart Tint, Gauzy | Liquid crystals dispersed in polymer, scatter when off | Milliseconds | Clear ↔ frosted/translucent | **No — privacy only, frosted state still passes heat** | No |`
`| **SPD** — Research Frontiers SmartGlass | Suspended dark particles align under voltage | 1–3 seconds | 50% clear → ~1% tinted | Yes, but requires continuous power in clear state | Niche |`

`**For Austin Climate Zone 2A and Sŏn's design intent — coordinating window tint with interior tunable white to maintain a consistent perceptual color temperature throughout the day — the answer is electrochromic.** EC is what View Smart Windows and SageGlass deliver. PDLC is a privacy product (a frosted bathroom partition); it would not address solar heat gain on south- and west-facing window walls in Austin summer. SPD is fast but still rare in commercial hospitality.`

`EC trade-offs to know:`
`- **40–50% premium over standard double-pane low-E glazing** at the curtain wall level`
`- 1–10 minute transition (View Maestro / SageGlass predictive control mitigates by anticipating)`
`- Even at 1% VLT, occupants can still see *out* (it's tinted, not opaque) — preserves the "connection to outdoors" the designer cares about`
`- HVAC load reduction in hot climates: **20–25% cooling load** (LBNL on SAGE; SageGlass blocks up to 93% solar heat)`

`### Smart glass + tunable white integration — *the "scene"*`

`The technical achievement to push for: **a scene where the smart glass tint state, the interior CCT, and the interior intensity are coordinated as one cue**, so the room reads as a consistent light temperature throughout the day.`

`**Daylight scene (lunch/coffee, hypothetical):** EC glass at 30% VLT (medium tint), interior tunable white at 3500K / 40% intensity. The cool incoming daylight is partially attenuated and the interior fills with neutral light; the eye perceives a clean, balanced room.`

`**Dinner scene:** EC glass at full clear (sun has set), exterior dark; interior tunable white at 2700K / 25% intensity; cove lighting at 2400K / 15%; accent at 3000K / 60%. Warm, layered, intimate.`

`**Late-night scene:** EC glass clear; interior at 2200–2400K / 10% ambient; bar accents at 2700K / 50% (functional task); cove at 2200K / 20%. Quiet, candlelit, present.`

`**Technical integration:** SageGlass exposes BACnet/IP; View exposes a local API and BACnet via gateway; Lutron HomeWorks QS speaks **BACnet, dry contact, Telnet/IP, and has a published integration API**. The systems integrator (typically your Lutron programmer) writes scene logic that simultaneously commands the glass tint state, the lighting CCT/intensity per zone, and (ideally) the audio scene via the HWQS-to-DSP integration. Single button press → whole-room cue.`

`### Skylight treatment`

`Sŏn's skylights are the highest-leverage piece of glazing in the building (overhead = the most direct solar exposure in Austin summer). Options, in order of escalating capability:`

`1. **Static 3M Prestige Series exterior film** (VLT options 40–70%): rejects up to 97% IR, blocks 99.9% UV, no electrical, no controls. Cheapest, durable, invisible. The minimum acceptable treatment.`
`2. **Motorized roller shades inside the skylight well** (Lutron Sivoia QS / Hunter Douglas / Mechoshade): blackout or solar-screen fabric, integrated into HWQS scene logic. Adds full controllability but adds visual mass and a maintenance item at height.`
`3. **EC glass for the skylights themselves** (View Smart Canopy, SageGlass Skyworks for overhead): the integrated answer — same control system, same scene logic, no shades. Most expensive, longest-lead, but architecturally cleanest. Overhead EC requires structural review (skylight framing must support the IGU spec) and proper drainage detailing.`

`**Recommendation for Sŏn:** if the budget supports it, EC for the skylights to maintain the integrated scene logic — otherwise 3M Prestige film as a baseline + motorized blackout shade in the skylight well wired to HWQS. **Whatever you do, do not leave the skylights untreated** — Austin summer sun through a vaulted skylight in a stone-and-hardwood room is brutal both thermally and visually.`

`### Austin solar context & dark-sky compliance`

`- **Climate Zone 2A (hot-humid).** Solar heat reduction from EC glass is documented at 20–30% of cooling load in this climate.`
`- **Texas state law (post-HB 2439 / SB 1090):** Outdoor lighting ordinances are restricted to certified IDA Dark Sky Communities, certain communities pursuing certification, and observatory/military zones. The City of Austin proper is **not currently a certified IDA Dark Sky Community**, but the Austin Land Development Code (Title 25) and the design community broadly apply the 3000K cap and full-cutoff fixture norm to commercial outdoor lighting near residential edges as professional best practice and Site Plan review standard.`
`- **For 207 E St Elmo Rd specifically:** verify zoning and adjacency at site plan review. As a defensible default, **specify 3000K maximum CCT for all exterior fixtures** (the patio lighting, façade, parking-adjacent), use full-cutoff/U0-uplight fixtures, and design photometric spill to ≤0.1 fc at any residential property line. This protects you on site plan review, satisfies any future ordinance update, and aligns with DarkSky-Approved-luminaire criteria. The IDA recommends ≤2700K for the most sensitive sites.`

`### Interior lighting — four-layer doctrine`

`IES (Illuminating Engineering Society) recommended practice for restaurant lighting layers:`

`1. **Ambient** — 5–20 footcandles at table height (lower for fine dining; Sŏn dinner target ~5–8 fc)`
`2. **Task** — 30–50 fc at menu height (delivered via decorative pendant or accent, not ambient)`
`3. **Accent** — 3:1 to 5:1 accent-to-ambient ratio on focal elements (food-on-plate, fireplace, art)`
`4. **Architectural** — cove wash, ceiling reveals, structural element grazing; the layer that makes the vaulted ceiling read as a designed object rather than a void`

`The vaulted ceiling complicates ambient: photometric calculations must use the **actual cavity reflectance and ceiling height per zone**, not a flat 9' assumption. A point-by-point study from your lighting designer is required, not optional.`

`### Red Flags`

`- Brings a fixture catalog and starts pointing at downlights before measuring the room`
`- Quotes CRI but not R9`
`- Proposes 4000K interior ambient ("more lumens per watt") — wrong for fine dining`
`- Doesn't know the difference between dim-to-warm and tunable white`
`- Has no smart-glass integration experience`
`- Recommends a wall dimmer for tunable white`
`- "We can program it ourselves" without a Lutron-certified programmer`

`### Austin 2026 Cost Range — Lighting Package`

`- **Lighting design fees** (architectural lighting designer): $25–55K for this scope`
`- **Fixtures (Ketra-tier interior + Erco/Lumenpulse accents + decorative pendants + exterior architectural)**: $90–220K`
`- **Lutron HomeWorks QS controls hardware** (processor, panels, keypads, drivers if not bundled with fixtures): $35–75K`
`- **Lutron programming and commissioning**: $8–20K`
`- **Smart glass — electrochromic** (View / SageGlass) for the window walls and skylights: **$75–150 per square foot of treated glazing** installed. Sŏn's glazing area is sized in the architectural set; if total treated glazing is, say, 600 SF, that's **$45–90K in smart glass**, plus $5–12K for the controller, sensors, and integration.`
`- **Static skylight film alternative** (3M Prestige): $12–18/SF — much cheaper if budget caps`
`- **Total interior lighting + controls + smart glass envelope: $200–470K**, heavily dependent on smart glass scope`

`---`

`## SECTION 4 — AUDIO SYSTEM: HIGH-FIDELITY INTERIOR & OUTDOOR (Domain 12)`

`### Philosophy: distributed vs. high-fidelity`

`There are two coherent approaches to restaurant audio, and Sŏn's music direction (Arooj Aftab, Nala Sinephro, Tirzah, Sault, Kelela — emotionally present, dynamic-range-heavy, low-frequency-rich, *not* background) demands the second:`

`- **Distributed audio**: 8–20 small ceiling speakers (QSC AcousticDesign, Atlas Sound, TOA F-series, JBL Control) on a 70V transformer-tapped line, driven by a single small amp, set to a uniform low SPL throughout. Easy to design, cheap, and acoustically forgettable. **Wrong for Sŏn.**`
`- **High-fidelity / point-source / architectural**: fewer, better speakers — full frequency range, controlled directivity, time-aligned, DSP-corrected, on a serious amp, fed from a lossless source. Designed to make music *present*, with the dynamic range and texture intact. **Right for Sŏn.**`

`"Audiophile in a restaurant" means the four conditions are simultaneously true:`
`1. **Speakers** capable of full-range reproduction without compression at the SPL the room requires`
`2. **Amplification** that preserves transient detail and dynamic range (not 70V transformer-coupled, which softens both)`
`3. **Room acoustic treatment** preventing standing waves, flutter echo, and slap (covered in the Acoustics Guide cross-reference)`
`4. **Lossless source material** (Tidal HiFi, Apple Music Lossless, Roon-managed local library) — Bluetooth from a phone is *never* the source`

`Plus: **DSP room correction.** Without DSP, expensive speakers in a hard-surfaced, vaulted, parallel-walled room sound *worse* than a properly tuned distributed system. DSP isn't a luxury here; it's the part that makes the fidelity audible.`

`### Acoustic challenges Sŏn presents`

`- **Vaulted ceiling**: parallel walls + sloped ceiling create flutter echo and increase RT60 in the dining cavity`
`- **Hard surfaces**: concrete, hardwood, stone fireplace — every surface is reflective; cross-reference the Acoustics Guide for absorption strategy`
`- **Skylights**: glass adds reflection in the upper register`
`- **Open plan to bar/entry**: bass leak between zones, level matching becomes critical`

`How speaker selection and placement address these:`
`- **Directional speakers** with controlled dispersion (Meyer UP-4slim's 100° pattern, B&W CCM bezel with directional control) avoid pumping energy into the ceiling`
`- **Mount lower and angle toward listener height** rather than firing straight down from vault apex`
`- **DSP time-alignment** between zones eliminates comb filtering when guests are in coverage overlap`
`- **Use the Haas effect** in distributed fills: any speaker arriving within ~35ms of the primary fuses perceptually into one source — the basis for delay-aligned fill speakers near the kitchen pass`

`### Speaker as architectural object`

`Three integration approaches:`

`1. **Specified speakers in their own enclosures** — B&W 700 series, KEF Reference, Focal Utopia. Finishable to match palette; enclosure cannot be redesigned without affecting acoustics.`
`2. **Driver-into-custom-enclosure** — buy raw drivers from Seas, ScanSpeak, Accuton, RAAL, integrate into a custom architectural baffle/enclosure designed by your fabricator working with an acoustic engineer. **Maximum design freedom; the highest-end approach in fine-dining hospitality.** The enclosure must be sized correctly per driver T/S parameters, sealed or ported per spec, and damped (Dynamat, fiberglass batting). A carpenter's "let's just build a box" produces a box that resonates and colors the sound.`
`3. **Architectural OEM speakers designed for custom integration** — B&W CI series, KEF Ci, Focal 100 series, Sonance Custom Visual Performance. Minimal enclosure requirements, designed to drop into framed-out cavities. Middle path between freedom and predictability.`

`The **KEF LS50 Meta** in the FF&E (the C variant is a center-channel for in-wall/custom-baffle installations) is a strong single-driver-baffle option for architectural integration — Uni-Q driver array, controlled dispersion, paintable.`

`### Recommended interior configuration for Sŏn`

`For the 988 SF vaulted dining room:`

`**Tier 1 — Audiophile-commercial benchmark:**`
`- **Pair (or quad) of Meyer Sound UP-4slim** in custom architectural housings, positioned at the ends of the dining room and angled to converge at table height. The UP-4slim is the speaker used at Eleven Madison Park, multiple Michelin-starred rooms, and in commercial/hotel-lobby fine-dining contexts where the speaker must be small, beautiful, and full-fidelity. 65Hz–18kHz, 116.5dB peak SPL, 100° dispersion, IntelligentDC powered (remote PSU, single 5-pin connector).`
`- **Two delay-aligned fill speakers** (Meyer UPM or smaller) near the kitchen pass to fill the open-plan bleed zone without fighting the mains.`
`- **Optional discreet subwoofer** (Meyer X-400C or USW-112P) hidden in millwork for the actual low-frequency content of Tirzah, Sault, and Kelela — without it the bass is implied, not delivered.`

`**Tier 2 — High-end architectural integration:**`
`- **B&W CCM 8.5D or 7.5 Custom Install** (paintable, large coaxial driver, hi-fi grade), 4–6 units in custom architectural housings`
`- Or **KEF Ci5160REF** Reference series in-wall`

`**Tier 3 — Distributed point-source:**`
`- Genelec 4040 series self-powered (built-in DSP and room correction)`
`- Sonance VP series with Sonance amp/DSP`

`**Recommendation: Tier 1 Meyer UP-4slim** as the anchor — hospitality pedigree, the right size/visual restraint, and self-powered IntelligentDC eliminates separate amp rack for the mains.`

`### Signal chain & DSP`

` ``` `
`Source → Network transport → DSP → Amplifier → Speaker`
` ``` `

`- **Source**: Bluesound Node (the practical workhorse — Tidal HiFi, Apple Music AirPlay 2 Lossless, Roon endpoint, Dante optional via add-on), or a dedicated Roon Nucleus + streamer for the Roon-native shop. **Never Bluetooth from a staff phone.**`
`- **Network transport**: Dante or AES67 for clean digital routing if amp/DSP supports; otherwise balanced analog from source to DSP.`
`- **DSP**: QSC Q-SYS Core Nano or Core 110f (the modern restaurant standard — networked, software-defined, EQ + delay + zoning + limiting in one box), or Symetrix Composer/Radius, or BSS Audio Soundweb London. For room correction specifically, **Dirac Live** (now available in many DSP front-ends) or **Trinnov** (audiophile-grade) layered on top.`
`- **Amplifier**: Crown DCi 2|600N (Dante-enabled), Powersoft M-series, or Lab.gruppen E-series. For Meyer UP-4slim, the IntelligentDC PSU (MPS-482HP for two channels, MPS-488HP for eight) replaces the discrete amp.`
`- **Speaker**: as above.`

`**What DSP actually does for Sŏn:**`
`- Notches the room modes specific to the vaulted volume (typically 35–80Hz peaks that bloom uncontrolled bass)`
`- Time-aligns all zones so a guest at the bar/dining boundary doesn't hear comb filtering`
`- Limits SPL per zone (protects the system AND respects late-night noise compliance)`
`- Routes zones (dining = full-range, bar = full-range with slight mid-presence lift, entry = brief intelligibility-tuned, patio = separate)`
`- Stores scenes that link to lighting cues via the HWQS-DSP integration`

`**DSP is not optional in this room.** Specifying high-end speakers without DSP is paying for capability you can't hear under the room's reflections.`

`### Zoning`

`- **Dining room main** — primary high-fidelity zone, full-range, scene-controlled`
`- **Bar fill** — supplementary architectural speakers, delayed feed from main, slightly leaner low end so bar conversation can ride on top`
`- **Entry/approach** — brief coverage zone, low SPL, clean intelligibility-tuned EQ`
`- **Trellis patio** — outdoor zone 1`
`- **Covered patio** — outdoor zone 2 (the late-night zone — see below)`
`- **Enclosed patio** — outdoor zone 3`
`- **All zones level-matched** in DSP so a guest moving from indoor to covered patio doesn't experience SPL discontinuity`

`### Outdoor speakers`

`**IP rating** is the durability spec. For Austin Climate Zone 2A (hot, humid, full UV, occasional severe weather):`
`- **IP54 minimum** (dust-protected, splash-resistant)`
`- **IP65 preferred** (dust-tight, low-pressure water jet) — required for any speaker exposed to direct rain or wash-down`
`- **UV-stabilized cabinet polymers** — consumer outdoor speakers fail in 2–3 Austin summers`
`- **Thermal cycling rated** for −20°C to 50°C minimum`

`What happens to consumer-grade outdoor speakers in continuous commercial use: cabinet color shifts, surrounds dry-rot, terminals corrode, woofers sag. Then they sound bad and you replace them. Commercial-grade IP65 lasts 10+ years.`

`### Covered patio 1,186 SF — the late-night zone`

`You already have **B&W AM-1** in FF&E — pair, currently $1,000-tier per unit (4 units in your inventory). Spec on the AM-1: 1" Nautilus aluminum tweeter + 5" glass-fiber midwoofer + auxiliary bass radiator (sealed for weather), rated 100W RMS program (the "200W program" figure may be a marketing rating; confirm against B&W datasheet — nominal IEC rating is 100W program, music handling higher), frequency response ~51Hz–22kHz wall-mounted, weather-resistant aluminum grille and glass-filled plastic cabinet, 220° rotation in the wall bracket. **Architecturally appropriate, sonically credible, weather-rated for Austin.**`

`For a 1,186 SF covered patio with high-fidelity intent, four AM-1s are correct — distributed at corners, angled inward, all driven from a dedicated outdoor zone amp channel through DSP. Add:`
`- **A direct-burial or hidden subwoofer** for actual low end. Options:`
`- Sonance Sonarray SR1 buried sub`
`- Episode Landscape ELS-XSUB-10 buried sub`
`- SpeakerCraft OE Series or Atlas Sound outdoor sub mounted in millwork`
`- The bar/sub-frame can hide a James Loudspeaker outdoor sub`
`- **Cardioid or directional sub configuration** — critical for noise compliance (see below). Multiple subs in a cardioid array radiate forward into the patio and cancel rearward toward the property line.`

`Alternative speaker tiers for covered patio:`
`- **Sonance Professional Outdoor** — IP65, transformer-tap option for distributed runs, pro-grade`
`- **Stealth Acoustics SR6/SR8** — IP68, *invisible* (flush-installed in wall/ceiling substrate, plastered over)`
`- **Klipsch AW-650/800** — value tier, durable, less refined`
`- **Bose FreeSpace DS** — distributed/commercial, not high-fidelity`

`### Speakers as architectural objects on the patio`

`- **Pendant/hanging speakers** — Cabasse Bora outdoor finish, custom-fabricated pendant enclosures housing high-quality coaxial drivers (commission with a fabricator + acoustic engineer)`
`- **In-post / in-column** — Stealth Acoustics flush-in-column, or custom aluminum/PVC column housing a driver`
`- **Ground-stake landscape subs** — buried, terminal cap at grade, fed by direct-burial 12/2`

`### Subwoofer strategy for late-night outdoor`

`Sŏn's music — Tirzah's bass-forward production, Sault's basslines, Kelela's R&B low-end — has real bass content. A patio system without a sub turns those tracks into thin, anemic versions of themselves. **Yes, install a sub.**`

`But: **City of Austin Code Chapter 9-2 Noise and Amplified Sound** governs late-night outdoor sound. Key provisions for Sŏn:`

`- A commercial outdoor amplified sound permit is required for any outdoor sound equipment in any space not enclosed by four walls and a roof. **Apply through Austin Development Services Entertainment Services Group.**`
`- Section 9-2-3: in public, no noise/sound equipment between 10:30 PM and 7:00 AM`
`- Amplified sound on residential property or audible to a residence: limits and audibility tests apply`
`- The "audible at 50 feet" standard appears in older versions and other jurisdictions; Austin's current Chapter 9-2 uses an audibility-at-property-line and decibel-at-residence standard (see the ordinance for current decibel limits, which the Planning Commission has been pushing to tighten).`
`- Late-night (post-10 PM/10:30 PM) compliance is the operational constraint. Sŏn must design the system to **be audible inside the patio at musically meaningful levels but inaudible at the nearest residential property line.**`

`How to engineer this:`
`- **Cardioid sub configuration** (multiple subs phase-aligned to radiate forward, cancel rearward) — reduces low-frequency radiation toward neighbors by 12–20dB`
`- **Pole-mounted directional mid/high speakers** angled downward into the patio rather than horizontally outward`
`- **DSP-enforced SPL limit** that physically caps the system at a level the operator cannot exceed — this is a feature, not a constraint`
`- **Acoustic fence or mass-loaded perimeter element** if site allows`
`- **Operational scene** that automatically reduces SPL and rolls off bass after, e.g., 10 PM via the lighting/audio scene control`

`### Infrastructure rough-in`

`**Interior:**`
`- Acoustic backboxes for in-wall/in-ceiling speakers (Dynamat-lined, sealed, prevents uncontrolled cavity resonance) — Atlas Sound or Speakercraft enclosures, or fabricator-built per acoustic spec`
`- **16 AWG minimum** in-wall speaker wire CL2/CL3 (NEC 800/725); **12 AWG for runs over 50 ft** — the runs from the LV room amp rack to the dining room ends will all be over 50 ft in this footprint`
`- Always in dedicated conduit, never sharing with data or line voltage`

`**Exterior:**`
`- Direct-burial 12/2 or 16/2 CL3/FT4 in 1" PVC, 12" min cover (NEC 300.5)`
`- Splice-free pulls from amp rack to each speaker location wherever possible`
`- Conduit to subwoofer location during foundation/hardscape work (this is the most-missed item — buried subs have to be set before pavers)`

`**Amp rack:**`
`- Co-located with network rack in LV room`
`- Dedicated 30A circuit (120V or 208V depending on amp choice)`
`- Active ventilation`
`- Network drop for Dante / Q-SYS / Roon`

`### Vendor evaluation — *the right sequence*`

`For Sŏn, three roles, in this order:`

`1. **Acoustic consultant** (independent, not selling product) — characterizes the vaulted dining room with measured RT60 and modal response, recommends absorption strategy in coordination with the architect and the Acoustics Guide cross-reference. Fee, not commission.`
`2. **CEDIA-certified custom AV integrator with fine-dining hospitality experience** — designs the speaker placement, integrates with HWQS, programs DSP, commissions the system. Look for integrators who reference projects like McGuire Moorman Lambert restaurants, Hai Hospitality, June's All Day, or similar Austin/Texas fine-dining audio installations.`
`3. **Commercial AV integrator** (often the same firm) for patio infrastructure, zoning, outdoor speaker mounting, and long-term service.`

`### 12 Questions to Ask an Audio Consultant / AV Integrator`

`1. Show me three fine-dining projects with comparable music programming and acoustic profiles.`
`2. What's your speaker recommendation for the vaulted dining room, and why is it that and not a distributed ceiling system?`
`3. What's your DSP platform, and have you implemented Dirac Live or Trinnov room correction in a restaurant?`
`4. How are you going to measure RT60 and room modes before you spec — what's the measurement protocol?`
`5. What's the source chain — Tidal HiFi via Bluesound? Roon? Dante? Walk me through.`
`6. How do the indoor and four outdoor zones level-match?`
`7. Show me your subwoofer plan for the covered patio and how it complies with Austin Chapter 9-2 for late-night.`
`8. How do you integrate with Lutron HomeWorks QS for scene-linked audio cues?`
`9. What's your IP rating spec for outdoor speakers and what's your warranty against UV/thermal failure?`
`10. What's your conduit and cable separation plan from the data and lighting control runs?`
`11. What's your commissioning process and what does the closeout package look like?`
`12. Who maintains this system in years 2, 5, 10 — is that you or a service contract?`

`### Red Flags`

`- Wants to put ceiling speakers throughout without measuring RT60`
`- Proposes 70V distributed for the high-fidelity dining zone`
`- Specs consumer-grade outdoor speakers (Polk Atrium, Klipsch entry-level) for the covered patio`
`- Bluetooth streaming from a phone as the source`
`- No DSP, "the speaker is so good it doesn't need correction" — wrong in this room`
`- No discussion of acoustic measurement, just speaker placement intuition`
`- Doesn't know Austin Chapter 9-2 or "we'll deal with that later"`
`- Proposes a single amp without zoning capability`
`- "You don't need a sub for a restaurant" — wrong for this music direction`

`### Austin 2026 Cost Range — Audio System`

`- **Acoustic consulting (RT60 measurement, treatment recommendation, coordination)**: $5–12K (separate from the audio installer)`
`- **Interior speaker package (Meyer UP-4slim quad in custom housings + fills + IntelligentDC PSU)**: $22–38K hardware + $8–15K custom architectural housing/fabrication`
`- **Outdoor speakers** (4× B&W AM-1 already in FF&E at $4K + supplemental + buried sub + brackets): $5–12K supplemental`
`- **Amplification and DSP** (QSC Q-SYS Core 110f, Crown DCi 2|600N for outdoor zones, Bluesound Node source, Dirac license): $12–25K`
`- **Cabling, conduit, terminations, racks**: $8–15K (separate from the LV scope or bundled)`
`- **AV programming, commissioning, scene integration with HWQS**: $8–18K`
`- **Total audio package: $68–135K**, with the high end approaching $150K if the custom-architectural-housing approach is fully realized and outdoor subs/cardioid array are spec'd`

`---`

`## CROSS-REFERENCES & SEQUENCING`

`The four systems in this document are deeply interdependent. The owner's job is to enforce the sequence:`

`1. **Architect's RCP and finish plan locked first** — every conduit and backbox depends on this.`
`2. **Lighting designer + acoustic consultant + audio integrator engaged before MEP rough-in starts** — they generate the conduit demand schedule.`
`3. **Smart glass vendor field-engineering visit** before glazing rough — EC requires specific framing and DC bus routing.`
`4. **Lutron HomeWorks QS programmer engaged at design phase**, not at commissioning — they specify the panel size, control wire pulls, and integration protocols.`
`5. **Outdoor circuits/conduit before hardscape pours** — patio heaters, audio, lighting, cameras, future raceway. The most expensive mistake at this scale is paving over conduit you didn't pull.`
`6. **Lighting scenes and audio scenes triggered simultaneously** via HWQS keypads or the operator's iPad — this is the integration that makes the daypart arc legible to a guest. Lutron HomeWorks QS integrates natively with Crestron, Control4, Savant, and Lutron's own Athena cloud, and via BACnet/Telnet/IP with Q-SYS, Symetrix, and BSS DSPs.`
`7. **Smart glass controller integrated into HWQS** via BACnet (SageGlass Maestro is BACnet-native) or dry contact (View has a published API and BACnet gateway). The systems integrator owns the protocol-level wiring.`
`8. **Low-voltage conduit planned before electrical rough-in closes** — separation of data, speaker wire, lighting control, and line voltage is impossible to fix after walls close.`
`9. **Network architecture (VLANs) defined before Toast install** — Toast's installer expects a configured network ready to receive their gear; surprises here delay opening.`
`10. **Audio room treatment coordinated with architect's finish palette** — the Acoustics Guide cross-reference covers absorption strategy in detail, but absorption placement and speaker placement must be designed together.`

`---`

`## RECOMMENDATIONS`

`**Do this now (pre-CD / before drawings finalize):**`

`1. **Engage the lighting designer (IES/LC), the acoustic consultant, and the AV integrator on retainer this week.** They feed the architect's drawings before they go to permit. Total upfront fees: ~$40–80K. The cost of skipping this and "value-engineering" later is 3–5× that in change orders.`
`2. **Specify Lutron HomeWorks QS + Ketra (or near-equivalent CRI 95+/R9 80+ tunable white) as the lighting backbone in the OPR (Owner's Project Requirements) document.** This is the single decision that protects every other lighting decision downstream.`
`3. **Decide on smart glass scope.** If budget supports, electrochromic on south- and west-facing window walls and on skylights. If not, electrochromic on the worst solar-exposure walls + 3M Prestige film + motorized shades on skylights, integrated to HWQS.`
`4. **Reject any "Bluetooth audio from staff phone" or "we'll just put Sonos" proposal.** Specify high-fidelity architectural integration with DSP room correction and a Tidal HiFi / Apple Lossless / Roon source.`

`**Do this before electrical rough-in (next 60 days):**`

`5. **Lock the load schedule and panel architecture** with the electrical contractor. Demand the actual NEC 220.88 calculation, not a per-square-foot estimate.`
`6. **Lock the conduit plan** — every Bromic heater, every speaker, every camera, every lighting zone, every smart glass run, every spare. This is the single drawing that kills change orders.`
`7. **Apply for the City of Austin Outdoor Amplified Sound permit** through Development Services Entertainment Services Group (Bryan Walker, 512-974-2686). 30+ days for approval.`

`**Do this before ceilings close:**`

`8. **Verify every backbox, junction box, and conduit termination is in place** for the lighting fixture schedule, the speaker plan, the camera plan, and the smart glass run. Walk the space with the lighting designer, AV integrator, and electrician simultaneously.`
`9. **Pre-install the HWQS panel and run all control wire** with a Lutron-certified installer. Programming happens later but the wiring must be in.`

`**Do this at commissioning:**`

`10. **Schedule a half-day on-site programming session** with the Lutron programmer, AV integrator, lighting designer, and owner — together, in the actual room, at dusk. Define and lock the daylight, dinner, and late-night scenes. Walk away with a printed scene list and a programmer's contract for two follow-up tuning sessions in months 1 and 3 of operation.`

`**Benchmarks/thresholds that change the recommendation:**`

`- If the smart-glass budget can't reach $60K minimum, switch to 3M Prestige film + motorized shades on skylights — *don't half-do EC*.`
`- If the audio budget can't reach $60K, drop the buried sub but keep the Meyer UP-4slim mains + DSP — *don't drop DSP*.`
`- If the project goes over 90-day permit timeline at City of Austin, expedite by removing scope (defer one patio zone's audio and lighting to a phase 2) rather than by skipping the consultant team.`
`- If a contractor pushes back on Lutron HWQS as "overkill," walk to RadioRA 3 only if the smart-glass integration is demonstrated to work over BACnet on RA3 (it's more limited). Do not drop to a residential dimmer system.`

`---`

`## CAVEATS`

`- **Bromic heater wiring specifics vary by exact model.** The brief specifies "120V/15A per unit," which is correct for the smaller Bromic Tungsten 2000W single-element heaters but understates the larger 4000W and 6000W units that draw two 15A elements (often spec'd on 240V/30A circuits per the field reports cited above). Confirm the exact model SKU and the manufacturer's installation manual at the time of order, and have the electrician size each circuit per that specific spec — do not generalize "120V/15A" across the patio.`
`- **City of Austin noise ordinance Chapter 9-2** has been the subject of active Planning Commission review (a July 2024 recommendation to drop mechanical equipment limits from 70 to 45 dB; a City Manager response in 2025 declining broader enforcement). The ordinance can change. Verify current decibel limits and audibility tests with Development Services at permit time, and design the audio system with 6–10 dB of headroom against the strictest plausible enforcement.`
`- **Austin's IDA Dark Sky status:** Austin proper is not a certified IDA Dark Sky Community, and per Texas HB 2439 / SB 1090, lighting ordinance enforceability is limited. The 3000K-max recommendation in this document is professional best practice and Site Plan review norm, not a current Austin code requirement at every site. Verify zoning-specific requirements at Site Plan review for 207 E St Elmo Rd.`
`- **Smart glass cost data** ($75–150/SF) reflects industry ranges from BuiltWorlds reporting (40–50% premium over standard curtain wall) and aggregated dealer pricing; project-specific quotes from View and SageGlass field engineering may differ materially based on IGU spec, shape, control system, and quantity.`
`- **Cost ranges are 2026 Austin estimates** synthesized from EB3 Construction's restaurant build-out data, contractor surveys, and product MSRPs at the time of writing. Final pricing is project-specific; treat these as planning ranges, not bids.`
`- **Toast's published network requirements** are accurate as cited but Toast updates them periodically; verify against the current Toast Network Requirements document at install time. The Toast 192.168.192.0/24 default, 5GHz-only WiFi, and dedicated VLAN guidance are stable, but firmware version requirements change.`
`- **Meyer UP-4slim datasheet variations**: Meyer publishes both an older datasheet citing 85Hz–18kHz / 112dB and a newer one citing 65Hz–18kHz / 116.5dB depending on test signal (M-noise vs. pink noise). The newer figures reflect the current production unit measured with M-noise; specify against the current datasheet revision.`
`- **PCI-DSS compliance** is the merchant's ongoing operational responsibility, not a one-time install. Toast's SAQ-C eligibility and the ongoing inventory/access controls described in the Toast PCI Instruction Guide must be operationalized by the manager team — this document covers the infrastructure, not the operational compliance.`
`- The **B&W AM-1 "$1,000/unit × 4 in FF&E"** figure in the brief reflects approximate retail; current pair pricing is typically $999–1,199. Confirm against the actual FF&E PO.`

`# Reference Document 7 — Domain 12: Outdoor BBQ Pit Compliance & Operations Guide`
`## Sŏn — 207 E St Elmo Rd, Austin, TX 78745`

`---`

`## TL;DR`

`- **A 4–6 foot wood/charcoal commercial BBQ pit at Sŏn is permitted by rule under TCEQ 30 TAC §106.242 (no registration, no fee), but only if it does not create a nuisance condition under 30 TAC §101.4 / Texas Health & Safety Code §382.085 — the office tenants on your campus are the single largest regulatory risk factor and dictate placement, fuel choice, and stack design more than any code citation.**`
`- **The covered-vs.-open-air decision is the master decision: putting the pit under the covered patio (weatherproof roof) triggers full NFPA 96 Chapter 14 treatment — Type I hood, dedicated grease duct, UL 300 wet-chemical suppression, makeup air, and AFD plan review identical to an indoor solid-fuel installation; placing it in the open under the trellis (no weatherproof roof) substantially reduces — but does not eliminate — the hood and duct burden, because Austin Public Health still requires an "overhead cover" at any commercial BBQ pit under DSHS retail-food guidance (Pub #23-14842).**`
`- **Sequence the work in this order: (1) lock pit location and covered/open status, (2) AFD pre-submittal meeting, (3) Austin Public Health (EHSD) plan-review consult, (4) structural/civil for pad and clearances, (5) fabricator selection from a vetted Texas commercial pit shop (Mill Scale, Moberg, Pitts & Spitts, J&R, Pitmaker, Primitive Pits), (6) building permit + trade permits, (7) installation and AFD/EHSD inspections, (8) operational training and ash/fuel SOPs.**`

`---`

`## Key Findings`

`1. **TCEQ air permitting is the easiest gate, not the hardest.** §106.242 is a "one-liner" permit by rule for food-prep equipment in eating establishments. There are no BTU or burn-rate caps in §106.242 itself, and no registration is required. The substantive constraint is the §106.4 general conditions — primarily the prohibition against creating a nuisance condition. If smoke drift to office tenants becomes a documented nuisance under TCEQ's FIDO methodology (Frequency, Intensity, Duration, Offensiveness), you lose the PBR shelter and become subject to a New Source Review (NSR) permit, which is materially more expensive and time-consuming.`

`2. **NFPA 96 Chapter 14 governs the fire-safety envelope and is binding regardless of TCEQ status.** Austin adopts the IFC, which incorporates NFPA 96 by reference for commercial cooking. Solid fuel triggers a separate, dedicated exhaust system (§14.3.3), spark arresters (§14.1.6), grease-removal devices of steel or stainless steel (§14.5.1), filters at least 4 ft above the cooking surface (§14.5.3), a fixed water-pipe system for fireboxes over 5 cu ft (§14.7.6) or a 2-A water/Class K extinguisher within 20 ft for smaller fireboxes (§14.7.8), and ash removal at least daily into a covered, noncombustible container (§14.9.5).`

`3. **The "covered patio" location triggers a Type I hood requirement; the "open trellis" likely does not — but Austin Public Health still requires overhead cover at the pit for any commercial outdoor BBQ.** The DSHS Standard Operating Procedure "Minimum Requirements for Outdoor Barbeque Pits" (Pub #23-14842, rev. 09/05/19) requires fixed food establishments to provide at minimum overhead cover, an enclosed screened shelter, and a surfaced floor (concrete/asphalt/gravel). This is enforced locally by Austin Public Health Environmental Health Services Division (EHSD).`

`4. **City of Austin adopted the 2024 technical codes effective July 10, 2025** (Ordinance 20250410-045 for the IBC; companion ordinances for the Existing Building Code, Energy Code, Plumbing Code, and Mechanical Code). The Austin Fire Code remains the IFC 2021 with local amendments (Article 7 of the Land Development Code, §25-12-173) until separately updated; AFD inspectors will reference IFC 2021 plus referenced NFPA 96 (currently 2021 edition adopted; 2024 edition pending).`

`5. **The pit itself is exempt from a building permit, but its pad, shelter, and gas/electric service are not.** Detached accessory structures under 200 sq ft are permit-exempt under Austin's adopted 2024 IBC. A 4–6 ft pit on its own pad is below this threshold, but: (a) any roof or shade structure built specifically for it, (b) any extension of the building's gas service, and (c) any electrical work for lighting/exhaust will each require trade permits through Austin Development Services Department (DSD).`

`6. **The wind at 207 E St Elmo Rd is your operational reality.** Austin's prevailing winds are south-southeast (SSE) most of the year, shifting to north in winter cold fronts. SE Austin (St Elmo industrial campus) shares this profile. A pit placed on the south or southeast side of the patio will push smoke into the building and your own dining patios. A pit placed on the north or northwest side will push smoke onto whatever sits north — including any office tenant on that side of the campus. Map adjacencies before you finalize location.`

`7. **Texas has a deep, mature commercial BBQ-pit fabricator ecosystem within 30 minutes of the site.** Mill Scale Metalworks (Lockhart), Moberg Smokers (Dripping Springs), Franklin Barbecue Pits (Austin), Cen-Tex Smokers, Pitts & Spitts (Houston), Pitmaker BBQ Pits (Houston), Primitive Pits (Georgia, but ships to Austin), and J&R Manufacturing (the only major commercial smoker maker that is both NSF-certified and UL-listed) cover the spectrum from custom artisan offsets to production NSF-listed commercial units. The owner's choice between a custom Texas-style offset (raw aesthetic, no NSF listing, AHJ-approved as a "site-built" appliance under NFPA 96 §14.9.4.3) and a listed/NSF-rated production unit (J&R Oyler, Holstein, SmokinTex commercial) is one of the most consequential decisions in the project — it changes the permit pathway.`

`## Details`

`### A. Permits and Regulatory`

`#### A1. TCEQ 30 TAC §106.242 — Food Preparation PBR`

`Equipment used in eating establishments to prepare food for human consumption is permitted by rule under §106.242. This is a "one-liner" PBR per TCEQ's Recordkeeping One-Liners list — no registration, no fee, no proactive recordkeeping beyond demonstrating compliance on request. Two related PBRs may apply depending on how the unit is described in your fabricator's documentation:`

`- **§106.243 (Smokehouses)** caps qualifying units at 100 sq ft maximum horizontal inside cross-sectional area. A 4–6 ft commercial BBQ pit is well below this threshold (a 6-ft × 3-ft pit is 18 sq ft).`
`- **§106.244 (Ovens, Barbecue Pits, and Cookers)** is the most directly applicable — it permits by rule "ovens, mixers, blenders, barbecue pits, and cookers if the products are edible and intended for human consumption." Also a one-liner.`

`**The substantive limit is 30 TAC §106.4 (General Requirements for Permits by Rule)**, which requires:`
`- The facility cannot exceed certain de minimis emission thresholds (25 tpy NOx, 25 tpy VOC, 25 tpy CO, 25 tpy SO2, 25 tpy PM10 — a single restaurant pit is far below all of these).`
`- The facility cannot create a "nuisance condition" as defined by Texas Health & Safety Code §382.085(a) (interference with the normal use and enjoyment of property).`
`- All emissions must comply with applicable rules, including those related to opacity and visible emissions.`

`**What it means for Sŏn:** Under normal operating conditions, the pit qualifies for §106.242/§106.244 by rule. The owner does not file anything with TCEQ. The qualification is jeopardized only if a documented nuisance complaint from an adjacent office tenant is sustained under TCEQ's Odor Complaint Investigation Procedures (FIDO methodology). If TCEQ confirms a nuisance, the agency can (a) require corrective controls, (b) assess penalties, or (c) in the most extreme case, require the operator to obtain a New Source Review (NSR) air permit under 30 TAC Chapter 116. NSR permits for a barbecue pit are unusual but not unheard of — they typically arise after enforcement and involve formal emissions modeling, control technology demonstrations, and public notice.`

`**Practical takeaway:** Treat §106.242 as a default authorization that depends on you keeping the pit's smoke from being a documented nuisance. Don't volunteer information to TCEQ; do build your operation so that no neighbor has cause to file an odor log.`

`#### A2. City of Austin Building Permit through DSD`

`The pit unit itself is portable equipment (skid-mounted or trailer-mounted), and a freestanding equipment installation does not in itself require a building permit. However, the following ancillary scopes will trigger DSD permit review:`

`- **Concrete pad or foundation extension:** A new isolated footing or slab extension to support a 4,000–6,000 lb skid-mounted pit triggers either a building permit (if the slab is structural) or, more commonly, is included as a deferred submittal under the existing tenant improvement (TI) permit for the patio buildout.`
`- **Shade/shelter structure built specifically for the pit:** A new accessory structure ≥200 sq ft, ≥15 ft tall, or attached to the building requires a building permit. A trellis or shed kept under 200 sq ft, ≤15 ft, freestanding, no plumbing, no electrical, and not in a flood hazard area is exempt. A roof to satisfy DSHS overhead-cover requirements should be sized to clear this exemption if possible.`
`- **Gas line extension to the patio for a gas-assist ignition:** Plumbing trade permit through DSD plus AFD review of IFGC compliance.`
`- **Electrical service** for hood lights, exhaust fan, GFCI receptacles, and patio lighting: electrical trade permit.`

`Austin currently enforces the **2024 International Building Code as locally amended (Ordinance 20250410-045, effective July 10, 2025)**, the 2024 Uniform Mechanical Code (Ordinance 20250410-044), the 2024 Uniform Plumbing Code (Ordinance 20250410-042), and the 2021 International Fire Code with local amendments (Article 7 of City Code Chapter 25-12). Confirm the IFC edition that applies at the time of permit submission — Austin's IFC update is on a separate cycle.`

`The Austin Building Criteria Manual, Section 2 (Food Establishments) provides Austin-specific design criteria that DSD plan reviewers will reference.`

`#### A3. Austin Fire Department (AFD) Plan Review`

`AFD reviews any commercial cooking installation for compliance with the adopted IFC and referenced standards (NFPA 96, NFPA 17A, NFPA 13, NFPA 10). For an outdoor commercial BBQ pit, AFD plan reviewers will look for:`

`1. **Site plan with dimensioned clearances** to all combustible construction, property lines, building openings (doors, windows, fresh-air intakes), egress paths, and adjacent tenants.`
`2. **NFPA 96 Chapter 14 conformance** — listed or AHJ-approved appliance, separate exhaust system if hooded, spark arresters, fire suppression sized for solid-fuel fire load.`
`3. **Fuel storage location and quantity** with NFPA 96 §14.9 separation, suppression, and noncombustible enclosure where required.`
`4. **Ash management protocol** — designated noncombustible covered container, designated cool-down area away from combustibles.`
`5. **Documentation of the appliance's listing or "site-built" approval submission** under NFPA 96 §14.9.4.`

`**Most common AFD citations on outdoor commercial BBQ in Austin:**`
`- Fuel pile within 3 ft of the firebox (§14.9.1).`
`- Missing or improperly sized water-pipe system / fire extinguisher (§14.7).`
`- Ash storage in combustible container or within combustible area.`
`- Pit located too close to combustible eaves, soffits, or wood trellis members.`
`- Spark arrester missing or improper.`
`- Fire-suppression coverage gap if hooded — most UL 300 systems were designed for indoor fryers/charbroilers, and solid-fuel coverage requires a system listed for that fuel.`

``Schedule a **pre-submittal meeting with AFD's Fire Prevention / Plan Review Section** (`fireprevention@austintexas.gov`) before fabrication. This is free, lasts 30–45 minutes, and saves weeks of redlines.``

`#### A4. Austin Public Health (APH/EHSD) — Retail Food Plan Review`

`The relevant authority is **Austin Public Health Environmental Health Services Division (EHSD)** at 1520 Rutherford Ln, Austin TX 78754. Their Plan Review Desk (512-974-3325 or main line 512-978-0300) reviews all food establishment build-outs and significant remodels under Texas Food Establishment Rules (TFER, 25 TAC Chapter 228, which incorporates the 2017 FDA Food Code by reference) and Austin/Travis County local food code.`

`Adding an outdoor BBQ pit to an already-permitted food establishment is treated as a **plan-review modification**, not a separate permit. EHSD will look for:`

`- **Compliance with DSHS Pub #23-14842 ("Minimum Requirements for Outdoor Barbeque Pits", rev. 09/05/19)** — overhead cover, enclosed screened shelter (where preparation occurs at the pit), surfaced floor (concrete preferred).`
`- **Handwashing facility within reach** — handwash sink within 25 ft of any food-preparation activity at the pit, with hot and cold water under pressure, soap, paper towels.`
`- **Food protection from overhead contamination** — the pit's smoke stack and any combustion residue/condensate cannot drip onto food contact surfaces; food covers, lid timing protocols, and overhead cleanability matter.`
`- **Pest control** at fuel storage — wood and charcoal stockpiles attract rodents and insects; storage must be off the ground, in a managed enclosure, with rotation.`
`- **Food-contact surfaces (grates, cutting boards, holding pans)** of NSF-listed or AHJ-approved materials. Bare carbon steel is acceptable for the cooking chamber (industry standard), but grates that contact food must be either stainless steel or seasoned cast iron consistent with TFER §228.66.`
`- **Adequate lighting** at the pit (10 foot-candles minimum on food-prep surfaces under TFER 6-303).`
`- **Drainage** — the surfaced floor must drain away from the food-handling areas; no standing water, no contamination of grease drainage.`

`**No new "outdoor pit permit" exists** — it is a modification to your existing Food Enterprise permit. EHSD plan review fee is set by the Austin/Travis County fee schedule (current as of October 1, 2025).`

`#### A5. Covered vs. Open-Air — The Master Decision`

`NFPA 96 §1.1.1 states the standard applies to ventilation control and fire protection of commercial cooking operations within buildings. NFPA 96 Chapter 14 (solid-fuel cooking) is invoked whenever solid-fuel equipment is "served by a hood and duct system" (§14.3.3). The interpretive question is whether your patio's overhead structure constitutes a "roofed enclosure" that captures effluent and therefore demands a hood.`

`**Three placement scenarios at Sŏn:**`

`| Placement | NFPA 96 Treatment | Practical Implications |`
`|---|---|---|`
`| **Open trellis (pergola with open beams above; effluent rises freely to atmosphere)** | Generally outside NFPA 96 §1.1.1 / §14.3 hood-mandate scope. NFPA 96 still governs grease, fuel storage, and spark arresters in §14.5–14.9 by reference and by AFD interpretation. Listed appliance not required, but AHJ approval still required for site-built unit (§14.9.4.3). | Lowest-cost path. Still requires DSHS overhead cover, surfaced floor, fuel storage controls, ash management, and AFD clearances. AFD inspector retains discretion to require a partial hood/duct if smoke drift is observed. |`
`| **Covered patio (weatherproof roof; effluent captured under roofing)** | Within NFPA 96 §1.1.1 — full Chapter 14 applies. Type I hood, dedicated grease duct, UL 300 wet-chemical fire suppression listed for solid fuel, spark arrester ahead of the grease filter, makeup air, exhaust fan listed under UL 762 / UL 705 SC. | Highest cost (hood + duct + fan + suppression + makeup air = roughly $40–80K of equipment plus structural and electrical). Cleanest regulatory story; quietest neighbor relations because effluent is captured and exhausted vertically above the roofline. |`
`| **Enclosed uncovered patio (walls but no roof)** | Treated like open-air for hood mandate; treated like enclosed for clearance to combustibles. AFD may require additional separation distances and combustion-air analysis. | Mid-cost. Risk: walls can trap smoke and create localized nuisance for diners; requires careful airflow design. |`

`**Recommendation:** Place the pit in the **open trellis area or in the enclosed uncovered patio**, not under the covered patio roof. The cost and complexity differential is large enough that the pit should drive the layout, not the layout drive the pit.`

`#### A6. TCEQ and Local Smoke / Air Quality Treatment`

`There is no Austin city ordinance specifically targeting commercial BBQ smoke. Open burning is prohibited in Austin, but commercial cooking on a barbecue pit is explicitly excepted under the IFC's definition of "open burning" (an outdoor fire contained in "an incinerator, outdoor fireplace, portable outdoor fireplace, barbeque grill or barbeque pit" is not open burning). The relevant nuisance pathway is therefore **TCEQ's nuisance authority under Texas Health & Safety Code §382.085(a)** plus the §106.4 general conditions on your PBR. TCEQ regional investigators (Region 11, Austin) evaluate complaints using the FIDO chart described in TCEQ's Odor Complaint Investigation Procedures. A confirmed nuisance violation (frequency × intensity × duration × offensiveness above the threshold for the relevant offensiveness category) can lead to corrective orders, penalties, and loss of PBR shelter.`

`In a multi-tenant office campus, also consider **landlord lease provisions** — most commercial leases include "nuisance" clauses that the landlord can enforce independent of any regulatory action. Read your lease for smoke, odor, and operating-hours language before pit placement is finalized.`
