`### B. NFPA 96 Outdoor Cooking — Specifics`

`#### B1. Chapter 14 Requirements That Apply Outdoors`

`NFPA 96 Chapter 14 (Solid Fuel Cooking) is written assuming an indoor or hooded installation but applies to outdoor cooking when (a) the operation is under a roofed enclosure or (b) the AHJ extends Chapter 14 by interpretation. Key provisions that apply regardless of whether a hood is required:`

`- **§14.1.6** — Spark arresters to prevent airborne sparks/embers from passing into ducts (or, in the open case, to prevent embers from reaching combustible structures).`
`- **§14.5.1** — Grease removal devices of steel or stainless steel (or approved for solid fuel).`
`- **§14.5.2** — Spark arrester ahead of the grease removal device.`
`- **§14.5.3** — Filters minimum 4 ft above cooking surface.`
`- **§14.7.6** — Solid fuel appliances with fireboxes exceeding 5 cu ft must be provided with a fixed water-pipe system with a hose, equipped with adjustable nozzle and capable of reaching the firebox.`
`- **§14.7.8** — Appliances with fireboxes ≤5 cu ft must have at least a listed 2-A water spray extinguisher or a 1.6-gal Class K wet chemical extinguisher within 20 ft.`
`- **§14.9.1** — Solid fuel cooking appliances must be installed on noncombustible floors that extend at least 3 ft in all directions (unless listed for less).`
`- **§14.9.2** — Fuel storage requirements (see §B6 below).`
`- **§14.9.4.1–.3** — Listing or AHJ approval for the appliance itself.`
`- **§14.9.5** — Ash removal at least daily; ash container must be noncombustible, covered, dedicated to that purpose, easy to handle, and always covered when transported.`

`**A 4–6 ft commercial pit's firebox is typically 2–4 cu ft** for a smaller offset, and 4–6+ cu ft for larger pits — confirm with your fabricator. If your firebox is ≥5 cu ft, plan on the §14.7.6 fixed water pipe (essentially a permanently plumbed hose bib with a stored hose within reach of the firebox).`

`#### B2. Hood, Grease Duct, and Exhaust Fan — When and What`

`If the pit is sited under a weatherproof covered roof or under a soffit that captures effluent:`

`- **Type I hood listed under UL 710** sized to overhang the cooking surface adequately (typically 6 in. on all open sides for a wall-canopy hood; more for solid-fuel given the vertical plume).`
`- **Dedicated grease duct** per NFPA 96 Chapter 7 — minimum 0.054-in. carbon steel or 0.043-in. stainless steel, fully welded, with cleanouts on each floor and at each change of direction. Solid-fuel duct must be **separate from any other exhaust system** (§14.3.3).`
`- **Spark arrester** ahead of grease filters (§14.5.2) — typically a stainless mesh screen rated for 1/4-inch maximum opening, recognized in the field as a diamond-pattern grate.`
`- **Exhaust fan listed under UL 762 and meeting UL 705 Supplement SC** for restaurant exhaust appliances on solid-fuel applications.`
`- **Makeup air** balanced per Mechanical Code; for an open patio installation, ambient air typically counts, but the AHJ may require directed makeup air for hooded installations.`
`- **UL 300 fire suppression listed for solid-fuel cooking** — note that not all UL 300 systems carry solid-fuel listings; this is a specific sub-listing your fire-protection contractor must confirm.`

`**Cross-reference:** This domain ties tightly to **Reference Document 1 (Solid Fuel Exhaust Ventilation Compliance Guide)** and **Reference Document 2 (Fire Suppression & Fire Alarm Compliance Guide)**. If the pit is hooded, those two documents govern the hood, duct, fan, and suppression scope and should be re-read in their entirety before vendor selection.`

`#### B3. Clearances`

`NFPA 96 §4.2 establishes baseline clearances for hoods, ducts, and grease-removal devices to combustibles (18 in.), limited combustibles (3 in.), and noncombustibles (0 in.). For the appliance itself, clearances are governed by the appliance listing, AHJ approval, and NFPA 96 §14.4 (location and application restrictions). In the absence of a listing, AFD will typically require:`

`- **Minimum 36 in. (3 ft) clearance** from any combustible wall, post, or trellis member, increasing to 48 in. or more for a wood-fueled pit at full burn.`
`- **Minimum 10 ft horizontal separation** from any building opening (per IFC 308 analogues) and from any combustible structure overhead.`
`- **Documented site plan** showing pit location, dimensions, all clearances called out, and overhead structure indicated.`

`Use these clearance numbers to test your three patio zones against the candidate pit footprints. A 6-ft pit with skid extensions, fuel staging, and ash drop zone wants roughly a **12 ft × 18 ft working envelope** with 3 ft clear behind and on the firebox side.`

`### C. Construction`

`#### C1. Pad, Foundation, and Structural Considerations`

`Commercial offset smokers on skids are heavy. Reference weights:`
`- **500-gallon offset** (3 ft × 7 ft cooking chamber, typical Mill Scale/Moberg construction): roughly **2,500–3,500 lbs** depending on steel thickness (1/4 in. vs. 5/16 in. wall).`
`- **1,000-gallon offset** (3.5 ft × 16 ft chamber, 1,000-gallon decommissioned propane tank base): **4,000–6,000 lbs** (J&R 1000-gallon offset is published at 6,000 lbs).`
`- **A purpose-built 4–6 ft commercial barbecue pit with insulated firebox** in steel: typically **1,800–4,000 lbs**.`
`- **Brick/masonry built-in pit**: significantly heavier (5,000–10,000+ lbs) and requires structural review for any existing slab.`

`The existing patio slab at 207 E St Elmo Rd was poured for general patio loading (typically 50 psf live load). A 4,000-lb pit on a 4 ft × 6 ft footprint imposes **roughly 165 psf** — within typical slab design but worth confirming. **Have a Texas-licensed structural engineer review the slab** before placing the pit. Cost is typically $1,500–$3,500 for a site visit, calculations, and a sealed letter — cheap insurance against future cracking, settlement, or differential movement under the pit.`

`If the slab is undersized, the standard remedy is an isolated footing extension: a 6 in. thick reinforced pad poured on prepared subgrade, isolated from the existing slab with an expansion joint. The pad should extend at least 3 ft beyond the appliance footprint (NFPA 96 §14.9.1.4) in noncombustible material.`

`#### C2. Fuel Storage (NFPA 96 §14.9 / §14.9.2)`

`- Fuel **shall not** be stored in the path of the ash removal route (§14.9.1.6).`
`- Where fuel is stored in the same building as the appliance, it must be in an enclosure with walls/floor/ceiling of noncombustible construction extending at least 3 ft past the outside fuel dimensions, and that enclosure must have automatic sprinkler protection.`
`- For an outdoor installation, the fuel pile must be **at least 8 ft** from the appliance per general fire-safety practice (and AHJ direction), under noncombustible cover protecting from precipitation, with managed rotation to prevent infestation.`
`- If the fuel pile **exceeds 5 cu ft**, sprinkler protection is required; if ≤5 cu ft, a 2-A or Class K extinguisher within 20 ft is acceptable (§14.9.2.8).`

`For Sŏn doing dinner service 5 nights per week at a Korean-Texas fine-dining concept, expect daily fuel use of:`
`- **Texas BBQ low-and-slow (overnight smokes):** 30–60 lbs of post oak per long cook; 1/4 to 1/2 cord weekly during peak.`
`- **Korean tabletop direct grilling:** charcoal binchotan or hardwood lump at 5–15 lbs per service.`

`Plan for a **dedicated fuel storage shed** or covered rack with 1/2 to 1 cord of seasoned post oak rotation, plus 50–100 lbs of charcoal on hand. Locate at least 8 ft from the pit, on the leeward side relative to summer SSE winds (so smoke from the pit doesn't drift over the fuel pile and the staff handling it).`

`#### C3. Grease Drainage`

`NFPA 96 §14.5.1 requires steel or stainless-steel grease removal devices in the hood path (if hooded). The pit itself produces grease drippings into the cook chamber, which most commercial pits route via a **drip line and ball valve** to an external drip pan or grease-collection vessel. For Sŏn:`

`- **The pit's drip pan is not directly connected to the building grease interceptor.** Outdoor pit drippings are typically managed manually — drip pan emptied into a sealed grease container, hauled to the rendering/recycling vendor.`
`- **Austin Water Industrial Waste division** does not require an outdoor pit to be plumbed to the GI provided the operator does not pour pit grease into building drains. Document this in your operations SOP.`
`- **Where the pit is hooded** (covered patio scenario), the hood and duct must comply with the grease-collection requirements in **Reference Document 3 (Plumbing/Grease Interceptor Compliance Guide)** — specifically, any hood-side grease should be collected at the hood termination and not allowed to enter the storm drain.`
`- **Surface drainage** at the pit area should slope away from food-handling zones and toward a permeable area or a sand/oil interceptor if the local Austin Water reviewer requires it.`

`#### C4. Gas-Assist Ignition`

`If you want gas-assisted ignition (a gas burner that lights the wood/charcoal load and shuts off):`

`- Adds **plumbing trade permit** for the gas line extension to the patio.`
`- Adds **AFD review of IFGC compliance** — Austin enforces the International Fuel Gas Code via the adopted Mechanical Code.`
`- Requires an **emergency shutoff valve** at the pit and a **flexible connector listed for outdoor commercial use**.`
`- For LP-gas (propane) cylinders, requires submission of an **Outdoor LP-Gas Installation Request to AFD** for any commercial container; AFD processes commercial requests within 14 days. Single LP container >2,000 gal water capacity or aggregate >4,000 gal triggers full plan submittal.`
`- **NFPA 96 §14.7.11** — when a solid-fuel appliance also has gas (or electric/oil) auxiliary fuel for ignition or supplemental heat, the auxiliary fuel must shut off automatically upon activation of the fire-extinguishing system.`

`For a 4–6 ft pit, a **natural gas line** (preferred over LP for commercial reliability and cost) sized for a 100,000–150,000 BTU/hr ignition burner is typical. Run the line during the patio TI buildout — running gas later means tearing up patio surfaces.`

`### D. Operations`

`#### D1. Smoke Management for a Multi-Tenant Campus`

`Austin's prevailing wind at 207 E St Elmo Rd is **south-southeast (SSE)** the majority of the year (April through November), shifting to **north** during winter cold-front passages (November through March). This is the single most actionable piece of operational information for your pit placement.`

`**Decisions driven by wind direction:**`

`1. **Pit position.** Place the pit on the **north or northeast edge** of the patio so that summer SSE winds carry smoke away from the dining patios and toward the office buildings only if those buildings are *south* of you. If the office tenants are north of the patio, you have a structural problem — summer winds will push smoke directly at them. Map the campus carefully before placing the pit.`
`2. **Stack height.** A taller stack (10–14 ft above the cooking chamber) lifts effluent above the recirculation zone of nearby buildings, dramatically reducing ground-level concentrations. Most production commercial offsets have a 6–8 ft stack from grade; a custom build can specify taller.`
`3. **Pollution Control Unit (PCU)** — for the covered/hooded scenario, an electrostatic precipitator (ESP) with HEPA after-filter can remove visible smoke from the exhaust before it reaches atmosphere. Cost is significant ($30–60K+ for solid-fuel-rated units per Halton/CaptiveAire), but for a fine-dining Korean-Texas hybrid in a mixed-use campus, this may be the only path to neighbor harmony.`
`4. **Operating hours.** Most office tenants leave by 6 PM. Dinner service starts at 5–6 PM. Heavy smoke production should align with after-hours, when offices are empty. Long Texas-style overnight smokes (8 PM – 4 AM) are friendlier to neighbors than hot-and-fast cooks during business hours.`

`**Fuel choice and smoke profile:**`

`- **Post oak** (the Texas BBQ standard) — clean, mild smoke; lowest-particulate hardwood available locally.`
`- **Pecan, mesquite, hickory** — heavier, more aromatic, more particulate; use sparingly.`
`- **Lump charcoal (binchotan or domestic hardwood lump)** — lowest smoke output of all solid fuels; ideal for Korean tabletop grilling.`
`- **Briquettes** — higher ash, more smoke, more odor; avoid for fine dining.`
`- **Wood pellets** (in a pellet smoker) — very low visible smoke; cleaner profile but loses some of the Texas BBQ character; not appropriate for an offset.`

`**A nuisance complaint sequence to anticipate:** an office tenant smells smoke → emails you or the landlord → if not resolved, files a TCEQ complaint → TCEQ Region 11 investigator visits → conducts a FIDO assessment → may issue a nuisance violation. Best defense: establish a written **good-neighbor protocol** with the landlord, exchange contact info with adjacent tenants, respond to complaints within 24 hours, document operational changes.`

`#### D2. Health Code Compliance for Outdoor Cooking`

`Integration with the existing Sŏn Food Enterprise permit requires:`

`- **Modification submittal to APH/EHSD** with revised plans showing the outdoor pit, handwash station, food storage, ash management area, and fuel storage.`
`- **Handwash station within 25 ft** of the pit if any food preparation (slicing, plating, seasoning) occurs at the pit. If only cooking occurs at the pit and prep happens inside, this distance is more flexible.`
`- **Overhead cover** at the pit per DSHS Pub #23-14842.`
`- **Surfaced floor** (concrete preferred) under and around the pit.`
`- **Lighting** ≥10 foot-candles on food-preparation surfaces, ≥20 foot-candles for cleaning.`
`- **Pest control** — covered, off-the-ground fuel storage; managed wood rotation; rodent program documenting the patio area.`
`- **Food protection** — covered hot-holding for finished products; protection from overhead drip and ash; no exposed food when the firebox is being loaded or ash is being removed.`

`The Health Inspector's pre-opening inspection for the modified permit will verify all of the above plus standard food-safety items. Schedule the inspection through the My Health Department customer portal at least 7 days before opening.`

`#### D3. Operational Fuel and Ash Management`

`- **Daily ash removal** from the cook chamber and firebox is required (NFPA 96 §14.9.5.1 and Austin Public Health pest/sanitation expectations).`
`- **Ash cooling protocol:** after removal, ash goes into a **dedicated, covered, noncombustible (steel) container** and sits in a designated cool-down area for **at least 72 hours** before disposal. Some AHJs accept shorter periods if ash is verified cool by IR thermometer (<150°F). This is not stated as 72 hours in NFPA 96 — the standard says ash containers "shall always be covered when being moved through the premises" and ash must be removed daily. The 72-hour cool-down is industry best practice and consistent with TCEQ guidance treating hot ash as a fire hazard until fully cooled.`
`- **Ash disposal:** when fully cooled, ash is non-hazardous solid waste under Texas standards and can be disposed in regular waste streams. Some operators repurpose hardwood ash for landscaping or distribute to staff for home use. Do not dispose of hot ash in dumpsters — this is the leading cause of dumpster fires at restaurants and a frequent AFD citation.`
`- **Document the ash protocol** in writing as part of your operations manual; AFD inspectors will ask to see it during annual inspection.`

`Fuel inventory management: **first-in, first-out rotation** of seasoned wood (12–18 months minimum seasoning for post oak); covered storage with airflow; off-the-ground pallets; weekly rodent inspection by your pest-control vendor.`

`### E. Vendor Evaluation`

`#### E1. Fifteen Questions to Ask a Pit Fabricator`

`1. **Construction materials:** What gauge steel for the cook chamber (5/16 in. and 1/4 in. are standard for commercial), the firebox (typically 1/4 in. or insulated double-wall), and the stack?`
`2. **Firebox volume:** What is the internal volume of the firebox in cubic feet? (Drives NFPA 96 §14.7.6/14.7.8 fire-protection requirements.)`
`3. **Cooking surface materials:** Stainless steel grates (preferred for Korean tableside service and food-contact compliance), expanded metal carbon steel grates (Texas BBQ standard), or both? Cast iron for galbi presentation?`
`4. **Airflow control:** What dampers, baffles, and tuning plates are included? Can the pit run both at 225–275°F low-and-slow and at 500–600°F direct-grilling temperatures?`
`5. **Weight (dry):** What is the shipped weight, and what is the recommended foundation?`
`6. **Listings:** Is the pit UL-listed for commercial use? NSF-certified? Or is it to be approved as "site-built" under NFPA 96 §14.9.4.3?`
`7. **Documentation provided for permitting:** Will you provide cut sheets, weight calculations, listing certificates (if any), installation instructions, and operations/maintenance manuals stamped or signed for AFD and EHSD review?`
`8. **Grease management:** How does the pit handle grease drippings? Is there an integral drip pan with ball valve drain to an external collection vessel? Can the grease tray be removed and washed in a 3-compartment sink?`
`9. **Health code surface cleanability:** Are food-contact surfaces NSF-listed materials (304 stainless or seasoned cast iron)? Are non-food-contact surfaces smooth, durable, and easily cleanable?`
`10. **Ash cleanout:** Is there a dedicated ash drawer or cleanout door? Is it sized for shovel access? Is it positioned away from the firebox loading door?`
`11. **Heat distribution:** What is the temperature differential across the cooking grate at 250°F? (The industry benchmark for premium commercial pits is ±5°F across the grate, achieved through computational fluid dynamics design — Mill Scale, Moberg, and Primitive Pits all publish this number.)`
`12. **Lead time:** What is the realistic delivery date? (Premium custom builders run 12–24 months; production builders run 6–12 weeks.)`
`13. **Commercial Texas/Austin experience:** Have you supplied pits to permitted commercial restaurants in Austin or Travis County in the last 3 years? Can you provide three references?`
`14. **Service and warranty:** What is the warranty period? Who handles service calls in Austin? What is your typical response time for an emergency repair (e.g., a stuck damper or warped door) during a service week?`
`15. **Korean BBQ/Texas BBQ hybrid configuration:** Have you built a pit that supports both tableside Korean direct grilling and Texas-style offset smoking on the same unit? If so, what was the design solution?`

`#### E2. Design Specifications for the Korean BBQ + Texas BBQ Hybrid Vision`

`Jun's culinary direction wants both:`
`- **Texas-style low-and-slow:** offset firebox feeding indirect heat into a horizontal cook chamber; 200–275°F; brisket, beef ribs, pork shoulder over 8–14 hours.`
`- **Korean galbi/bulgogi/samgyeopsal:** higher-heat direct grilling, 500–700°F radiant from charcoal/binchotan, with an adjustable grate height for fine control.`

`Design features that enable both on a single 4–6 ft commercial pit:`

`1. **Offset configuration with reverse-flow plate** — gives clean indirect heat for low-and-slow.`
`2. **Auxiliary direct-fire grilling section** (often a separate firebox door / grilling well at one end) where charcoal can be staged for Korean direct grilling. Mill Scale and Moberg both build pits with optional asado/yakitori-style direct grilling sections.`
`3. **Adjustable cooking grates** — height adjustable in 2–3 inch increments, ideally on a crank or pulley, to control distance from the heat source for galbi (close, hot, fast char) vs. brisket (further, cooler, slow render).`
`4. **Grate material flexibility** — interchangeable stainless-steel grates for tableside-style proteins and seasoned heavy-gauge carbon steel grates for Texas brisket. Cast iron is acceptable for galbi presentation but requires careful seasoning and hand-cleaning.`
`5. **Firebox airflow control** — both an intake damper (for low-and-slow) and a high-flow grilling damper (for direct grilling); two distinct burning modes with mechanical changeover.`
`6. **Charcoal staging** — a charcoal chimney/lighting station integrated into the pit footprint or immediately adjacent, with safe staging for hot lump charcoal during service.`

`The conversation with the fabricator should center on **dual-mode airflow and a configurable cooking surface**. Mill Scale, Moberg, Pitts & Spitts, and Pitmaker are all capable of this kind of custom build; the production NSF-listed brands (J&R, Holstein, SmokinTex) are typically less flexible because their designs are optimized for one mode (usually low-and-slow smoking).`

`#### E3. Red Flags in a Vendor Proposal`

`- **No NSF listing on food-contact surfaces** and **no AHJ-approved site-built submission** prepared in advance — this is fixable but it's the fabricator's job, not yours.`
`- **No grease management system** drawn into the cut sheet.`
`- **No documentation prepared** for AFD or EHSD plan review; fabricator says "you'll handle that" — wrong answer for a commercial install.`
`- **Undersized firebox airflow** for the cooking volume planned (a 4-ft chamber that runs at 175°F max because the firebox can't draft is a useless commercial pit).`
`- **No ash cleanout provision** other than reaching into the firebox — a daily-use restaurant pit needs a dedicated ash drawer.`
`- **No structural engineering review** of the supporting pad ("just put it on your slab").`
`- **No spark arrester** included or specified.`
`- **No fire-extinguishing equipment** specified or sized to NFPA 96 §14.7.`
`- **No reference list** of commercial restaurants currently using the fabricator's pits.`
`- **Lead time discrepancy** — quoted lead time materially shorter than industry norms is suspicious; quoted lead time materially longer than 18 months may not align with your opening schedule.`
`- **Vague paint/finish spec** — Texas BBQ shops typically leave the cook chamber raw or high-temp painted; the fabricator should specify which.`
`- **Stack with no spark arrester or rain cap** — both AFD and your roof will care.`

`---`

`### F. 12-Step Recommended Sequencing Plan`

`1. **Decide covered vs. open-air pit location** within the three patio zones. Walk the campus, map adjacencies (especially north-side office tenants), and pick the placement that puts smoke into the prevailing wind path away from neighbors and dining patios.`
``2. **Schedule a pre-submittal meeting with AFD Fire Prevention** (`fireprevention@austintexas.gov`). Bring a draft site plan, conceptual pit cut sheet, and the placement decision. Get AFD to weigh in on hood requirement and clearance interpretation before you commit dollars.``
`3. **Schedule an EHSD plan-review consult** (Plan Review Desk 512-974-3325). Confirm the path is a permit modification rather than a new permit, and identify any handwash, lighting, and overhead-cover requirements specific to your patio configuration.`
`4. **Engage a Texas-licensed structural engineer** to evaluate the existing patio slab and design any required pad extension or isolated footing. Cost: $1,500–$3,500. Deliverable: sealed letter or stamped detail.`
`5. **Engage a civil/MEP design team** (likely your existing project architect plus a kitchen-design consultant or commercial cooking specialist) to draft hood/duct/suppression design if you go covered, or fuel-storage and clearance details if you go open-air. Cross-reference Reference Documents 1, 2, and 3.`
`6. **Solicit fabricator proposals** from three to four shortlisted vendors (recommended: Mill Scale, Moberg, Pitts & Spitts, Pitmaker, J&R if you want NSF). Use the 15 questions in §E1 above. Score on listing/documentation, lead time, design fit for the Korean-Texas hybrid vision, and references.`
`7. **Select fabricator and place order.** Lock the firebox volume, materials, listings, weight, and accessories in the purchase order, including the documentation deliverables for permitting.`
`8. **Submit building permit and trade permits to DSD** through the AB+C portal (Austin Build + Connect). Include: site plan, structural pad detail, electrical for lighting/exhaust/GFCI, plumbing for handwash sink and any gas-assist line, mechanical for any hood/duct/fan. Cross-reference your fabricator's documentation.`
`9. **AFD plan review concurrent with DSD permit review.** Clearances, fuel storage, ash management plan, fire-extinguishing equipment, spark arrester, water-pipe system if firebox >5 cu ft.`
`10. **APH/EHSD plan-review modification submittal.** Revised floor plan, handwash station, food protection details, fuel storage, lighting, and surfaced flooring under the pit.`
`11. **Construct the pad and shelter, install the pit, complete trade work, and request inspections.** Sequence: structural inspection → electrical rough → plumbing rough → final building → AFD final → EHSD pre-opening inspection.`
`12. **Operationalize:** train staff on fuel handling, ignition protocol, ash-removal SOP (cool-down container, 72-hour protocol, disposal), grease drainage and disposal, fire-extinguisher use, and the good-neighbor smoke-management protocol. Document everything in the operations manual; keep it onsite for AFD and EHSD inspectors.`

`---`

`## Recommendations`

`**Stage 1 — Lock the placement decision (next 30 days).** The single most important action is finalizing where the pit goes within the trellis / covered / enclosed-uncovered zones. Walk the site with a compass and the campus tenant map. Confirm office tenant locations relative to the prevailing SSE summer wind. **Recommended position:** the **enclosed uncovered patio** if it is on the north or east edge of the building footprint, or the **trellis area** if positioning there pushes smoke south or southwest into open campus space rather than into adjacent office windows. Avoid the covered patio unless you are committed to a Type I hood + ESP installation budget of $40–80K beyond the pit itself. *Threshold that changes the recommendation:* if the only non-conflicting location is under the covered roof, do the hood and PCU rather than re-fight the placement.`

`**Stage 2 — Run the AFD and EHSD pre-submittal meetings before fabricator selection (next 60 days).** Both meetings are free and substantively change what you order from the fabricator. Bring concept drawings, not finished plans. Get the AHJ to commit, in writing if possible, to whether the placement requires a hood, what fire-extinguishing scope is required, what overhead-cover form satisfies DSHS, and whether the existing food permit can be modified rather than reissued. *Threshold:* if AFD insists on a Type I hood for any of your candidate locations, return to Stage 1 and re-evaluate.`

`**Stage 3 — Choose the fabricator on documentation quality, not just craft (months 3–4).** A pit with stunning welds and no NFPA 96 §14.9.4.3 site-built submittal package is a 6-month permit fight. A pit from J&R with full UL/NSF listings and weaker aesthetic warmth is a 6-week permit story. For Sŏn — a **fine dining concept** integrating Texas BBQ with Korean technique — the right answer is most likely a custom build from Mill Scale, Moberg, or Pitmaker that includes (a) a complete site-built approval package prepared by the fabricator, (b) NSF-grade stainless cooking grates, and (c) the dual-mode firebox/direct-grill configuration from §E2. Budget $25K–$60K for the pit alone depending on size and configuration; add 30–50% for installation, pad, shelter, and trade work. *Threshold:* if no premium custom shop can deliver within your opening window, default to a J&R Oyler or similar NSF/UL-listed production smoker and pair it with a separate Korean tabletop grilling station.`

`**Stage 4 — Build the smoke-management and good-neighbor protocol into the lease and operations from day one (concurrent with construction).** Exchange contact information with the landlord and adjacent tenants. Establish a written 24-hour response protocol for any odor or smoke complaint. Consider a **stack height of at least 12 ft above grade and 2 ft above the highest point within 10 ft horizontally** (NFPA 211 chimney guidance applied by analogy). For a fine-dining operation, pre-budget for an **electrostatic precipitator (ESP)** retrofit if early operational data shows nuisance risk — this is far cheaper to design in than retrofit. *Threshold:* if a single TCEQ-investigated nuisance complaint is sustained against the operation in the first 12 months, immediately install an ESP or PCU regardless of cost — losing the §106.242 PBR shelter is more expensive than any control technology.`

`**Stage 5 — Do not skip the structural engineer.** $3,000 of engineering up front prevents $50,000 of slab repair and operational disruption two years in. *Threshold:* if the engineer recommends a new isolated footing rather than reliance on the existing slab, do the footing.`

`---`

`## Caveats`

`- **Code edition timing:** As of May 2026, Austin enforces the 2024 IBC, IECC, IPMC, IWUIC, ISPSC, UPC, and UMC effective July 10, 2025. The Austin Fire Code remains based on the **2021 IFC with local amendments** at the time this guide was prepared. Confirm the exact IFC edition in force at the time of permit submission directly with AFD; the city sometimes updates these on a separate cycle. NFPA 96 is referenced through the IFC and through Austin's Mechanical Code; the 2021 NFPA 96 edition is most commonly enforced, with the 2024 edition pending. Chapter and section numbers cited in this document reflect the 2021 NFPA 96 numbering (Chapter 14 = solid fuel cooking); in the 2024 edition some content moves to Chapter 15. Verify section numbers in the edition cited on your permit set.`

`- **TCEQ §106.242 limits:** This PBR is a "one-liner" with no specific BTU or burn-rate cap in the rule itself. Some online guidance materials reference burn-rate caps from §106.243 (smokehouses) or §106.244 (ovens, cookers, barbecue pits) that don't exist or are not currently in force. Always confirm the specific §106.4 general conditions and the most current TCEQ checklist for the relevant PBR before relying on it.`

`- **NSF listing for site-built BBQ pits is rare.** Most Texas custom offset smokers are not NSF-listed as a complete unit. The path to compliance is typically (a) NSF-listed food-contact components (304 stainless steel grates) plus (b) AHJ approval of the appliance under NFPA 96 §14.9.4.3 ("site-built solid-fuel cooking appliances shall be submitted for approval to the AHJ before being considered for installation"). Do not reject a fabricator because the complete pit lacks an NSF listing — the question is whether the food-contact surfaces meet TFER §228.66 standards and whether the fabricator will prepare the §14.9.4.3 submittal.`

`- **Wind patterns are a long-term average, not a daily forecast.** Austin's winds vary dramatically day-to-day. Cold-front passages bring strong north winds; spring storms bring east winds; summer high-pressure ridges give long stretches of consistent SSE. Operational smoke management requires daily judgment and, ideally, a wind sensor and smoke-camera at the pit so the pitmaster can see effluent dispersion in real time. Treat the SSE prevailing-wind information as the planning baseline, not a guarantee.`

`- **The DSHS Standard Operating Procedure on outdoor BBQ pits (Pub #23-14842) was last revised September 5, 2019.** Austin Public Health applies it as guidance. Confirm with EHSD that the current 2026 plan-review interpretation has not shifted; the document is non-regulatory in form but is treated as binding by DSHS field inspectors.`

`- **Lease and landlord constraints often supersede regulatory minimums.** A multi-tenant office campus lease frequently has nuisance, hours-of-operation, exterior modification, and smoke-related provisions independent of TCEQ or city authority. The landlord can shut down a compliant operation if the lease language permits. **Read the lease carefully before any pit work begins**, and if necessary negotiate a written acknowledgment of the BBQ pit operation and smoke as part of the project record.`

`- **The §106.242 PBR is only as good as your operations.** A pit that runs cleanly and serves a small fine-dining dinner service rarely produces complaints. A pit that runs sloppily, with green wood or smoldering charcoal that produces visible plumes during business hours, will produce complaints quickly. The compliance posture depends on operations, not on paper.`

`---`

`## Cross-References to Prior Documents in the Series`

`- **Reference Document 1 (Solid Fuel Exhaust Ventilation):** governs hood, grease duct, exhaust fan, makeup air for any covered/hooded pit configuration. The decision in this domain (covered vs. open-air) determines whether Document 1's full scope applies.`
`- **Reference Document 2 (Fire Suppression & Fire Alarm):** governs UL 300 wet-chemical suppression sized and listed for solid-fuel cooking, integration with the building fire alarm, and Class K extinguisher requirements. Cross-reference §B1 of this document for the specific NFPA 96 §14.7 requirements that bridge this domain to Document 2.`
`- **Reference Document 3 (Plumbing/Grease Interceptor/Roof Penetrations):** governs hood-side grease collection, building grease interceptor sizing, and roof penetration treatment for any hood/duct termination above the covered patio. The pit's drip-pan grease management described in §C3 of this document is specifically *outside* the GI scope but must be coordinated with Document 3 to avoid stray drainage into building sanitary or storm systems.`
`- **Reference Document 4 (Flooring):** the surfaced floor under the pit per DSHS Pub #23-14842 should be specified consistent with Document 4's exterior patio flooring scope. Concrete is the standard.`
`- **Reference Document 5 (HVAC/Walk-In/Acoustics):** if a hood is required, makeup air and acoustic treatment of the exhaust fan tie back to Document 5. For an open-air pit, the smoke effects on patio HVAC outdoor-air intakes need attention — verify outdoor-air intake locations against the pit position to avoid pulling smoke into the dining room.`
`- **Reference Document 6 (Electrical/Low-Voltage/Lighting/Audio):** the patio lighting at the pit, GFCI receptacles for any hood lights or fans, and any low-voltage thermometer/probe wiring tie to Document 6. Coordinate the pit's electrical loads (typically 20–40A for a hooded installation; minimal for an open-air installation) with the patio panel sizing.`

`The thread that binds this domain to Documents 1, 2, and 3 is **NFPA 96 solid-fuel cooking**: the same standard governs the hood and duct (Document 1), the suppression system (Document 2), grease collection (Document 3), and the appliance and fuel handling (this document, Domain 12). Read NFPA 96 Chapters 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, and 14 together; the standard is intended to be applied as a whole, not in fragments.`

pages.name: Sŏn Restaurant Bar Build-Out: Millwork, Masonry, and LHI Budget Guide
pages.content:
`# Sŏn — Millwork, Casework, Masonry & Custom Bar Build-Out Knowledge Base`
`**207 E St Elmo Rd, Austin, TX | Korean Fine Dining | Owner Reference Document, Series Supplement**`

`---`

`## TL;DR`

`- **The bar, server station, and coffee station are 80% LHI scope and 20% FF&E by spend, but you must categorize line-by-line — the plywood substrate is LHI, the stone slab is FF&E; the 220V circuit is LHI, the espresso machine is FF&E; the cement-board backer is LHI, the stone veneer is debatable (treat as LHI for budget integrity). Get this split right before you start signing contracts because miscategorization is the single biggest source of double-billed scope and missed line items in fine dining build-outs.**`
`- **For Sŏn's positioning, the right specification is AWI Premium-grade custom millwork from a QCP-licensed shop, marine-grade plywood throughout, a quartzite or honed limestone bar top with a continuous welded steel angle supporting the 24-inch guest overhang, and a thin-set natural stone veneer bar face that visually echoes the fireplace. Anything less — particleboard cores, paint-grade carpenter work, decorative brackets instead of structural steel — will fail visibly and structurally inside three years in a working bar environment.**`
`- **Total realistic LHI budget for the three custom elements at mid-range: roughly $35,000–$45,000; with FF&E (stone slab, espresso machine, undercounter refrigeration, POS hardware, finished casework panels) layered on top, the all-in invested capital for the bar room and server station lands between $95,000 and $145,000 in Austin 2025–2026 pricing. The biggest swing factor is the back bar treatment (open shelving with integrated lighting versus closed lit cabinetry can move that bar room number $15,000+ on its own).**`

`---`

`## Key Findings`

`1. **The bar room is the most coordination-dense 174 SF in the entire restaurant.** Stone fabricator, GC, plumber, electrician, lighting designer, and millworker all converge on one room, and the order of operations matters. Sequence locks must be agreed in writing before demo: GC frames bar box → plumber sets stub-outs and electrician runs rough → GC installs plywood substrate → stone fabricator templates → millworker installs back bar and bar face millwork → stone install → final connections.`
`2. **Plumbing stub-out misalignment is the single most expensive avoidable mistake.** Landlord-provided stub-outs for cold water and drain are typically located based on the previous tenant's layout or a generic plumbing plan. They must be re-located (or extended) to match the actual ice bin, hand sink, glass washer, and espresso machine positions on Sŏn's bar drawings before walls close. Re-locating a stub-out after drywall is up adds $500–$2,000 per fixture; re-locating after the bar box is built can run $3,000–$5,000.`
`3. **The 24-inch guest overhang is structurally non-trivial.** Natural stone slabs cannot cantilever beyond 8–12 inches without engineered support. A 24-inch overhang on quartzite at this length requires a continuous steel angle (commonly 2×2 or 3×3 structural angle, ¼"–⅜" wall) welded to the bar frame and running the full 18 LF — not decorative corbels and not surface-mounted brackets. This is LHI scope and must be specified by the stone fabricator before the bar frame is built.`
`4. **Premium-grade AWI millwork costs 20–35% more than custom-grade and is the correct specification for a fine dining bar.** The cost premium buys tighter tolerances (touch-ups indistinguishable at 24 inches versus 48 inches), grain-matched veneers, marine-grade plywood substrate throughout, and a documented QCP audit trail that gives you recourse if something fails.`
`5. **The Toast Flex is a 14-inch terminal with a base/stand, not a small handheld unit.** The exact dimensions referenced in the project brief (8.5" × 8.5" × 1.75") more closely match a Toast Tap on-counter card reader (≈8 × 8 × 5 cm per Toast's spec guide) than the Flex terminal itself. The Flex requires a different recess strategy — typically a flush-mounted swivel base rather than a flat upward-facing screen recess. Confirm exact hardware with Toast and the millworker before cutout dimensions are finalized.`
`6. **A 2-group La Marzocco Linea PB requires a 20A 240V circuit (NEMA L6-20), not 30A — but spec-ing 30A is the right call for future-proofing.** Actual published Linea PB 2-group dimensions are 28" W × 23" D × 21" H (71 × 59 × 53.3 cm), 135 lbs, not the figures listed in the brief. A 30A circuit gives Sŏn the option to upgrade to a 3-group (L6-30) without rewiring.`

`---`

`## Details`

`---`

`### SECTION 1 — LHI vs. FF&E Split`

`**The principle:** Leasehold Improvements (LHI) are the things that physically remain with the building when you walk away — framing, substrate, masonry, electrical and plumbing rough-in, blocking, drywall. FF&E (Furniture, Fixtures & Equipment) are the things you could, in theory, unbolt and take with you — the stone slab, the casework panels, the espresso machine, the refrigerator, the POS terminals. The split matters for three reasons: (a) your contractor bills LHI on the GC contract and FF&E typically through separate vendor POs; (b) your investor/lender capital budget separates depreciable improvements from owned equipment; (c) lease language often defines which line items qualify for the landlord's TI allowance and which do not.`

`**The grey zone:** Built-in casework (the back bar millwork, the server station cabinet, the coffee station counter section) is technically FF&E but is often categorized as LHI when it is permanently affixed and built-to-fit. For Sŏn's purposes, treat permanently-fixed millwork as LHI for accounting clarity, and treat removable equipment (machines, refrigerators, POS hardware, stone slabs that could in theory be lifted) as FF&E. Document the split in the project budget and confirm it with both the GC and the accountant before the LOI to the contractor is signed.`

`#### Component-by-component split`

`**Bar (18 LF, 174 SF room):**`
`| Component | Scope |`
`|---|---|`
`| Bar box framing (steel or dimensional lumber) | LHI |`
`| Plywood substrate under bar top (¾" marine-grade) | LHI |`
`| Cement board backer behind stone face | LHI |`
`| Continuous steel angle for overhang support | LHI |`
`| Plumbing rough-in connections from stub-out | LHI |`
`| Electrical rough-in (circuits, conduit, boxes) | LHI |`
`| Bar face stone veneer or wood slat panel (installed) | LHI (treat as building finish) |`
`| Bar face millwork panels (if removable wood slat) | FF&E if panelized; LHI if fully integrated |`
`| Stone bar top slab | FF&E |`
`| Back bar shelving / casework | FF&E (built-in millwork) |`
`| Back bar integrated LED strips and drivers | LHI (if hardwired into Lutron HWQS) |`
`| Bar stools | FF&E |`

`**Server Station:**`
`| Component | Scope |`
`|---|---|`
`| Wall niche framing / partition framing | LHI |`
`| Blocking for casework mounting | LHI |`
`| Electrical rough-in (POS low-voltage, lighting, refrigeration circuit) | LHI |`
`| Drywall and finish | LHI |`
`| Casework (drawers, doors, dividers) | FF&E |`
`| POS terminal and cable management box | FF&E |`
`| Undercounter refrigerator (Perlick HC24RS or True equivalent) | FF&E |`
`| Steel/aluminum POS recess frame | FF&E (delivered as part of casework package) |`

`**Coffee Station:**`
`| Component | Scope |`
`|---|---|`
`| 220V/30A dedicated circuit, conduit, breaker, outlet | LHI |`
`| Cold water supply line tie-in from stub-out | LHI |`
`| Drain tie-in | LHI |`
`| Plywood substrate at machine location (¾" marine grade) | LHI |`
`| Counter casework panels | FF&E (millwork package) |`
`| Recessed grinder platform millwork | FF&E |`
`| La Marzocco Linea PB espresso machine | FF&E |`
`| Espresso grinder(s) (Mahlkönig, Mazzer, etc.) | FF&E |`
`| Pentair Everpure or equivalent water filtration | FF&E |`
`| Shut-off valve, supply line from filter to machine | LHI (final connection labor) |`

`#### Landlord stub-outs — what "provided" actually means`

`The lease describes "plumbing stub-outs provided" for the bar room, typically meaning the landlord delivers cold water supply (usually ½" or ¾" copper) and a sanitary drain (1½" or 2" PVC) terminating in capped pipes a few inches above floor or behind the back bar wall, in pre-defined locations from the building's previous fit-out or generic plan.`

`Tenant scope from there:`
`- **Quarter-turn ball valve / shut-off valve** at each connection point (mandatory; allows individual fixture isolation): $30–$80 per valve in materials, installed labor brings total to **$150–$300 per shut-off**.`
`- **Supply line from valve to fixture** (braided stainless flex line, copper, or PEX): $20–$80 per line in materials, $80–$200 installed.`
`- **P-trap and drain tie-in** at each waste fixture (ice bin drain, hand sink, glass wash, espresso drain): $80–$200 in materials, $200–$500 per fixture installed including venting.`
`- **Order-of-magnitude per connection in a restaurant context: $500–$2,000 fully connected**, varying with run length, accessibility under the bar box, and whether the plumber needs to re-route or extend the stub-out.`

`**The critical owner question:** Where exactly does each stub-out land relative to the equipment that will eventually use it? Have the GC's plumber walk the bar with the bar designer and the Toast/POS layout in hand, mark each stub-out location, and compare to where the ice bin, three-compartment wash sink, hand sink, glass washer, and espresso machine will actually sit. Misalignment found at this stage is cheap to fix; misalignment found after the bar frame is built is not.`

`#### Electrical — from panel to fixture`

`Landlord delivers a panel with capacity. Tenant scope:`
`- **220V/240V dedicated circuit to espresso machine**: NEMA L6-20 receptacle (20A) for a 2-group Linea PB; NEMA L6-30 (30A) if upgrading to 3-group. Wire run typically 30–50 LF from sub-panel; #10 AWG copper for 30A, #12 for 20A. **Installed cost: $800–$1,500.** Spec the 30A circuit even if running a 2-group machine — the cost delta is minimal and it preserves upgrade flexibility.`
`- **Dedicated 20A 120V circuits** for: undercounter refrigeration (×2 — bar and server station), grinders (×1–2), bar lighting (Lutron-controlled), POS terminal low-voltage power, blender or smoothie equipment if present. Budget $300–$600 per circuit installed.`
`- **Lutron HQWS (HomeWorks QS) or equivalent control system coordination**: the bar's integrated back bar LED lighting, undercabinet lighting, and any decorative cove lighting must run through dimmable LED drivers compatible with Lutron's load schedule. The electrician needs the lighting designer's load schedule and dimmer locations before rough-in.`

`**What the electrician needs from the millworker before rough-in:**`
`1. Exact location of each junction box and outlet relative to the millwork (knockouts in the back bar wall for LED driver, outlets behind the espresso machine, low-voltage chase to POS recess).`
`2. Cable-management chase locations (typically a 2"–4" diameter grommet through the millwork down to a junction box).`
`3. Confirmation of LED strip wattage, dimming protocol (0–10V, ELV, or DALI), and driver location so the electrician can verify circuit sizing and switch leg routing.`
`4. Whether the POS terminal is hardwired or plug-in (Toast Flex is plug-in via a single power adapter; the Flex's base typically needs a 120V receptacle within 6" of the unit).`

`---`

`### SECTION 2 — Millwork and Casework`

`#### Who builds what`

`There are four distinct vendor categories that will all claim they can build a fine dining bar. They are not equivalent.`

`- **Custom millworker (small artisan shop):** Excellent for one-off pieces, may lack commercial volume capacity, often does not carry AWI certification, and may not have experience coordinating with stone fabricators or producing AWI-compliant shop drawings. Right for a residence; risky for a restaurant on a deadline.`
`- **Commercial AWI-certified casework manufacturer (QCP-licensed shop):** Operates against published quality standards, produces AWI-grade shop drawings, carries general liability insurance with tenant-improvement language, and has the production capacity to deliver an 18 LF bar package on a 10–14 week lead time. **This is the right vendor category for Sŏn.**`
`- **Restaurant equipment company that "does millwork":** Stainless steel BOH specialists who occasionally fabricate FOH wood casework. Excellent for the back-of-house cooks line and stainless server station BOH components; rarely the right choice for a fine dining FOH bar where finish quality is paramount.`
`- **GC's finish carpenter:** Builds trim, handles install, may build the bar box framing. Should not be building the finished bar face millwork or back bar casework on a project at Sŏn's positioning. The materials, joinery standards, and finish techniques are different categories of work.`

`**What to look for when vetting an AWI-certified shop:**`
`- Active QCP license and a QCP project audit certificate from a recently completed project.`
`- A portfolio of restaurant millwork in the Austin / Texas market within the last three years.`
`- Marine-grade plywood as the standard substrate, not particleboard or MDF (MDF is fine for non-water-exposed cabinetry but should not be used in the bar core).`
`- In-house shop drawing capability with an AutoCAD or Cabinet Vision/Microvellum workflow.`
`- Field measurement and stone-fabricator coordination as a documented part of their process.`
`- Commercial general liability insurance ≥ $2M aggregate, with the owner namable as additional insured during installation.`

`#### AWI quality grades`

`AWI publishes three quality grades. They differ primarily in tolerances, materials selection, and the strictness of finish quality.`

`- **Economy Grade:** Minimum acceptable quality. Reserved for back-of-house, mechanical rooms, anywhere the woodwork is not in public view. Not eligible for QCP certification. **Not appropriate for any FOH element at Sŏn.**`
`- **Custom Grade:** AWI's default. The sensible specification for most commercial woodwork — schools, hospitals, mid-tier restaurants. Touch-ups and repairs must be indistinguishable at 48 inches. Adequate but not exceptional.`
`- **Premium Grade:** Highest grade. Specified for the most visible architectural features — executive offices, courtrooms, high-end hospitality. Touch-ups must be indistinguishable at 24 inches. Grain matching, veneer selection, and joinery tolerances are significantly tighter. **The right specification for Sŏn's bar, server station, and coffee station — these are the three most-touched and most-photographed surfaces in the restaurant.**`

`**Cost premium of Premium over Custom:** typically 20–35% on the millwork line item. For an 18 LF back bar at $800–$1,400/LF Premium, the same package at Custom grade would run roughly $640–$1,050/LF. The premium buys roughly 5–7% of the total bar room invested capital — a low cost for the most visible feature in the room.`

`#### Bar top material — 18 LF run`

`| Material | Installed Cost / LF | Pros | Cons | Sŏn Fit |`
`|---|---|---|---|---|`
`| Natural stone slab (quartzite, marble, honed limestone) | **$250–$450/LF** | Beauty, character, gravitas, visual continuity with fireplace | Sealing required, etch risk from citrus and acid (esp. marble), seam management required | **Recommended (quartzite preferred for durability)** |`
`| Engineered quartz (Caesarstone, Silestone, Cambria) | $180–$320/LF | Non-porous, no sealing, consistent pattern, durable | Lacks veining variation and natural depth | Acceptable backup if owner prioritizes maintenance over character |`
`| Concrete (cast or poured-in-place) | $200–$350/LF | Custom texture, custom color, modern aesthetic | Cracking risk at joints, requires sealing, expansion control needed | Possible but reads more industrial than Sŏn's warm aesthetic |`
`| Hardwood + bar-top epoxy | $150–$280/LF | Warmth, tactile quality, organic | Moisture swelling/warping in cocktail bar environment, edge wear | Wrong for cocktail bar; right for a wine-focused dry bar |`
`| Stainless steel | $120–$200/LF | Indestructible, sanitary | Cold, industrial; wrong aesthetic | **No** — appropriate only for BOH |`

`**Recommendation for Sŏn: quartzite, honed finish.** Quartzite gives marble's visual depth with significantly better durability and lower etch risk from acid. Honed (matte) finish reads more refined and Korean-aesthetic-aligned than polished, and hides minor surface wear better. Budget $300–$400/LF installed for a mid-tier quartzite (Classic White, Super White, or similar), $400–$500+/LF if Sŏn lands on a more exotic slab (Taj Mahal, Calacatta-pattern quartzite). For an 18 LF run that's roughly **$5,400–$9,000 in stone fabrication and install** — FF&E line.`

`#### Seam strategy on 18 LF`

`Standard quartzite slabs are 9'–10' long by ~5.5' wide. An 18 LF run will require **two slabs, one seam.** Three rules:`

`1. **Place the seam strategically.** Ideal locations: directly above the service well or ice bin, at a defined material break (e.g., where the stone bar top meets the recessed coffee station counter), or at the back bar's corner. **Never** in the center of an open guest section — the seam will catch every glass slide and become the surface's most-noticed feature.`
`2. **Book-match if visually appropriate.** Two consecutive slabs from the same quarry block, opened like a book, give continuous veining across the seam. Specify book-matched slabs with the stone yard at selection (MS International Austin, Stratus Surfaces, Architectural Tile & Stone, or CRS Marble & Granite are the primary slab houses in Austin).`
`3. **Lock the seam location before bar design is finalized.** The bar millworker, stone fabricator, and bar designer should be in the same room (or at minimum a shared markup PDF) when seam location is decided. Once placed, the seam location dictates the bar box framing module.`

`**Slab selection process:** Owner should physically visit the slab house and tag specific slabs. Photograph slab IDs and bundle numbers. Insist that the fabricator photographs the slab in the order it will be installed and that the installation order matches the visual flow you approved.`

`#### Overhang support`

`Per the design intent, **24" guest overhang on the front of the bar.** Natural stone in 3cm thickness can cantilever 8"–12" unsupported; 24" requires engineered support.`

`**The correct solution:** continuous structural steel angle (typically 2×2 or 3×3, ¼"–⅜" wall) welded to the bar's steel frame and running the full 18 LF, with the angle's horizontal leg supporting the underside of the stone overhang and the vertical leg bolted/welded to the bar frame. This distributes point loads (someone leaning hard on the bar edge) across the full length of the angle, eliminating local stress concentrations. Bracket spacing on the vertical (mounting) leg is typically 16"–24" on center.`

`The continuous angle is **LHI scope** (welded into the bar frame before substrate goes on). The welder fabricates it; the GC installs it; the stone fabricator confirms specifications during templating. Budget **$1,200–$3,800** for the steel angle work depending on welder rates and design complexity.`

`Hidden-bracket systems and decorative corbels are inadequate for 24" overhang in commercial use. Do not let the GC value-engineer this down.`

`#### Back bar — 18 LF, floor-to-ceiling`

`This is the highest-impact aesthetic surface in the restaurant after the fireplace. Three primary treatment options (or hybrid):`

`1. **Open floating shelves with integrated lit display.** Visually lightest, shows off bottles and glassware. Requires 2× wall blocking at every shelf bracket location (specified in the LHI table before drywall closes — minimum 2× framing 16" o.c. behind the entire shelf elevation; for shelves carrying >40 lbs add additional blocking). LED strip channels routed into the underside of each shelf with the driver concealed behind the back bar wall or in an adjacent cabinet. **Premium millwork cost: ~$700–$1,100/LF installed.**`
`2. **Integrated lit display cabinets (closed glass front).** Mid-weight visually. Better for protecting expensive bottles from dust and (for some Korean spirits) light. Heavier electrical scope — each cabinet needs its own LED channel and driver. **Premium millwork cost: ~$1,000–$1,400/LF installed.**`
`3. **Closed cabinetry (back-bar storage).** Heaviest visually. Hides bottles. Inappropriate for the front-and-center back bar of a fine-dining cocktail program. Use only for portions concealed behind the espresso station or against a service-only wall.`
`4. **Hybrid (recommended for Sŏn):** Open floating shelves at eye level (visible to guests) with grain-matched stained hardwood and integrated LED cove lighting; closed cabinetry below counter and above eye level for bulk storage; stone shelves at the bottom display row to tie back to the bar top material.`

`**Total Premium AWI back bar millwork (18 LF, floor-to-ceiling, hybrid): $14,400–$25,200** for the millwork scope alone, plus separate budget for the LED system, driver, dimmable Lutron load, glass shelves (if specified), and stone accent shelves.`

`**LED integration specifics for the millworker:**`
`- Specify **LED strip in aluminum channel with frosted diffuser** — never bare strip on a refined back bar. Bare strip shows hot spots; channel diffusion gives a uniform glow.`
`- **Driver location:** in a dedicated, ventilated, accessible cabinet (not buried in a sealed cavity). Drivers fail more often than the LED itself; access for replacement is mandatory.`
`- **Dimming protocol:** confirm the lighting designer's specification — typically ELV (electronic low voltage) or 0–10V dimming. Lutron HomeWorks QS supports both with the appropriate dimmer module. Specify a dimmable driver matched to the chosen protocol.`
`- **Color temperature:** 2700K for fine dining warmth; 3000K is the maximum acceptable. Anything cooler will read as institutional.`
`- **Cove vs. visible:** for refined aesthetics, conceal the LED strip in a routed cove on the underside of each shelf so only the wash of light is visible. Surface-mounted strips are acceptable for budget back bars but do not match Sŏn's positioning.`

`#### Bar face — 18 LF × ~42" tall`

`Total bar face surface: ~63 SF.`

`| Material | Installed Cost / SF | Note |`
`|---|---|---|`
`| Thin-set natural stone veneer (matching fireplace) | $25–$55 | **First choice** — visual continuity with fireplace |`
`| Large-format porcelain tile (≥24"×24") | $20–$45 | Cleaner lines, modern; less warmth |`
`| Wood slat panel (vertical or horizontal slats) | $30–$60 | Warm; contributes acoustic absorption; reads as Korean/Japanese aesthetic |`
`| Resin / decorative panel | $45–$80 | High style cost; specialty fabrication |`
`| Venetian or limewash plaster | $18–$35 | Soft, matte, very Texas-aesthetic-aligned |`

`**Recommendation for Sŏn: split decision.**`
`- The **front face of the bar** (visible to seated guests and the dining room beyond) should be **natural stone veneer that visually echoes the fireplace** — this creates the single most powerful design tie between the two stone elements in the room.`
`- The **lower kick / toe-kick recess** can be matte black painted MDF or stained wood — it disappears in shadow.`
`- Optionally consider a **wood slat accent** on the side return faces (the ends of the bar) to introduce warmth at the visual transitions.`

`**Bar face substrate buildup (LHI):**`
`- ¾" plywood on the framed bar box (LHI)`
`- ½" cement board over plywood for stone or tile veneer (LHI; required by tile/stone manufacturers for adhesion and crack isolation)`
`- Thin-set mortar bed and stone veneer (this is the line item that crosses LHI/FF&E — treat the installed veneer as LHI for budget integrity since it's permanently bonded to the building)`
`- Final sealing with penetrating stone sealer (LHI; final finishing labor)`

`For a wood slat panel: the substrate is ¾" plywood, then a felt or acoustic backer, then the slat panel mounted on furring strips. No cement board needed.`

`### SECTION 3 — Server Station`

`#### POS terminal flush/recessed installation`

`**IMPORTANT — verify hardware before millworker begins:** The dimensions referenced in the project brief (8.5" × 8.5" × 1.75") more closely match Toast's Tap on-counter card reader (≈8 × 8 × 5 cm per Toast's published spec guide) than the **Toast Flex 14**, which is a 14-inch full-screen terminal mounted on a stand or wall-mount arm. Confirm with Toast and the millworker which exact unit is being deployed before locking cutout dimensions.`

`Two likely configurations:`
`1. **Toast Flex 14 on a low-profile wedge stand**, semi-recessed into the counter (the stand base nests into a routed pocket so the screen sits at a comfortable upward viewing angle without floating high above the counter). This is Toast's recommended configuration for "server stations, bar backs, and expediting areas" per their hardware documentation.`
`2. **Toast Tap (8 × 8 cm) flush-mounted face-up** for tap-only payment processing, with a separate Flex screen positioned vertically. This is closer to the brief's described 8.5" × 8.5" footprint.`

`**What a flush/recessed installation requires either way:**`
`- A **steel or aluminum recess frame** (custom-fabricated, typically powder-coated black) built into the countertop with a precise cutout sized to the terminal base or stand foot, with a 1/16" tolerance shadow gap.`
`- **Cable management chase:** 2"–3" diameter grommet down through the casework to a low-voltage box mounted inside the cabinet. Power cable, ethernet (if not WiFi), and any peripheral cables route through this chase.`
`- **Ventilation clearance:** Toast requires minimum 1" clearance on sides and back of the unit per their installation guide. The millworker must build this into the recess design.`
`- **Locking tray or retention bracket:** secures the terminal against accidental displacement or theft. Toast offers proprietary locking accessories; specify these in the FF&E procurement.`

`**The millworker must receive the exact POS hardware spec sheet (model number, base dimensions, cable exit location, mounting hole pattern) before finalizing cutout dimensions.** This is the single most common field coordination failure in restaurant millwork — the casework is built to a generic POS dimension and the actual hardware doesn't fit. Get the spec sheet from Toast in writing, share it with the millworker, and have the millworker confirm receipt before shop drawings are issued.`

`#### Server station placement`

`In a ~988 SF dining room, **one well-positioned server station serves up to ~60 covers**. Two stations (at opposite ends of the dining room, or one mid-room concealed behind a partition wall) serve more, and reduce server walk distance during peak service.`

`Industry standard: a server should not walk more than ~30 feet to reach a station mid-service. Placement criteria:`
`- **~15 step radius from all dining tables** — measure on the floor plan.`
`- **Shielded from direct sightlines from primary dining tables** — achieved by placing in a hallway knee wall, behind a partition, in a service corridor, or as a recessed niche in a non-primary wall.`
`- **Adequate circulation space** so two servers can access simultaneously without crowding (minimum 4' clear floor in front of the station).`
`- **Path to kitchen** — should not require crossing a primary dining sightline.`

`For Sŏn's layout (vaulted ceiling dining room with the bar room separated), the right move is likely a single concealed station in a service-side niche or behind a floor-to-ceiling partition wall, with the bar serving as effective overflow for cocktail and coffee orders.`

`#### Contents required for a 50–75 cover dinner service`

`Designed to support full service without trips to the kitchen:`
`- **Flatware storage:** 6–8 organized drawer dividers covering forks, knives, dessert spoons, soup spoons, teaspoons, chopsticks (Korean fine dining requires both Western and Korean utensil sets — plan for 8 dividers minimum).`
`- **Napkin/linen storage:** pullout shelf or large drawer, depth ~22", typically two stacks of folded napkins.`
`- **Check presenters:** 30–50 count storage, vertical slot.`
`- **Pen caddy, straw/pick caddy, salt cellar, citrus tray.**`
`- **Undercounter refrigeration or wine storage (FF&E):** 24" Perlick HC24RS commercial undercounter refrigerator (~5.3 cu ft, all-stainless interior, R600a refrigerant, NSF-rated) at **$2,500–$4,500**, or a 15" wine refrigerator at $1,500–$3,000. True 24" commercial undercounter is the equivalent and often slightly less expensive.`
`- **POS terminal** as described above.`

`**Casework dimensions:**`
`- Width: 36"–48" (48" preferred — gives room for refrigerator + drawer stack + POS)`
`- Depth: 24" (standard counter depth)`
`- Counter height: 36" (standard)`
`- Overhead storage: optional cabinet up to 72"–84" total height, only if the station is in a niche where overhead doesn't read as intrusive`

`### SECTION 4 — Coffee Station`

`#### Machine and equipment specifications — verified`

`**La Marzocco Linea PB 2-group (per La Marzocco's published spec sheet):**`
`- **Width: 28" (71 cm)**`
`- **Depth: 23" (59 cm)**`
`- **Height: 21" (53.3 cm)**`
`- **Weight: 135 lbs (61 kg)**`
`- Voltage: 200V single phase, 220V single/3-phase, or 380V 3-phase (US installations: 220V/240V single phase)`
`- Wattage: 3,750–5,450W`
`- Power: NEMA L6-20 plug, **20A dedicated circuit** for 2-group (3-group requires NEMA L6-30, 30A)`

`**3-group Linea PB:** 38" W × 23" D × 21" H, 170 lbs, NEMA L6-30 / 30A circuit.`

`**The brief's listed dimensions (32.3" × 20.3" × 18.5") do not match the current published Linea PB spec sheet.** Use the verified dimensions above in the millwork shop drawings.`

`**Spec the 30A circuit even if installing a 2-group machine.** A 30A NEMA L6-30 circuit can power any 2-group or 3-group La Marzocco; downsizing later to a 2-group is trivial; upsizing later to a 3-group requires rewiring. Cost delta is roughly $100–$200 in wire/breaker. This is the single highest-value future-proofing decision in the coffee station scope.`

`#### Counter substrate at the machine`

`The 135 lb (or 170 lb if 3-group) machine sits in one location for the life of the bar. The substrate must be **¾" marine-grade plywood minimum (not particleboard, not MDF).** Marine-grade plywood (Douglas fir or Western larch, A-B grade, fully waterproof structural adhesive, 1/8" max core gap per APA spec) is the right substrate for any restaurant bar substrate but is non-negotiable beneath an espresso machine due to weight, heat, and inevitable water spillage.`

`#### Steam wand and overhead clearance`

`Steam wand swing radius requires **minimum 24" from the counter surface to the underside of any overhead cabinet, shelf, or pot rack.** Closer than that and the barista cannot freely position the steaming pitcher. Open above the machine is preferred at fine dining bars; if a shelf is required for cup warming, it must be at least 24" up and ideally 30"+.`

`#### Electrical and plumbing rough-in locations`

`The millworker must coordinate with the electrician and plumber on **exit/entry knockouts in the substrate**:`

`- **Power knockout:** 220V circuit terminates within 6" of the machine's power cord exit point. Cord typically exits the rear-bottom of the machine. Confirm exact cord exit location with the spec sheet; mis-located by more than 6" and the cord must run exposed across the back of the machine.`
`- **Cold water supply knockout:** within 12" of the machine's water inlet (typically at the rear-bottom). 3/8" supply line standard.`
`- **Drain knockout:** within 12" of the machine's drain outlet. 1/2" or 3/4" PVC drain to the under-counter waste line.`

`These knockouts are **drilled into the substrate before the substrate is set on the bar frame.** Re-drilling after install is possible but disruptive and risks splitting the plywood. Get the locations right the first time.`

`#### Recessed grinder platform — the refined detail`

`Off-the-shelf coffee station design puts the grinder on the same 36" counter as the machine. The result: a 14"–18" tall grinder sticks up to ~50" from the floor, dominating the visual silhouette of the bar and forcing the barista to reach high during dosing.`

`**The fine-dining detail:** Drop the grinder section of the counter 2"–3", to ~33"–34". The grinder now sits visually 2"–3" lower, the dosing cup landing is at a more ergonomic level, and the grinder reads as integrated rather than perched. Frame the recess in the bar millwork as a deliberate "station" with a slightly different finish or material edge to reinforce the intentionality.`

`This detail must be specified in the millwork shop drawings before the bar frame is built. Add to the millworker's RFI list.`

`#### Barista ergonomics and workflow within 4'–5'`

`**Counter height for tamping: 34"–35" is the consensus ergonomic range.** Standard 36" counters force shoulder-tense tamping; 32"–34" reduces shoulder fatigue and back pain over a multi-hour shift. The barista's forearm should be vertical at the moment of tamping; the elbow, shoulder, and wrist in line.`

`**Workflow sequence in 4'–5' (right-handed barista, standard left-to-right flow):**`
`1. **Grinder position** (in the recessed platform)`
`2. **Dosing/tamping zone** — 6"–10" of clear counter, with a tamping mat or built-in tamper holder`
`3. **Espresso machine** (group heads and steam wands face the barista)`
`4. **Service landing** — 8"–12" of clear counter where the finished drink lands for garnish, plating, and handoff`

`**Designing a continuous counter at 36" with a recessed grinder/tamping section at 34"–35":** the millworker creates an inset section ~14"–18" wide at the grinder/tamping zone. The transition between heights is a clean reveal (¼" hardwood return) — not a stepped riser, not a curved transition. The reveal reads as intentional architecture, not as a mistake.`

`#### Water filtration under the bar`

`**System type:** for an espresso program, a multi-stage system combining sediment filtration, carbon filtration (chlorine/taste), and either softening or reverse osmosis is standard. Pentair Everpure is the commercial-foodservice gold standard; alternatives include 3M CUNO and direct-from-La-Marzocco specified systems.`

`**Recommended for Sŏn (a fine-dining espresso program with moderate volume):** Pentair Everpure Conserv 75E (high-efficiency RO system) or an Everpure QT-style multi-cartridge system, depending on incoming Austin water hardness (test before specifying — Austin water is moderately hard and chlorinated).`

`**Dimensions to allocate in the under-counter cabinet:**`
`- Filter canister stack: 12"–14" wide × 5"–8" deep × 14"–20" tall`
`- RO storage tank (if RO): 3–5 gallons, ~10"–14" diameter, 14"–18" tall`
`- Service clearance: minimum 18" vertical clearance below the canister to allow rotating cartridges out for replacement (~2.5" minimum per Everpure documentation, plus working room)`
`- Total under-counter cabinet allocation for filtration: **roughly 18" wide × 24" deep × full cabinet height**`

`**Placement:** directly below the espresso machine for the shortest water line run. Must not be blocked by adjacent plumbing or by the espresso machine drain.`

`**Critical detail:** install a **self-closing quarter-turn ball valve** between the cold water stub-out and the filtration system inlet. The technician needs to be able to isolate the filter for cartridge changes without shutting off water to the rest of the bar.`

`### SECTION 5 — Masonry`

`#### Where masonry shows up in the bar build-out`

`1. **Bar face (highest visibility — 63 SF, 18 LF × ~42"):** thin-set stone veneer matching the fireplace stone aesthetic. **First choice for design continuity.**`
`2. **Back bar lower base or recessed shelf supports:** stone shelves or stone base course (1–3 SF each) tying the back bar visually to the bar top and bar face.`
`3. **Server station surround (optional):** if integrated into a stone-clad wall niche, the surround can be the same stone family as the fireplace.`
`4. **Stone bar top itself:** technically masonry installation by the stone fabricator.`
`5. **Coffee station counter:** if Sŏn's design extends the bar top stone through the coffee station, the stone wraps the 4'–5' coffee section.`

`**Design intent: visual continuity.** The fireplace, bar top, and bar face should read as a single material vocabulary. The bar face does not need to be the *exact same* stone as the fireplace (often impractical given that fireplace stone is often full-bed and the bar face is thin-set veneer), but should be the same family — same color palette, same texture grammar, same finish (honed, split-face, or smooth-face).`

`#### Masonry types`

`| Type | Application | Cost / SF Installed (Austin 2025–2026) |`
`|---|---|---|`
`| **Thin-set stone veneer** (¾"–1.5" thick natural stone, panels or pieces, adhered with thin-set mortar to cement board on plywood) | Bar face, server niche, back bar accents | **$25–$55** |`
`| **Cast stone** (precast architectural panels, consistent pattern) | Feature walls, columns | $35–$65 |`
`| **Large-format tile in mortar bed** (porcelain or natural stone ≥24"×24") | Bar face alternative | $20–$45 |`
`| **Full-bed masonry** (real brick or stone in mortar on structural footing) | Fireplaces, structural feature walls | Overkill for a bar face — not specified |`

`**For Sŏn's bar face, specify thin-set natural stone veneer in the same family as the fireplace, ¾"–1" thickness, with sealed thin-grout or tight-butt joints, and a penetrating stone sealer applied after install.**`

`#### Stone countertop installation — coordination sequence`

`Who does what:`

`1. **GC builds the bar frame** (welded steel box or dimensional lumber) — including the continuous steel angle for the 24" overhang.`
`2. **GC installs the plywood substrate and cement board backer** (LHI scope).`
`3. **Stone fabricator templates** — a site visit where the fabricator creates an exact profile of the counter shape, confirms seam locations, and verifies the steel support angle is in place. Templating typically uses laser measurement or rigid template stock.`
`4. **Stone fabricator cuts, finishes, edges, and seals the slab** at their shop.`
`5. **Stone fabricator installs the slab** on the substrate, with structural silicone or epoxy at support points and along the angle.`
`6. **Stone fabricator returns** for final sealing and seam fill (typically 24–48 hours after install).`

`**Total templating-to-install timeline:** typically 2–3 weeks. Plan accordingly in the construction schedule.`

`The **continuous steel angle is LHI scope** (welded into the frame by the GC's metal sub before substrate goes on). The **stone slab itself is FF&E.** This is the cleanest LHI/FF&E split in the entire project.`

`**Why the split matters:**`
`- **Investor-facing capital budget:** LHI items depreciate over the lease term; FF&E typically depreciates faster (5–7 years). Mis-categorizing changes your tax depreciation schedule.`
`- **Landlord TI allowance:** Most leases reimburse LHI but not FF&E. Mis-categorizing a $9,000 stone slab as LHI when it's FF&E means you tried to bill the landlord for something the lease excludes — and you'll lose the dispute.`
`- **Contractor billing clarity:** The GC bills LHI on the construction contract. FF&E is procured separately. Mis-categorizing creates disputes about who is responsible for damage during install, who carries warranty, and whose insurance covers field damage.`
