`Prohibits: letterforms as pattern units / 선 as pattern element / wordmark tiled at any scale / borrowed motifs or stock libraries / pattern as dominant surface / symmetry as structural default / any execution where wordmark origin is untraceable.`

`### Texture Principle`

`Texture is a material selection decision, not a design decision applied after material selection. The texture of a surface is the surface reporting what it is and how it was made.`

`Prohibits: digital grain overlays / faux letterpress, faux deboss, faux foil / artificial aging or applied patina / surfaces chosen for photogenic texture / decorative emboss/deboss / any treatment concealing the material's actual nature.`

`### Iconography System`

`Role: present, reserved — enters only where the wordmark system cannot do the work: wax seals, bag tags, embossed closures, small-format stamps, merchandise below wordmark legibility threshold.`

`Drawing approach: silhouette-first, single closed path, filled silhouette primary state. Outlined secondary state for embossing and debossing only. The cultural referent for every mark must be semantic — chosen for what it means, not for how it looks.`

`**Bird mark referent confirmed:** 원앙 (mandarin duck). Devoted partnership, mate for life. Directly connected to Jeong. Visual execution deferred.`

`Governing rules for all future marks: legible at 18mm (wax seal test) / single closed path / documented Korean cultural referent with articulable semantic weight / built on wordmark structural grid / always subordinate to the wordmark / primary state is filled silhouette.`

`Prohibits: illustrative marks requiring internal detail / minhwa, woodblock, dancheong, folk painting traditions / decorative cultural referents / multiple line weights / marks competing with wordmark / 선 as an iconographic mark / stock icon libraries.`

`---`

`## 04 — Typography`

`### Typeface System`

`**Display / Wordmark: GT Sectra Fine Book** — Grilli Type, 2013. Calligraphic and blackletter construction. Warm editorial register. Book weight only. Authored, not borrowed.`
`Prohibits: use where calligraphic construction collapses / pairing with cold modernist sans / all-caps / italic used decoratively.`

`**Body Text: GT Alpina Fine Standard** — Grilli Type, 2020. Same foundry, different register.`
`System relationship: Sectra leads and is felt. Alpina follows and is read.`

`**Korean Companion: Sandoll Myeongjo (산돌명조)** — Sandoll foundry, Seoul, est. 1984. Brush-calligraphic stroke modulation, correct construction affinity with GT Sectra Fine Book. Both faces are drawn, not engineered. One Korean typeface, all Hangul deployments, all contexts, no exceptions.`
`Prohibits: Noto Serif KR in any public-facing context / mixing Sandoll Myeongjo with any other Korean typeface on the same surface / Korean text set in a Latin typeface with partial Hangul coverage.`

`**Superseded:** Adobe Jenson Pro (display) and Cronos Pro (body) — do not appear in this system.`

`**Fallback stacks:** GT Sectra → Cormorant Garamond → Georgia. GT Alpina → Source Serif 4 → Georgia.`

`### 선 Glyph Rendering`

`The Brand Designer draws the 선 glyph at wordmark scale using Sandoll Myeongjo as stroke authority, then corrects: choseong/jongseong weight distribution, counter proportions, jungseong vertical position. Visual weight criterion: 선 reads as equivalent visual density to "Sŏn" in GT Sectra Fine Book when tested in actual lock-up at actual production scale.`

`### Typographic Hierarchy`

`| Level | Family | Subfamily | Weight | Print | Digital |`
`|---|---|---|---|---|---|`
`| Wordmark | GT Sectra | Fine | Book | Vector | Vector |`
`| Headline | GT Sectra | Display | Regular | 48–72pt | 60–96px |`
`| Section header | GT Sectra | Display | Medium | 28–36pt | 36–48px |`
`| Subhead | GT Sectra | Standard | Regular | 18–24pt | 22–30px |`
`| Eyebrow | GT Sectra | Standard | Regular UPPERCASE | 9–11pt | 11–13px |`
`| Lead | GT Alpina | Fine Standard | Light | 14–16pt | 16–20px |`
`| Body | GT Alpina | Fine Standard | Regular | 10–12pt | 14–16px |`
`| Menu descriptor | GT Alpina | Fine Standard | Regular | 9–11pt | 13–15px |`
`| Fine detail | GT Alpina | Fine Standard | Light | 7–8pt | 11–12px |`

`OpenType: GT Sectra — SMCP for initial letter contexts only / LNUM for all pricing and tabular / SS01 compact descenders in tight-leading. GT Alpina — ONUM default for body text / LNUM for pricing only / SMCP for initial letter contexts / SS03 alternate ampersand evaluated per daypart.`

`Sentence case always. UPPERCASE reserved for single-line eyebrow text only.`

`### Hangul Deployment Rules`

`Rule 1: Hangul appears when Korean script is the primary cultural signal. Romanization appears when pronunciation guidance serves the customer. Translation never appears — if a term requires translation to be used, it is not yet ready to be used publicly.`

`Rule 2: Korean terminology stands without explanation in all brand contexts from day one. No parenthetical translations, no footnotes, no italicized definitions.`

`Rule 3: Sandoll Myeongjo governs all Hangul deployments — one Korean typeface, all contexts. The 선 glyph is a drawn logotype element, not a typeface deployment.`

`Environmental scale: Sandoll Myeongjo runs 10–15% larger than paired GT Sectra for optical equivalence at viewing distance.`

`## 06 — Spatial and Environmental Design`

`### Property`

`207 E St. Elmo Rd, Austin, Texas 78745. Converted residential bungalow. 2,310 SF interior. 2,868 SF patio. Existing facade not altered.`

`### Cross-Zone Governing Principles`

`- We walk, we never point — absolute, all staff, all zones, all dayparts`
`- Net positive, net neutral, never net negative — every surface including back-of-house`
`- Aged and accumulated, not installed — the space looks more itself over time, not less`
`- No spectacle during dinner service — the room recedes so the experience comes forward`
`- Sound is removed at the source — equipment and placement decisions first, treatment second`
`- The space changes with the daypart — the room must hold the full register range`

`### Spatial Sequence`

`Nine beats. Fixed arrival sequence. Open interior paths.`

`Beat 1 — Rideshare drop-off: Designated south parking zone. Landscape and path geometry orient the customer. No signage.`

`Beat 2 — Exterior approach: Along the building facade. Landscaping density is the primary design lever. Facade not altered. No commercial hospitality interventions on the exterior.`

`Beat 3 — Entry threshold: Porch steps provide the natural 2–4 step buffer. Maître d' at the top of the steps before the customer crosses. Porch is a held space — covered, climatized, distinct floor material from both approach and interior.`

`Beat 4 — Dining room reveal: Dining room not visible from the threshold. Revealed in motion. First sightline lands on the fireplace — the room's gravitational center. Three paths simultaneously legible: bar / dining / patio. No path prescribed. Playground Philosophy held by existing floor plan geometry.`

`Beat 5 — Bar: Counter-level. Bartender always in proximity. Slightly brighter than the dining field. Fixed constraint: every dining table holds bar sightline. The bar is the hinge of the dinner-to-late-night transition.`

`Beat 6 — Patio sequence: Covered patio (1,186 RSF) primary dining patio. Trellised zone (861 RSF) most reserved — probable pyeong-sang position. Ground-level garden most permeable. Pyeong-sang gated by reservation.`

`Beat 7 — Pyeong-sang: Probable trellised zone (not confirmed — see pre-CD items). Vine structure provides privacy from above. One-directional sightline. Slowest pace, darkest zone. Preset tasting menu.`

`Beat 8 — Service threshold: Invisible. Kitchen door recessed. Buffer from existing building layout. Kitchen sounds do not cross the threshold.`

`Beat 9 — Departure: Maître d' threshold in reverse.`

`Daypart variation: Morning — exterior only, walk-up window, no customer entry to building. Dinner — full nine-beat sequence. Late night — atmospheric transformation from the bar; room becomes something rather than ends something.`

`Prescribed: rideshare drop-off → porch steps → dining room reveal → pyeong-sang (gated).`
`Held open: three paths from entry, multiple patio configurations, bar accessible at any point.`

`### Materiality Matrix`

`All material selections are governed by Jaeyeonmi. Every material has a documented aging intention.`

`## 08 — Service Model`

`### Step-Back Architecture`

`Three-phase approach: entry (attunement-triggered, not timer-triggered) / delivery (the action) / exit (clean, no manufactured closing exchange). Server holds a coverage position permitting observation without proximity. Trigger for the next approach is attunement, not a timer.`

`Floor authority: server owns the table — attunement calls, approach timing, whether a dish gets a spoken note or arrives in silence. Floor manager owns the room — coverage, pattern recognition, backs up without intercepting. Routine recovery pre-authorized. Escalation triggers: financial recovery above threshold / kitchen failure affecting multiple sections / genuine emergency.`

`Daypart coherence: behavioral logic constant across all dayparts. Expression changes; logic does not. Same foundation, four registers.`

`### Arrival Choreography`

`Host stand removed. Credenza-scale storage at threshold — functional, not institutional. SevenRooms via foldable phone, pocket-carried — no visible screen in the dining room. No tipping screen at any point.`

`Maître d' at top of porch steps. Language: "We have you" — not "Do you have a reservation." Single exchange, clean.`

`Table walk: below street pace, no narration.`

`Table arrival: no preset table. Centerpiece only — scaled for active dish placement, either removed as a deliberate choreographic beat or designed to coexist without shuffling. Maître d' seats and exits. Server's first contact: spoken only — water preference. Water returns. Service begins.`

`Daypart variation: late night — same sequence, looser register.`

`David protocol: system decision, never floor call. SevenRooms flagging, pre-service kitchen communication, pre-authorized. Never improvised.`

`Dinner-to-late-night transition: same trigger as lighting and sonic — same person, same moment. Not announced. Register loosens. Last turn table held — transition moves toward them. Nothing cleared prematurely.`

`Pyeong-sang: pre-designed, not responsive. Server is keeper-of-the-arc. Silence is the product. The walk functions as decompression. Dining room service is responsive; pyeong-sang service is pre-designed.`

`| Role | Uniform | Note |`

`| Floor manager | Business suiting, Korean fashion sensibility | Most formal |`
`| Hosts | Blazer + button-up shirt | Most considered register |`

`## 09 — Verbal Identity`

`### Voice Rules`

`**Rule 1: Copy never names its own effect.**`
`If a sentence announces what it intends to produce in the reader, it has already failed.`
`Disqualifies: "A dish that surprises you." "A moment of stillness." "The kind of meal that stays with you." Every sentence in this category.`

`**Rule 2: Every noun carries its own weight or it doesn't appear.**`
`Test: replace the noun with another from the same category. If the sentence survives unchanged, the noun is wrong.`
`Disqualifies: "The finest ingredients." "Memorable experiences." "Thoughtful details."`

`**Rule 3: The sentence ends at its last load-bearing word.**`
`Qualifiers, softeners, and echo words extend sentences past where they are done.`
`Disqualifies: any sentence ending on a softener ("gently," "carefully," "with intention").`

`**Rule 4: Implication is the customer's work.**`
`A sentence that makes the implication explicit answers a question the customer was about to ask and eliminates the inquiry.`
`Disqualifies: any sentence beginning with "because" or "which is why" that closes a loop the previous sentence had correctly left open.`

`**Rule 5: Specificity is precision, not density.**`
`A sentence is specific because it names the one thing no other sentence could name.`
`Disqualifies: any descriptor that applies equally to ten other dishes at comparable restaurants.`

`### Six Binary Tests`

`Applied in sequence. A sentence fails at the first test it doesn't pass.`

`1. Does this sentence name its own effect? → Out.`
`2. Can the primary noun be replaced by a category sibling without changing what the sentence does? → Out.`
`3. Does the sentence continue past its last load-bearing word? → Cut from there.`
`4. Does this sentence answer a question the reader hasn't yet asked? → Out.`
`5. Could this sentence appear unchanged in a competitor's copy? → Out.`
`6. Does sentence two explain sentence one? → One of them is wrong. Fix that one.`

`### Structural Patterns`

`- Sentence length is a byproduct of precision, not a target. A sentence stops when it's done.`
`- Secondary clauses must introduce contrast or friction — elaboration is wrong.`
`- Default clause structure: subject + verb. No nominalization. Passive only where the absent actor is itself the statement.`
`- Sentences in sequence do not explain each other — they accumulate.`
`- The statement ends before the implication. The brand fills the honesty. The customer fills the meaning.`

`### Register Matrix by Surface`

`**Menu / Sŏn dinner:** maximum precision, minimum surface area. Dish name carries identity. Descriptor names what identity doesn't contain. Execution assumed. No adjectives performing quality. No sequential or spatial language.`
`Example: *Galbi / Aged thirty days. Scored before the fire.*`

`**Menu / Dosi:** short enough to read at decision speed. Descriptor closes the decision. No dinner register. No explanation of Korean food.`
`Example: *Dosirak / Braised short rib, multigrain rice, four banchan. Eat in or out.*`

`**Short-form digital:** one statement. All binary tests at compression. No setup sentences. No emojis. No exclamation points.`
`Example: *Scored before the fire. Table available tonight.*`

`**Longer-form digital:** statements accumulate without explaining each other. Brand position named directly. No "We believe," no "journey," no founder hero narrative.`
`Example: *Most restaurants are pointed at the plate. We are pointed at the relationship. The plate is how we earn the right to have one.*`

`**In-space copy:** present when found, not announcing itself. Korean terminology stands without explanation. No instructional copy.`
`Example: *선 / 207 E St. Elmo Rd*`

`**Correspondence:** names what it knows specifically. Confirms without reselling. No hospitality-speak.`
`Example: *Your table is confirmed for Saturday at 7. Outdoor seating, as requested. We'll see you then.*`

`### Preferred Terms`

`Korean culinary and cultural terminology — stands without translation: Jeong, Nunchi, Jaeyeonmi, Ma, Mahk, Galbi, Dosirak, Banchan, Buncheong, Baekja, Pyeong-sang, Ganjang, Doenjang, Gochujang, 선.`

`Preparation as decision, stated factually: scored, aged, braised, pressed, set, rendered, reduced.`

`Specific over categorical: "thirty days" not "long-aged" / "white oak" not "hardwood" / "onggi clay" not "traditional vessels."`

`Customer relationship: "return" not "loyalty" / "table" as primary reservation term / "record" for what the brand holds about a customer.`

`### Forbidden Lexicon`

`**Forbidden in all contexts — no exceptions:**`
`Elevated / experiential / innovative / disruptive / authentic / delicious / mouthwatering / vibrant / seasonal / chef-driven / hand-crafted / house-made / community-driven / passion / journey / curated / curated experience / farm-to-table / artisanal / crafted / must-try / amazing / incredible / thoughtful / intentional / memorable / unforgettable / beautiful / stunning / barbecue as genre descriptor / any emoji / exclamation points in any written brand voice context.`

`**Forbidden in specific contexts:**`
`"Inspired by" — forbidden in menu copy and in-space copy.`
`Quality-signal adjectives (crispy, tender, rich, bright, bold, complex) — forbidden when functioning as reassurance; test: does this adjective appear in competitor copy at comparable caliber? If yes, cut.`
`"Welcome," "enjoy" — forbidden in all written copy; acceptable as in-person service language only.`
`Duration and quantity descriptors (extensive, wide selection, long-standing) — forbidden in all contexts.`

`### Menu Copy Governing Principles`

`**Governing principle:** a menu entry names what is present, how it is present, and the role of its presence. The descriptor is a statement of the decisions that produced the dish — not a description of the finished dish.`

`**Name to descriptor relationship:** name carries identity; descriptor names what identity doesn't contain. They do not overlap. If the descriptor restates the name in other words, one of them is wrong.`

`**Sŏn dinner entry structure:** Korean dish name, no translation. One to two declarative sentences naming decisions not outcomes. No adjectives performing quality. No sequential or spatial language. Execution assumed.`

`**Dosi entry structure:** English primary; Korean where it is the correct and only term. More complete than the dinner entry — customer is deciding at speed. What's in it. How it's assembled. Format options.`

`**The test:** can this descriptor apply to a different dish at a comparable restaurant without modification? If yes, the entry is wrong. Secondary test: does the descriptor answer a question the customer was about to ask? If yes, stop at the statement.`

`## 10 — Photography`

`### Philosophy`

`Photographs as memories, not documents. People always present. Light found, not lit. Composition decentered. Frame imperfect. Closer than comfortable. Film grain accepted. AI-generated imagery prohibited on all public-facing surfaces — absolute, no exceptions. AI-assisted minor edits permitted under the Harvard SEAS disclosure tag convention.`

`### Three Photography Contexts`

`Context A — The Room: space, atmosphere, time-of-day. People as animating evidence that the room is inhabited — not as performers.`

`Context B — The Table: food in the context of consumption or service. Vessel and surrounding hands always present. Food alone is prohibited. Exception: food in preparation where the cook constitutes the human context.`

`Context C — The People: portraits and relationships. Customers, kitchen, service team. No role photography. No subject is backdrop.`

`Non-negotiable across all three: no image in which the subject has adjusted posture, expression, or gaze in response to the camera. Awareness is permitted. Alteration is not.`

`Two production modes: Produced (scheduled, crew-supported, Contexts A and B primarily) and Ambient (photographer during service/preparation, minimal footprint, Context C primarily).`

`Temporal arc governs capture conditions — not post-production: Morning shot in morning light. Dinner shot at dinner. A single-day shoot cannot cover all dayparts.`

`### Light Direction`

`Found light: window light, candlelight, installed 2700K CRI 95+ architectural lighting, firelight, ambient outdoor glow, reflected light from warm materials.`

`Rules out: strobe, flash, ring lights, softboxes, beauty dishes, reflector panels, any crew-introduced light source.`

`Footprint rule: no production lighting in the dining room for ambient or Context A/C shoots. For Context B produced shoots: negative fill only. No light addition.`

`Daypart variation: morning — window light at low angle, shadows not filled. Dinner — installed warm white lighting plus candlelight, no flash. Late night — high-ISO required; grain at ISO 3200–6400 is the honest record, not a defect.`

`The camera adapts to the room. The room does not adapt to the camera.`

`### Subject and Framing`

`People: present in every frame. In Contexts A and B, never looking at camera. In Context C, direct gaze permitted but not posed.`

`Food in context: only in transactional context. Vessel and hands always present. Food alone prohibited.`

`Composition governing rules:`
`- Decentered: subject's primary element at or outside inner thirds intersection; center may be empty.`
`- Imperfect: horizon not level, visible motion blur in at least one element; no tripod with plumb line.`
`- Closer than comfortable: move forward until something important is cropped — hand at wrist, face at jaw, dish at rim.`

`Never in the frame: brand signage as primary subject / introduced props not belonging to space or service / visible production equipment / tables styled for camera / compositions communicating transaction over exchange.`

`### Post-Production Parameters`

`Color: grade toward confirmed palette. Skin warms to Onggi. Shadows deepen to Aubergine — not cool blue-black. Highlights hold in Parchment/Bone. Outdoor greens hold in Jade/Peacock. Prohibited: cooling, blue shadows, muted-neutrals register.`

`Grain: preserved not removed. ISO 800–3200 consistent grain as specification. Late-night ISO 3200–6400 grain is correct. Artificial grain added in post is a Jaeyeonmi violation.`

`Retouching: Permitted — exposure, color balance, dust removal, incidental equipment removal. Prohibited — skin retouching beyond blemish, food texture correction, architectural surface correction for actual imperfections.`

`AI-assisted editing: Permitted under disclosure tag — noise reduction, lens correction, distortion/perspective correction within actual capture geometry. Prohibited outright — any generative AI creating content not in original capture (sky replacement, object generation, background extension, skin synthesis, generative content-aware fill). The prohibition is absolute.`

`### Photographer Selection Criteria`

`Must demonstrate: inhabited spaces with unaltered people / available light and high-ISO comfort with grain / decentered composition as deliberate choice / portraiture without performance.`

`Immediate disqualifiers: food-only portfolio / heavy post-production visible / overhead tabletop dominant / strobe as primary light source / technically proficient commercial restaurant photography aesthetic / standard AI-processing rights contract without modification.`

`Cultural fluency evaluation: briefed on Jaeyeonmi, Ma, and Mahk before confirmation. A photographer who asks how to make food look more appetizing after reading the Mahk standard has failed the evaluation.`

`Photographer reference library (sensibility anchors — not style targets):`
`Daniel Krieger, Heami Lee, Lukas Wassmann, Adrianna Glaviano, Wolfgang Tillmans, Nan Goldin, Ryan McGinley, Joshua Gordon, Quil Lemons, Heather Glazzard, Grant Cornett.`

`---`

`## 12 — Digital Identity`

`### Component Library`

`**Atomic level:** the token layer made visible. No new values. Everything references the token system. Governed exclusively by the Design Systems Architect. A request requiring a value outside the token system is an RFC, not a design decision.`

`**Composed level:** functional units from atoms. Three simultaneous requirements that all must be met: (1) token compliance, (2) state completeness — all six states (default, hover, focus, active, disabled, error) across all four daypart themes, (3) brand exclusion list. All three required.`

`**Template level:** composed components assembled into full-screen layouts. Governed by the digital touchpoint hierarchy — not by convention.`

`**New component criterion:** warranted only when no existing component can produce the required semantic function without modifying structure — not token values, structure. Extension is the default. "We need more flexibility" is not a structural justification.`

`**Daypart theme governance:**`
`Invariant across all four themes: 8pt grid / type scale hierarchy / component structure / interaction behavior / iconography construction.`
`Variable across themes: all semantic color token resolutions / type weight and leading within the type scale (theme-aware variants, not different sizes).`

`**Must never contain:**`
`- Components routing customers through single prescribed sequences`
`- Hardcoded values outside the token system`
`- Decorative dividers, colored left-border accents, 2px borders, double rules`
`- AI-generated imagery on any public-facing surface`
`- Loading states performing urgency or apologizing for wait time`
`- Components pre-selecting defaults encoding customer assumptions`
`- Components animating to signal importance rather than state change`
`- Social proof widgets`
`- Components announcing what they intend to do to the customer`

`### Digital Touchpoint Hierarchy`

`**Reservation flow:** profile lookup at initiation (not post-submission). SevenRooms profile match triggers merge before data collection. Clara conversion dependency addressed structurally — daypart visit history informs confirmation and pre-visit register. The customer does not feel processed. No tipping screens. No upsell. No forced account creation.`

`**Post-reservation:** Confirmation — functional, not congratulatory; "We can't wait to see you" is prohibited; present without performing. Pre-visit — profile-aware; warmer register for returning Good Energy customers. Post-visit — does not solicit a review; does not present a rating scale.`

``**Good Energy digital presence:** `son.theme.morning` token resolution. Prohibits: any visual marker of the specialty coffee category / chalkboard aesthetics / hand-drawn elements / countdown timers / urgency signals / social proof widgets / neighborhood café signifiers.``

`### Interaction Principles`

`Motion: marks state change, not importance. Motion as emphasis is prohibited — an element that pulses or blinks because it wants attention is a brand register violation.`

`Duration tokens: fast 100ms / standard 200ms / slow 400ms.`
`Easing tokens: standard cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1) / enter cubic-bezier(0, 0, 0.2, 1) / exit cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 1, 1).`
`` `prefers-reduced-motion`: one token override disables all non-essential animation. ``

`Feedback: communicates confirmation, process state, and specific errors. Does not communicate enthusiasm, urgency, social proof, or commentary. A successful reservation is confirmed — not celebrated. No confetti. "Something went wrong. Please try again." is prohibited.`

`Error and empty states: Ma/Yubaek-ui-mi governs. Empty is not absence to apologize for. The action is present and accessible. The interface does not direct. "No reservations yet — book your first visit!" is prohibited.`

`Prohibited interaction patterns: forced sequences without documented data dependency / pre-selected defaults / tooltips explaining how to use an interface element (redesign the element) / confirmation dialogs on non-destructive actions / progress indicators not reflecting actual progress / any pattern announcing what it intends to do to the customer.`

`Accessibility: WCAG 2.2 AA minimum; AAA target for type-heavy surfaces. Full accessibility constraints including Peacock on Pale Jade resolution, restricted color combinations, and token enforcement are documented in Section 05.`

`---`

`## What Remains`

`### [HELD] — Pending Executive Chef Hire`

`Chef onboarding sequence (in this order, before anything else):`

`1. **Session 1B — Culinary Philosophy** (Korean Hospitality Consultant)`
`The brand owns the culinary identity. The chef executes within it. Mahk standard is an explicit hiring criterion.`

`2. **Brand Narrative** (Brand Strategist + Brand Copywriter)`
`The structural argument for the brand exists. The kitchen voice — the part of the story only the kitchen can write — waits for the chef.`

`3. **Session 7C — Tableware Taxonomy** (Industrial Designer)`
`A culinary decision, not a decorative one. Requires: course structure and format / cold versus warm preparation assignments / chef's relationship to Bangjja Yugi, Baekja, Buncheong, and Cheongja (a hiring criterion) / back-of-house realities.`

`4. **Session 11A — Menu Design System** (Print Production Manager)`
`Gate-fold presentation card proposed for Sŏn dinner; single flat card printed both sides proposed for Dosi. Neither confirmed. Requires: course structure, tasting menu versus à la carte, change cadence, number of items at service.`

`### [DEFERRED] — Governing Principles Established, Execution Pending`

`**9B — Microcopy Standards:** governing register in Section 12. Korean terminology deployment rules must close before this runs.`

`**Korean Terminology Deployment Rules:** Korean Hospitality Consultant follow-up. Required before Section 09 is complete.`

`**Bird Mark Visual Execution:** 원앙 (mandarin duck) referent confirmed. Governing rules in Section 03. Deferred until explicitly opened.`

`**Loyalty Layer:** unnamed. Governed by Sections 05 and 12 when built. Requires naming session.`

`**Sub-Concept Marks — Good Energy, Dosi:** triggered by spin-out decision at a future location.`

`**Website IA and Templates:** IA must precede template-level component work.`

`**Tagline Architecture:** unlocks after Brand Narrative closes.`

`**Olfactory Designer:** session unslotted.`

`**Type Weight and Leading Theme Variables:** specific token values require Typographer and Multiscript Specialist coordination.`

`**Centerpiece Design:** constraints set — scaled for table, remove-or-coexist, cannot be shuffled. Industrial Designer new brief.`

`**Section 13 — AI Production Appendix:** builds last from all of the above.`

`---`

`*Sŏn Brand Guidelines v1.0 — Future Nostalgia Hospitality Group*`
`*207 E St. Elmo Rd, Austin, Texas*`
`*Brand guidelines build sprint: complete.*`
`*Living document: ClickUp You do not have access to this Doc`

`---`

`## 14 — Deck Design Governing Principles`

`**Internal production standard — not a public-facing brand guideline.**`

`This section governs all presentation decks generated using the Sŏn brand system — investor decks, brand decks, operational decks, vendor presentations. Decks are an editorial format, not a brand expression format. They use the brand's identity system without mimicking its environmental or spatial register. A deck is not the restaurant. It is a document about the restaurant.`

`The governing standard: the most editorial expression of the brand. Think high-end architecture monographs, Kinfolk, Cereal, or Apartamento — not brand presentations for a hospitality company. The restraint that makes the physical environment feel luxurious must operate with the same authority on the page.`

`Decks are not public-facing. They do not appear to customers. They will be used actively during the pre-opening funding and partnership phase, then recede. They do not require a separate brand identity — they require the brand's identity applied with editorial discipline.`

`---`

`### Background Hierarchy`

`**Primary slide background: Bone #EDE7D8 and Parchment #DBC9B0.**`

`The overwhelming majority of slides — content slides, evidence slides, diagram slides, photography slides — use Bone or Parchment as the background. These are not safe or neutral choices. They are the warm, considered, editorial register of the brand applied to a page.`

`| Background | Use |`
`|---|---|`
`| Bone #EDE7D8 | Default content slide background |`
`| Parchment #DBC9B0 | Secondary content background; warm variation |`
`| Plum Ink #120916 | Section title slides only; maximum one per section |`
`| Aubergine #2E1F31 | Major statement callout slides; maximum two or three per deck |`
`| All other colors | Accent use only — never as slide background |`

`**Prohibits:** Aubergine or Plum Ink as the background for content slides / gradient fills / any color background that competes with the content for attention / running more than two consecutive dark-background slides without returning to a neutral.`

`The deep colors are not prohibited in decks. They are controlled. A section title slide in Plum Ink followed by four slides in Bone is correct use. Twelve consecutive slides in Aubergine is not.`

`---`

`### Layout and Negative Space`

`**Negative space is a specification, not unused space.**`

`The Ma / Yubaek-ui-mi principle applies to the deck page as it applies to the physical environment. An empty slide margin is held intentionally. A slide that looks underbuilt is not underbuilt — it is disciplined.`

`Governing rules:`

`- **One primary idea per slide.** A slide that presents two competing ideas presents neither well. If two ideas need to appear together, one is subordinate to the other — not equal.`
`- **Generous margins.** Slide content does not extend to the edge of the frame. The deck is not a container to be filled. Minimum margin: 10% of slide dimension on each side.`
`- **Content does not center by default.** Centered layouts read as symmetrical and decorative. Left-aligned or asymmetric layouts read as editorial and considered. Centering is a deliberate choice, not a default.`
`- **Asymmetry over symmetry.** A single column of text on a slide with significant empty space to the right or left is correct. A perfectly balanced two-column grid is a template, not a decision.`

`**Prohibits:** centered text as a default layout / content extending to slide edges / multiple competing visual elements at equal weight on a single slide / decorative frames or borders around content / persistent header or footer chrome that adds visual noise without structural function.`

`---`

`### Typography in Decks`

`The typeface system is identical to the brand system. The application rules adjust for the presentation format.`

`**Headlines and section titles:** GT Sectra Fine Book. Large. Generous leading. The headline does not compete with body copy — it stands alone on the slide or dominates the upper register clearly.`

`**Body and supporting text:** GT Alpina Fine Standard, Regular or Light weight. Smaller. More generous leading than print — decks are read at distance. Tracking slightly open.`

`**Minimum sizes:** Headlines — minimum 48pt equivalent. Body text — minimum 18pt equivalent. Anything smaller is illegible in presentation conditions and should not appear in the deck.`

`**Sentence case always.** UPPERCASE reserved for single-line eyebrow labels only — category markers, section identifiers.`

`**No bullet point forests.** A slide is not a listicle. If content requires a list, the list has a maximum of four items, each is a complete thought, and the list does not occupy the entire slide. If the content requires more than four list items, it requires a different approach to the slide.`

`**Prose over fragments.** A single complete sentence in 72pt GT Sectra Fine Book on a Bone background is more powerful than eight bulleted fragments in 18pt body text. The deck should make arguments, not transmit data.`

`**No em dashes.** Same rule as all brand copy.`

`---`

`### Color Use on the Slide`

`**The temporal arc does not govern deck color.** The temporal arc — Jade/Peacock opening the day, deepening to Plum Ink/Aubergine, Jade re-entering at late night — is a sensory environment principle for the restaurant. It does not apply to a presentation deck.`

`**What does govern color in the deck:**`

`Gold Foil: not applicable in digital deck format. The brand's foil is a physical production specification. In deck contexts, Gold Foil is referenced typographically or in material specification slides — it is not simulated as a flat fill or gradient. If a deck slide references Gold Foil, the text names it as a physical material.`

`Color accents in decks: Jade, Peacock, and Onggi may appear as accent colors — a colored rule, a category label, an icon. They are never a dominant element.`

`Type on dark backgrounds: when a Plum Ink or Aubergine slide is used, type is in Bone or Parchment only. No Jade or Peacock type on dark backgrounds.`

`**Prohibits:** Gold Foil simulated as flat digital fill / full-slide color backgrounds on consecutive content slides / more than one accent color in use on a single slide / gradient fills of any kind.`

`---`

`### Image Use in Decks`

`Photography in decks follows all Section 10 governing principles. The following rules are specific to the deck format.`

`**Full bleed or large format.** A photograph in a deck occupies at least 50% of the slide, or it is full bleed. Thumbnail-sized photography next to a block of text is a PowerPoint default, not a design decision.`

`**One photograph per slide.** Two photographs on the same slide compete for attention. One photograph is a statement.`

`**No captions unless functionally necessary.** A photograph of the property does not require a caption explaining it is a photograph of the property. If a caption is required, it is minimal — a single short line in GT Alpina Fine Standard Light, small, recessive.`

`**Prohibits:** stock imagery / AI-generated imagery / photographs with watermarks / photographs with production equipment visible / photographs that violate any Section 10 governing principle / photograph thumbnails arranged in grids as slide filler.`

`---`

`### Deck Architecture and Sequence`

`**Slide count is not a measure of effort or thoroughness.** A 30-slide deck that makes its case with precision is stronger than an 80-slide deck that repeats itself. When evaluating deck length, the question is not "what else can we add?" but "what can we remove without losing the argument?"`

`**Section dividers:** Plum Ink or Aubergine background, single line of GT Sectra Fine Book in Bone or Parchment, generous negative space. No decorative elements. No icons. The section title is the entire content of the slide.`

`**Opening slide:** the brand mark and the single most important thing the deck is for. Nothing else.`

`**Closing slide:** direct and complete. Either a clear call to action or a closing statement. Not a "Thank you" slide with contact information that could have appeared on any deck from any company.`

`**Slide templates:** the deck should not read as templated. Slides that vary in layout — a full-bleed photograph followed by a single-statement text slide followed by a spare diagram — read as editorial. Slides that use the same layout repeated sixteen times read as a template output.`

`---`

`### What This Standard Prohibits Outright`

`- Full-slide gradient fills`
`- Drop shadows on text or images`
`- Beveled or embossed elements`
`- Decorative frames or borders`
`- Clip art or icon library illustrations`
`- Charts or graphs with heavy grid lines, unnecessary data labels, or default application styling — if a chart appears in the deck, it is styled to the brand's typographic and color system`
`- Transitions or animations beyond the simplest fade`
`- Multiple fonts beyond the two-typeface system (GT Sectra, GT Alpina)`
`- Any slide that requires the presenter to apologize for or explain — if a slide is confusing without narration, redesign the slide`

`---`

`### The Governing Test for Any Deck Slide`

`Could this slide appear in a premium editorial publication — a monograph, a brand book, a high-end print journal — without embarrassment?`

`If yes, it is ready.`

`If no, identify what makes it wrong and remove or redesign that element until the answer is yes.`

pages.name: The Gladwell Style Engine: A Claude Knowledge File for Revising Writing into Malcolm Gladwell’s Style
pages.content:
`The Gladwell Style Engine: A Claude Knowledge File for Revising Writing into Malcolm Gladwell’s Style`

`## TL;DR`

`- **The deliverable is below in Part B — a ready-to-paste Claude Project knowledge file** organized into eight sections (Philosophy & Voice, Structural Templates, Rhetorical Move Catalog, Sentence-Level Guide, Integration Techniques, Anti-Patterns, Revision Checklist, Prompting Instructions), every rule written as an instruction to *do*, not a description of what Gladwell is like.`
`- **Gladwell’s style reduces to a reproducible engine:** open on a named person in a specific physical moment → plant a withheld puzzle → deliver a counterintuitive reframe powered by a “missing variable” → coin a sticky portable label → braid supporting cases → close by returning to the opening figure with a lens-shift the reader can use tomorrow. Sentences run short and declarative with the occasional long “payoff” sentence; research enters through named characters, never as “studies show.”`
`- **The single biggest adaptation for Medium** is compression: Gladwell’s native form is the ~5,000–8,000-word New Yorker piece built in 5–6 numbered sections, so the file carries an explicit short-form layer (800–2,000 words, five beats) specifying which moves are non-negotiable (named-person open, counterintuitive turn, reframe close) and which are droppable (extra cases, historical parallels, extended objection-handling).`

`-----`

`## Key Findings`

`**1. Actionable beats descriptive, and examples beat adjectives.** Both the professional AI-style-guide literature (Every’s Spiral system) and Anthropic’s own Claude Projects guidance converge on the same principle: AI changes behavior when given concrete paired examples and explicit “do not” lists, not flattering descriptors. Anthropic’s best-practice guidance is to “start with constraints, not capabilities” and that “one example is worth ten rules.” The knowledge file below is therefore built almost entirely from named moves, verbatim micro-examples, and a banned-patterns list.`

`**2. Gladwell’s architecture is unusually well-documented — by Gladwell himself.** His MasterClass, his *What the Dog Saw* preface, and close readings (Henry Oliver’s *Common Reader* analysis of *The Tipping Point*; the Draftly craft breakdown) independently describe the same machine: story-first/example-before-explanation, strategic withholding, the small→big→small loop, and the counterintuitive reframe. This convergence means the style can be specified precisely rather than impressionistically.`

`**3. The short-form gap is real and must be engineered.** Gladwell’s purest form is long. His essay collection *What the Dog Saw* (his favorite New Yorker pieces) is the closest model to Medium length and the highest-priority reference, but even those run several thousand words. A Medium post needs a deliberate compression layer, included below.`

`**4. Critics articulate the mechanics most precisely — and flag the ethical risk.** Steven Pinker, reviewing *What the Dog Saw* in The New York Times (Nov. 7, 2009), wrote that “the reasoning in ‘Outliers,’ which consists of cherry-picked anecdotes, post-hoc sophistry and false dichotomies, had me gnawing on my Kindle.” Michiko Kakutani separately dismissed the Gladwell “shake-and-bake” recipe applied “in such a clumsy manner that it italicizes the weaknesses of his methodology.” For thought-leadership use, this is the load-bearing caveat: adopt the *style* (mechanism-driven storytelling) without manufacturing false dichotomies or overclaiming beyond evidence.`

`-----`

`## Details: How the Research Maps to Each Section`

`- **Voice** is sourced to Gladwell’s own standard from the *What the Dog Saw* introduction and his MasterClass reading-level admission, plus the Draftly “prosecutor who moonlights as a raconteur” framing.`
`- **Structure** is sourced to the *Common Reader* section-by-section anatomy of *The Tipping Point* (nine chapters; varying section lengths; “example before explanation”), the MasterClass “Imperfect Puzzle” lesson, and Rob Biesenbach’s “start small → go big → return small” formulation.`
`- **Rhetorical moves** are grounded in verbatim openings/closings verified against primary sources (The New Yorker, the books themselves), plus the puzzle/mystery framing from “Open Secrets.”`
`- **Sentence mechanics** come directly from Gladwell’s MasterClass “Structuring Language” lesson (the “rat-a-tat then one long payoff” method; eighth-grade reading level).`
`- **Anti-patterns** are assembled from the craft analyses (no thesis-first openings, no listicles) and the critical literature (false dichotomies, cherry-picking).`

`-----`

`# PART B — THE KNOWLEDGE FILE`

`### (Paste everything below into the Claude Project knowledge base)`

`-----`

`## 1. Philosophy and Voice`

`You are revising prose to read like Malcolm Gladwell. Gladwell’s worldview: the world does not accord with our intuition, and there is a hidden mechanism beneath ordinary surfaces that, once revealed, makes everything click. He does not present himself as an original thinker; he finds research and brings it alive through people. (In a 2012 talk at Yale he described his role this way: “There’s that bird on the back of the elephant that picks off the ticks — I am the bird.”)`

`His own stated standard, from the introduction to *What the Dog Saw and Other Adventures* (2009): **“Good writing does not succeed or fail on the strength of its ability to persuade. It succeeds or fails on the strength of its ability to engage you, to make you think, to give you a glimpse into someone else’s head.” **`

`The voice is a prosecutor who moonlights as a raconteur: warm, curious, slightly mischievous, confident without superiority. It treats the reader as a smart partner who is missing exactly one piece of context. The emotional residue should be delight (at seeing a hidden mechanism) mixed with mild unease (at how often common sense misleads). Conspiratorial curiosity — “here is something hidden in plain sight” — is the keynote. Per his MasterClass (“Structuring Language” chapter), the target is sophisticated ideas delivered at an eighth-to-ninth-grade reading level with short sentences: “I’m writing at the eighth grade level, or maybe the ninth. And my sentences are super short compared to my peers.”`

`## 2. Structural Templates`

`**LONG-FORM (the native architecture, for reference).** Gladwell builds in numbered sections (typically 5–6), each a single-task unit. The macro-shape is **small → big → small**: open on an individual, object, or moment; expand to research and implication; return at the end to the opening figure. Sections start with a story, expand into social-science exposition, then revert to explaining the story in light of the research — *example before explanation, always*. Section lengths vary deliberately (uniform lengths are “the enemy of clear exposition”). Themes recur like motifs in music. (Anatomy verified against *The Tipping Point*: nine chapters, sharply varying section lengths, Hush Puppies referenced across seven separate places.)`

`**SHORT-FORM TEMPLATE (Medium, 800–2,000 words) — USE THIS BY DEFAULT.** Compress to five beats:`

`1. **The Scene (≈15–20%)** — Open on one named person in one specific physical moment. Plant a puzzle. Withhold why it matters. End the opening on a clean one-sentence question.`
`1. **The Puzzle (≈10%)** — Name the counterintuitive question explicitly. Frame what “everyone assumes.”`
`1. **The Turn (≈25%)** — Introduce the expert/study/mechanism that contradicts common sense. Hand the reader the missing variable. This is the counterintuitive reframe.`
`1. **The Widening (≈25%)** — One or two more cases that test or complicate the pattern (example braiding). Concede the obvious objection, then show why the mechanism still holds.`
`1. **The Reframe Close (≈15%)** — Return to the opening person/scene, now re-seen through the mechanism. End on a portable lens-shift the reader can apply tomorrow — not a summary.`

`**Non-negotiable beats even at 800 words:** the named-person scene opening, the counterintuitive turn, and the reframe close. **Droppable when tight:** the second/third case, the historical parallel, extended objection-handling.`

`## 3. Rhetorical Move Catalog`

`Each move is a reusable, named technique. Apply by name during revision.`

`- **The Named-Person Cold Open.** Begin inside a specific person’s specific moment, not a thesis. *Verified models:* “On the afternoon of October 23, 2006, Jeffrey Skilling sat at a table at the front of a federal courtroom in Houston, Texas. He was wearing a navy-blue suit and a tie. He was fifty-two years old, but looked older.” (“Open Secrets,” The New Yorker). “Murray Barr was a bear of a man, an ex-marine, six feet tall and heavyset… On the street, they called him Smokey.” (“Million-Dollar Murray,” The New Yorker). “For Hush Puppies—the classic American brushed-suede shoes with the lightweight crepe sole—the Tipping Point came somewhere between late 1994 and early 1995.” (*The Tipping Point*).`
`- **The Named Phenomenon.** Coin a sticky, portable label for a social observation, then immediately narrow its domain so it doesn’t become a slogan (“guardrails”). Models: *the Tipping Point, the Stickiness Factor, the Law of the Few, Connectors/Mavens/Salesmen, thin-slicing, the 10,000-Hour Rule.* In revision, take the piece’s core idea and give it ONE memorable, ownable name.`
`- **The Counterintuitive Reframe (signature move).** Set the reader up to predict a conclusion, then replace their explanation with a better one that accounts for more of the details they already saw. Earn surprise by showing the missing variable, not by provoking. The reader should feel “of course” right after “no way.”`
`- **The Puzzle/Mystery Reframe.** Recast the question itself. Verified model from “Open Secrets”: “But the prosecutor was wrong. Enron wasn’t really a puzzle. It was a mystery.” A puzzle needs *more* information; a mystery has *too much* and needs better interpretation. Use this to flip what the reader thinks the problem even is.`
`- **The Expert Who Contradicts Common Sense.** Introduce a researcher/practitioner whose finding upends intuition. Introduce them as a *character* — physical description plus a quote that reveals their working model of the world — never as a citation.`
`- **The Historical Parallel as Proof.** Reach into the past for an unexpected case (Paul Revere; a WWII intelligence unit listening to public Nazi broadcasts) and use it as the interpretive key.`
`- **Example Braiding.** Weave multiple cases so each adds a new variable — one introduces the pattern, the next complicates it, a third tests its limit. Never repeat the same point with a new name.`
`- **Objection Preemption.** Anticipate the reader’s best skepticism, concede part of it, then show why the mechanism still points your way.`
`- **Strategic Withholding / The Imperfect Puzzle.** Ration explanations; delay the “why” to create micro-cliffhangers. Gladwell (MasterClass, Lesson 1): “Amateur storytellers withhold valuable information because they are oblivious. Pros withhold information for suspense, surprise, or humor.” And (MasterClass, “Imperfect Puzzle”): the best arguments are imperfect “because the perfect argument is too obvious.” The reader must have everything needed to solve the puzzle by the end.`
`- **The Portable Ending Reframe.** Close by changing how the reader interprets a familiar thing, not by recapping. Verified model (*The Tipping Point* close): “Look at the world around you. It may seem like an immovable, implacable place. It is not. With the slightest push—in just the right place—it can be tipped.” A second verified model (the close of “Small Change: Why the revolution will not be tweeted,” The New Yorker): “What happens next is more of the same. A networked, weak-tie world is good at things like helping Wall Streeters get phones back from teen-age girls. Viva la revolución.” Endings change the reader’s lens, they do not recap points.`

`## 4. Sentence-Level Style Guide`

`- **Rhythm: rat-a-tat then reward.** Stack short, declarative sentences to build rhythm, then deliver one long, winding sentence as a payoff. Gladwell on his own method (MasterClass): short sentence, short sentence, short sentence, “and then the payoff is this one long, windy, super fun [sentence], with a little punch there at the end.” Use long sentences sparingly; the reader has “a limited appetite for them.”`
`- **The suspended opening sentence.** Occasionally delay the main verb behind a prepositional phrase or parenthesis to build suspense (the “For Hush Puppies—…” construction delays its first verb to the 18th word). Starting a sentence with “For…” is a signature.`
`- **One paragraph, one job.** Single-task paragraphs that behave like steps in a guided walk. Vary paragraph length sharply.`
`- **Rhetorical questions as steering, not filler.** Use a question to tell the reader what to wonder next, then pay it off quickly with something concrete. Do not let questions accumulate as decoration.`
`- **Register: accessible but not simplistic.** Concrete nouns (places, roles, objects) and causal verbs (drives, triggers, predicts, undermines). Avoid ornate synonyms. Specialist terms are allowed as *anchors* — introduce the jargon, then translate it immediately into a human example so the reader feels initiated, not excluded.`
`- **Plain rule** (Gladwell, MasterClass): “Write on sophisticated topics, but at an eighth-grade reading level. Writing should be simple enough that it doesn’t defeat the reader. Write with mostly short sentences, so that the long ones stand out.” The reader should never have to ask, “Wait a minute — where did this sentence start?”`

`## 5. Integration Techniques (research, experts, and data the Gladwell way)`

`- **Research is a bridge, not a badge.** Never drop a study to borrow authority. Use research as connective tissue: it translates one story into a general claim and sets up the next story as a test. Make the reader *want* the statistic before you give it.`
`- **Introduce studies through people.** Replace “Studies show X” with a named researcher who discovered X, given a face and a quote. When building a character, Gladwell advises describing them “by what they keep in their bedroom,” not just how they look.`
`- **Statistics without slowing pace.** Deploy numbers as the payoff to a question the reader is already asking, or as a small surprising cluster (e.g., the run of nearly identical birthdates of tech-company founders in *Outliers*). Keep them embedded in narrative — never in a table or bullet list.`
`- **Dialogue as evidence.** Quote a person to capture how they justify a decision or what they notice; trim to the single revealing line, then move on before it becomes biography.`

`## 6. Anti-Patterns (identify and strip during revision)`

`- **Never open with a thesis statement or a 30,000-foot summary.** If the draft starts with the main point or an overview, replace it with a named-person scene. A summary paragraph, if truly required, goes in a sidebar — never the lead.`
`- **No academic hedging.** Cut “it could be argued,” “somewhat,” “arguably,” “studies suggest.” State the mechanism.`
`- **No listicles or numbered “X tips” structures.** Gladwell never writes listicles; convert any list into narrative sections.`
`- **No second person / no “you should.”** He writes about people, not instructions to the reader. (The lens-shift close is the one place reader-implication is allowed — and even there it is a reframe, not a command.)`
`- **No “studies show” boilerplate** — name the study or delete it.`
`- **No tidy summary ending** that recaps points. End by extending or reframing.`
`- **No quirky-anecdote-as-insight.** Every anecdote must sit on a load-bearing mechanism connecting the individual to a system. A scrapbook of eccentric stories is not Gladwellian.`
`- **No contrarian twist for shock value.** A reframe must explain *more* with fewer assumptions, or it reads as a stunt.`
`- **No correlative “not X, but Y” scaffolding and no generic transitions.** State Y directly.`
`- **Guard against the documented critique.** Per Steven Pinker’s New York Times review of *What the Dog Saw* (Nov. 7, 2009): “The reasoning in ‘Outliers,’ which consists of cherry-picked anecdotes, post-hoc sophistry and false dichotomies, had me gnawing on my Kindle.” Michiko Kakutani made the same charge about Gladwell’s “shake-and-bake” recipe applied “in such a clumsy manner that it italicizes the weaknesses of his methodology.” When revising real thought-leadership, keep the storytelling *style* without manufacturing false dichotomies or overclaiming beyond the evidence. Style must not become intellectual dishonesty.`

`## 7. Revision Checklist (quick-apply)`

`1. Does it open on ONE named person in ONE specific physical moment — not a thesis?`
`1. Is there a single clean question driving the piece, answerable in one sentence?`
`1. Is there a genuine counterintuitive turn — a missing variable that makes the surprise feel inevitable?`
`1. Does every anecdote connect to a system/mechanism, not just sit there as color?`
`1. Is research introduced through named people, never as “studies show”?`
`1. Does the rhythm alternate short declaratives with an occasional long payoff sentence?`
`1. Is there ONE coined, portable label for the core idea (with guardrails so it isn’t a slogan)?`
`1. Are examples braided (each adds a new variable) rather than repeating the point?`
`1. Does the ending RETURN to the opening figure and deliver a lens-shift, not a summary?`
`1. Have all listicles, second-person instructions, hedges, and thesis-first openings been stripped?`
`1. Could a reader repeat the core insight at dinner tonight?`
`1. Is the reading level accessible (short sentences, concrete nouns, translated jargon) — and is any claim honestly supported, not a false dichotomy?`

`## 8. Prompting Instructions (how to invoke this file)`

`Store this file in a Claude Project. In the **Project Instructions** field, add:`

`> *“You are the Gladwell Style Engine. Apply the attached knowledge file to every revision. When I paste a draft, revise it into Malcolm Gladwell’s style using the SHORT-FORM TEMPLATE by default, then list which rhetorical moves you applied and which anti-patterns you stripped. Preserve all my factual claims; never invent research, quotes, or statistics. If a Gladwellian move would require evidence the draft lacks, flag it instead of fabricating.”*`

`To revise a piece, paste the draft and use one of these invocations:`

`- **Full revision:** “Revise this into Gladwell’s style. Use the short-form template. Open on a named person, deliver one counterintuitive turn, and close with a reframe. Show the revised piece, then a 3-line note on what changed structurally.”`
`- **Diagnostic only:** “Don’t rewrite yet. Run this draft against the Revision Checklist and tell me which items it fails and why.”`
`- **Opening fix:** “Rewrite only the opening as a Gladwell named-person cold open with a withheld payoff and a closing question.”`
`- **Move injection:** “Identify the core idea and coin one sticky Named Phenomenon for it, with guardrails.”`
`- **Tone calibration:** “Keep my content and structure but adjust prose rhythm and voice to Gladwell’s — short declaratives with occasional long payoff sentences, conspiratorial curiosity, concrete nouns, jargon translated on first use.”`

`-----`

`## Recommendations (staged)`

`**Stage 1 — Stand it up now.** Create a Claude Project named “Gladwell Style Engine,” paste Part B as the knowledge file, and add the Project Instructions pointer from Section 8. Test it on two of your existing Medium drafts using the “Full revision” invocation. This is a Level-2 “working guide” in Every’s framework — appropriate for someone drafting regularly.`

`**Stage 2 — Calibrate against real output (after ~5 revisions).** Anthropic’s guidance is explicit that first instructions are never perfect. Track which anti-patterns Claude keeps reintroducing (the most common will be tidy summary endings and thesis-first openings). Each time you make the same correction twice, add a sharper line to Section 6 with a before/after example. **Threshold to act:** if the same correction recurs across three drafts, it belongs in the file.`

`**Stage 3 — Add your own verified example bank.** The file currently uses verbatim Gladwell openings/closings as models. Add 3–5 of *your own* best Gladwell-style paragraphs once you produce them, labeled “good,” plus 2–3 “bad” examples (AI-generic or thesis-first) labeled with *why* they fail. Per the AI-style-guide literature, paired good/bad examples move model behavior more than any rule.`

`**Stage 4 — Decide your honesty guardrail explicitly.** Because the Gladwell style’s central critique is overclaiming, add a house rule to Section 6 stating how far you’re willing to generalize from a single anecdote. **Benchmark that should change your approach:** if a revised piece’s core claim rests on one example with no supporting mechanism or second case, treat it as a draft failure regardless of how good the prose sounds.`

`## Caveats`

`- **The “bird on the back of the elephant” quote** is reported from a 2012 Yale Daily News account of a Gladwell talk; it is reliable as reportage but is not a published Gladwell text, so treat it as a talk paraphrase rather than a canonical line.`
`- **MasterClass quotes** (the withholding line, the reading-level admission, the “imperfect puzzle” rule, the rat-a-tat method) are verbatim within the course but are transcribed in widely circulated reviews/summaries rather than a single official transcript; wording is consistent across sources and was cross-checked, but minor punctuation may vary from the video.`
`- **The opening/closing micro-examples** in Section 3 were verified verbatim against primary sources (The New Yorker article pages and the books themselves) for “Open Secrets,” “Million-Dollar Murray,” *The Tipping Point*, and “Small Change.” Two literal *final* sentences (“The Ketchup Conundrum” and “What the Dog Saw”) could not be confirmed word-for-word and were therefore not quoted as closings; do not present unverified closings as exact.`
`- **Style is not substance.** This file reproduces Gladwell’s *method of presentation*. The persistent expert critique (Pinker, Kakutani, the *If Books Could Kill* podcast) is that the method can outrun the evidence. For thought-leadership under your own name, the file’s anti-pattern and checklist guardrails against false dichotomies and single-anecdote overreach are the most important parts to enforce, not the most fun.`
`- **Reading-level targeting is a tool, not a mandate.** The eighth/ninth-grade figure is Gladwell’s own self-report from a readability analysis; treat it as a directional target for sentence simplicity, not a metric to optimize mechanically at the expense of your ideas.`

pages.name: The Paul Graham Filter: A Claude Project Knowledge File for Investor-Facing Business Writing
pages.content:
`# The Paul Graham Filter: A Claude Project Knowledge File for Investor-Facing Business Writing`

`**Purpose:** Use this file to revise and generate all investor-facing copy for a Korean fine-dining concept (Austin, TX; targeting VC/tech-adjacent investors) so it reads with Paul Graham’s clarity, logic architecture, and conviction model. Every section is written as an instruction set. Apply it; don’t just read it. Where quotations appear, they are verbatim from the named Graham essay so you can calibrate against the real source.`

`-----`

`## SECTION 1 — PHILOSOPHY AND CONVICTION MODEL (apply this lens to everything)`

`Operate from these principles. They come from specific essays: principle 1 from “The Age of the Essay” (Sept. 2004); principles 2–5 from “How to Convince Investors” (Aug. 2013); principle 6 from “Write Like You Talk” (Oct. 2015); principle 7 from “How to Present to Investors” (Aug. 2006, rev. 2010).`

`1. **Aim to be right, not to be convincing.** From “The Age of the Essay”: “But the aim is never to be convincing per se. As the reader gets smarter, convincing and true become identical, so if I can convince smart readers I must be near the truth.” DO NOT perform conviction. Establish that the claim is true, then state it plainly. A smart skeptic is persuaded by a correct argument, not an energetic one.`
`1. **Let the thing do the work, not the pitch.** From “How to Convince Investors”: inexperienced founders “try to convince with their pitch” when they “would be better off if they let their startup do the work — if they started by understanding why their startup is worth investing in, then simply explained this well.” INSTRUCTION: Before writing any investor copy, write the plain answer to “Why is this actually worth investing in?” Then just explain that.`
`1. **Convince yourself first; truth is the source of confidence.** From “How to Convince Investors”: “Convince yourself that your startup is worth investing in, and then when you explain this to investors they’ll believe you.” And: “As long as you stay on the territory of truth, you’re strong. Make the truth good, then just tell it.” INSTRUCTION: Never write a sentence the founder cannot defend as literally true. Drop any claim that requires exaggeration to land.`
`1. **Matter-of-fact register beats marketing-speak.** From “How to Convince Investors”: “use the same matter-of-fact language you used to convince yourself. You wouldn’t use vague, grandiose marketing-speak among yourselves. Don’t use it with investors either. It not only doesn’t work on them, but seems a mark of incompetence. Just be concise.”`
`1. **Clarity is evidence of understanding.** From “How to Convince Investors”: investors “use [conciseness] as a test, reasoning (correctly) that if you can’t explain your plans concisely, you don’t really understand them.” Also (Note 13): the explanation “has to work not just on the partner you talk to, but when that partner re-tells it to colleagues.” INSTRUCTION: Every core claim must be re-tellable in one sentence by someone who heard it once.`
`1. **Write like you talk.** From “Write Like You Talk”: “If you simply manage to write in spoken language, you’ll be ahead of 95% of writers… just don’t let a sentence through unless it’s the way you’d say it to a friend.” Same essay: “the harder the subject, the more informally experts speak… Informal language is the athletic clothing of ideas.” And: “You don’t need complex sentences to express complex ideas.” Test: read each sentence aloud; if you wouldn’t say it to a friend, rewrite it.`
`1. **Hostility to jargon, buzzwords, and abstraction.** From “How to Present to Investors,” Graham’s warning about vague descriptions: “as you approach… a description of something that could be anything, the content of your description approaches zero.” A line like “a system to allow people to collaboratively leverage the value of information… will go in one investor ear and out the other.” INSTRUCTION: Prefer the narrow, concrete, even “misleadingly narrow” description over the grand vague one.`

`**The conviction test for any sentence:** (a) Is it true? (b) Would I say it to a friend? (c) Could a skeptic re-tell it accurately? If any answer is no, rewrite.`

`-----`

`## SECTION 2 — REGISTER 1 TEMPLATE: ESSAY / WHITE PAPER (1,500–4,000 words)`

`Use this to make the case for a new concept (e.g., “why Korean fine dining is a venture-scale category now”) to a sophisticated investor audience. Follow the labeled beats in order.`

`**BEAT 1 — THE PLAIN-SENTENCE THESIS OPENER (sentence 1–2).**`
`State the conclusion flatly in the first one or two sentences. No scene, no question, no buildup. Verbatim models from Graham:`

`- “The way to get startup ideas is not to try to think of startup ideas. It’s to look for problems, preferably problems you have yourself.” (“How to Get Startup Ideas”)`
`- “One of the most common types of advice we give at Y Combinator is to do things that don’t scale.” (“Do Things That Don’t Scale”)`
`- “There are great startup ideas lying around unexploited right under our noses.” (“Schlep Blindness”)`
`- “One of the more surprising things I’ve noticed while working on Y Combinator is how frightening the most ambitious startup ideas are.” (“Frighteningly Ambitious Startup Ideas”)`

`EXCEPTION (permitted, used sparingly): a single concrete physical analogy that resolves into the thesis by sentence 3. “How to Convince Investors” opens: “When people hurt themselves lifting heavy things, it’s usually because they try to lift with their back… Inexperienced founders make the same mistake.” Use this ONLY when the analogy is concrete and immediately mapped to the real subject. Default to the flat thesis. (Note: the “always open with the thesis” rule is a strong tendency, not a universal law — Graham himself sometimes opens with a concrete analogy-scene.)`

`**BEAT 2 — NAME THE HIDDEN TRUTH / DEFINE THE TERM.**`
`Introduce the one counterintuitive idea the piece exists to deliver, and if useful, name it (see Section 5). Use the “most people don’t realize” setup without condescension — Graham: “One reason we don’t see them is a phenomenon I call schlep blindness.” Then define any pivotal term in plain words immediately (Definitional Pivot, Section 6).`

`**BEAT 3 — THE ADDITIVE PROOF STACK.**`
`Each subsequent paragraph adds ONE more reason the claim is inevitable — not a new topic, a new load-bearing reason. The paragraphs should feel like links in a chain. Each paragraph’s first sentence is a flat topic sentence; the rest of the paragraph proves it. Do not pile up parallel angles; build a single ascending argument.`

`**BEAT 4 — EMPIRICAL PROOF BY EXAMPLE.**`
`Prove abstract claims with specific real cases, the way Graham uses Stripe, Airbnb, and Facebook. Use named, concrete proof: a specific sold-out service, a named chef, a real waitlist number, a specific repeat-guest rate. One vivid real example outperforms a paragraph of adjectives.`

`**BEAT 5 — OBJECTION PREEMPTION (mid-essay, never saved for the end).**`
`Name the smartest objection a skeptical investor would raise, in their words, and answer it in the same passage. Graham models naming why investors reject the scary-but-good idea, then showing why they’re wrong; he advises tackling the worry “head-on… instead of seeming evasive.” INSTRUCTION: Place the hardest objection roughly two-thirds through, address it directly, and concede the genuinely weak part (Self-Undermining Concession, Section 6) — this increases trust.`

`**BEAT 6 — THE “WHY NOW.”**`
`Identify the specific external wave. From “How to Convince Investors”: “to make a convincing case for becoming huge, you have to identify some specific trend you’ll benefit from. Usually you can find this by asking ‘why now?’ … Ideally the answer is that it only recently became a good idea, because something changed, and no one else has noticed yet.” INSTRUCTION: State the one thing that recently changed (a shift in diner behavior, a demographic or cultural change, a supply-chain shift) that makes this category investable now and wasn’t true five years ago.`

`**BEAT 7 — THE HIGHER-LEVEL REFRAME CLOSE.**`
`Close by restating the opening thesis at a higher level of generality, or by stating the practical implication. Graham ends “How to Convince Investors” with a compressed restatement: “Make the truth good, then just tell it.” Do not summarize; reframe. Leave the reader with the thesis enlarged.`

`**Paragraph and section rules for Register 1:**`

`- Short paragraphs dominate. Reserve longer paragraphs for the single most complex logical step.`
`- Use bold section headers of one or two plain words (Graham’s own in “How to Convince Investors”: “Formidable,” “Truth,” “Market,” “Rejection,” “Different”). Each header names the reason that section proves.`
`- Signal transitions through logical sequence, not transition words. Each paragraph’s first sentence should make the connection obvious without “Furthermore” or “Moreover.”`
`- Use footnotes/endnotes to hold digressions out of the main line of argument.`

`-----`

`## SECTION 3 — REGISTER 2 TEMPLATE: INVESTOR DECK (slide-level logic)`

`Compress the essay architecture to slide units. The deck mechanics below come from “How to Present to Investors” (Aug. 2006, rev. 2010), Graham’s distinct demo-day essay, which is the source of the “first sentence,” “four or five numbers,” and “under 20 words” rules.`

`**Rule for every slide: one claim, stated as a flat conclusion in the slide title, then 2–3 compressed proofs.** The title carries the argument; the body proves it. Graham: “look at your slides and ask of each word ‘could I cross this out?’… Try to get your slides under 20 words if you can.” And: “Specific numbers are good… Numbers stick in people’s heads.”`

`**Slide-type instructions:**`

`- **Title / concept slide.** State what you’re doing in the first line, plainly: “Say what you’re doing as soon as possible, preferably in the first sentence.” Pair with the soundbite (Section 5). NOT a mission-statement abstraction. Good model: a one-line description a non-foodie investor could re-tell.`
`- **Problem slide.** Frame the problem as a real, specific pain, told through users. Graham: “Tell stories about users… talk about problems specific users have and how you solve them.” Look for the “proxy for demand” — “What are people doing now, using inadequate tools, that shows they need what you’re making?” DO NOT open with market size. State the human problem concretely.`
`- **Solution slide.** State the plain-English mechanism: what you built and why people want it. Graham’s two demo-day goals: “(a) explain what you’re doing, and (b) explain why users will want it.” Show the mechanism, not adjectives about it.`
`- **Why-now slide.** One slide on the specific trend you’re riding (Beat 6 above). State the single thing that changed.`
`- **Traction slide.** Empirical proof by example, with 4–5 specific numbers maximum. From “How to Present to Investors”: “don’t give them more than four or five numbers, and only give them numbers specific to you.” Use a weekly/monthly growth figure, a repeat rate, a waitlist, covers-per-night, revenue per seat. Real and specific beats large and vague.`
`- **Market slide.** Graham’s view (from “How to Convince Investors”): “Founders think of startups as ideas, but investors think of them as markets.” Show a “plausible path to owning a big piece of a big market” — and note it’s fine to “start in a small market that will either turn into a big one or from which you can move into a big one.” Frame the path of hops to a big market; don’t lead with a “$X billion TAM” headline (see anti-patterns). If you cite TAM, it’s support, never the opening claim.`
`- **Team / founder slide.** Frame founder credibility as **domain expertise and formidability**, not titles. Graham: “To evaluate whether your startup is worth investing in, you have to be a domain expert… investors can tell fairly quickly whether you’re a domain expert by how well you answer their questions.” Formidable = “seems like they’ll get what they want, regardless of whatever obstacles are in the way.” Keep it brief: flash credentials for “15 seconds.” Show, don’t tell: “Never say ‘we’re passionate’ or ‘our product is great.’ People just ignore that — or worse, write you off as bullshitters.”`
`- **Ask / close slide.** State the amount and what it buys plainly. No grandiosity.`

`**Language that NEVER appears in a Graham-style deck:** “synergy,” “ecosystem,” “leverage” (as a verb), “scalable,” “robust,” “utilize,” “disruptive,” “revolutionary,” “best-in-class,” “world-class,” “passionate,” “seamless,” “next-generation,” “paradigm,” “we believe / we think / we hope,” “the [Famous Company] of [X],” and any sentence whose content “approaches zero” when you ask what it concretely means.`

`-----`

`## SECTION 4 — REGISTER 3 TEMPLATE: INVESTOR WEBSITE (one idea per unit)`

`Goal: make the concept feel like an obvious bet to a VC who arrives cold. Short paragraphs, one idea per unit, plain words, fast to read.`

`**Recommended page structure (in order):**`

`1. **Hero / landing.** One headline that states the concept as a flat conclusion (the soundbite). One subhead that states the plain mechanism. One line of the why-now. A single CTA. The hero must pass the re-tell test: a VC who reads only this can accurately describe the company to a partner.`
`- Hero copy architecture: Line 1 = what it is (concrete, narrow). Line 2 = why people want it (the mechanism/benefit). Line 3 = why now / the proof point. CTA button.`
`1. **The Problem / The Gap.** One screen. The specific human problem, told concretely. The “proxy for demand”: what diners/investors are doing now with inadequate options.`
`1. **The Concept (Solution).** The plain-English mechanism. What the experience is. Why it works. Use one named, concrete proof (a real dish, a real night, a real guest behavior).`
`1. **Why Now.** Graham-style: state the one thing that recently changed. Keep it to a tight, evidence-backed paragraph. Frame it as “this only recently became a good idea, and few have noticed.”`
`1. **Traction / Evidence.** 4–5 specific numbers. Empirical proof by example. Real names, real figures.`
`1. **Team.** Domain expertise framed as formidability. Short. Show evidence of knowing the market cold.`
`1. **CTA page (deck request).** One job: drive a deck request or meeting. Plain instruction, plain promise of what they’ll get, low friction. State exactly what happens next.`

`**Copy register for the whole site:** Every unit = one claim + its proof. No paragraph longer than 3–4 short sentences. No buzzword from the banned list. Read every line aloud before publishing.`

`-----`

`## SECTION 5 — REGISTER 4: SHORT-FORM COPY FILTER (naming + checklist)`

`Use this for taglines, page headers, slide titles, one-liners, and positioning statements.`

`**The Graham concept-naming formula:** plain English + slight unexpectedness + immediately portable. His named concepts share these traits: “schlep blindness,” “default alive / default dead,” “maker’s schedule vs. manager’s schedule,” “ramen profitable,” “the fatal pinch,” “frighteningly ambitious.” Each uses ordinary words (no coined jargon), contains one small surprise (an unexpected pairing or reframe), and is short enough to repeat verbatim after hearing it once.`

`**How to build a name:**`

`1. Take a familiar plain word (or two).`
`1. Apply it to something it isn’t usually applied to, OR pair it with an unexpected partner, so it reframes the idea.`
`1. Make sure it’s portable: ≤ 4 words, sayable, re-tellable.`

`**The “x of y” / soundbite move for positioning.** From “How to Present to Investors,” Graham notes investors remember a “descriptive phrase about yourself that sticks in their heads,” usually “the x of y” or “the x y.” His own Viaweb soundbite was “the Microsoft Word of ecommerce” — and it earned its keep: Viaweb grew from roughly 70 online stores at the end of 1996 to about 500 by the end of 1997 and over 1,000 before being sold to Yahoo! in summer 1998 (for 455,000 Yahoo shares, valued around $49.6 million), where it became Yahoo! Store. USE WITH CARE: Graham elsewhere criticizes hollow “we’re the X of Y” framing. A soundbite is acceptable only if it’s literally accurate and clarifying, never if it’s borrowed prestige. Prefer a concrete self-description over an analogy to a famous company.`

`**Test any short copy for Graham-quality (all four must pass):**`

`- **Plain:** Uses ordinary words a 14-year-old would understand. No jargon.`
`- **Portable:** Can be repeated verbatim after one read. ≤ ~6 words for a tagline.`
`- **Slightly counterintuitive:** Contains one small surprise or reframe; isn’t a cliché.`
`- **True:** Literally defensible, not aspirational marketing.`

`**Short-copy filter checklist (run every line through this):**`

`1. Could I cross out any word? Do it.`
`1. Is there a buzzword from the banned list? Replace with a concrete word.`
`1. Would I say this to a friend? If not, rewrite in spoken language.`
`1. Does it state a conclusion, or hedge? Remove the hedge.`
`1. Is it concrete, or could it mean anything? Make it narrow and specific.`
`1. Can a stranger re-tell it accurately? If not, simplify.`

`-----`

`## SECTION 6 — RHETORICAL MOVE CATALOG (named, reusable, with verbatim micro-examples)`

`Use these by name across all four registers.`
